title: Too Weak to Learn All God Wants to Teach

body.text: Apparently, a solution to being “weak,” or being unable to learn and understand more from God’s revelation and word is to “ponder upon the things [that you have heard from God], and ask of the Father, in [the name of Jesus] that ye may understand, and prepare your minds…” (3 Nephi 17:3).
Maybe this is the same sort of weakness mentioned in Ether 12:27

title: Moses’ Seven Days of Creation Also Being a History
metadata_raw: When Bad Things Happen to Good People, by Harold S. Kushner, pages 81-88 | #Creation #Evolution #Dual-Symbolism #7-Seals

body.text: I was reading my book, When Bad Things Happen to Good People, and the author mentioned an interpretation of the creation in Genesis that I hadn’t ever considered before. He suggested that the seven days of creation could still be ongoing; i.e., we’re in the sixth day right now and the seventh day of rest will be the millennium. I took it a little further and added my own spin on it—maybe it could be a dually symbolic story. The seven days of creation could have been the real explanation of God’s creation and could also be an explanation of history where we, now, are in the sixth day (evening of the sixth day to be more precise). In this case each day of creation could be suggestive of historic events; e.g., maybe the separation of light and dark could have been a racial separation or some other war or something. Who knows. I did some searching online but couldn’t find any research already done on the subject. I’m sure there’s stuff on it but I just don’t know how to find it or what to search for.

The more I read through these juxtaposed sections and compare them the more I think it’s less cryptic than I supposed and more of a mere repetition for importance or continuity of God’s rule of three. Not sure but I can’t find anything else of seeming significance that is repeated three times.

It’s a common saying in mainstream Christianity that “God can do all things.” This sounds good and is probably said with good intent but it’s not true and would cause lots of problems if it were true. God cannot do anything for several reasons. One is that He cannot deny His word. He cannot do things that would betray His law and truth. He cannot save us in our sins, only from our sins. He cannot infringe upon the agency of man here in this life, at least to a degree. This helps to make sense of suffering in the world. God probably would stop it if He could but He can’t—not without causing some greater evil, such as ruining our agency, or maybe He just really can’t do this at all while being God.

Moroni and Mormon have a lot to say about faith and hope. The relationship between these two attributes is a bit confusing for me. Is hope a part of faith or vice versa. And does one produce the other?
For starters, there are some details you can catch from Moroni 7, Ether 12, and earlier war chapters of Mormon that give some context to why Mormon and Moroni say some of the things they say.
Ether 12:4 says,

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.
This tells of the possibility that if one believes in God they can eventually come to a sure hope that they will end up in a better world where they have a place at the right hand of God.
One note on this section of Moroni 7, apparently there were believers, enough for Mormon to give sermons and for there to be a synagogue.
Moroni 7:40-42 has a lot to say about hope and faith.
And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning . How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?

And what is it that ye shall  for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have  through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life , and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.
Wherefore, if a man have  he  needs have hope; for without faith there cannot be any hope.
In my interpretation Mormon is saying, “How can you have faith unless you have hope? ...If you have faith you’ve got to have hope because there can’t be hope without faith.”
Later, in an interesting verse, Mormon says that both faith and hope can fail, but not charity (Moroni 7:46). This makes a little more sense when you consider some earlier words of the same Mormon:

●“Behold, ...I had led them many times to battle, and had loved them, ...and my soul had been poured out in prayer unto my God all the day long for them; nevertheless, it was without faith, because of the hardness of their hearts.” (Mormon 3:12, emphasis added)
●“...Behold, I was without hope, for I knew the judgements of the Lord which should come upon them; for they repented not of their iniquities…” (Mormon 5:2, emphasis added)

●“...Behold, I had led them, notwithstanding their wickedness I had led them many times to battle, and had loved them, according to the love of God which was in me, with all my heart...” (Mormon 3:12, emphasis added)

●“...And I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love; wherefore, all children are alike unto me; wherefore, I love little children with a perfect love; and they are all alike and partakers of salvation.” (Mormon 8:17, emphasis added)
By these excerpts we can see that, indeed, faith and hope can fail while charity remains.

I don’t know if I take ordering too far by noting that Mormon first lost faith for his people, then hope. To be absolutely precise, it’s only recorded in that order. This doesn’t necessarily mean he lost faith first, then hope. Though, if it were true that he lost faith before hope, how are we to interpret Moroni 7:42, “...without faith there cannot be any hope”? We could see this as a cause and effect relationship—loss of faith results in loss of hope.
Anyway, on to the real question intended for this section, Is faith a part of hope or is hope a part of faith?
Idea 1: Faith → Hope → Charity
Faith precedes hope and hope precedes charity. This ascending ordering also applies their respective power and import. Support for this idea follows:
●“...faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13; see also Alma 7:24; Moroni 7:1; 8:14; D&C 18:19).

This conclusion relies on the idea that the ordering of these attributes is intentional. It also relies upon the manifest teaching that charity is the greatest of the three, which merely leaves us uncertain regarding faith and hope.
●“Whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith” (Ether 12:4, see also verse 9).
Here we answer the question of which of hope and faith are first—faith precedes hope.

●“And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope? And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise. Wherefore, if a man have faith he must needs have hope; for without faith there cannot be any hope” (Moroni 7:40-42).

This is the main source of confusion when considering the question posed above. This seems to say that you must have hope in order to gain faith. This is backwards from what I’ve gathered from other Book of Mormon sources.

Abinadi teaches the people of King Noah about Jesus Christ and His true role of Savior. This is a hard teaching for them. The idea of a Son of God seems to be new to these people. They have a hard time accepting that God would condescend to us. In fact, they eventually kill Abinadi on this charge:

...Abinadi, we have found an accusation against thee, and thou art worthy of death. For thou hast said that God himself should come down among the children of men; and now, for this cause thou shalt be put to death unless thou wilt recall all the words which thou hast spoken evil concerning me and my people. (Mosiah 17:7-8)
Anyway, Abinadi taught the people about Jesus Christ’s relationship to the Father in a way that has been confusing to me. I’ll quote Mosiah 15:1-4 to start, because it’s the basis of my questions:

And now Abinadi said unto them: I would that ye should understand that  himself shall  down among the children of men, and shall  his people. And because he  in  he shall be called the , and having subjected the flesh to the  of the , being the Father and the Son—The Father,  he was  by the power of God; and the Son, because of the flesh; thus becoming the Father and Son—And they are , yea, the very   of heaven and of earth.

It makes sense that God himself (Jesus) will come down and redeem his people. It makes sense that because He dwelt in the flesh He’s the Son of God. I don’t understand the next line. How does subjecting flesh to the will of the Father make Him the Father? Further, how does being conceived by the power of God make Him the Father? Those are two lines of reasoning that I don’t understand. I’ve read some commentaries online from Bruce R. McConkie or James Talmage where they explain how Jesus is the Father in at least three ways, by virtue of being Creator, the Father to whom we give our acceptance of the gospel, being Atoner, divine investiture, etc. I get that; but it doesn’t answer the question.

I came across a publication by Jeffery R. Holland called, The Father and the Son — The Roles of Jesus Christ. He made a point that may answer one of my questions. He stated, “First and foremost, as Abinadi taught, Christ was ‘conceived by the power of God’ (Mosiah 15:3) and therefore has the powers of the Father within him.”, I continue the quote as the rest is relevant to the topic:

In addition to that divine lineal relationship, Christ also acts as the Father in that he is the Creator of heaven and earth, is the father of our spiritual rebirth and salvation, and is faithful in honoring—and therefore claiming the power of—the will of his Father above that of his own will. Because of this inseparable relationship and uncompromised trust between them, Christ can at any time and in any place, speak and act for the Father by virtue of the “divine investiture of authority” (A Doctrinal Exposition by The First Presidency and The Twelve, Ensign, April 2002, pp. 13-17) the Father has given him.
In an article on Forbes, Bowyer described an interesting chiasm found in Genesis 2-3. He describes it somewhat as follows:
A.Adam and Eve (note that Adam is mandated to cleave unto his wife) (Genesis) 2:23
B.Smooth, as in being naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25)
B.Smooth, as in the serpent who was shrewd (apparently the words ‘shrewd’ and ‘naked’ are similar in Hebrew) (Genesis 3:1)
A.Woman (note that now the woman is unguarded, which may have been Adam straying from a commandment to be with the woman) (Genesis 3:1)

The reason this chiasm is important to the author is that it shows that although Adam was told to “keep” (, perhaps meaning, to guard) the Garden, the serpent was in the midst of the Garden Tempting Eve. I’m not sure if Adam’s job was to protect her from the serpent, but, apparently, he didn’t interfere. This latter deduction is implied via the chiasm above: Adam and Eve start out together and by the end it is only Eve. The question may seem present of whether Adam was even with Eve during this temptation and thus whether he would have been able to interfere. Bowyer must have taken evidence from Genesis 3:6, “and [Eve] gave also unto her husband with her…” This could mean that Adam was standing with her the whole time. It could also mean not this.

body.text: The other day I listened to an interview of a man named Bob Lazar who used to work at Area 51. He gave a really good case, including personal witness, that technology has been found that is far beyond what humans are capable of making right now. An interesting implication he made regarding the creators behind this technology is that their size would have had to be about half that of the adult human. He asserts this based on the fact that the UFO he went into had seats about that small and a ceiling that low. This is a very curious fact. When trying to reconcile it with what I know about God and His plan for us it is hard to fathom. If this idea were true, what are the possible ways to interpret it in harmony with my current understanding?
●These short creatures could be mere shells that act on behalf of a higher and more intelligent human race.
●There could be short, odd-looking aliens living in this universe with us and with God. Perhaps God could be friends with the other high intelligences in this universe and live in harmony together.
●The seats were for short humans who came to earth either from another part of space or from within our own earth (hollow-earth theory).

I was just reading Lehi’s dream in 1 Nephi 8 and I wonder how much of it is symbolic or whether he actually saw the symbols named rather than creating symbols himself to protect certain historical aspects of the vision. I’ve taken from Nephi’s vision, which was answered in response to his plea to see the dream his father, Lehi, had, that the dream was only a symbol of Christ’s life, history of the Lehites, and some apocryphal prophecies. In fact, Nephi’s account tells only of being shown these events which he then relates to the symbols in Lehi’s dream. Could it have been the same? Could Lehi have seen the same events of Christ and His ministry and invented or be shown the symbols later?
I guess this question has a somewhat inconsequential answer, but it’s still interesting.

title: Can We Be Given Something We Cannot Bear?

body.text: At church today someone made the comment that we won’t ever be given any trial or temptation that we cannot bear. I think that comment needs some qualification in order to be correct. In addition, there can be, and are, interpretations of comments like these that are very harmful to followers of Christ; e.g., ‘I should be able to fight this urge myself but I can’t… I must be evil and a shame to God,’ ‘Why can’t they just stop sinning? I was able to resist the temptations they’re falling for. They could stop. They must just not care enough.’ Statements like the ones mentioned are horrible to read, I’m not sure how often these ideas or thoughts exist but I’m sure they could be lessened if this misunderstanding were corrected.
So here’s the question, Is it true that you can’t be tempted or tried beyond what you can bear? I think this subject gets its attention from the following scriptures:

●Alma 13:28, “But that ye would humble yourselves before the Lord, and call on his holy name, and  and pray continually, that ye may not be  above that which ye can bear, and thus be  by the Holy Spirit, becoming humble, , submissive, patient, full of love and all long-suffering;”

●1 Corinthians 10:13, “There hath no temptation  you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be  above that ye are able; but will with the  also make a way to , that ye may be able to  it.”

●Doctrine and Covenants 95:1, “Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you whom I love, and whom I  I also chasten that their sins may be , for with the  I prepare a way for their  in all things out of , and I have loved you”

Let’s start with Alma 13:28. This scripture seems to say that we should humble ourselves and pray often so we don’t get tempted beyond what we can bear—which would imply that such an unbearable temptation exists! Secondly, 1 Corinthians 10:13. If we only read the first half of this verse it might seem that Paul is teaching us that we can’t be tempted beyond our ability to resist. But if we continue reading we see that he gets this point across: ‘God won’t suffer you to be tempted beyond what you can bear unless He makes a way for you to escape, so you can bear that experience.” This is my interpretation. Lastly, Doctrine and Covenants 95:1 says that God will always prepare a way for deliverance to each temptation. This doesn’t mean that you’ll be able to resist every temptation; i.e., if you don’t heed God’s chance(s) for deliverance, there may come a time when you will be stuck with an unbearable load, a slave to the devil—”and we become devils,  to a , to be  from the presence of our God…” (2 Nephi 9:9).

Having given my take on the scriptures on the subject, I think my case presents good support for my understanding, which is: God will provide us with grace and opportunities for deliverance and has been more merciful than I could have imagined, by often giving me chances and forgiveness when I thought I had gone too many times astray. But it is surely possible to ignore God’s hand and end up with temptations which no man could bear. Indeed, no man can bear temptation except through God’s grace. Even when we think we resist, if we do so relying only upon our abilities and not God, we’re poisoned by the devilish touch and would be inevitably fated to succumation.

I think it’s so important to realize this distinction! Realize that it is impossible for us to live a sinless life—if it were true that we would never be given something we couldn’t bear then that would mean it would be possible for us to live a sinless life; therefore, at least one of the two ideas must be false. If we were able to bear all things alone we wouldn’t need Christ—this is a horrible false doctrine, of course. These are just implications of the false doctrine as I see it.

title: Who is ‘The Spirit of the Lord’?

body.text: In 1 Nephi 11, Nephi is guided through a vision by a heavenly messenger. In 1 Nephi 11:11 we learn that this messenger is ‘The Spirit of the Lord.’ Preceding verses in the chapter make me hesitate to accept that this is Jesus Christ, or even the Holy Ghost.

“...chapter 11 teaches that the Spirit of the Lord is in the form of a mortal man (see 1 Nephi 11:11). I take this to mean that the Holy Ghost is in the form of a man, though I am aware that others have believed it to be the preexistent Christ, such as is described in Ether 3:14–17” ().

To me, it’s just odd that, if this were the preexistent Christ, He would say also to Nephi, “Hosanna to the Lord, the most high God; for he is God over all the , yea, even above all. And blessed art thou, Nephi, because thou  in the Son of the most high God; wherefore, thou shalt behold the things which thou hast desired.” (1 Nephi 11:6) Maybe He could be talking in third person.

It’s interesting that in verse 14, the first messenger, supposedly Jesus Christ, leaves and an angel comes down. Why would He have to leave unless this was Jesus Christ—for the scene He leaves is the scene of His birth—maybe He can’t be in two places at once, even in vision? I’m not sure about that one. This fact could also be true if we interpreted the first being to be the Holy Ghost. In fact—that might make more sense. Remember how the Holy Ghost seems to be restricted when Jesus is present?—”Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is  for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the  will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you” (John 16:7). The problem is, both Jesus and the Holy Ghost could have reason to depart at this point in the dream, because, evidently, the Holy Ghost cannot minister in fullness while Christ is present (ibid), and supposably, Jesus Christ could not be present in a vision about His mortal life—especially when He is in His premortal state(?). Third, and final, attempt to explain the identity of this being is that identity of an Angel invested with the temporary vestige and divinity of Christ. Perhaps this would be why he can speak on behalf of the Lord, rejoice for the words of the Lord—”Hosanna to the Lord, the most high God; for he is God over all the , yea, even above all. And blessed art thou, Nephi, because thou  in the Son of the most high God”, and appear as the Lord—”he was in the  of a man; yet nevertheless, I knew that it was the Spirit of the Lord.”  The only oddity I see with this option is that this being did leave, or have to leave, when the vision started showing the mortal Christ. Why would the angel have to leave—he’s not Christ or the Holy Ghost, so does he have any necessity to leave? Perhaps it could have to do with the way that divine investiture would work.
After taking a couple Calculus classes, I now understand a bit more about infinity. I think we humans understand very little about infinity, but enough to make a few guesses and speculations.

2 Nephi 9:7 says that the atonement must be infinite or else “...this corruption could not put on incorruption… [and our] flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.” So basically, if the atonement was finite, it wouldn’t have worked to the extent that we would have been able to be resurrected.
Alma 34 talks a lot more about the topic and reasoning. I’ll summarize it in my own words below:
●Verse 9: An atonement has to be made or all mankind would die in a lost and fallen state, to rise no more.
●Verse 10: This verse is a bit more complex. I see at least two ways to interpret it:
○There must be a great and final sacrifice, not a sacrifice of any animals or even humans, but a sacrifice of an infinite and eternal Being.
○There must be a great and final sacrifice, not a sacrifice offered by man—who is finite, but one offered by the eternal, infinite Beings.

This latter interpretation is the one I’m leaning toward. The reason is because it says, “for it shall not be a human sacrifice; but it must be an infinite and eternal sacrifice.” Why would Amulek say the words “for” and “but” unless they were clarifying, as in: “This sacrifice won’t be of man, beast, or fowl; for (you see), it won’t be a human sacrifice (or offering); but (rather than being an offering made by humans) it must be an infinite and eternal sacrifice.”
●Verse 11: No man can offer his blood to make up for a crime of another man—it doesn’t work like that; e.g., if a man murdered, would our just law exact death of his brother as punishment? No way.
●Verse 12: But a just law would require the life of the murderer; that’s why nothing short of an infinite atonement could satisfy for the sins of the world.

Verses 11-12 are difficult for me to interpret. One idea is that, perhaps, Amulek isn’t explaining why an infinite and eternal sacrifice works, rather, he explains that a sacrifice or offering of a man would not work; ergo, an infinite and eternal sacrifice is the only other option—and we are to assume that it does work. Another interpretation could be that Amulek is saying that mankind can’t invoke redemption or mercy on behalf of another, but God can ().

title: What Did the Atonement Involve as Payment for Sins?

body.text: “He suffereth the pains of all men, yea, the pains of every living creature, both men, women, and children, who belong to the family of Adam” (2 Nephi 9:21).

My first question is this: In what way did Christ pay for our sins? I wonder if He merely felt the pains that any human has ever felt, though I use the word “merely” to say that, perhaps, there’s more He felt and went through, not that this pain was a small measure. And why did He have to feel the pain we’ve felt? Was that the price of our sins? Is that the remedy to our estrangement from God? I remember the scripture that gives one reason why He felt this pain, “that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities” (Alma 7:12).
Side question

Why did Christ have to suffer to learn something new? I thought He already knew everything by virtue of his title of god. The next verse may be a response, “Now the Spirit knoweth all things; nevertheless the Son of God suffereth according to the flesh that he might take upon him the sins of his people, that he might blot out their transgressions according to the power of his deliverance; and now behold, this is the testimony which is in me” (Alma 7:13). This would be to say that He wasn’t only learning how to succor, but He was making a payment. It doesn’t necessarily answer the question about Christ already knowing everything, it just states that there were also other reasons, in addition to learning, for the atonement.

As referenced in my side question above, Alma taught why Christ felt pain during the atonement, “...the Son of God suffereth according to the flesh that he might take upon him the sins of his people, that he might blot out their transgressions according to the power of his deliverance; and now behold, this is the testimony which is in me” (Alma 7:13).
Apparently, this was Christ taking sins of mankind upon himself, and doing so allows his power of deliverance to blot out our transgressions.
2 Nephi 9:22 says that Christ suffered all these things so that everyone could be resurrected.

title: Let Thy Bowels Also Be Full of Charity

body.text: I was just thinking how it’s interesting wording in this verse (D&C 121:45) “Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men, and to the household of faith, and let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly…” Is it merely an old fashioned way of speaking, saying “let”? If not, it sounds like charity and virtue can naturally flow in us if we let them in. This is different than what I’ve sometimes thought, as if they are so foreign and unfound to us that we have to strive with great willpower to create them or find them within us. It reminds me of the Toaist thought, Wu Wei, doing without doing, or finding success and harmony without trying, or without fighting.

I like the idea that we just let go and let in and magic can happen in our lives. Western thought strongly advocates willpower and if your will isn’t working, you just need to put more power into it. Wu Wei says, “Be like water; if you hit a rock in your path, let that be a turn in the road and find that it brings you on the right path in the end.”
The question about this scripture here is whether I’m interpreting it correctly and whether charity and virtue will flow within us if we just let them. If so, how do we “let” in these virtues?
Temples
Bodies
You have to have a recommend to get inside
We don’t let things into our bodies or minds that would harm us; e.g., drugs, vulgar media, etc.
Temples are beautiful
Our bodies are very beautiful, as if a master architect designed them
The Holy Spirit can dwell in temples
The Holy Spirit can dwell in our bodies if we keep them sacred

title: Is Jesus Christ God of Beings on Other Worlds?

body.text: I referenced the scripture 2 Nephi 10:3 as the inspiration to this question because it says, “...there is none other nation on earth that would crucify their God.” This implies that there are more nations than the Jews (not a new idea), and it seems like I’ve heard people use this verse to go beyond this implication and say that “...there is none other [people in any other world in the universe] that would crucify their God.” This seems like a stretch and I wonder if there really are other people in other worlds. This is what I want to look into here—quotes, scriptures, talks, etc. about this question.

Fairmormon has an article on this subject of Jesus Christ being the Savior of other inhabitants on other worlds as well as this at . D&C 76:23-24 is referenced in this article and may be the most relevant scripture, and also the most corroborating scripture for this theory: “For we saw him [Jesus Christ], even on the right hand of God; and we heard [a] voice bearing record that he is the Only Begotten of the Father—that by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.”

The article has this quote from Joseph Fielding Smith, “Perhaps this is the reason Jesus Christ was sent here instead of some other world, for in some other world they would not have crucified Him, and His presence was needed her because of the extreme wickedness of the inhabitants of this earth” (The Signs of the Times, pg. 5).

Another quote, now by the President of the church, though he wasn’t the president at the time he said this, “The mercy of the Atonement extends not only to an infinite number of people, but also to an infinite number of worlds created by Him” (Russell M. Nelson, The Atonement, November 1996 Ensign, pg. 35. As cited in Tad R. Callister’s, The Infinite Atonement).

The only reference cited that might lead to an opposite conclusion is a quote of Brigham Young, “Let me open the eyes of your understanding. There has never been a time when the creations of worlds commenced. They are from eternity to eternity in their creations and redemption. After they are organized they experience the good and the evil, the light and the dark, the bitter and the sweet as you and I do. There never was a time when there were not worlds in existence as this world is, and they pass through similar changes in abiding their creation preparatory to exaltation. Worlds have always been in progress, and eternally will be. Every world has had an Adam and an Eve, named so simply because the first man is always called Adam and the first woman, Eve. And the oldest son has always had the privilege of being ordained, appointed and called to be the heir of the family if he does not rebel against the Father, and he is the Savior of the family. Every world that has been created has been created upon the same principle. They may vary in their varieties, yet the eternity is one: it is one eternal round” (Brigham Young, For This is Life Eternal, in Eldon Watson (editor), Brigham Young Addresses (1982).

I somewhat like this latter quote by Brigham Young. It seems that if any prophet taught different or opposing views from what we now believe in general consensus, it is Brigham Young. Though, this view would resolve some things. Namely, if Jesus were the Savior of infinite worlds, that wouldn’t necessarily mean all worlds, for that would mean that if Heavenly Father ever lived on a world that Christ, His Son, would have been His Savior, yet, Christ wouldn’t have existed yet, right? Christ still could be the Savior for infinite worlds without being the Savior for any worlds before His own time. Infinity can be all backward, all forward, or both—the all-forward view would be applicable in this case; and I speak respecting time when saying “backward” and “forward”.

It’s a little interesting to think about in what ways the Atonement can be infinite. It can be infinite in the number of people it applies to—infinite people; it can be infinite in the cost per each individual—infinite payment for sin per each individual.

Anyway, I would say we probably don’t know precisely if or how Christ was the Savior for any world beyond our own, or even if other worlds that He was Savior for had inhabitants at all; let alone being in need of atonement. Maybe would would say that it’s generally believed that He’s the Savior of inhabitants on other worlds, but He doesn’t have to be in order for His atonement to be infinite. He atonement could still be called infinite even if it were for only one individual by virtue of the definition of infinite in the sense of paying an infinite cost. On the note of being infinite in application to number of recipients, there can only be a finite number of recipients living at any given time in the universe, so the infinite nature must come from length of time, meaning that either new recipients will be made as time continues, or that the finite number of recipients receive continued (infinite) application of the atonement as their glory continues and their seed preliforates. This last description might denote a new, third type of infinite application.

There are so many symbols of Christ in the Old Testament. There’s Abraham sacrificing Isaac—Isaac symbolizing Christ, who was offered as sacrifice by Heavenly Father. Quick tangent on that, Isaac was the only son of Abraham who was from his wife. Is this similar to how Christ is the only begotten Son of Heavenly Father? Anyway, there’s also Jonah and the Whale, where Jonah being in the belly of the whale for three days was like Jesus dying for three days, then being resurrected. I was reading in Corinthians the other day where Paul points out some symbolism where the rock from which water flowed and the manna from heaven represented Christ to the children of Israel. Even the serpent that was raised up to heal the children of Israel seems to be a great symbol of Christ. In fact, it seems like the ministry of Christ was somewhat symbolized to the children of Israel: they “were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:2), then had the teachings, miracles, healing, etc. I wanted to spend this study looking at these examples of Christ in the Old Testament, and perhaps in other scriptures too.
●Prophecy of the seed of woman (Christ) crushing the serpent’s head (Satan)

○The act of the serpent bruising the seed of woman and also getting its head bruised/crushed is the same instance, the atonement. This was Satan’s triumph in crucifying Christ, the Son of God, but also the victory of Christ, in paying for all the sins of the world and leading to the overcoming of death through resurrection. (Genesis 3:15; Moses 4:21)
●Joseph of Egypt
●The Passover Lamb

○Every house whose door had blood of a sacrificial lamb on either side was passed over by the curse which would have caused death to the firstborn of the house. This is symbolic of how the plagues of spiritual sickness and death pass over those who are washed clean by the blood of Jesus Christ. I’m not sure why this curse just killed the firstborn of every house and animal. There’s probably a reason. I’ll have to study that another time. (Exodus 12)
●Animal sacrifice
○An animal free from blemish is sacrificed for the sins of the people. Jesus Christ is even called the Lamb, showing His fulfillment of this long-practiced, symbolic tradition.
●Rock of Horeb

○Moses is commanded to stand upon the rock in Horeb and smite it for water to flow out of it. Moses does this and the water flows out and is drank by the people and their flocks. During Jesus Christ’s ministry, He often taught that He was the living water; “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink” (John 7:37). (Exodus 17:6; John 4:10, 7:37; Revelation 7:17, 21:6; 1 Nephi 11:25)
●Quails and manna from heaven

○In the wilderness, God provides sources of food for the children of Israel. In one of these instances the children of Israel wake up to find quail covering the ground for them to cook and eat. Another instance, they wake up to find manna covering the ground and are to take what they need for the day, no more, and eat. The first of these examples could be like God sending angels from heaven; it seems birds often symbolize angels. The second example is like Christ Himself being sent. Christ often taught that He is the Bread of Life and that we must eat of Him to live. “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). (Exodus 16:12-35; Revelation 2:17; Alma 5:34)
●Serpent raised up on a pole

○God sent fiery flying serpents among the children of Israel that had deadly bites. Moses was commanded, “Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live” (Numbers 21:8). So Moses did this and it worked as the Lord said. This is like Christ being raised up on the cross and having power that if we look to Him, we will live. (Numbers 21:8-9; Johny 19:17-31; 3 Nephi 27:14; Alma 33:19)
●Jonah and the whale

○Jonah was swallowed by a whale for three days, then came out alive. This is symbolic of Christ being swallowed by death for three days, then being resurrected. In this case, going under water symbolizes death. (Jonah 1:15-17; Matthew 16:4)
●Pharaoh of Egypt killed all the male babies and Moses escaped (Exodus 2) like Herod killing all the male babies (Matthew 2)—”The Massacre of the Innocents”.

●Melchizedek, though much of his information comes from Pseudepigrapha and Alma 13, “he was called the prince of peace, for he was the king of Salem; and he did reign under his father.” (Alma 13:18) This is just as Christ is the prince of peace (Isaiah 1:23; 2 Nephi 13:4)

I’m trying to understand better what Nephi is saying in 2 Nephi 32. From what I gather, the statement made in the reference I gave for this entry regards the sermon given beginning at 2 Nephi 31:2. I’ll try to summarize his teachings and hopefully that will guide me as to what he is referring to later on.
●God speaks to men according to their language of understanding
●Reminder that John the Baptist will baptize Jesus Christ
●If Jesus was holy and baptized nevertheless, we really need to be baptized
●After Jesus was baptized the Holy Ghost descended upon Him
●Christ said, “Follow thou me.”
●The Father said, “Repent ye, repent ye, and be baptized in the name of my Beloved Son.”
●The Son said, “He that is baptized in my name, to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost, like unto me; wherefore, follow me, and do the things which ye have seen me do.”
●Nephi testifies that if you truly follow the Son by repentance and baptism, you will receive the Holy Ghost and then be baptized by fire and speak with the tongue of angels
●When one speaks with the tongue of angels, if they then deny God, it would have been better that they were never born
●The Father said, “Yea, the words of my Beloved are true and faithful. He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved.”
●If you don’t endure to the end, like the Son, you can’t be saved
●The gate to enter is repentance and baptism, then comes a remission of sins by fire and the Holy Ghost
●Then you’ve done what the Father and Son commanded and will receive
●But after you enter the gate, you must keep going with hope, love, and might; then the Father says, “Ye shall have eternal life”
●This is the way to be saved and the doctrine of Christ—the only, true doctrine of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Amen
●Now why are you guys pondering about the path after entering the gate?
●Didn’t you guys hear me say that after you get the Holy Ghost you can speak with the tongue of angels?
●Angels speak by the Holy Ghost; i.e., the words of Christ. So feast on the words of Christ. They tell you what to do.
●If you still don’t understand then you must not be asking or knocking. You’re just not getting it.
●Again, if you enter the gate and receive the Holy Ghost, it will show you what to do
●This is the doctrine of Christ. There won’t be more doctrine until after he manifests himself unto you in flesh and person. When He does this, you should do what He says.

This is the point where Nephi says that I can’t say more because the Spirit stops him. Then he talks about how sad he is that people will be stuck in unbelief and ignorance. He says that they won’t search knowledge or understand great knowledge when it is given in plainness, “even as plain as word can be.” He closes these words by saying that the evil spirit is the one that teaches a man not to pray and that we have to always pray unto the Father in Christ’s name.

My question: am I missing something in my interpretation? Is there some great meaning behind this doctrine of Christ? I mean, I think I get it. It seems straightforward. But, then again, if speaking with the tongue of angels is a consequence of following his instructions from the Father and the Son, apparently, I haven’t done this or reached that point. I don’t think I’ve reached a knowledge or assurance that, if I denied God, would put me in such an awful situation of being worse off than if I hadn’t been born. That’s what really makes me wonder what part I’m not getting.

Joseph M. Spencer wrote in his article, , about this topic, saying, along with some other pretty interesting stuff about Nephi’s words, that Nephi was referring to coming into the presence of angels, at least, and perhaps even Jesus Christ. He pointed out that when Nephi tries to clear up the apparent confusion and misunderstanding at his words, he mentions asking to receive and knocking at the door. Spencer relates this to asking and knocking at the veil. “Nephi then promises that those who do knock at the veil will be able to part it, and Christ ‘shall manifest himself unto [such] in the flesh’(32:7). Finally, mourning that he ‘cannot say more’ (32:7), Nephi explains that he is not allowed to describe what lies beyond the veil—though he does say that ‘what [he] seal[s] on earth, shall be brought against [his readers] at the judgement bar’(33:15).” said Spencer.

After reading more of Spencer’s words, I’m starting to see a bigger meaning in Nephi’s account. A suggestion was made that Nephi’s narrative could all be a giant, four-fold symbol of creation, fall, atonement, and veil.

Bookofmormoncentral.org interpreted Spencer’s words in their article,  They said that there is commonality between the way of speaking in reference to Lehi’s vision of God sitting on his throne with angels surrounding Him and singing praises (1 Nephi 1:8) with Nephi saying, “ye speak with the tongue of angels, and shout praises unto the Holy One of Israel” (2 Nephi 31:13). They also say that joining in the heavenly host in praising is to join their rank and class, as inheritors of that kingdom.

This high privilege seems to be confirmed as such when we consider that Nephi had to be first interviewed by the angel before being rewarded (1 Nephi 11:1-6). Another point on that is that Nephi told how the Holy Ghost was Nephi’s witnessing medium of that experience.

The article also references and implies a correlation with baptism of the Holy Ghost and of fire with Isaiah’s purging (Isaiah 6:6-7). Perhaps this is why Nephi thought it important enough to include Isaiah’s account of this in his own book. Perhaps Nephi related well to Isaiah’s process of joining the heavenly hosts.

title: How Old Was Nephi in the Wilderness?

body.text: Assuming that 1 Nephi 18:7, “my father had begat two sons in wilderness” was through Sariah, we can make some conclusions about her age, and thus, the possible ages of her sons.

Sariah bore children in the wilderness (~595 B.C. - 589 B.C.). How young must Sariah have been according to reasonable child-bearing limits of women? Research from yourfertility.org.au stated that women 40-44 years old have a 7% chance of becoming pregnant, and women over 45 years old have less than 1% chance of becoming pregnant.
If we then consider that Sariah’s age at the birth of her last son, Joseph, was within a particular range, we can then produce approximations of birth ranges for her sons.
Sariah’s age at Joseph’s birth (estimated): 38 (min) to 45 (max)
Sariah’s age at Lemuel’s birth (estimated): 14 (min) to ? (max)
Sariah being 38 to 45 during the time range of 595 to 589 B.C. implies the following:
●Sariah was born during 640~627 B.C.
●Sariah’s fertility range was from age 14 (626~613 B.C.) to age 45 (595~582 B.C)
●Sariah had at least 6~12 children consisting of 6 sons and, supposably, several daughters

○A woman’s gestational period of pregnancy is approximately 9 months, which is followed by 2 to 6 months of infertility, or at least a period where sex is much less likely. For the sake of simplicity, let us use a general number of 15 months as the minimum space of time taken out of fertility per child. If Sariah had 6 to 12 children, this equates to 90 to 180 months, or 7.5 to 15 years, of infertility during Sariah’s period of fertility. From the estimations above we also obtain minimum buffer space between births of Sariah’s children:

●Sariah’s 4 oldest sons were very likely to be at least teenagers at 600 B.C., meaning that although she theoretically possible that her fertility range began at 613 B.C., it’s not plausible because her youngest son at 600 B.C.—Nephi—was probably at least 12 (min) years old. This would mean that the youngest possible age Laman could have been would be 12 (Nephi’s minimum age at 600 B.C.) + 15 (minimum months of infertility per birth) * 3 (3 sons older than Nephi: Laman, Lemuel, and Sam) / 12 (convert month total into year total) = 15.75, which we’ll round up to 16. If Laman was 16 at 600 B.C., then this pushes Sariah’s plausible child-bearing years starting at 600 B.C. minus 16 (Laman’s age) = 616 B.C.

○If Sariah was at her youngest fertility/marrying age when she had Laman in 616 B.C. (which is the minimum), which age would probably be 14 when married, and 15 when birthing Laman, that would make her 31 years old at 600 B.C. and 36 to 42 years old during the births of Jacob and Joseph.

■If we push Laman’s birth back at all, it starts to create problems of improbability in the story of her 4 oldest sons going to get the plates of Laban and Nephi, her youngest at the time, overpowering a full-grown man-servant, Zoram.
■If we push Sariah’s fertility/marrying age back earlier, it starts to create problems of improbability with being fertile during Jacob and Joseph’s births.
I’ve created a bit of a mess of thought here, but can end with some conclusions. The two big facts that help me in these conclusions are
1.Sariah’s max probable age at Joseph’s birth
2.Nephi’s (and consequently, Laman’s) min age at obtaining the plates from Laban
Taking the estimations above, here are the estimated ages of Lehi’s family:
●Sariah
○Born: 630 B.C.
○Birthed oldest child at age 14~18 in 616~620 B.C.
○Birthed youngest child at age 35~41
●Laman
○16~20 years old at obtaining of Laban’s plates
●Lemuel
○14~18 years old at obtaining of Laban’s plates
●Sam
○13~17 years old at obtaining of Laban’s plates
●Nephi
○11~16 years old at obtaining of Laban’s plates
●Jacob
●Joseph

Last thought: a maximum drawn. If we say Nephi was older than the suggestion here, say 20 years old, that makes Laman at least 24 and means Sariah birthed Laman at 624 B.C., and even if she was very young at the time, giving a minimum of 14 years old, which means she would be born at 638 B.C., and would have been 43~49 during Jacob and Joseph’s births during 595~589 B.C. This isn’t impossible. It just seems less likely. So I think Nephi was probably more like 16~18 years old. I know this is different from the conclusion made above in the bullet points; it’s a work in progress!

In Jacob 5:7, Jacob tells about the antiChrist, Sherem. He tells how Sherem thinks that he could shake Jacob from his faith despite the fact that Jacob has had “many revelations and ...seen angels, and they had ministered unto [him]. And also, [he] had heard the voice of the Lord…” I just thought it was interesting that Jacob didn’t mention what I thought would have been his greatest assurance for his testimony—the fact that he had seen Jesus, the Redeemer: “...my brother, Jacob, also has seen [the Redeemer] as I have seen him” (2 Nephi 11:2). Instead, he names off the other means of assurance he’s had. Anyway, not much else to say about that here.

title: Tactics of Sherem, the First Lehite Antichrist

body.text: Summary and commentary of dialog:

●(7-6) Sherem comes to Jacob and says that he heard that Jacob was twisting the law of Moses into the worship of Christ, who is taught to come. He tells how he thinks this is blasphemy and no man can know of things to come.
●(9) Jacob’s first response is a question of whether Sherem denies the Christ who will come.

●(9) Sherem responds to the question saying that if there were a Christ he would not deny, but he knows that there isn’t one, never has been one, and will not ever be one. This is odd knowledge to have seeing that Sherem said that no man can tell of things to come. How then could he tell that a Christ certainly would not come? If this discussion were happening today, I could imagine the following dialog occurring: “How come I cannot know of things to come but you can know with certainty of things not to come? Is there a difference?” “Anyone could prophecy of some unfalsifiable, future event. I can say that in 20 years a magic unicorn will fly down from the skies and destroy the earth. How could anyone deny my claim except to say it’s very unreasonable. Yet, no one could prove me wrong, just as I cannot prove you wrong. I can only say we have no reason to accept your claim.” At least, this is how I imagine it. But I could be wrong. They may have treated knowledge differently back then.
●(10) Jacob asks him if he believes the scriptures.
●(10) Sherem affirms that he does believe in the scriptures.

●(11-12) Jacob explains that Sherem then must not understand the scriptures, for they testify of Christ, the being whom Sherem denied. How could you believe the words which testify of Christ but not believe in Christ? Jacob also explains that not only the scriptures tell him that there will be a Christ, but he has “heard and seen” and learned through “the power of the Holy Ghost,” such that he knows that if there’s no Christ, there’s no atonement, and no salvation; thus all men would be lost.

●(13) Sherem asks that Jacob may show him by the same sign—the sign of the Holy Ghost. It seems apparent the both parties realize that they couldn’t resolve their difference of opinion with scripture alone—Jacob gave scripture as one of the sources for his belief and Sherem didn’t ask about it; he didn’t say, “Oh yeah? What scriptures talk about Christ.” Maybe this was because he saw subjectivity in Jacob’s latter claim and thought it a good target to attack, thinking that Jacob was just making up these claims. A person could say God revealed to them many things, but the hearer of these things does not have to believe, and really shouldn’t believe, unless the same Spirit manifests the truth of the words to them as well.

●(14) Jacob tells that he is not in power to command God what to do—especially when that involves proving to a sign-seeker something he already knows. Jacob then tells that he knows Sherem will deny the sign anyway, because he’s of the devil, but God’s will be done; and if God smites him, that will be a sign unto him that God has power in heaven and in earth and also that Christ will come. He closes with a prayer, “thy will, O Lord, be done, and not mine.”

The dialogue is really simple. Sherem tells Jacob he doesn’t believe what Jacob teaches. Jacob asks Sherem if he believes what he teaches. Sherem says he doesn’t. Jacob says why he knows what he knows. Sherem asks for the same proof that Jacob has earned to believe and again denies. Jacob tells that he can’t command God to give Sherem a sign, especially since he knows the thing, but if God smites him, that will be a sign. Jacob ends with a submission prayer to God.

I think many of the same arguments are used on both sides of the discussion still today. Ultimately, reason, scripture, etc., cannot be enough in order for someone to believe in God truly. The Spirit has to corroborate the truth to the individual, and this is a subjective experience in our world. Many could claim things, and do, that were revealed from God or some supernatural source. Sometimes things are claimed that are flat-out wrong. So, we can’t use the supernatural source as a valid ground for such claims. It comes down to a personal experience we each can have, but cannot share. It’s sort of like the parable of the ten virgins. They couldn’t share their oil; why not? Because their oil is their testimony. How can someone believe based on the personal, subjective experiences of another?

I am reading the story of Enos and saw that he first prayed for himself and got a response that his sins were forgiven. Then he prayed for the Nephites and the Lord tells him that He will be just and merciful to them and will not destroy them unless they bring it upon themselves through transgressions. After this happens, Enos’ faith begins “to be unshaken in the Lord.” It seems like he realizes that God can do many great things and is hearing Enos’ prayer.

Enos begins praying for the Lamanites and God grants to Enos according to his desires, which is odd, because Enos desires what was already going to happen according to the future that God knew, and others apparently knew.

Enos then continues praying about the records being preserved and other things. I’m not sure why Enos took this preservation upon his own shoulders, I wouldn’t have been surprised if he had assumed God was able to, and would, preserve what needed to be preserved. Was it then by God’s will that the records were preserved, or by Enos’? I think Enos’ desires and will just began to align with God’s so, naturally, common desires surfaced.

Anyway, I wanted to write about how I saw Enos pray for himself, then his family and people, then everyone else he knew. I wonder if this has to do with where he had love. Did he first gain love and validation for himself, then want it for others? Can we love others before we love ourselves? I know that if I cannot connect with myself in love, it’s hard to connect with anyone else and have love with them.

I was just reading Onmi 1 and realized that the people of Zarahemla, who joined the Nephites, weren’t even deists. They “denied the being of their Creator.” This would have had a major impact on the Nephites. This would be especially true because they were more than double the population of the Nephites at the time they joined (Mosiah 25:3-4). Is this the time when a lot of wickedness happened? How did they handle conversion? Was this why King Benjamin’s sermon was so impactful, because it was largely to new converts or people who didn’t really understand the gospel?

Another note is that Coriantumr being discovered by the people of Zarahemla in vs. 21 seems to imply that this finding of him occurred before the meet-up of the people of Zarahemla with the people of Mosiah. This would make more sense with the Jaradite timeline and the fact that the Nephites had stumbled upon the dead civilization already, implying that they had been dead for some time, else, wouldn’t the Nephites have noticed a thriving civilization right next door to them?

title: What is God’s Will For Cleanliness in Language?

body.text: I was thinking about profanity this morning. I have noticed that profanity has become commonplace in the world, especially outside of the U.S. I’ve been taught that profanity and vulgar speech should be avoided. I’ve even been taught, via parents and culture, that there are certain words which have the status of ‘swear words’ which are considered officially profane.

I now can look at the things society and my parents have taught me and see them in a more objective light, where authority and culture have less sway. I see that some of these official swear words mentioned above have a translated meaning which is far less crude or vulgar than other non-swear words, which I technically would be allowed to use. I also see how technicalities have been made which assert that certain euphemisms can replace official swear words in order to fill in the blank, but soften the intensity, so to say.
So my questions are: What is right and good? How should I conduct myself and how should I teach my kids? Should I only watch or listen to media that matches my standards?
I’ll examine a few different approaches I have in mind and explore the consequences of each.

This is one way to demonstrate my interpretation of how swear words are perceived by varying standards.

Here is a chart showing my estimation of the intensity of vulgarity that each swear word has, compared with it’s most commonly interpreted meaning, and shows whether the interpreted intensity of vulgarity accurately reveals the meaning of the word.
Rated Intensity

This chart is just my interpretation and estimation, but it reveals my thinking here. My thinking is that many of the official swear words, which I dare say here in my Gospel Study Journal for their lack of severity; e.g., Ass, Damn, Hell, and Shit—are rated as being worse than some other words whose meaning is much more severe and/or vulgar, mostly, this is the case with God, whose name is taken in vain commonly and colloquially.
Now that I’ve exposed my feelings of misinterpretation in society of these words, I’ll consider some of the questions I mentioned above.
What is right and good?

I think it is right and good to use words that edify, depict our intentions with clarity, and respect the sacred and the just. This means using God’s name in vain, or using slang terms such as ni***r are inappropriate, at least in most all context. I think it would be good to use words that relay information in a pure and good way, sometimes, when speaking of grotesque, scandalous, biological, or religious things, it may be pure and accurate to use words that otherwise would be out of place. Examples of this include using the word “rape” to describe a crime of such nature; or “sex outisde of marriage”, “pornography”, “nude”, etc., to refer to scandals or events which are such; “penis” or “vagina” to refer to sexual organs in education or proper contexts; “God”, “Hell”, “damn”, “ass”, when used in religious texts or when referring to their religious meanings.
How should I conduct myself and how should I teach my kids?

I want to use language that is helpful, informative, clear, and accurate. This would mean that I would want to refrain from using slang or vulgar terms out of context or for mere sake of cursing. But I also don’t want to associate unnecessary shame with usage of words such as damn, ass, hell, or shit, when they refer to petty or unoffensive ideas. I admit, these words have a sharp ting to their usage. I can’t think of any instance where it would be more purely accurate or helpful to say “ass” instead of “butt” or “bum”, or to say “shit” instead of “poop” or “feces”. This being the case, I prefer using less offensive words to these, but do not mind so much that other people say them. However, I not only think words such as “B**ch” and “F**k” fall into a category of intensity, lewdness, and offensiveness, but I think that making a point to avoid hearing these words or choosing media that uses them is useful and expedient for a pure and good life. This could be compared to how we hold standards of modesty that include women not wearing tank tops in public, but this doesn't mean we can't be around women in public who have different standards and do choose to wear tank tops. Neither do we shun or shame people whose standards do allow them to wear tank tops.

In teaching my children, I think it would be useful for their upbringing to be as free of shame and secrecy as possible. This would mean that rather than scolding any use of a swear word, especially if said without proper knowledge and understanding, I would teach the meaning of the word and explain what I think about its use—when and where it might be proper and how it can be used in an offensive or crude and unuseful way. Rather than saying “Bad bad bad boy for saying that!” I say, “Do you know what that means? I’ll teach you. I want you to understand.” I also don’t want my kids to feel like saying the words like “damn” are necessarily bad. Why shame them for knowing or saying a word that is said in the Bible? Of course, I would encourage proper usage of the word—not using it out of context. But I don’t want them to be afraid of the words themselves. When it comes to words that express ideas or intensity unknown to my children because of their young age and innocence; e.g., “F**k”, I would do the same as above in explaining briefly what the word means, perhaps saying that it is a very rude word that really hurts people’s feelings and refers to painful ideas, or implies something lustful or lewd, etc.

An additional subject here is euphemisms. There are many replacer words I’ve been taught such as “flip”, “shoot”, “geeze”, etc. These words often replace, or are variations of, very vulgar and intense swear words; e.g., “Freaking” replacing “F***ing”, or “Geeze” replacing, “Jesus” (used as a curse). Are these euphemisms more appropriate or acceptable? They are just as much or more meaningless and vague. Sometimes I find them harmless, but I do cringe at the idea that some of them sound close to the actual word in meaning and pronunciation. In this latter case, this is not much better than saying the word itself. Then I say here that I shouldn’t use euphemisms which depict other words that I would not say. Don’t beat around the bush. Who am I fooling? Here I can’t go through every euphemism or say which case is right or wrong, but must use wisdom and go by the principles I’ve established.
Should I only watch or listen to media that matches my standards?

Here I go off of the words’ meanings’ intensity. I don’t usually care if I hear the words, “ass”, “damn”, “Hell”, or “shit” used in media. They are sharp, and I can’t find usage for them in most all contexts, but I don’t think their meaning is offensive. Thus, I justify using media that uses them moderately.

When it comes to words whose meaning is sexual, promiscuous, demeaning, or prejudice, allowing media in my life which uses them is similar to allowing media which displays them. Perhaps I could use this rule: The word’s usage is generally acceptable in media if its visual depiction is acceptable. This would outrule hearing the word, “F**k”, “B***h”, and many others. I wouldn’t watch a movie with a sex scene, then how much better am I if the movie uses words pertaining to a sex scene? Of course, words are less intense than images; but words depict the same feelings, ideas, and expressions that may be expressed in image or video.
