In Mosiah 8, King Limhi tells Ammon about how he sent 43 of his people to search for the land of Zarahemla in order to get aid and deliverance from bondage. I found a couple points interesting in how they paint a picture where there could have easily been other people than the Lehites in the Americas during this time.

Verse 8 says that the 43 explorers found a land that “had been peopled with a people who were as numerous as the hosts of Israel.” I’m not sure exactly when the Jaredites became extinct, but, apparently, Coriantumr had been found among by the descendants of Mulek (or the people of Zarahemla). These people arrived in the Americas sometime between 600 B.C. and 550 B.C. I assume this because Mulek was still alive when they arrived—I suppose that’s an assumption too. And they had been dwelling in the Americas until they were found by the people of King Mosiah. This was around 323-130 B.C. So, sometime within that range, Coriantumr was found.

My point here is that the Nephites and Lamanites had apparently lived for some three or four hundred years before even realizing there was a giant civilization, larger than the Nephites in population, living next to them. If they were so ignorant of their surroundings, what other people could they have been unaware of? And how are we to interpret the writings in the Book of Ether when they tell of the great war where “...they did gather together all the people upon all the face of the land” (Ether 15:12)? This war was likely going on while the Lehites and Mulekites both also dwelt on the American continent. How could such large civilizations have been ignorant of each other’s existence? Or were they aware of each other and merely ignored contact or mention of them? I prefer the former theory.

In addition to this fact that the early inhabitants of the Americas mentioned in the Book of Mormon were incredibly ignorant of the size and inhabitation of their land, there’s a subtle clue in verse 11, “...and there is no one in the land that is able to interpret the language or engravings that are on the plates.” This doesn’t imply much, but it allows for an interpretation that they may have met inhabitants other than themselves in the land they had visited and those inhabitants couldn’t interpret the records, or couldn’t communicate with the explorers requesting the translation. Of course, it could be just as easily said that this land they refer to is the land of Limhi’s people and they were only asking for translators among their own people. I don’t know. But at least we could entertain the idea that other people could have easily existed.
When Abinadi comes to King Noah the second time, he is questioned by King Noah’s priests. We don’t hear what they questioned him about, except for one question that was asked:

What meaneth the words which are written, and which have been taught by our fathers, saying: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings; that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good; that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth; Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing; for they shall see eye to eye when the Lord shall bring again Zion; Break forth into joy; sing together ye waste places of Jerusalem; for the Lord hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem; The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God?
This question was about the meaning of Isaiah 52:7-10. I wonder why, of all scripture, and even of all of Isaiah’s words, this priest asked a question about this scripture.
In my pursuit of this question’s answer, I found this article:

It helps explain a lot. It suggests that the priest asking this question was not asking without confidence in understanding. Apparently, the priests had used this scripture to confirm that their lifestyle of display of joy and pleasure was a fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy; “Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the Lord hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.” If they thought they were living the fulfillment of this prophecy in their hedonistic pursuits, they could condemn anyone who contradicted this as a false prophet, a crime worthy of death.

This was new to me. I had assumed that the priest asking this question was actually doing so with real intent, thinking, “This guy might actually be a man of God. I’ll ask him that question I had about Isaiah.” This view made me think it might actually even be Alma who asked it. But this interpretation doesn’t make as much sense. Would the priests really not have a clue what that scripture meant?

Anyway, so what is Abinadi’s message? So far, Abinadi has been asked some questions by the priests, including the one mentioned above, and he confounded them in their words (Mosiah 12:19). Abinadi follows by telling them they’ve “[perverted] the ways of the Lord!” He then asks them what they teach the people, since they are supposed to be teachers. The priests answer, “We teach the law of Moses.” Abinadi asks them why they don’t keep the law of Moses if that’s what they teach. He calls out their sins of using prostitutes and being set upon riches.

Then he challenges their understanding of the law of Moses and asks them a question to gage their understanding, “Doth salvation come by the law of Moses?” They answer in the affirmative. Abinadi qualifies their answer by telling them that keeping the commandments does lead to salvation. He then iterates through the first three of the ten commandments and tells the priests they haven’t even taught these first three commandments.

It’s at this point where King Noah commands for Abinadi to be taken away. After withstanding this attempt, Abinadi says that he hasn’t delivered the message God sent him to tell initially, and he hasn’t yet finished answering the question that they asked. Abinadi continues with a face shining with the luster of Moses’ face after coming down from Mount Sinai. He acknowledges the powerful effect of his words upon the people and their fear and anger.

Abinadi finishes answering the question he was asked by continuing on the seven of the ten remaining commandments. He then asks the priests if they have taught these things and without giving time for, or perhaps receiving, an answer, he tells them they have not taught them.

He brings the focus back to his earlier question of whether salvation comes by the law of Moses, saying that the priests had said that salvation comes through the law of Moses. Abinadi teaches that “...the time shall come when it shall no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses.” He continues, “...salvation doth not come by the law alone; and were it not for the atonement, which God himself shall make for the sins and iniquities of his people, that they must unavoidably perish, notwithstanding the law of Moses.”

Abinadi explains how the law of Moses was a symbol of Christ and was given as a strict law to the people because of their wickedness. Abinadi explains how not all people understood the law. Moses did prophecy about Christ, the Messiah, just like “all the prophets who have prophesied ever since the world began.” Abinadi asks,

Have [all the prophets] not said that God himself should come down among the children of men, and take upon him the form of man, and go forth in might power upon the face of the earth? Yea, and have they not said also that he should bring to pass the resurrection of the dea, and that he, himself, should be oppressed and afflicted?
Later we’ll find out that this teaching will be grounds for an accusation worthy of death according to the priests.

Abinadi then quotes the first 12 verses of Isaiah 53, which speak of the condescension of God, who will come down to earth in humility, without beauty, despised and rejected, sorrowful, bearing griefs and sorrows, and to be wounded for the transgressions of His people. He will make his grave with the wicked even though He had done no evil. He will have a portion of the great because He has been counted as a transgressor and “[bourne] the sins of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” (Mosiah 14:12)

Abinadi then expounds the doctrine of the purpose of Christ’s condescension and atonement. He explains how God must come down to redeem his people. He explains how Christ is the Son of God, but also the Father through His submission to God—how Christ will be crucified and slain in subjection to death, according to the will of the Father, and “thus… [breaking] the bands of death, having gained the victory over death; giving the Son power to make intercession for the children of men.” (Mosiah 15:8)

He continues by explaining how He will pay the ransom for His seed, and redeem them by satisfying the demands of justice. He then answers the question about Isaiah that was asked by the priest initially by saying that the prophets who teach this great message of Christ are the ones who publish peace “And O how beautiful upon the mountains were their feet!” He also teaches that this prophecy applies to the founder of peace, “even the Lord, who has redeemed his people.”

Abinadi teaches the cruciality of the atonement, how that all men would perish if it weren’t for the atonement of Christ. He teaches about the resurrection. He teaches that the wicked receive no such redemption as being numbered among the first resurrection and having such a magnificent salvation as do the righteous.
Now it seems that Abinadi has finished answering the question of the priest. He goes on to deliver the message that he was sent by God to deliver, and does so with “stretched forth [hands]”:

The time shall come when all shall see the salvation of the Lord; when every nation, kindred, tongue, and people shall see eye to eye and shall confess before God that his judgments are just. And then shall the wicked be cast out, and they shall have cause to howl, and weep, and wail, and gnash their teeth; and this because they would not hearken unto the voice of the Lord; therefore the Lord redeemeth them not. For they are carnal and devilish, and the devil has power over them; yea, even that old serpent that did beguile our first parents, which was the cause of their fall; which was the cause of all mankind becoming carnal, sensual, devilish, knowing evil from good, subjecting themselves to the devil. Thus all mankind were lost; and behold, they would have been endlessly lost were it not that God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state. But remember that he that persists in his own carnal nature, and goes on in the ways of sin and rebellion against God, remaineth in his fallen state and the devil hath all power over him. Therefore, he is as though there was no redemption made, being an enemy to God; and also is the devil an enemy to God. And now if Christ had not come into the world, speaking of things to come as though they had already come, there could have been no redemption. And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection. But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ. He is the light and the life of the world; yea, a light that is endless, that can never be darkened; yea, and also a life which is endless, that there can be no more death. Even this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruption shall put on incorruption, and shall be brought to stand before the bar of God, to be judged of him according to their works whether they be good or whether they be evil—If they be good, to the resurrection of endless life and happiness; and if they be evil, to the resurrection of endless damnation, being delivered up to the devil, who hath subjected them, which is damnation—Having gone according to their own carnal wills and desires; having never called upon the Lord while the arms of mercy were extended towards them; for the arms of mercy were extended towards them, and they would not; they being warned of their iniquities and yet they would not depart from them; and they were commanded to repent and yet they would not repent. And now, ought ye not to tremble and repent of your sins, and remember that only in and through Christ ye can be saved? Therefore, if ye teach the law of Moses, also teach that it is a shadow of those things which are to come—Teach them that redemption cometh through Christ the Lord, who is the very Eternal Father. Amen. (Mosiah 16)
I found a great article that explained this section of scripture in a way that clicked with me. Here is the article for reference:

A note for starters is that Abinadi intended to teach King Noah and his people that the Messiah would be their God, Jehovah, in the flesh. I always thought that Abinadi was trying to teach the Godhead, but this is false. In fact, I only counted one reference to Elohim, and no references to the Holy Ghost.
Here are the verses of Mosiah 15:1-6 with replacement as I understand them now:
1 And now Abinadi said unto them: I would that ye should understand that [Jehovah] himself shall come down among the children of men, and shall redeem his people.
2 And because he dwelleth in flesh he shall be called the [Messiah], and having subjected the flesh to the will of the [Jehovah], being the [Jehovah] and the [Messiah]—
3 The [Jehovah], because he was conceived by the power of [Elohim]; and the [Messiah], because of the flesh; thus becoming the [Jehovah] and [Messiah]—
4 And they are one God, yea, the very Eternal Father of heaven and of earth.

5 And thus the flesh becoming subject to the Spirit, or the [Messiah] to the [Jehovah], being one God, suffereth temptation, and yieldeth not to the temptation, but suffereth himself to be mocked, and scourged, and cast out, and disowned by his people.
6 And after all this, after working many mighty miracles among the children of men, he shall be led, yea, even as Isaiah said, as a sheep before the shearer is dumb, so he opened not his mouth.

Another important detail that helps is understanding why Abinadi quoted Isaiah 53 right before he said this. Isaiah 53 was his reference of scripture for proof to the priests and King Noah that he is not a false prophet and therefore not worthy of death. Isaiah 53, in the Hebrew text, references Jehovah and one can see how it could be interpreted that the person Isaiah is talking about in chapter 53 is actually Jehovah himself. But it’s not such a clear interpretation, which is why, even after Abinadi quoted this and gave his explanation, the priests still refuted his claim, or tried to, that Jehovah would come down and be the mortal Messiah.
Here is the Hebrew replacement for divine references (Isaiah 53:1-12):
1 Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of [Jehovah] revealed?
2 For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
3 He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
4 ¶ Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of [Elohim], and afflicted.
5 But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
6 All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and [Jehovah] hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
7 He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
8 He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.
9 And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

10 ¶ Yet it pleased [Jehovah] to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of [Jehovah] shall prosper in his hand.
11 He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.

12 Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

A good cross-reference here is . It also is confusing if not interpreted as Abinadi’s words are above. Jehovah argues that He will perform the will of the Father because of Him and the Son because of His flesh. That wouldn’t make sense unless you interpret Father to be Jehovah and Son to be Messiah. This is another reason why I think the title of Father is more appropriate than brother for Jesus.

My comments aren’t directly about what’s contained in the reference, but I think they’re related. I was just thinking about grace and the gift of the Holy Ghost and how we qualify for such. There seems to be a common idea, at least I’ve believed this, that perfection—or something close to it, is the prerequisite for God’s acceptance, love, or the gift of the Holy Ghost. The truth, though, seems closer to the inverse—God’s acceptance, love, or the gift of the Holy Ghost is the prerequisite to perfection—or anything close to it. Even this can be misleading. We’re not perfect and we won’t be perfect in this life.

You know how God is able to make beautiful results out of the worst things? This is what happens when we go to Him broken and defeated. He doesn’t cause the bad, that’s the result of a fallen world and choices made by a fallen people. He didn’t cause the Holocaust or sickness and disease. Rather, He takes these things and somehow uses them to bring about a good that couldn’t have been anticipated. It doesn’t justify the existence of the bad, it just shows how powerful and of what nature God is.

title: The Priesthood in Book of Mormon Times

body.text: I looked this up and it seems that most quotes just say that it is implied that the Lehite people of the Book of Mormon times had the Melchizedek priesthood. Apparently, the Nephites exercised this priesthood often and consistently up to the coming of Christ. Alma the older is a priest who was once a member of the priesthood council of the wicked King Noah. He later flees from Noah after suggesting to save a prophet who threatened King Noah by calling out his wickedness. Alma uses priesthood authority to baptize some 450 people.

title: Why is Ammon a Leader Even Though He’s Younger?

body.text: I was wondering why Ammon, among the sons of Mosiah, is presummedly a leader among his brethren, at least during their missions among the Lamanites, while he is younger than his brother, Aaron. Their culture, especially as shown by Lehi’s sons, designates the oldest brother to be the leader by default.

I read an article called In His Footsteps: Ammon1 and Ammon2, by Val Larsen. He talks about a lot of interesting correlations between Ammon1, the Ammon who leads a group of explorers to find Lemhi’s people, and Ammon2, who is the son of Mosiah. He suggests that Ammon2 tried to follow the pattern of Ammon1 after being converted. This pattern is that of an explorer, one who was initially unworthy but who does great things and is a leader and converts and becomes an instrument in God’s hands.

Another interesting point from the article is that Mosiah could have been half Mulekite and his sons could have been half or three-fourths Mulekite. This would explain why the people supported and desired the idea of one of the sons of Mosiah being their king. But then when Alma is made chief judge and high priest, the people revolt against his authority and show great disrespect. This could have been because Alma was a pure-blood Zeneffite and Nephite. They could have had discomfort with those who didn’t mix with or understand the Mulekites. The Mulekites were, mind you, more than double the number of the Nephites when the two civilizations united. This would have been a big culture transition and there were likely many Nephites who pridefully resisted integration with the Mulekites. This bigotry could have supported the resistance Mulekites would have had against Alma, a pure blood.

Anyway, the reason why Ammon2 could have been the leader among his brethren during their missions could have been in order for Ammon2 to fulfill his mission and role of representing the pattern of Ammon1. Aaron could have condescended to allow his brother to rule over them as a leader for this cause.
One other parallel between the Ammons is that they both had three brothers on their journeys. Ammon1 had Amaleki, Helem, and Hem, while Ammon2 had Aaron, Omner, and Himni (Mosiah 7:6).

Ammon1 went to the land of their inheritance and was taken and bound by Limhi’s guards and proved to be a savior to them. Ammon2 went to the land of his inheritance (see ) and was taken and bound by Limoni’s guards and proved to be a savior to them. There are parallels between Limhi and Limoni.

In Alma 1, Nehor rises in popularity and teaches several things, one of which is “that all mankind should be saved at the last day, and that they need not fear nor tremble, but that they might lift up their heads and rejoice; for the Lord had created all men, and had also redeemed all men; and, in the end, all men should have eternal life.” (Alma 1:4)

This teaching isn’t exactly true, but it’s also not totally false. D&C 76:43 says, “[Christ] saves all the works of his hands, except those sons of perdition who deny the Son after the Father has revealed him.” And Paul taught, “As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22).

It really depends on the context of the usage for salvation. Everyone will be resurrected and brought back into the presence of the Father, but not all will be able to stay in His presence and not all will be resurrected to the same resurrection.

title: Alma vs. Amlici and The Body Bridge

body.text: I interpreted the story of the battle between Amlici and the lamanites, and the Nephites with Alma a certain way and I’m not sure if I was correct. There’s one part, in verse 34, where the Nephites “[clear] the ground, or rather the bank, which was on the west of the river Sidon, throwing the bodies of the Lamanites who had been slain into the waters of Sidon, that thereby his people might have room to cross and contend with the Lamanites…” I used to think that they made a bridge out of the bodies in order to cross, but now it seems that they already had crossed almost to the east side and were just trying to clear the bank. So it’s not quite as cool, but still an interesting battle.

It’s odd to me that the righteous sons of Lehi are listed in this order, “Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam” (Alma 3:6). Why is Sam listed last, and in a way that seems he was almost forgotten?—the list was complete, grammatically, without him, then his name was appended to the list. Could just be human error.
Alma 3:14-17 tells of a prophecy which was not recorded in the plates of Nephi we now have in the Book of Mormon; these are the words Mormon tells the reader that the Lord spoke to Nephi:

Behold, the Lamanites have I cursed, and I will set a mark on them that they and their seed may be separated from the and thy seed, from this time henceforth and forever, except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me that I may have mercy upon them. And again: I will set a mark upon him that mingleth his seed with they brethren, that they may be cursed also. And again: I will set a mark upon him that fighteth against thee and thy seed. And again, I say he that departeth from they shall no more be called thy seed; and I will bless thee, and whomsoever shall be called thy seed, henceforth and forever.”
The only prophecy recorded by Nephi that’s similar to this is in 2 Nephi 5:20 - 25

Wherefore, the word of the Lord was fulfilled which he spake unto me, saying that: Inasmuch as they will not hearken unto thy words they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord. And behold, they were cut off from his presence. And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity. For behold, they had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint; wherefore, as they were white, and exceedingly fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them. And thus saith the Lord God: I will cause that they shall be loathsome unto thy people, save they shall repent of their iniquities. And cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed; for they shall be cursed even with the same cursing. And the Lord spake it, and it was done. And because of their cursing which was upon them they did become an idle people, full of mischief and subtlety, and did seek in the wilderness for beasts of prey. And the Lord God said unto me: They shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in remembrance of me; and inasmuch as they will not remember me, and hearken unto my words, they shall scourge them even unto destruction.

title: Conceive by the Power of the Holy Ghost

body.text: In Alma 7:10 it says that Mary will “conceive by the power of the Holy Ghost.” This is consistent with the wording in Matthew 1:20. Why did Mary conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost instead of by the power of God? Jesus was the Son of Elohim and Mary, right? Then how did the Holy Ghost put the seed of the Father in Mary to make a mortal man, Jesus?

On this topic, as I study, another question that I also had is brought up: How did Mary conceive?—did she have sexual intercourse with God somehow? Apparently this has been a subject of speculation and some of the early church leaders would have answered in the affirmative. Officially, the church doesn’t have a stance on this. We just don’t know the details here.

Some evidence that could be interpreted to support the claim that sexual intercourse of some sort did occur comes from 1 Nephi 11:19-20, “And it came to pass that I beheld that she was carried away in the Spirit; and after she had been carried away in the Spirit for the space of a time the angel spake unto me, saying: Look! And I looked and beheld the virgin again, bearing a child in her arms.” Why did the angel skip over the conception part unless it were a scene of sexual intercourse? I think that there could be other reasons why the angel would skip over that scene—perhaps the scene included non-sexual but intimate or personal interaction between the Spirit and Mary. I would expect privacy in such personal and spiritual experiences, so this claim holds little weight to me.
Brigham Young was one of the prominent believers and teachers of the idea that Mary and the Father had sexual intercourse. This is all but explicitly stated in a quote of his:

...[T]here is no act, no principle, no power belonging to the Deity that is not purely philosophical. The birth of the Saviour was as natural as are the births of our children; it was the result of natural action. He partook of flesh and blood—was begotten of his Father, as we were of our fathers. (Character of God and Christ, etc., July 8, 1860)

One issue I find with this idea is that how would the Father’s wife feel if He had sex with a mortal woman? Of course, maybe God is a polygamist. I really don’t know. I feel like this topic is sacred and perhaps speculation should be left aside until a greater source teaches the truth of the matter. I don’t want to trifle with sacred things. The last source I think relevant on the matter is that in 1 Nephi 11:20, quoted above, Mary is referred to as a virgin both before and after she gave birth.

Back to my original question of why the Holy Ghost instead of the Father. Harold B. Lee said, “Remember that the being who was brought about by [Mary’s] conception was a divine personage. We need not question His method to accomplish His purposes.” (Teachings of Harold B. Lee, 14) I suppose that any member of the Godhead often has acted and does act as the Father. Then there should be now question as to why or how the Holy Ghost could have been the representative or instrument of God in Mary’s conception. Isn’t it true that the scriptures say that Jesus is the Son of the Father and not that He is the Son of the Holy Ghost? Then why should we worry about the wordage of Mary’s conception in referring to the Holy Ghost?

title: Omniscient God, Before and After Atonement

body.text: Alma teaches the church of Zarahemla, as recorded in Alma 7:12, that Jesus “will take upon him death… and he will take upon him [man’s] infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.” (emphasis added) Now this sounds like Christ was in some way deficient of mercy and/or knowledge and thus needed to suffer and learn to obtain sufficient mercy and knowledge according to the infirmities and such. My question is, didn’t Christ already know everything? Then why would He have had to learn through suffering, etc.?

Doctrine and Covenants 88:6 implies a similar idea, that Christ somehow learned when He atoned and suffered, “He that ascended up on high, as also he descended below all things in that he comprehended all things, that he might be in and through all things, the light of truth.” So did He not comprehend all things before descending below? Or had He descended below all things before the atonement?

Alma does seem to anticipate this question as he continues in verse 13, “Now the Spirit knoweth all things; nevertheless the Son of God suffereth according to the flesh that he might take upon him the sins of his people, that he might blot out their transgressions according to the power of his deliverance”. This reasoning for answering why Christ suffered in the atonement makes sense—He had to suffer to pay for our sins. But what about the other reason, did He also have to suffer to learn?

If we say that Christ did have to suffer to learn then it implies a great deal of things, some of which seem improbable. If one must suffer all things in order to learn all things, then any omniscient being must have suffered all things, this includes the Father, the Holy Ghost, and prospectively speaking, any and all who will inherit celestial glory. We musn’t all perform an atonement, right? This implication seems far off from the truth as I presume it to be understood.

Then what other interpretation can be suggested? Perhaps Alma and Joseph Smith were saying that we can be personally assured that Christ knows our pain because He literally suffered them all. Of course, He would have understood anyway by virtue of His knowledge of all things, but this is perhaps a more personal and relatable way of understanding.

title: Bible Verses in The Book of Mormon

body.text: The scriptures referenced above say the same phrase, “lay aside every sin which easily doth beset you.” One part of me says, “Wow, it must be important to be said twice in almost the same way.” But another part of me wonders why Joseph Smith would use the same wording. Why would an ancient American people be using the same sentence structure and words from a New Testament apostle? I think Moroni does the same thing with Paul’s words on charity.

One theory I’ve heard about this says that perhaps they were both quoting an old source of scripture that both of them had but that we don’t currently have. This would make sense. It’s sort of like how they both quote Isaiah, except that we do have Isaiah. One issue with that is that everywhere else that Old Testament prophets in the Book of Mormon, the quoter references who they’re quoting; e.g., Isaiah, Zenos, Zenock, etc.

Perhaps Joseph Smith’s subconscious memory was used to best describe the meaning when translating the Book of Mormon. This would mean that the words he had read in the Bible might appear exactly as they did in the Bible when they described what a Book of Mormon prophet had said.

When Alma went to the land of Ammonihah, he didn’t have much success and the people were very wicked. After his first attempts were made, he “labored much in the spirit, wrestling with God in mighty prayer, that he would pour out his Spirit upon the people who were in the city” (ibid).

What does it mean that Alma “labored much in the spirit”? I suppose this is referring to Alma’s spirit and not the Spirit of God based on the lack of a capitalized “s”. So Alma labored with his spirit, “wrestling with God in mighty prayer.” Now, what does that mean? Why do they call it a “wrestle”?
Genesis 32:24-25 has an odd story where Jacob wrestles with a man, supposably an angel, all night, and Jacob’s thigh got pulled out of its socket.
There’s also the story in Enos 1 where Enos wrestles in mighty prayer. That’s a pretty good example.

Alma 13:2 refers to priests that “were ordained after the order of [God’s] Son, in a manner that ...the people might know in what manner to look forward to his Son for redemption.” I suppose that these priests were symbols of Christ and became the instruments acting as Christ whereby we would receive redemption.

Alma 13:3 describes this manner referred to above—“being called and prepared from the foundation of the world”—as Christ was called and prepared before the world began—“according to the foreknowledge of God, on account of their exceeding faith and good works… and exercising exceedingly great faith, are called with a holy calling, yea, with that holy calling which was prepared with, and according to, a preparatory redemption for such.” This last part sounds similar to Christ. He was righteous from the beginning and chosen for a holy role. I suppose all leaders and prophets were thus called in a similar way, but for a role much different from and only symbolically like Christ’s.

My question is about the preparatory redemption part. Were the priests referred to above, and Christ whose manner of calling theirs symbolized, receivers of a preparatory redemption. If so, what does that even mean?

I looked this up and read a lot of discussion boards and quotes. I don’t think we know exactly what this text means. I think it can be interpreted that high priests were foreordained to their callings and that God at least had some sort of foresight and knowledge about what the future would be like. We also know that Christ’s atonement was foreknown and perhaps was even retroactive, or eternally active, once Christ was ordained to this calling of the Savior.

What is an accurate way to describe the balance of works and grace? On one hand the scriptures say “Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only” (James 2:24). On the other hand, “...whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all” (James 2:10). Everyone, then, is guilty! So no one is saved by their own works. No one is righteous by their own works. But “Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness” (James 2:23). Was this a work of Abraham that justified him? But hadn’t he offended the law in keeping not all points? This must have been the grace of God. I think that we are never counted righteous by the law, only by God, through grace! We cannot be righteous without the atonement. We cannot be justified without Christ.

What about this scripture: “There is a law, irrevocable decreed in heaven before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated—And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated” (D&C 130:20-21). Can this system of salvation be reduced to the idea that each action has a set consequence and that when we perform a particular set of actions, we can expect a natural array of consequences associated with such actions to occur. This could make it sound like we earn our salvation by just doing the actions that yield the effects of salvation. This is a big problem. We don’t earn our salvation and it’s not our works that give it to us. True, if we receive Christ and have faith, etc., Christ’s grace will save us, but not by our merit, by Christs. How can this be stated better? I feel like it’s still not a simple way of putting it.
One suggested change in the punctuation of Alma 13:3 did resonate with me. It goes like this:

...being called and prepared from the foundation of the world according to the foreknowledge of God on account of their exceeding faith and good works in the first place [this is referring to premortality]; being left to choose good or evil [now referring to their mortal time], therefore they having chosen good and exercising exceedingly great faith, are called with a holy calling…”

When Korihor receives empirical proof of God, he tells the story of where he got his philosophies. Supposedly, the devil appeared to him as an angel of light and told him there was no God, etc. How did that work? The context seems to disagree with the story. How could a phony angel of light attempt to convince someone that there was no God? Wouldn’t the fact that angels exist corroborate God’s existence? I’m confused how that worked. How could someone accept the fact that angels exist but deny God’s existence? Maybe I’m missing something here. It just seems confusing to me.

title: Lightened Burdens Through Faith in Christ

body.text: Alma told the poor Zoramites that if they planted the word of God in their hearts and let it grow to faith, “then may God grant unto you that your burdens may be light, through the joy of his Son” (Alma 33:23).

I was somehow surprised that we need to have faith to have our burdens lightened. Well, to be technical, I guess this doesn’t necessarily say that you can’t have your burdens lightened without faith, it just says that if you do have faith, God may grant you lightened burdens. Maybe it implies this, but that’s beside my point. I think it’s cool. It seems like a simple concept, but it stood out to me.

Why does having faith in Christ allow my burdens to be lightened? What is my burden? I think the Zoramites had a burden of poverty and ostracization. I have a burden of struggling with stress and negative emotions. I struggle with being free and not struggling. Can having faith in Christ help me? I’m sure it could.

I was reading in Alma where Amulek teaches the Zoramites the teachings of Zenos’ teachings. One line says this: “Yea, cry unto him against the power of your enemies” (Alma 34:22). How is this to be reconciled with Matthew 5:44, “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.”
I guess you could say that you should be compassionate toward all but don’t pray that your enemies will overtake you. Pray against their success inasmuch as they seek to harm you and others.

Amulek teaches the Zoramites that after they pray unto God for all things, if they do not serve the poor, love the needy, and have charity, they are worthless. This sounds pretty extreme. I don’t mean to focus on the negative aspect of this, rather, about how we are forgiven if we forgive and are shown mercy if we show mercy. It’s as if there’s some principle of reflection in the universe. I’ve noticed that if I give to others and have an outward feeling of love and goodness, I receive more of the same in my life.

It reminds me of something that I heard from Alan Watts. He said that if you hold your breath, you lose it. If you let it go, you receive more. He related this to Christ’s teaching of “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it” (Matthew 16:25). If you hold on to your life, your life becomes miserable and loses its effervescence and vivacity. Only by letting go and trusting can you receive more. It’s an odd paradox.

How is it that to keep, we must let go—to gain, we must lose? I must give and love to receive and be loved. It begins with me. I am the center of my reactions—the main causer, it seems. Perhaps I am given all my virtues by God, but I must let them ensue within me. I must love myself and be honest with myself, then all things fall into place.

This is much like the principle of Karma. If we show goodness, we will reap goodness. But I need to qualify this. We can’t show goodness for the cause of reaping goodness. We must show goodness out of the sincerity of our heart, expecting nothing in return, being satisfied with the deed itself as the end to the means.

It’s all too easy to fool ourselves into doing things for the wrong reasons. I’ve noticed that I want to have the appearance of honesty more than the actuality of personal honesty. Perhaps this is because we’re taught to do these things. Those who teach us to do good will be sad if we don’t heed them. We know this and sometimes submit out of obligation or evasion of shame. If we act out of shame or obligation, though, we find ourselves in a terrible situation—we do the deed expecting something in return, such as reward, prestige, or satisfaction, and may thus pervert the natural way of things. Remember I said that you cannot do good for the cause of receiving good alone; you must sincerely do it for the sake of itself.
I think teaching is a necessary evil. Teaching others to do things may lead them to doing those things for the wrong reasons and ending up in a mess of shame and ulterior motives that lead to misery.

Imagine the mother who tells her son, “You should love God. That’s the first commandment! You shouldn’t break commandments!” The son realizes that he doesn’t know God and doesn’t find love for God within himself. He then attempts to love God by flexing his forehead, etc., all the while feeling ashamed and wretched for not loving God. What a conundrum. But the one who already loves God finds it a great benefit of fulfillment and goodness. Then should they not teach others? This all is taught by Alan Watts in his lectures.
The main principle here is to be the good and the good will fill you. You can only deprive yourself of love and goodness if you do not give or express any at all. Then it dries up.

This is sort of going on a limb, but I really think we affect so much of our environment. What I think about myself becomes what others think about me. What I think about others becomes what others think about others. If I think the world is hostile, the world becomes hostile and everyone on the road is an idiot who’s trying to cut me off. If I think the world is full of hope and love, I find so many good people who inspire me and bless me by their virtue.
Alma 41:6 says, “If he hath repented of his sins, and desired righteousness until the end of his days, even so he shall be rewarded unto righteousness.”

This stuck out to me because it seems to say that desiring righteousness is virtuous. Often, I’ve found myself desiring that which I cannot attain to—righteousness, or perfection? I don’t know that my desire is godly; it may even be damning—some shame-induced perfectionism of not reaching the standard I’ve been taught and thus condemning myself to be some devilish creature.
“For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.” (Romans 7:15)

Why must we contrast our desires? Are we to desire to be what we never can be in this life? I can’t be perfect. I can’t be free from all lusts and envies and strifes. Then seeking what I cannot have is my way? That sounds miserable. Isn’t there some way to accept the reality that I live in without submitting to sin? I must accept that I will sin but also desire righteousness.

It seems like the people in the Book of Mormon times often were praying to Jesus. In fact, it seems like most Old Testament prayers were really to Jehovah. Jehovah was the God of the Old Testament. Heavenly Father was infrequently referred to, if I understand correctly.

In the referenced verses, Nephi prays to “God in behalf of his people,” yet God is identified in the next verse when He answers Nephi saying, “...on the morrow come I into the world, to show unto the world that I will fulfill all that which I have caused to be spoken by the mouth of my holy prophets.” (3 Nephi 1:13)
What’s up with this? Jesus is the one who comes to the world as the mortal Messiah. So this was the premortal Jesus Nephi was praying to and who answered his prayer? Why is this?

title: Love, the law, and the prophets

body.text: I was just reading in the Sermon on the Mount when given to the Nephites and noticed there’s a connection between the Golden Rule and the first and greatest commandment.
“Therefore, all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them, for this is the law and the prophets.” (3 Nephi 14:12)

“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all they mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” (Matthew 22:37-40)

I suppose that the Golden Rule is perhaps one of the laws among the prophets and not necessarily all of the laws. But it still may be helpful to say “On the commandments to love God and love our neighbors hangs the Golden Rule.” Maybe it’s not supposed to be understood this way, though.

title: Eye hath not seen, neither hath ear heard

body.text: It’s incredible to hear that my own ability to imagine and conceive ideas of joy and marvelous things is incapable of conjuring the true blessings and glory God can give. I mean, I can imagine what seems to be pretty good—I see a future where all mankind live together with compassion and peace, having lust, greed, envy, hatred, and suffering all removed. Here all could live with surplus and live out their days seeing progress and prosperity. Even this is not as good as GOd has prepared? How great is it?

title: Why have so few known the true God?

body.text: Last night I was talking with Kaylene about a question that I had. The question came up while I was listening to a podcast talking about Buddhism. I was thinking, how come so few people in the world knew the God of Abraham and worshipped the way that was taught him? I mean, so many people desperately wanted to find truth; Siddhartha Gautama, the man now know as the Buddha, wasn’t alone in his quest for knowledge and enlightenment which, in his case, involved such drastic measures as eating only one grain of rice a day, abstaining from pleasures and worldly vices, and meditating for long periods.

Surely, many people have sought knowledge with greatest fervor. But the gospel has been given to only a small percentage of the earth’s inhabitants. It seems that there is some great restraint in God’s will to bless all people with the gospel.

The small sliver of people who have been privileged to have the gospel are those who are, in some way, biologically related to a chain of covenant people. Is the covenant all that holds the gospel on this earth? Why could the truth-seeker Abraham have heavenly manifestations and revelations when Socrates, Epicurious, and Buddha left to their own wisdom? Each of these I named had every intention to do good and to be moral, but why were they kept from that which they apparently desired?

If I had to estimate, I would say that 99.9% of all the people to have ever lived on the earth have not known the God of Abraham. What is the reason for this? Is it so difficult for God to send angels and prove to people that He is the true God? Is it so difficult for God to give dreams and visions to truth seekers to guide their minds to know of Him and the plan of salvation that He has designed? Kaylene suggested that it’s not that God is unable to do these things, but that mankind has been so unprepared for these things. Perhaps the world just wasn’t ready for true religion.

I suppose that God reaching out in such apparent manifestations also brings condemnation and He considers this and perhaps decides that the people are better wicked and ignorant than wicked and accountable. But then, doesn’t that reflect some issue with the fairness of judgement?—wouldn’t a fair judgement have to judge the person equally, despite their external circumstances? Of course, external circumstances are taken into account, but not in the way I mean. Let me explain. A person is not charged of murden when their grandparent dies of old age in the room next to them. But that same person very-well might be charged of murder in the same case if they had known some way to stop the death but did nothing—say an act of great negligence on their part.

What I’m getting at is that an identical person born as an untouchable in ancient India should be judged the same in the end as in the case where they, identical in soul and mind, etc., are born as prince of Persia. Of course, one may turn out differently, but aren’t they the same person? Are we products of our environments or of our choices? To say that this identical person whose environment differs could be judged differently by God would be to say that environment determines the person, rather than that the person determines the person. Then the accountability for a person’s eternal well being rests upon the factors that contributed to their environment placement rather than the person themself.

Lastly, there’s the question of why the covenant people are strictly commanded to preach the gospel, at least as they are in this day. If heaven did refrain from manifesting true teachings to mankind for the sake of avoiding the wicked to be condemned, why would we be commanded to teach all mankind the gospel? Is the condemnation that was an issue beforehand no longer an issue?
I was wondering about this old question again this morning. I know it’s not God’s way to work by proof, but why not? I read an article online that helped me to find a satisfying answer.

The article said that one of the amazing things about God is His meek restraint of power. When Jesus was about to be taken for crucifixion, He said, “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?” Of course, God could be the kind of God where He rules by power and proves to us that He is supreme, above all, and more powerful and knowledgeable than us. But God doesn’t do this. He can’t achieve the desired effect in us unless we have the scenario allowing for us to disbelieve Him. We can deny Him, spit in His face, reject Him, follow our own paths. This option is necessary in allowing the alternate option of believing purely because of faith and subtle whisperings of the Spirit. We can then say, “I could have denied Him, I could have rejected Him, but I didn’t.”

title: Can ye behold the Lamb of God?

body.text: This scripture stood out to me. It applies in a context where in my life there are many signs and witnesses of Christ—the way things have been working out with our home buying, the way we were taken care of during my lightheadedness’ worst, etc. There are many invisible acts of God that can act as witnesses of Him if we can behold Him in the works. This question made me think of this sort of thing. I asked myself, “Can I behold the Lamb of God in all these things or will I deny the Christ?” The second part of that sounds drastic. But I think it’s important to have eyes that are willing to see, even when we’re seeing things that are personal to us and cannot be used as validation or proof to others of our convictions.

title: Whatsoever he shall ask… shall be granted him

body.text: “Behold, I say unto you that whoso believeth in Christ, doubting nothing, whatsoever he shall ask the Father in the name of Christ it shall be granted him; and this promise is unto all, even unto the ends of the earth.” (Mormon 9:21)

How can I interpret this? It’s an amazing promise, first off. But is it true? Can I really ask anything and the Father will grant it as long as I believe in Christ and doubt nothing? It seems too simple. On top of that, I have asked God many things that haven’t come true. I asked him to take away my lightheadedness, though it has gotten much better, it’s not gone. I asked him to help me in certain ways throughout my life but they didn’t happen. I’ve even asked for visions and spiritual manifestations but they didn’t happen. I fervently believed when I asked these things. Why didn’t they come true?

I’m content with the way things are. I understood that God’s will is higher than mine and my desires are sometimes not in my best interest and I ask things that will not be for my good. God knows this and tries to help me through understanding these things instead of being a Santa Claus who grants all my wishes.

With this being said, what does this verse mean? Most commentaries and comments I found online interpret it literally. They feel that God means that we really can pray for anything and it will be granted if we don’t doubt.

I want to believe this is true. I just think to all the desperate times I’ve prayed with all the faith in my being and felt that all doubt was removed only to find that as the days passed and then the weeks, my prayer would not be granted as I thought it would. Again, I think God’s way of responding to me in these times has been for the greater good. I’m grateful He loves me enough to be patient with my pleas and work in my best interest. I’m grateful that He has given me peace in times of despair. I do believe He’s there and hears me. Perhaps there is more insight I’ll learn later on this verse.

When the Brother of Jared prays to God asking Him to touch the stones and make them lighted, the Brother of Jared sees the finger of God and asks to see more. God first qualifies him by asking, “Believest thou the words which I shall speak?” (verse 11) I thought it was kind of odd that this question asked the Brother of Jared if he believed words that were only yet to be spoken. One could ask, “How is this possible to believe something that hasn’t been defined yet?” I thought about that but then the next verse helped me understand how he could believe in such a way. “And he answered: Yea, Lord, I know that thou speakest the truth, for thou art a God of truth, and canst not lie.” (verse 12) Because the Brother of Jared knew that God could not lie, he could confess belief in any words that God had or would speak.
The question came to my mind, “Do you believe that God cannot lie?” That would mean that I already decide to believe anything God tells me. He really cannot lie. It’s sort of an interesting idea.

There was a test of faith involved, as the Lord asked: 'Believest thou the words which I shall speak?' (Ether 3:11. Italics added.) Interesting, isn't it, that he was not asked, 'Believest thou the words that I have spoken?' It didn't relate to the past. It related to the future. The brother of Jared was asked to commit himself on something that had not yet happened. He was to confirm his belief in that which the Lord had not yet spoken. . . . Faith, to be faith, must center around something that is not known. Faith, to be faith, must go beyond that for which there is confirming evidence. Faith, to be faith, must go into the unknown. Faith, to be faith, must walk to the edge of the light, and then a few steps into the darkness. If everything has to be known, if everything has to be explained, if everything has to be certified, then there is no need for faith. Indeed, there is no room for it. (quoted in We Talk of Christ, by Neal A. Maxwell, p. 66)

I was reading in Ether and wondered why there was a Hebrew name used among them. If this was the Jaredites, this is before Hebrew. At least, we would think so. We presume that the Jaredites’ language was not confounded and they therefore kept what they had of the Adamic language.

Perhaps the Hebrew language borrowed elements of the Adamic language. Anyway, I found a great article discussing this topic and going into further analysis of language in the Book of Mormon. It’s called, .

They mentioned the fact that Moroni could have just been inserting the Nephite name of the hill called Ephraim in the verse I referenced in the heading. This could be true, but there still are names such as Noah and Seth that are Hebrew biblical names. Maybe they’re the Hebrew equivalent names.

In 1 Nephi 3:19 Nephi says that one good thing about the Brass Plates is that they would “preserve unto our children the language of our fathers.” Does this mean that this language he’s referring to is different from the language he speaks? I assumed it would be written in Hebrew. Didn’t Lehi and his family mainly speak Hebrew? Even Moroni is confident in his Hebrew a thousand years after Lehi. So what language is being preserved here? Maybe it’s just worded in an ambiguous way but both the plates and language are Hebrew.

title: Things the Author of The Book of Mormon Would Have to Had Known

body.text: I remember on my mission I was teaching a member family and I said that there are many individual proofs of the Book of Mormon’s authenticity, but none are as powerful or important as the testimony of the Spirit. The wife in this family asked out of curiosity what some of the proofs I was talking about were. I could only think of the chiasma in Alma 36 at the time. I know I’ve found many evidences that the Book of Mormon was not written by Joseph Smith, but I never compiled them into one list. Perhaps I can do that here. I will try to mainly list the points that would be most difficult or impossible to access during the time of the writing of The Book of Mormon; e.g., not points that could easily be learned via The Holy Bible or other documents and books common during the time period.
●The approximate date of (589 - 587 B.C.). The Book of Mormon dates this event sometime between 588 - 570 B.C. Lehi has a vision that Jerusalem was destroyed during this time (see 2 Nephi 1:4).
●Understanding and proper implementation of , an ancient Hebrew and Greek poetic structure. Although many are found in The Book of Mormon, the most manifest and popular example is Alma 36.

●The name of a remote Yemen village NHM (Nahom), a city referenced in 1 Nephi 16:34 as the city where Ishmael was buried. Also see Yemen altars in this location dating to the time Lehi traveled through.

A friend of mine who has a doctorate in theology suggested the sources named above in response to me asking for some early christian interpretations of the creation account. I’ve been curious about the creation for a long time. It seems like one of the most curious stories in the Bible. Here are my notes and summaries as I read each of the documents named above.
This source only allows me to read 2 pages because it’s a preview and not a full document. Because of such, it’s not very insightful.
St. Basil apparently believes in creation out of nothing. I do like his style of preaching or writing.
St. Basil doesn’t go so far as the garden of Eden and the fall in this writing. I need to find that.
This is on the right material.
Garden of Eden is like meaning Paradise of Delight

THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH. And that Paradise is earth, and is planted on the earth, the Scripture states, saying: “And the Lord God planted Paradise in Eden eastwards, and placed man there; and out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food.” By the expressions, therefore, “out of the ground,” and “eastwards,” the holy writing clearly teaches us that Paradise is under this heaven, under which the east and the earth are. And the Hebrew word Eden signifies “delight” … And God transferred him from the earth, out of which he had been produced, into Paradise, giving him means of advancement, in order that, maturing and becoming perfect, and being even declared a god, he might thus ascend into heaven in possession of immortality. For man had been made a middle nature, neither wholly mortal, nor altogether immortal, but capable of either; so also the place, Paradise, was made in respect of beauty intermediate between earth and heaven. [To Autolycus 2.24 ANF v.2]

Ambrose of Milan is quoted discussing the necessity of opposition, including the existence and creation of the devil and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—good must actually exist in order to conceive of good and evil; likewise evil.

AMBROSE OF MILAN. There was a tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Paradise. This was so because 'God made to grow a tree pleasant to sight and good for food, the tree of life also in the midst of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.' {Gen 2:9) We shall see later whether this tree, like the others, was pleasant to sight and good for food. The question will be more fittingly discussed at the point where, on tasting the fruit of this tree, we find that man was deceived. Meantime, we should no[t] reproach ourselves for not being able to know precisely the reasons behind these facts. We should not form a hasty judgment in respect to this product of creation, if it presents to our intellect what seems to us—like the creation of serpents and certain poisonous creatures-difficult and incomprehensible. In fact, we are unable, owing to human weakness, yet to know and understand the reason for the creation of each and every object. Let us, therefore, not criticise in holy Scripture something which we cannot comprehend. There are very many things which must not be subjected to the judgment of our intellect. Rather, these should be surveyed from the lofty heights of Divine Providence and from the intentions of God Himself. Without prejudice, then, to what we shall say hereafter, set it down as a first principle that the subject of this tree of the knowledge of good and evil is to you a displeasing one. After men had tasted of this tree, they realized that they were naked. [ Gen 3:7 ] Nevertheless, I will state for your benefit that as a consummation of God's creation this tree grew in Paradise and that it was permitted by God, in order that we might be able to know the preeminence of good. How could we learn to know that there was a difference between good and evil, if there existed no knowledge of good and evil? We could not have come to realize that evil was evil, unless there was knowledge of good, and that there could not be knowledge of good, unless there was actual good. Again, we could not have known what in itself was good, unless there was knowledge of evil. Take an example from the nature of the human body. There exists as a matter of fact a certain bitter and poisonous substance which has been discovered to have a general salutary effect on the health of men. Hence, what we regard as evil frequently turns out to be not in every respect evil, but to be advantageous for general use. Just as poison exists in a part of the body but has a beneficial effect on the body as a whole, so God established the knowledge in part of what is good and evil, in order that the whole might be benefitted. Hence it follows that the serpent in Paradise was certainly not brought into being without the will of God. In the figure of the serpent we see the Devil. That the Devil existed even in Paradise we are informed by the Prophet Ezekiel, who in discussing the Prince of Tyre says: 'Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God.' [ Ezek 28:13 ] We maintain that the Prince of Tyre stands for the Devil. Shall we, therefore, accuse God because we cannot comprehend the treasures-with the exception of those which He has deigned to reveal-of His majesty and wisdom which lie hidden and concealed in Christ? Yet He did reveal to us the fact that the wickedness of the Devil is fruitful for man's salvation. This would not be the Devil's intention, but the Lord makes the wickedness of him who stands in opposition to us contribute something to our salvation. The wickedness of the Devil has caused the virtue and patience of one holy man to shine in a clearer light. The justice of Job was so disciplined and exercised by the wickedness of his opponent that eventually he gained the crown of victory over his adversary, the Devil. No one is crowned 'unless he has competed according to the rules.' [ 2 Tim 2:5 ] Joseph's chastity, too, would never have been recorded for us, if it did not happen that a woman, the wife of his master and friend, incited and goaded by the Devil's allurements, had not played with his affections. [ Gen 39:17 ] This woman finally endeavored to bring about his death. This event added more to the fame of a man who by his continence faced death in defense of chastity. Do you desire to know God's plan? Here is an instance. Through the instrumentality of the Devil there was once an occasion when a just man prepared to perpetrate manslaughter. The situation was one that involved the murder of one's own son. Yet, for all that, the Lord tempted Abraham in this wise. He demanded that Abraham sacrifice his son to Him. By reason of this temptation he was able to prove himself faithful to the Lord, since compliance to his vow and not pity for his beloved son brought about repeal of the order. [ Gen 22:1 ] There was, therefore, in Paradise a tree of knowledge of good and evil which appeared to the eye to be beautiful and to the taste to be edible. It was not actually good to eat, for its fruit appeared to have a harmful effect on man. What is injurious to individuals may nevertheless have a beneficial effect on men as a whole. The Devil, for example, did harm to Judas, [ Luke 22:3 ] but he bestowed the wreath of victory on all the other Apostles, inasmuch as they were able to face and overcome the force of his temptation. Accordingly, let it not be a subject of reprehension or doubt that the Devil existed in Paradise. As a matter of fact he was powerless to bar from the saints the way of their ascent. As one who had the right of possession, he did not evict the just from their habitation. It may be that he turned away from the occupancy of that high estate some who were in fact slothful and vicious. There is a recorded event that arouses to a much greater degree our regard and our admiration. This is the fact that the Devil was excluded from the prayers of the saints as the result of an event which was to take place: 'I was watching Satan fall as lightning from heaven.' [ Luke 10:18 ] Let us, therefore, not fear one who is so weak that he is destined to fall from heaven. He actually received the power to tempt us but not the competency to subvert us, except when our weak and unassisted will falters because it is powerless to summon aid. For that reason we need to know what was the nature of the deceit inflicted on the first man. We ought to know, too, the method and manner of the Devil's procedure and what in man he thought was subject to temptation, so that we, in knowing this, may proceed to take precautions. Many people nevertheless are of the opinion that the Devil was not in Paradise, although we read that he stood with the angels in heaven. [ Zech. 3:1 ] These persons interpret the statement of Scripture according to their own fancy. In this way they put aside any objection which they may have to the words of Scripture. We stand by the conviction held by one who preceded us that sin was committed by man because of the pleasure of sense. We maintain that the figure of the serpent stands for enjoyment and the figure of the woman for the emotions of the mind and heart. The latter is called by the Greeks aisthesis. When according to this theory, the senses are aisthesis deceived, the mind, which the Greeks call nous , falls into error. Hence, not without reason the to whom I refer [Cf. Philo, De opificio mundi 59; Legum allegoriae I 29.] accepts the Greek word nous as a figure of a man and aisthesis as that of a woman. Hence, some have interpreted Adam to mean an earthly nous . In the Gospel the Lord sets forth the parable of the virgins who awaited the coming of the bridegroom with either lighted or extinguished lamps. Thus He exemplifies either the pure emotions of the wise or the impure senses of the unwise. [ Matt 25:1 ] If Eve, that is, the emotions of the first woman, had kept her lamp lighted, she would not have enfolded us in the meshes of her sin. She would not have fallen from the height of immortality which is established as the reward of virtue. Paradise is, therefore, a land of fertility-that is to say, a soul which is fertile-planted in Eden, that is, in a certain delightful or well-tilled land in which the soul finds pleasure. Adam exists there as nous [mind] and Eve as 'sense.' Take note of what this soul of ours has in the nature of defense against natural and weak tendencies or against situations which might be unfavorable to us in our attempts to avoid danger. [On Paradise]
All of the usages of “Lord” in Isaiah 53 are 3068, which is Jehovah. I guess this isn’t as elaborate as I thought.

title: Break the Bands of Death and the Bowels of Mercy

body.text: In Abinadi’s sermon to King Noah and his priests, he weighs heavily upon the mortal mission of Jehovah as the Messiah. Abinadi teaches how God will break the bands of death via the Messiah’s crucifixion and atonement. Abinadi uses a unique phrase used nowhere else in christian scripture, “God breaketh the bands of death”.

The words Abinadi taught had a major impact on at least one person, Alma the older. It’s not too surprising, though it is interesting, that after Abinadi’s four uses of this phrase during his sermon (; ), all other uses in The Book of Mormon are after Abinadi.
●Alma uses the phrase five times, three during a sermon to the saints in the land of Zarahemla (; ), once to the saints in the land of Gideon ()
●Amulek uses the phrase once when teaching Zeezrom ()
●Aaron uses the phrase once when teaching King Lamoni’s father ()

Abinadi’s teachings apparently became a large part of Alma the older’s life and thought. Alma the older would have had a large theological influence and it is apparent that his teachings made their influence on Amulek and at least one of the sons of Mosiah, Aaron.

This is a small witness that the story in The Book of Mormon is a true account of an ancient people and not an invented fabrication of Joseph Smith. How elaborate and thought out are the deliberations here? It is no invention of man. This is a complex story that involves real people and real events.

One last interesting note is that the “bands of death” is not the only phrase that Alma later uses, but he also uses the original phrase of “bowels filled with mercy.” Abinadi first uses this wording in Mosiah 15:9 in the same sentence as the “bands of death”, in fact:

And thus God breaketh the bands of death, having gained the victory over death; giving the Son power to make intercession for the children of men—Having ascended into heaven, having the bowels of mercy; being filled with compassion towards the children of men; standing betwixt them and justice; having broken the bands of death, taken upon himself their iniquity and their transgressions, having redeemed them, and satisfied the demands of justice. ()
Alma then uses the wording in a sermon to the people in the land of Gideon,

And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities. ()
It’s interesting that Christ later says in His post-resurrection visit to the Nephites,

Behold, my bowels are filled with compassion towards you. Have ye any that are sick among you? Bring them hither. Have ye any that are lame, or blind, or halt, or maimed, or leprous, or that are withered, or that are deaf, or that are afflicted in any manner? Bring them hither and I will heal them, for I have compassion upon you; my bowels are filled with mercy. ()

title: Not a Human Sacrifice, but an Infinite and Eternal One

body.text: Amulek expounds the atonement to the Zoramites of Antionum. In verse ten he teaches that the atonement “must be an infinite and eternal sacrifice.” This makes sense. But let me dissect his reasoning up to this point (verse 9):
●It is expedient that an atonement should be made
○Because God’s great plan says so
○If there isn’t an atonement, all mankind must perish
■All are fallen and lost and will perish unless redeemed
●It is expedient that an atonement should be made
There’s a sort of chiastic structure to Amulek’s reasoning here. Regardless, he says the atonement is necessary for the reasons named above.
He goes on to explain why and how an atonement solves the problem of mankind being fallen and lost (verse 10):
●It’s expedient that there should be a great and last sacrifice
○The sacrifices Zoramites may be familiar with but which are ineffective for the cause named:
■Not a sacrifice of man
■Not a sacrifice of beast
■Not a sacrifice of any manner of fowl
○For it shall not be a human sacrifice
○But an infinite and eternal sacrifice

I italicize “human sacrifice” because this is interestingly placed. One might interpret the face value of this to mean that the sacrificial offering won’t work if it is human (no man, beast, fowl, etc.), but with closer reading we see that Amulek already said this, “not a sacrifice of man, neither of beast…” Why would Amulek repeat himself and only repeat the human part?

My understanding of this phrase is that it is saying, “You see, this sacrifice can’t be offered by humans, therefore, it won’t be a ‘human sacrifice’.” This is significant when you see how this alters what follows. “But it must be an infinite and eternal sacrifice” comes to hold a different meaning as well. Instead of simply meaning that Christ, the sacrificial offering, is infinite and eternal (which He is), it means that the sacrificial offerer must be infinite and eternal. This Being is God, the Father. God, the Father, who is infinite and eternal, offers up a sacrifice which is also infinite and eternal.
This difference in interpretation seems significant to me.

title: Take away the sins of the world

body.text: I think the wording is cool in this verse: “...it is [Christ] that cometh to take away the sins of the world, yea, the sins of every man who steadfastly believeth on his name.”

title: The Wisdom of Ammon and Consent of Lamoni

body.text: There’s a cool reference I read about for the scenario of Ammon teaching King Lamoni. Alma 18:22 says, “Now Ammon being wise, yet harmless, he said unto Lamoni: Wilt thou hearken unto my words, if I tell thee by what power I do these things?” This sounds very familiar to Jesus’ advice in Matthew 10:16, “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.” Interesting that Ammon was sent as a sheep among wolves. Also, he gathered the sheep as a miraculous demonstration of the power of God within him before teaching King Lamoni.

There’s a question that I had when reading Alma 18:23, “And the king answered him, and said: Yea, I will believe all thy words. And thus he was caught with guile.” How was the king caught with guile? What sort of deceit or trickery had the king committed in order to be caught in such an act?

There are two answers I found online that take different routes to answer this. One answer suggests that the word “guile” in this context does not denote deceit, but rather surprise. This would make sense, but it would be odd to use the word if it doesn’t mean what the word means. Why not use the word “surprise”? The dictionaries of Joseph Smith’s time don’t change the meaning of the word “guile” either, so the definition still retained the meaning of being guilty of deceit or cunning.

This is why I think the second answer makes a bit more sense. It suggests that the king wanted to know who Ammon was and by what power he did the things he did. The king, however, committed a cunning act, perhaps even deceitful, which may have been more apparent in their culture than ours. He asked Ammon “tell me concerning these things; and also tell me by what power ye slew and smote off the arms of my brethren that scattered my flocks”. The king conditioned Ammon’s response telling him that he would pay a price of any worldly offering the king had if Ammon told him.

Apparently, this was insincere and even cunning or deceitful to Ammon, because Ammon changed the conditions the king had given, saying, “Wilt thou hearken unto my words, if I tell thee by what power I do these things?” After consenting to this request, king Lamoni was supposedly caught with guile.
I think this second answer makes sense. It does suggest that the culture of their time was a bit different and perhaps considered belief in one’s words more sincere and expected than worldly rewards.

I was just in a church lesson on faith and some comments and questions were said that got me thinking about this topic. I’ve studied faith in the past and feel like there’s a lot to study there. One of the questions was how we’re supposed to build faith if the things we pray for don’t always happen. A follow-up comment was made by the asker of this question that if you prayed for something and it happened right away it would build your faith but it’s not God’s way—something like that. I have some different thoughts on this.

Faith, a song in the Children’s Songbook, says, “Faith is knowing the sun will rise, lighting each new day. Faith is knowing the Lord will hear my prayers each time I pray.” This is technically inaccurate. Faith is not knowing. Knowing is knowing. I know that’s redundant but knowledge and faith are not the same thing. As Alma taught, “faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things.” (Alma 32:21) This means that faith must precede knowledge in their relationship.

But some criticize Christians for their supposed faith because, as they pose, it is blind obedience. This is a bad description and also shows misunderstanding. Faith, as stated above, is not knowledge, but it also isn’t blindness. “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). This means that faith is based on actual evidence. It’s not the empirical evidence deemed worthy by secularism, but it is even more personally corroborative. Alma taught, “therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true” (Alma 32:21). Faith can only exist when a truth-based hope exists and such a truth-based hope can only come by assurance of faith, or from the Holy Spirit.

The Nephite armies experienced the birth of a truth-based and God-given hope that enabled them to have faith in their times of trial, “Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him” (Alma 58:11).
