Moroni taught, “Wherefore, there must be faith; and if there must be faith there must also be hope; and if there must be hope there must also be charity” (Moroni 10:20). I believe this sets up a structural relationship between the three named attributes. Charity is first and most fundamental and critical, then hope, then faith. The latter depend upon the former. Without charity, there can be no hope, and without hope, there can be no faith.

This is further demonstrated when Mormon leads a wicked people and loses faith (Mormon 3:12) and then hope (Mormon 5:2) but does not lose the love or charity which he had for his people, “Behold, I had led them, notwithstanding their wickedness I had led them many times to battle, and had loved them, according to the love of God which was in me, with all my heart” (Mormon 3:12). Thus, “all things must fail… but charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever” (Moroni 7:46-47).

My point here is that faith is based on assurance, or evidence, given by the Spirit. It is not something weak people do to follow tradition. It is not something whimsical like having a hope for good weather. It is deep and based in truth. Of course, it is often used improperly and out of context, but the scriptures give a good and proper usage which shows the meaning that works well according to my understanding.
The great mission of the sons of Mosiah and their brethren is an amazing story. Here are details I’ve gathered.

Ammon, Aaron, Omner, and Himni, four sons of Mosiah, “took a small number with them and returned to their father, the king, and desired of him that he would grant unto them that they might,with these whom they had selected, go up to the land of Nephi that they might preach the things which they had heard, and that they might impart the word of God to their brethren, the Lamanites” (Mosiah 28:1).

King Mosiah prays about this, perhaps considering the great danger entailed. The Lord responds: “Let them go up, for many shall believe on their words, and they shall have eternal life; and I will deliver thy sons out of the hands of the Lamanites” (Mosiah 28:6). So with the promise of deliverance, Mosiah sends his sons out on their mission.

For reasons we can only speculate on, Ammon leads among his brothers and friends during their mission to the Lamanites. There is reason to believe that Aaron is the eldest brother—he is the first choice of the people as the successor of King Mosiah. Why else would the people desire him as the successor instead of Ammon unless Aaron were the eldest brother?

I suppose it’s possible that Ammon was the eldest but had offended the people so egregiously that they chose Aaron over him as the King’s successor. If it were the case that Ammon was the eldest, it would make sense why he would lead his brothers and friends on their mission.

If Aaron was, in fact, the eldest brother, it not becomes curious why Ammon led his brothers during their mission. There would have to be some reason why birthright and age could have been overridden so that Ammon led over Aaron. I’ve read someone’s thoughts on this who asserted that Ammon led so that he could fulfill a special calling that he had taken upon himself.

The special calling Ammon had may have been set by virtue of Ammon’s name. Apparently names had incredible significance among the Nephites—Nephites kings took upon themselves the name Nephi (Jacob 1:11), many fathers named their sons after themselves, namely Mosiah, Alma, Helaman, and Nephi. Nephi and Lehi were named after their namesake ancestors with hopes to yield to their righteous lives.

With all this emphasis on names, perhaps Mosiah had named his son after Ammon, the great exhibition leader whom Mosiah sent out to find the lost Nephites in the land of Lehi-Nephi. This Ammon is described as “a strong and mighty man” (Mosiah 7:3). After traveling forty days in the wilderness, they came to a hill north of the land of Shilom and Ammon took three of his men, Amaleki, Helem, and Hem, and went down into the land of Nephi where he and his men were surrounded by King Limhi’s guards, cast into prison for two days, and brought before King Limhi. At that point, Ammon was able to explain his identity and became well received by the King.

Later on, King Limhi and a sect of the people desired to be baptized but there was no one in the land who had authority to baptize except, apparently, Ammon, who declined performing the rite “considering himself an unworthy servant” (Mosiah 21:33).

It isn’t unlikely that King Mosiah would have named his own son after this first Ammon. If it were the case, then Ammon, son of Mosiah, may have desired to use his namesake as a model for his conversion, which did end up being quite a good model—both venture among the Lamanites on a mission of sorts, are taken by king’s guards and set before the king, Limhi in the first case and Lamoni in the second, and lead the new-found and converted people back to the land of the believers.
Perhaps Aaron stepped down from his position of seniority so that Ammon could fulfill his namesake’s model role.

Also, I don’t know if there’s any significance to this, but the first Ammon, just before being captured by King Limhi’s guards, had brought three of his brethren with him: Amaleki, Helem, and Hem… nevermind on this thought. I was going to compare it with “Aaron, and also Muloki and Ammah” (Alma 20:2) who are some of the brethren Ammon is accompanied by. The similarity of a count of three seemed interesting and perhaps of significance to me.

title: My Favorite Book of Mormon Studies & Analyses

body.text: This will likely be a large section and hopefully one that I can continue editing and appending to as I learn more. But I have come across so many insightful and powerful studies and analyses of The Book of Mormon that I’d like to compile a list. This also is an effort to organize the evidence I’ve found that support the idea that The Book of Mormon is a work of literary art of ancient date. It ought to be taken seriously. The evidence that it is the word of God must primarily come from God Himself. I leave that to each man and God. But these evidence will at least provide grounds to give a reasonable case that The Book of Mormon is what it purports to be.

Chiasmuses are poetic structures with ancient origin. They follow an inverted parallel structure; e.g., A B C D D C B A. These are found all over in the Book of Mormon. Some of the most renowned are 2 Nephi 25, Alma 36, Alma 39, but there are many others.
I see highly complex relationships between narratives and characters to be evidence supporting the Book of Mormon’s authenticity. Here are some examples:
Ammon and Ammon

King Mosiah, son of King Benjamin, sent a strong man named Ammon to lead an important expedition of a number of men to search for a group of Nephites who had, generations before, left the main group of Nephites and sought for the land of their inheritance in the land of Nephi among the Lamanites. Ammon, after wandering many days in the wilderness, finds his lost brethren and acquaints himself with their king, a man named Limhi. Ammon is received with joy and gives an accounting of the Nephites since Limhi’s people had departed from them. Ammon also gives to them an important sermon King Benjamin had recently given, a message of deep spiritual significance.
Limhi and his people are held captive by Lamanites. Limhi’s people and Ammon and his group escape from the Lamanites during the night while the Lamanite guards are drunk and sleeping.

Limhi desires to be baptized by forebears because no one has authority to baptize him except Ammon, and Ammon considered himself unworthy at the time. Eventually, Limhi and others are baptized by Alma when they reunite.
It may be that Ammon not only acted as a leader and restored his brethren to the fold, so to say, but that he also gained his own conversion.
The fact that his father, Mosiah, was the one who sent him on his quest gives support to the theory that the son of Mosiah who was named Ammon could have been named after this very same Ammon.

This supports a theory that Ammon son of Mosiah, when on his mission among the Lamanites, was attempting to fulfill the role of his name by being fully converted, leading an expedition, and bringing his brethren, the Lamanites, back to the fold. This would explain why he took the lead in the expedition he and his brothers and friends went on, rather than his older brother, Aaron.
… continue later

Samuel the Lamanite taught some great things about the Atonement of Jesus Christ. Last night Kaylene and I were talking about his teachings and I tried to teach Kaylene some doctrine about the Atonement—it was my turn to teach the lesson. I soon became curious about some areas of doctrine on the subject that I don’t understand. I wanted to address those curiosities today and I hope to learn something more about the Atonement.

“For behold, [Jesus Christ] surely must die that salvation may come; yea, it behooveth him and becometh expedient that he dieth, to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, that thereby men may be brought into the presence of the Lord.” (Helaman 13:15)

From this I understand that Christ must die so that we can be saved. Saved from what? Well Samuel teaches that this is salvation from “the first death” which he teaches is spiritual death. He also mentions that the fall brought about a temporal and spiritual death, both of which, presumably, we would be redeemed from by the death of Christ.
Anyway, before I get too far into these descriptions by Samuel and other teachers in The Book of Mormon, I want to see if I can articulate the questions I had last night.

So, my understanding is that the Atonement, meaning the suffering, death, and resurrection of Christ, allows all of us to repent and enables all of us to be resurrected. The resurrection part seems to be automatic, like Christ just solves our problem of temporal death. That makes sense because Adam partook of the fruit and brought this death upon all of us. It wasn’t our fault, right? Even Paul said “death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come” (Tomans 5:14). If death passed upon them which did not enact it by the same transgression Adam made, then it becomes all the more just that the redemption of this consequence comes as easily. “For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” (Romans 5:18) Aha! So we are made righteous by the products of the Atonement. Christ not only saves us from death, but He redeems us from the spiritual death which we have and also the cause of our spiritual death, unrighteousness.

I thought last night, what good would it do for Christ to redeem us of the debt we owe to justice by our sinful deeds if we were not purged of that which makes us sin to begin with!? We really must be “dead to sin” (Romans 6:2). But how? How will that happen? Cannot the redemption of our unrighteousness be as free and easy as the redemption of our physical death? At least, our redemption from death seems free and easy. We just receive it and all will have that gift. But why cannot all be saved from the cause of our spiritual death and not merely squared away as to our debt? I fear that every time Christ’s grace pays my debt I return to sin and incur more debt. What good is it to jettison the water filling my rowboat if there is a leak through which water continuously runs? Wouldn’t the solution be to fix the leak? Well then how will Christ fix the leak which causes unrighteousness to flow into me? For, like Paul, “that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.” (Romans 7:15)

Oh how I want to be dead to sin. But I seem enslaved to it without release. How will Christ redeem me? Because even though “no unclean thing can dwell in the presence of God”, even more, “No unclean thing can enter into his kingdom.” So only if I am clean, from sin I presume, can I dwell with God in His kingdom. Perhaps all men, righteous and unrighteous, will be enabled to be judged by God and stand in His presence even though some may be unclean, because of a technicality—the unclean cannot dwell with God and therefore cannot enter his kingdom, but that doesn’t mean that they cannot stand temporarily in His presence.

But again I ask, how will I ever become dead to sin? Does it happen when I’m resurrected? And if the resurrection allows us to somehow become masters over sin and be unaffected by sin’s power, then what is the point of repentance?

I’ve been taught that repentance is some condition of salvation that Christ imposed because He could—you know how the one who pays your debt now owns your debt? I don’t think this view is very accurate though. It’s not like Christ greedily took in His own hands our debt in order to exploit that leverage. Perhaps you won’t call His attempt to make us choose righteousness an exploitation of leverage or a means for manipulation, but even so, this all implies that the power for us to become righteous rests not in God’s hands alone, but, at least in part, in our own hands. Why not then would God just snap His fingers and redeem us of our sinful and fallen state as He so mercifully and gracious did, or will, for our physical death?

I admit that it makes sense that God could not impose a change of nature upon that which resisted His change. He cannot override our will, right? He wouldn’t take away our own autonomy of choice. If He could do this then there would be utterly no point to us being alive except to be God’s puppets. It would totally deprive us of absolutely any responsibility to be or do good. All responsibility would rest entirely in God’s hands. So no, this is not the case. God will not, or perhaps cannot, change us beyond our will to be changed.

One might then say, okay then there’s your answer: God provides repentance not as a means to manipulate us to do what He supposably cannot force us to do Himself, but as a means to proffer us change of heart from unrighteousness to righteousness. This too though seems to say that this power of change is a laborious journey on our part and puts a lot of it in our hands. I certainly feel that this power is not in my hands. No matter how hard I try, I seem to be enslaved to the sinful nature of mankind and no amount of meditation or self-will can change my nature to yield to greed, pride, lust, and envy. So how then will repentance enable me to change? I don’t merely need more probationary time to solve my dilemma of sin, I need someone to change my heart “[have] this wicked spirit rooted out of my breast” (Alma 22:15)?

Perhaps God’s grace does this for us, but we can only accept His gift grace for grace, day by day, until “the perfect day” when we will find our path and ways illuminated and righteous. Our “faith is counted for righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Is this because our faith enables God to be alive in us and for our sinful deeds to be overwhelmed by the good God pours into us through His grace? I am fine accepting a hard path for grace to work in us, but if it is not so, I don’t want to make things harder than God intends them to be.
Alma describes to the poor people among the Zoramites the process of gaining faith and how it grows. I want to understand the process better so here’s my summary of what I’m reading.
●Exercise a particle of faith, even if it’s just a desire to believe.
●Don’t cast out your faith or desire to believe. Don’t resist it. Give it room to exist.
●It will begin to swell and grow, which is evidence to you that the word you have faith in is good.
○This increases your faith, but it is not a perfect knowledge
●The word and your enlightenment will continue to expand and grow and your evidence along with it.
○Your knowledge will now become perfect in this particular thing and faith is less needed, therefore, it becomes dormant.
●At this point, your knowledge is not perfect; i.e., it had only been perfect in knowing that the word you had planted was good. But faith is still needed, somehow.(?)

○If you neglect your duty to nourish this seed sufficiently then it will not get any root and the heat, or trials, may come and your faith will wither, not because it was unfounded or false, but because you didn’t give it a fighting chance.
○You must nourish the word and look forward to its fruit with an eye of faith.
●By and by, you will pluck the fruit if you nourish the word and it will take root in you.

title: Praying to Jesus and Jesus as God

body.text: I have been curious why it seems that in the Old Testament and often in the Book of Mormon, they seem to pray to Jehovah, worship Jehovah, and treat Jehovah as the One True Father and God. Didn’t they have to still abide by the rule to pray to Elohim, the Father, through Christ, His Son?
I read a good article talking about how we have certainly been instructed, and even by Christ Himself, to pray to the Father in the name of Christ. Here’s the article:
But I wanted to see how supported my question is and clear it up in order to make sure my understanding is correct.
●Book of Mormon
○Mosiah 13:34, “Have they not said that God himself should come down among the children of men, and take upon him the form of man, and go forth in mighty power upon the face of the earth?”
■This references “God” as meaning Jesus Christ.
○Mosiah 15:1, “...I would that ye should understand that God himself shall come down among the children of men, and shall redeem his people.”
■This references “God” as meaning Jesus Christ
○Mosiah 15:1-5, multiple references to Jehovah being called “the Father” and only one reference to Elohim—“...conceived by the power of God” (verse 3).

○Alma 42:15, “And now, the plan of mercy could not be brought about except an atonement should be made; therefore God himself atoneth for the sins of the world, to bring about the plan of mercy, to appease the demands of justice, that God might be a perfect, just God, and a merciful God also.”
■The first usage of “God” is most-likely referring to Christ. The latter three are probably referring to Christ as well.

At least twice Kaylene and I have been reading the Book of Mormon in Alma 34 and come upon the question of what was meant by Alma 34:12. The context is that Amulek and Alma are teaching the Zoramites, whose teachings rejected the need for Christ. Amulek is teaching them to correct this false doctrine and goes into detail of what exactly the atonement is and why we need it.
He teaches that it’s necessary that there be a “great and last sacrifice” that will put a stop to the need for animal sacrifice as performed by the law of Moses. Then we come upon verses 11-12:

Now there is not any man that can sacrifice his own blood which will atone for the sins of another. Now, if a man murdereth, behold will our law, which is just, take the life of his brother? I say unto you, Nay. But the law requireth the life of him who hath murdered; therefore there can be nothing which is short of an infinite atonement which will suffice for the sins of the world.

If Amulek had just said that no man can sacrifice his blood for another man’s sins, how is Christ’s sacrifice any different? It almost sounded like Amulek was teaching that every man must pay his own sins and this is only fair.

What Kaylene and I concluded after discussion is that Amulek must have meant that mankind cannot offer a sacrifice to pay for another’s sins, but God, or the infinite offerer, can. Thus, nothing short of an infinite, or God-give, atonement will suffice.

It’s still not totally lucid to me. “But the law requireth the life of him who hath murdered;” If the law requires the sinner’s life, then how would an infinite sacrifice, whether that means God-offered sacrifice or God being the sacrifice, fix the dilemma? Maybe I’ll have to think more upon this.

I’ve been thinking about repentance lately and I’ve had more questions than I thought about the topic. For example, what does repentance really mean?—does it always entail change and what sort of change? If change doesn’t seem to happen, am I really repenting? The change that’s supposed to occur, does it come from God, our own efforts, or both? What hinders godly changes from occurring more often and in greater effect?
I’m going to research everything I can about repentance and see what conclusions I can make.
Guide to the Scriptures: Repentance

A change of mind and heart that brings a fresh attitude toward God, oneself, and life in general. Repentance implies that a person turns away from evil and turns his heart and will to God, submitting to God’s commandments and desires and forsaking sin. True repentance comes from a love for God and a sincere desire to obey His commandments. All accountable persons have sinned and must repent in order to progress toward salvation. Only through the Atonement of Jesus Christ can our repentance become effective and accepted by God.

Here are the parts about repentance that make sense to me. It is a change of mind and heart, a turning of one’s heart and will to God, a submission to God’s commandments and desires out of a love for God and a sincere desire to obey and follow Him. Although, I’m not sure I understand how turning away from evil and forsaking sin is possible. I know that may seem like an odd thing to say. Of course, many people make changes to quit bad habits or become nicer, more compassionate people through learning lessons of life, but the ultimate responsibility to turn away from evil and forsake sin as a requirement of the penitent assumes that the penitent has power to do such things. Perhaps the implication is that such are only possible and this would have to be the case, because if we all have power in and of ourselves to change our ways and to not ever sin, we would have no need for God’s grace except to excuse the sins we made along the way and for resurrection. And for those who could not sin because of the innocence of youth or mental handicap, they would have no need for God’s grace except for resurrection.

How could we assume the power to change ourselves on our own without removing our need for God? And if it were possible that a person could, by their own willpower, resist all sin, that yields the possibility that one could live their whole life sinless, which thing is impossible. Paul said, “All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23) Paul says even so much more that is relevant. Listen to his words and see if there could exist within us the ability to mend our own ways retreat from a sinful nature:

We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin. I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do. And if I do what I do not want to do, I agree that the law is good. As it is, it is no longer I myself who do it, but it is sin living in me. For I know that good itself does not dwell in me, that is, in my sinful nature. For I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. For I do not do the good I want to do, but the evil I do not want to do—this I keep on doing. Now if I do what I do not want to do, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it. So I find this law at work: Although I want to do good, evil is right there with me. For in my inner being I delight in God’s law; but I see another law at work in me, waging war against the law of my mind and making me a prisoner of the law of sin at work within me. What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body that is subject to death? Thanks be to God, who delivers me through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself in my mind am a slave to God’s law, but in my sinful nature a slave to the law of sin. (Romans 7:14-25)

Paul depicts my lament, “Who will rescue me from this body that is subject to death?” My pain is that I serve sin in my body but my mind desires the law of God. How could such a contrasted and opposing dichotomy exist within me? Why must I have a nature that contradicts my desired nature? It seems that my body desires to covet, injure, anger, and lust, but my mind desires holiness and grace. But the two fight each other and I am left attacking myself. Who can win when I am my own enemy?

But Paul ended with saying God delivers us through Jesus Christ. This is what I desire. But what will the deliverance be? Will it be a relief of the sinful nature? This is my deep desire. I no longer want to serve sin. Would it be possible to, like the people of Mosiah, “have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually”? (Mosiah 5:2). I feel that I truly am a slave to sin. I feel in bondage with desire for relief. How can I not despair unless I truly can be freed from the carnal and sinful nature? The people of Mosiah attributed their change to the “Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent.” Was their change a desire or a change of nature? Since they said their disposition changed, that makes me think it was truly a change of nature. This is my desire. I no longer wish to be bound to serving sin. Let me find respite and have these bounds broken.

Perhaps Nephi related to these feelings when he lamented “O wretched man that I am! Yea, my heart sorroweth because of my flesh; my soul grieveth because of mine iniquities. I am encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins which do so easily beset me. And when I desire to rejoice, my heart groaneth because of my sins.” (2 Nephi 4:17-18) Nephi does follow this lament with words of inspiration and hope. He talks about how he has seen such great things and surely been filled with God’s love. This is his resolution and cause to rejoice, not necessarily a reversal of his declared problem. He writes, “Why should I yield to sin, because of my flesh? Yea, why should I give way to temptations, that the evil one have place in my heart to destroy my peace and afflict my soul? Why am I angry because of mine enemy? Awake, my soul! No longer droop in sin. Rejoice, O my heart, and give place no more for the enemy of my soul.” (2 Nephi 4:27-28) Of course, this is encouraging, but does it mean that Nephi assumes responsibility and power to overcome sin and his enemy, the devil? Where is God’s place in all of this?
Bible Dictionary: Repentance
The Greek word of which this is the translation denotes a change of mind, a fresh view about God, about oneself, and about the world.

A change of mind. Well this makes sense in the contexts of God repenting, or not repenting. I remember in Genesis 6:6 it says, “And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” Speaking of this, I looked up the hebrew word that is used in this verse and it seems to be, by far, the most dominant hebrew word which gets translated into repent, or variations thereof. The hebrew word is nacham, naw-kham’; to sigh, i.e. breathe strongly; by implication, to be sorry or to pity, console, or avenge. This changes things because now we don’t assume that anytime one repents in the Old Testament it doesn’t imply that such a person has sinned, but is simply regretting, changing their mind, or sorrowing. God can change His mind, it seems. This does seem odd. I really think that we don’t understand God as much as we think we do. I thought He was some theoretical superlative of every good, which may still be true. But He is a man, a Man of Holiness, but a man. He has passion, personality, and desire. These are attributes that we often forget to attribute to Him.

The Bible Dictionary section on Repentance also says that it means turning your heart to God and renouncing sin. How do we abandon sin? Is it a choice? Maybe it is a choice that we can make because of what God has done for us. Maybe it’s a choice we can make, even before implementing it, even without God’s power to do so. I mean, of course we would definitely need Him to overcome sin, but the desire and choice alone to avoid sin may come to us and be our decision, perhaps.
Preach My Gospel: The Gospel of Jesus Christ: Repentance through the Atonement of Jesus Christ

Here repentance is defined as an action, “to change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with [God’s] will.” It also says that it includes feeling godly sorrow, returning to God with full purpose of heart, and stopping sinning. It also says that the grace and mercy of Christ is necessary to return to live with God the Father, and that we receive the mercy of Christ via the condition of repentance. Here’s a statement on my issue:

As we change, we recognize that we are children of God and that we need not continue making the same mistakes over and over. If we sincerely repent, we turn away from our sins and do them no more. We resist any desire to commit sin. Our desire to follow God grows strong and deeper.

We don’t repeat sins that we repent of, according to this, and we even resist the desire to commit sin, probably this sin in particular. This part is a bit harder. How can we do this? How can we stop repeating the same sins over and over? How could we? How can that desire leave us and our behavior change? This is especially crucial in addictions. How can an addict stop their behavior which they’re addicted to? I’m afraid that many times we simply don’t possess the power to stop sinning the sin that we’ve committed. It goes back to Paul and Nephi’s words which express and lament that they, and us, cannot seem to do the things we know are good and always avoid those that are bad.

Preach My Gospel mentions some results of repentance that I do see: “We feel God’s forgiveness and His peace in our lives. Our guilt and sorrow are swept away. We feel the influence of the Spirit in greater abundance. And when we pass from this life, we will be more prepared to live with our Heavenly Father and His Son.” I like this. I think if we follow the steps of repentance that we really will be freed of guilt and sorrow that often accompany sin in large degree.

This part is also comforting in relation to my issue: “Even after we have accepted Christ and repented of our sins, we may fall short and sin again. We should continually try to correct these transgressions…”.

There was a referenced scripture: “By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will  them and  them.” (D&C 58:43) A sign of repentance is when one has forsaken the sin. This reminds me of Jesus’ words to the woman taken in adultery, “go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11) Jesus wouldn’t have told the woman to stop sinning unless she could stop. Perhaps it would be only by His grace that she could leave the sin, but it was possible. This is how it must be with us—God commands us to forsake our sins, it seems, and this must be possible.

I was talking with Kaylene about this yesterday and I came to the conclusion that we really are able to recognize the wrong we did and repent, apologize, make amends, and stop doing the sin, just not in addiction. Addiction is a special case where we do things that we are, in all ways, trying our best not to do. It goes against our own desire and best effort. This is why it must be addressed differently.
True to the Faith: Repentance

Repentance is first described similarly to the other resources I’ve already read from. But I do like how they put it here. It seems nice and clear. I think I may even like it better than all the others for what it describes here:

Repentance is one of the first principles of the gospel (see ). It is essential to your happiness in this life and throughout eternity. Repentance is much more than just acknowledging wrongdoings. It is a change of mind and heart that gives you a fresh view about God, about yourself, and about the world. It includes turning away from sin and turning to God for forgiveness. It is motivated by love for God and the sincere desire to obey His commandments.
It goes on in more detail citing Alma 11:37, “no unclean thing can inherit the kingdom of heaven.” Our sins make us unclean, it says. Even on that note I wonder if that’s all that makes us unclean.

It says, “Jesus Christ suffered the penalty for your sins so you can be forgiven if you sincerely repent.” This leads me to ask, why is there a penalty for our sins? If God invented this penalty only to pay it Himself at such a high price, why would He even have invented it in the first place?
Lehi taught:

And if ye shall say there is no law, ye shall also say there is no sin. If ye shall say there is no sin, ye shall also say there is no righteousness. And if there be no righteousness there be no happiness. And if there be no righteousness nor happiness there be no punishment nor misery. And if these things are not there is no God. And if there is no God we are not, neither the earth; for there could have been no creation of things, neither to act nor to be acted upon; wherefore, all things must have vanished away. (2 Nephi 2:13)

This argues for the necessity of law and punishment. It doesn’t necessarily pose God as the author and enforcer of punishment. What I’m getting at is an alternate view of the consequences of sin. Perhaps wickedness is its own punishment. Perhaps God would not invoke any more suffering for a person’s actions than their own actions bring about. But I don’t know that this is true. It does seem that teachings of the scriptures imply that God takes vengeance and penal enforcement into His own hands.
Conclusory Remarks

Anyway, I guess my sole question of all this is do we have power to change? Repentance is a correction to unlawful behavior. Did we have power to change our behavior, thoughts, actions before sinning? Could we have resisted sin hypothetically? Could we resist all sin hypothetically and just by sheer bad luck and improbability we never do? It seems contrary in my mind. It seems that we have a sinful nature and are unable to conjure godly change alone and that it is the Spirit of God that must work in us which comes of the Atonement and through the grace of Jesus Christ that change may ensue. We could not change our very beings yet we can, because of Jesus Christ. We are changing and have great power invested in us through the grace of Jesus Christ. Our sins reap punishment by virtue of a just law and God, wanting to spare us suffering but being just and good, paid the highest price to allow a way for redemption of an inevitable damnation, making this plan merciful and just. It is the way to appease justice and yet offer us mercy. What a good plan! How it is permitted by just laws to allow for a Savior to redeem the sorry damned, I do not know. I just accept that based on scripture, I suppose.

title: The Davidic Covenant in The Book of Mormon

body.text: The Old Testament contains three major covenants, the Noachan Covenant that God will never again destroy humanity by a flood (Gen. 9:1-17), the Abrahamic Covenant that the descendants of Ahraham will inherit land, increase, and blessings, and the Mosiac Covenant that God will protect and prosper Israel on the condition of their righteousness. There is, however, a fourth and less popular covenant which is the Davidic Covenant that King David’s dynasty would last forever, or that his descendants would always be on the throne.

This fourth covenant is one which perhaps the people of Zarahemla in the Book of Mormon found relevant because they were the posterity of royal seed, that is, the seed of Mulek, son of Zedekiah. It is possible and likely that the insurrections of Nephites claiming right to the throne, Amalakiah, king men, etc., were descendants of Mulek. This explains why they might assume right to the throne—it would have been based upon scripture through the Davidic Covenant.

This also would explain why, soon after uniting with the people of Zarahemla which contained Davidic heirs of the right to rule, Mosiah dissolved the monarchy and proposed a system of judges. This at least relieved him of the controversy of ruling over rightful heirs through the Davidic Covenant.

But because of the faith of men he has shown himself unto the world, and glorified the name of the Father, and prepared a way that thereby others might be partakers of the heavenly gift, that they might hope for those things which they have not seen.
- Ether 12:28

The way the scriptures talk about this heavenly gift makes it seem to be something like a hope. It comes because of faith and isn’t seeing but allows some to hope in something they can’t see. It also seems like faith but it can’t quite be faith or hope because it’s description uses those words to describe it.
Here are the two other references to the phrase. I’ll see if the usage is consistent.
And they had all things common among them; therefore there were not rich and poor, bond and free, but they were all made free, and partakers of the heavenly gift.
4 Nephi 1:3
That one doesn’t really yield more information about what the phrase means but it does use it.

For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.
- Hebrews 6:4-6

This usage makes it sound like the heavenly gift is a sure knowledge of God. Perhaps it is the sure knowledge given through the Holy Ghost, hence the holy/heavenly gift. We also can receive the gift of the Holy Ghost, who apparently can offer this heavenly gift of knowledge.

title: Beholders of Visions and Their Preparations

body.text: I was reading 1 Nephi 1 and thought about Lehi’s vision and wondered what his life looked like soon before this vision. What sort of life was he living? The prayer during which the vision occurred was on “behalf of his people” and he was praying “with all his heart”. This made me want to search out what the scriptures teach about the events leading up to visions. I’ll go through several examples from the scriptures and examine what leads to the visions and if there are any themes.
●Samuel was retiring to bed but lived in a holy place (Samuel 3)
●Daniel received a vision at night (Daniel 7)
●Cornelius receives a vision after living a devout life and praying always (Acts 10)
●Joseph Smith had his vision in a field after praying (JSH 1)
I guess visions can come to anyone at any time but they often come to the righteous who pray often and spend time in the temple. Also, visions often occur at night, perhaps because it is in private.

Nephi begins by acknowledging the goodness of his parents and blessings and afflictions. It seems he writes this from a standpoint far in the future. I get the impression that by the time he writes this he is already in the Americas and all the major pieces of the story he will tell have transpired.
Nephi writes this record by his own hand and bears record of its truth.

Context of Lehi before his vision—it’s 600 B.C. and Zedekiah is king of Judah. Zedekiah, whose given name was Mattaniah, was granted his role as king over Judah when the Babylonians sieged Judah. Zedekiah soon conspired to rebel against king Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled the Babylonians. In 587 B.C., knowing of Zedekiah’s conspiracy against him with Egypt, king Nebuchadnezzar took Zedekiah, killed his sons, all but Mulek, before him and blinded him. Zedekiah was imprisoned until his death.

Jeremiah had prophesied of Jerusalem’s destruction and urged the king of Judah to allow the Babylonian rule, as he felt it was God’s will for Israel at the time. Other contemporary prophets among Lehi may have been Daniel and Ezekiel.

Lehi is apparently praying at some place not in his home with all his heart “in behalf of his people” when “there came a pillar of fire and dwelt upon a rock before him.” Lehi hears and sees things here that make him “quake and tremble exceedingly.”

The reason I take it that Lehi is not in his home during this occasion is that Nephi’s account says that after this instance, “he returned to his own house at Jerusalem,” after which he lays on his bed and is overcome with the Spirit.

In this state, he has another vision where “he saw the heavens open, and he thought he saw God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels in the attitude of singing and praising their God.”

What is this attitude of “singing and praising [God]”? Does this mean the angels were gesturing an action or expression that implicated rejoicing and praising? Or could Lehi comprehend some telepathic praise going on that could only be represented to mortals as an attitude of singing and praising?

In the opened heavens, or perhaps out of, Lehi sees One whose brightness is above the sun during its brightest hour. He also saw twelve others following Him whose brightness were above that of the stars.

It’s interesting that, according to Paul’s symbolic representation of the three kingdoms—sun, moon, and starts for the respective kingdoms of celestial, terrestrial, and telestial—the One, presumably Christ, has already the glory of, or beyond, the celestial kingdom while the twelve who follow Him have a glory of, or beyond, the telestial. Perhaps this was the glory of the twelve while in their premortal state. Or I could be digging too deep on this one.

The first apostle, Peter, I suppose, gives a book to Lehi and tells him to read it. Books often seem to be used to represent information or law in the scriptures. Ezekiel was given a book that told of lamentations and mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9-10). Revelation has many references to a book. One is sealed with seven seals. When Lehi reads the book given to him by the first apostle of Christ, “he [is] filled with the Spirit of the Lord. He also reads of God’s judgements toward Israel and His condemnation toward their abominations. Lehi reads that the Babylonians will slay many and take captive others into Babylon. This concurs with the actual history we have.

Apparently, Lehi reads more from this book because he also “did exclaim many things unto the Lord; such as: Great and marvelous are thy works… because thou art merciful, thou wilt not suffer those who come unto thee that they shall perish!” (1 Nephi 1:14)

Lehi’s soul rejoiced and “his whole heart was filled.” It’s crazy that he was feeling excitement and joy and gratitude despite the calamities and condemnations he read of his people. I mean, he started out praying on behalf of his people and didn’t really hear comforting news regarding them.
It seems that Lehi’s revelatory experiences weren’t limited to this occasion. As Nephi says, “he hath written many things which he saw in visions and in dreams”.
Lehi goes forth among his people and prophesies but is mocked. The people are angry and begin to want to kill him.

Nephi is constrained by the Spirit to kill Laban. This is an interesting story. Sometimes God gives commandments to His servants that make them question everything. For Abraham, it was sacrificing Isaac. For Nephi, killing Laban. In this day and age, it’s hard to understand that commandment. Of course, the times for Abraham and of Nephi were much different than current times. But still, Nephi must have really worked over this.

Something I hadn’t thought of before is what Laman, Lemuel, and Sam thought after Nephi had told them what he had done. He already had a strained relationship with the former two. Did this cause incredulity in them toward Nephi? Did they really trust him or think highly of him? It must have made them question him a bit knowing that he had actually killed a man, something none of them had likely done.
Zoram also would have had to hear the story and digest it in his own way. He likely knew of Laban’s wickedness and perhaps under their Jewish law Nephi was justified.
Zoram also, likely being older than Lehi’s sons, could have already had a wife and family. I hope not, but it is possible. I think if that were the case he would have wanted to go back and get them.

It’s interesting that throughout Abraham’s generations, God has stayed with His chosen people and repeatedly reached out to them through prophets. They have been the chosen generation and have been loved by God. They have often been wicked and rejected and killed the prophets. God didn’t give this kind of long-suffering reach-outs to other people, that I know of. The heathen nations continued in their ways often and did not have a covenant from God as the seed of Abraham did. Of course, God is no respecter of persons, but He did covenant with the ancient fathers which led Him to continue this kind of favor and long-suffering towards the seed of Abraham. Yet, it was this very seed which would kill the Savior. How is it? The lineage from which Christ came, the seed of David. His own people killed Him and rejected Him. How could this be?
There is also a poetic and symbolic statement in this verse:
It behooveth the great Creator that he suffereth himself to become subject unto man in the flesh, and die for all men, that all men might become subject unto him.

I know there’s another scripture that says something like this but I can’t find it. It says that Christ is lifted up upon the cross and judged by man that He may lift up man to be judged by Him. But the converse judgement from wicked to righteous is the beauty in the symbolism. The greatest suffers himself to condescend and put Himself in the hands of the wicked for an unrighteous judgement that He may cause the wicked to ascend to a righteous and merciful judgement by the righteous. It’s unthinkable that a God would do this for fallen man. But He already has.
...I found the scripture I was thinking of:

And my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and after that I had been lifted up upon the cross, that I might draw all men unto me, that as I have been lifted up by men even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil—And for this cause have I been lifted up; therefore, according to the power of the Father I will draw all men unto me, that they may be judged according to their works. - 3 Nephi 27:14-15

So, because of transgression—the transgression of Adam—man became fallen and was cut off from the presence of the Lord, which necessitated a power of resurrection in accordance with God’s merciful plan.

It’s interesting that Jacob says “For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection…” Was death the mercy or the power of resurrection? Did death pass upon all men to fulfill God’s merciful plan or was that the need for a power of resurrection?

Why must our spirits become subject to the devil if we rise no more? Perhaps it is the devil’s domain in that world of fallen spirits. For God couldn’t reign there, could he? It reminds me of the scripture in D&C 88:36-39:

All kingdoms have a law given; And there are many kingdoms; for there is no space in the which there is no kingdom; and there is no kingdom in which there is no space, either a greater or a lesser kingdom. And unto every kingdom is given a law; and unto every law there are certain bounds also and conditions. All beings who abide not in those conditions are not justified.

A kingdom is a place with a law detailing the bounds and conditions that must be kept within such space. Or else, beings who do not abide by the law are not justified. What does it mean to not be justified? Is this when justice is broken? Perhaps this is why God said justice must be served and had to judge Adam and Eve as He did? Perhaps He has declared His law within this space and we and He must abide by it. I trust that such a law would be in favor of superlative progress, joy, peace, and well being.

Connecting these thoughts, the devil, being the maker of the law of his dominion, and the fallen spirits being cast out of God’s dominion, fall under the law of the devil, which allegedly is a miserable kingdom (2 Nephi 9:9). But the kingdoms of glory must be in the kingdom of God, right? At least the celestial would surely be there.
10, Jacob’s terminology of death and hell

Jacob calls the separation of the body and spirit death. He calls the separation of the spirit from God hell, or, respectively, the death of the body and the death of the spirit. He lumps these together and calls it an “awful monster”, which he later names the devil (2 Nephi 9:19), but also later refers to these three things—death, hell, and the devil—separately and distinct (2 Nephi 9:26).

I thought the use of the word “monster” was interesting. Other uses of this word are when the Lamanites of King Lamoni’s kingdom speculate that Ammon is a monster sent by the Nephites to torment them (Alma 19:26). This usage implies a demonic tone to the word. The other use in The Book of Mormon is in the Jaradite record when it describes how no monster of the sea or whale could harm them in their vessels (Ether 6:10).
11-12, Kinds of death

Jacob teaches about the temporal death, which death is the grave, and the spiritual death, which death is hell. The power of the resurrection will restore both of these estrangements or separations. How is chaos reversed? This truly is a power beyond all comprehension of man.
13, Why does Jacob only talk about the resurrection of the righteous?
For on the other hand, the paradise of God must deliver up the spirits of the righteous, and the grave deliver up the body of the righteous;

Jacob mentions only the resurrection of the souls from paradise—which is a good reference to spirit paradise. He also only mentions that the grave will deliver up the bodies of the righteous, perhaps because he had already confined his group to the righteous of paradise. Did Jacob think that only the righteous would be saved and resurrected? I don’t think so. Earlier in this sermon Jacob said, “For as death hath passed upon all men… there must needs be a power of resurrection…” (2 Nephi 9:6). Further, he says “[Christ] suffereth himself to become subject unto man in the flesh, and die for all men, that all men might become subject unto him.” (2 Nephi 9:5). This names “all men” as the recipients of the atonement. So I guess Jacob is just talking about the first resurrection because that’s probably the one he knows more about. This is much like Abinadi only discussing the first resurrection in his sermon on the atonement (Mosiah 15:22).
14, the robe of righteousness
This would be a good study sometime, what is the robe of righteousness that Jacob and Nephi refer to. Is it the priesthood or some protection offered by Christ?
16, the righteous and the filthy

Am I righteous or filthy? How can we really know that we are righteous? Sometimes when I sin and break God’s commandments or do things I wish I didn’t do, I feel more like the filthy than the righteous. I suppose that’s where the atonement comes in.
Abinadi said that the seed of Christ, or the righteous, includes:

All the holy prophets who have prophesied concerning the coming of the Lord… all those who have hearkened unto their words and believed that the Lord would redeem his people, and have looked forward to that day for a remission of their sins, …these are his seed …that [have] not fallen into transgression  (Mosiah 15:11-13).
Oh, and if you read on, verse 18 of 2 Nephi 9 has Jacob’s description of the righteous:

...the righteous, the saints of the Holy One of Israel, they who have believed in the Holy One of Israel, they who have endured the crosses of the world, and despised the shame of it, they shall inherit the kingdom of God
At least I know I believe in the Holy One of Israel. What are the crosses of the world to me? Have I despised the shame of it? I don’t know exactly what that part means.

1 And it came to pass that as the disciples of Jesus were journeying and were preaching the things which they had both heard and seen, and were baptizing in the name of Jesus, it came to pass that the disciples were gathered together and were united in mighty prayer and fasting.

2 And Jesus again showed himself unto them, for they were praying unto the Father in his name; and Jesus came and stood in the midst of them, and said unto them: What will ye that I shall give unto you?
3 And they said unto him: Lord, we will that thou wouldst tell us the name whereby we shall call this church; for there are disputations among the people concerning this matter.
4 And the Lord said unto them: Verily, verily, I say unto you, why is it that the people should murmur and dispute because of this thing?
5 Have they not read the scriptures, which say ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is my name? For by this name shall ye be called at the last day;
6 And whoso taketh upon him my name, and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved at the last day.
7 Therefore, whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name; therefore ye shall call the church in my name; and ye shall call upon the Father in my name that he will bless the church for my sake.

8 And how be it my church save it be called in my name? For if a church be called in Moses’ name then it be Moses’ church; or if it be called in the name of a man then it be the church of a man; but if it be called in my name then it is my church, if it so be that they are built upon my gospel.

9 Verily I say unto you, that ye are built upon my gospel; therefore ye shall call whatsoever things ye do call, in my name; therefore if ye call upon the Father, for the church, if it be in my name the Father will hear you;
10 And if it so be that the church is built upon my gospel then will the Father show forth his own works in it.

11 But if it be not built upon my gospel, and is built upon the works of men, or upon the works of the devil, verily I say unto you they have joy in their works for a season, and by and by the end cometh, and they are hewn down and cast into the fire, from whence there is no return.
12 For their works do follow them, for it is because of their works that they are hewn down; therefore remember the things that I have told you.
13 Behold I have given unto you my gospel, and this is the gospel which I have given unto you—that I came into the world to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me.

14 And my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and after that I had been lifted up upon the cross, that I might draw all men unto me, that as I have been lifted up by men even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil—
15 And for this cause have I been lifted up; therefore, according to the power of the Father I will draw all men unto me, that they may be judged according to their works.

16 And it shall come to pass, that whoso repenteth and is baptized in my name shall be filled; and if he endureth to the end, behold, him will I hold guiltless before my Father at that day when I shall stand to judge the world.
17 And he that endureth not unto the end, the same is he that is also hewn down and cast into the fire, from whence they can no more return, because of the justice of the Father.
18 And this is the word which he hath given unto the children of men. And for this cause he fulfilleth the words which he hath given, and he lieth not, but fulfilleth all his words.

19 And no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom; therefore nothing entereth into his rest save it be those who have washed their garments in my blood, because of their faith, and the repentance of all their sins, and their faithfulness unto the end.

20 Now this is the commandment: Repent, all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name, that ye may be sanctified by the reception of the Holy Ghost, that ye may stand spotless before me at the last day.

21 Verily, verily, I say unto you, this is my gospel; and ye know the things that ye must do in my church; for the works which ye have seen me do that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do even that shall ye do;
22 Therefore, if ye do these things blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day.
23 Write the things which ye have seen and heard, save it be those which are forbidden.
24 Write the works of this people, which shall be, even as hath been written, of that which hath been.
25 For behold, out of the books which have been written, and which shall be written, shall this people be judged, for by them shall their works be known unto men.
26 And behold, all things are written by the Father; therefore out of the books which shall be written shall the world be judged.

27 And know ye that ye shall be judges of this people, according to the judgment which I shall give unto you, which shall be just. Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
28 And now I go unto the Father. And verily I say unto you, whatsoever things ye shall ask the Father in my name shall be given unto you.
29 Therefore, ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you; for he that asketh, receiveth; and unto him that knocketh, it shall be opened.

30 And now, behold, my joy is great, even unto fulness, because of you, and also this generation; yea, and even the Father rejoiceth, and also all the holy angels, because of you and this generation; for none of them are lost.
31 Behold, I would that ye should understand; for I mean them who are now alive of this generation; and none of them are lost; and in them I have fulness of joy.

32 But behold, it sorroweth me because of the fourth generation from this generation, for they are led away captive by him even as was the son of perdition; for they will sell me for silver and for gold, and for that which moth doth corrupt and which thieves can break through and steal. And in that day will I visit them, even in turning their works upon their own heads.

33 And it came to pass that when Jesus had ended these sayings he said unto his disciples: Enter ye in at the strait gate; for strait is the gate, and narrow is the way that leads to life, and few there be that find it; but wide is the gate, and broad the way which leads to death, and many there be that travel therein, until the night cometh, wherein no man can work.

title: Did Christ Suffer for All or Just the Righteous?

body.text: Mosiah 15:10-12

And now I say unto you, who shall declare his generation? Behold, I say unto you, that when his soul has been made an offering for sin he shall see his seed. And now what say ye? And who shall be his seed? Behold I say unto you, that whosoever has heard the words of the prophets, yea, all the holy prophets who have prophesied concerning the coming of the Lord—I say unto you, that all those who have hearkened unto their words, and believed that the Lord would redeem his people, and have looked forward to that day for a remission of their sins, I say unto you, that these are his seed, or they are the heirs of the kingdom of God. For these are they whose sins he has borne; these are they for whom he has died, to redeem them from their transgressions. And now, are they not his seed?

This says that Christ suffered for His seed. Who is His seed? The people who heard the holy prophets and hearkened unto their words and believed in the Lord’s redemption and looked forward to that day for remission of sins, etc. Well that is understandable but then what about the rest? What about the people who didn’t hearken unto the prophets or even hear them in the first place? Are they the seed of Christ? Did He bear their sins too? Naturally, one would probably say that He did bear the sins of everyone, but then why does Abinadi not say that here?

Abinadi goes on to say that there will be a first resurrection including the resurrection of all those who have lived and died up until Christ’s resurrection who have “kept the commandments of God” (Mosiah 15:22), have died in ignorance—”not having salvation declared unto them” (Mosiah 15:24), or were little children at the time they died (Mosiah 15:25). The rest are apparently not resurrected at this time but are left as disembodied spirits.

It seems that Abinadi was only discussing the part of the atonement that applies to the righteous, which is the bearing of their sins. But even this may not be true, did Christ only bear the sins of the righteous? Or is it that only the righteous will be benefited from His bearing of their sins?

I tried to research this topic but I can’t find anything. I saw that the Calvinists believe in Limited Atonement, a thought where Christ’s atonement, though capable of paying for the sins of the whole world, only pays for the elect and leads them surely to salvation. What an odd doctrine.
Anyway, I guess Abinadi’s words could apply some form of limited atonement by interpretation.
This scripture piqued my interest:
Mosiah 15:26

But behold, and fear, and tremble before God, for ye ought to tremble; for the Lord redeemeth none such that rebel against him and die in their sins; yea, even all those that have perished in their sins ever since the world began, that have wilfully rebelled against God, that have known the commandments of God, and would not keep them; these are they that have no part in the first resurrection. Therefore ought ye not to tremble? For salvation cometh to none such; for the Lord hath redeemed none such; yea, neither can the Lord redeem such; for he cannot deny himself; for he cannot deny justice when it has its claim.

What does this mean? Why does Abinadi have to be so interestingly contradictory at first? The same thing happened in my study of the first few verses of this chapter. I’ll have to continue this because I am still not satisfied. I wish I had a good resource or something that could make sense of this. So far, I think that Abinadi is largely focusing on the first resurrection which could help explain why his focus group which he talks about receiving salvation, etc., is only the righteous.

Alright, so Abinadi is teaching that redemption comes only to the righteous and part of redemption, or an indicator of it, is being part of the first resurrection. It would be important here to know what redemption means, especially what it meant to Abinadi. Perhaps he considered it to me freedom from the bondage of death, or death and hell, or just hell—in terms of Jacob (2 Nephi 9). One thing’s certain, Abinadi loved Isaiah. If Isaiah has anything on redemption I’ll want to look at that. Here are some relevant scriptures and my thoughts on them:
Redeem, Redeemed, Redemption, from the Bible Dictionary

To deliver, to purchase, or to ransom, such as to free a person from bondage by payment. Redemption refers to the Atonement of Jesus Christ and to deliverance from sin. Jesus’ Atonement redeems all mankind from physical death. Through His Atonement, those who have faith in Him and who repent are also redeemed from spiritual death.
This says redemption is the atonement of Christ delivering people from sin. But only the righteous are delivered from sin, right?

And surely every man must repent or suffer, for I, God, am endless. ...Therefore I command you to repent—repent, lest I smite you by the rod of my mouth, and by my wrath, and by my anger, and your sufferings be sore—how sore you know not, how exquisite you know not, yea, how hard to bear you know not. For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent; But if they would not repent they must suffer even as I; Which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit—and would that I might not drink the bitter cup, and shrink—Nevertheless, glory be to the Father, and I partook and finished my preparations unto the children of men. Wherefore, I command you again to repent, lest I humble you with my almighty power; and that you confess your sins, lest you suffer these punishments of which I have spoken, of which in the smallest, yea, even in the least degree you have tasted at the time I withdrew my Spirit.

This implies that if you don’t repent, you will have to suffer for your sins yourself. But not to the fullest extent, right? We will all still be resurrected. Perhaps our sins aren’t the cause of that part, though. I think Adam’s transgression caused us to be cursed with death, and our sins cause us the curse of hell. Is that right?
Genesis 3:15-16

I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.

What curse(s) does Eve bring to the human family? The pains of childbirth for womankind. In sorrow she’ll bring forth children. I don’t know what this means. Men will have dominion over women. Perhaps this means that women will be more feeble than men and will be physically subject to them because of this physical feebleness.
Genesis 3:17-19

And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

Adam is cursed with the cursed earth, which requires much work in order to bring forth fruit for meat. He also is cursed to return to the dust of the earth. This could be interpreted to mean that Adam is the one cursed with subjection to the powers of physical death.
I don’t know exactly what caused, or when, hell came into the picture. This might necessitate its own study topic. Continuing on with scriptures on redemption, to figure out what it means:
Isaiah 44:22
I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee.
So redemption might mean having transgressions and sins blotted out. So this isn’t talking about redemption from death, just from hell?
Hosea 13:14
I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction: repentance shall be hid from mine eyes.

Nevermind, redemption can refer to that of the grave or death. I can’t tell the context of this scripture, though. I’m not sure what the true meaning is or whether its usage of “redemption” can be taken as the common meaning.
Nephi says, “The Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell” (2 Nephi 1:15). This is redemption from hell and not death.
Mormon, in discussing infant baptism, talks about redemption as a means obtained through repentance.
Moroni 8:22

For behold that all little children are alive in Christ, and also all they that are without the law. For the power of redemption cometh on all them that have no law; wherefore, he that is not condemned, or he that is under no condemnation, cannot repent; and unto such baptism availeth nothing.
D&C 45:54 mentions that the heath nations and they which knew no law “shall have part in the first resurrection.”
Though I haven’t found clarity solely via scripture, I am concluding that redemption usually refers to such from hell and not death. Redemption from death is granted to all.
Wait a minute, here’s the scripture I’ve been looking for without knowing it!

And he shall come into the world to redeem his people; and he shall take upon him the transgressions of those who believe on his name; and these are they that shall have eternal life, and salvation cometh to none else. Therefore the wicked remain as though there had been no redemption made, except it be the loosing of the bands of death; for behold, the day cometh that all shall rise from the dead and stand before God, and be judged according to their works. Now, there is a death which is called a temporal death; and the death of Christ shall loose the bands of this temporal death, that all shall be raised from this temporal death. The spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form; both limb and joint shall be restored to its proper frame, even as we now are at this time; and we shall be brought to stand before God, knowing even as we know now, and have a bright recollection of all our guilt. Now, this restoration shall come to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, both the wicked and the righteous; and even there shall not so much as a hair of their heads be lost; but every thing shall be restored to its perfect frame, as it is now, or in the body, and shall be brought and be arraigned before the bar of Christ the Son, and God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, which is one Eternal God, to be judged according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil. Now, behold, I have spoken unto you concerning the death of the mortal body, and also concerning the resurrection of the mortal body. I say unto you that this mortal body is raised to an immortal body, that is from death, even from the first death unto life, that they can die no more; their spirits uniting with their bodies, never to be divided; thus the whole becoming spiritual and immortal, that they can no more see corruption.

But this scripture states that Christ took upon himself the transgressions of “those who believe on his name”. It doesn’t say that he took upon himself the transgressions of the unrepentant, and that’s my question. I can’t say that just because Amulek didn’t explicitly say that Christ didn’t take upon himself the sins of the unrepentant that such is the case. He only said the Christ atoned for the sins of the repentant. But what about the sins of the unrepentant? Did Christ not take these upon himself? For some reason I feel I was taught that he took upon himself every single person’s sins. Did he?
The Atonement Makes Repentance Possible; What We Believe; Ensign February 2011

He sent His Only Begotten Son, Jesus Christ, to suffer for our sins. That is, Jesus paid the penalty required by the law of justice for our breaking of God’s commandments. Because the Savior suffered for our sins, we will not have to suffer the full punishment for them if we repent (see). His Atonement “satisfied the demands of justice” (), allowing Heavenly Father to mercifully forgive us and withhold punishment.
The cross-reference of D&C 19:16 says that we won’t have to suffer if we repent. So I guess Christ really did only take upon him the sins of repentant?
Because of Jesus Christ, We Can Live with God, Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf; April 2018 General Conference

...we have all sinned. Our sins would forever keep us from living with God, because “no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom.” As a result, every man, woman, and child was shut out of His presence—that is, until Jesus Christ, the Lamb without spot, offered His life as a ransom for our sins. Because Jesus owed no debt to justice, He could pay our debt and meet the demands of justice for every soul. And that includes you and me. Jesus Christ paid the price for our sins. All of them.

Elder Uchtdorf said that Christ paid for all of our sins, but I guess that he actually only paid for sins we have repented of, or the sins of the repentant, at least? I guess you could also say that he paid for the sins we have repented, or will repent, of.
Here we go, there are teachings that explicitly state Christ paid for everyone’s sins and, implicitly, even the sins of the sinners:
The Atonement of the Savior, Marion G. Romney; The Improvement Era December 1953

The Savior … paid the debt for my personal sins. He paid the debt for your personal sins and for the personal sins of every living soul that ever dwelt upon the earth or that ever will dwell in mortality upon the earth.
I know this isn’t cannon, but it does seem to contradict the idea I’m getting from the scriptures.
Well, I found something that is cannon, I think…
The Living Christ: The Testimony of the Apostles, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

He instituted the sacrament as a reminder of His great atoning sacrifice. He was arrested and condemned on spurious charges, convicted to satisfy a mob, and sentenced to die on Calvary’s cross. He gave His life to atone for the sins of all mankind. His was a great vicarious gift in behalf of all who would ever live upon the earth.

I don’t know what to think now… I guess go back to the scriptures and make sure that there even is a problem or contradiction. Maybe the scriptures could harmonize with this statement? Or maybe this statement doesn’t have to imply that Christ atoned for the sins of the unrepentant… I don’t know about that latter idea. It says “the sins of all mankind.” That would include the unrepentant, I think.

Back to Amulek’s teachings, he said that “the wicked remain as though there had been no redemption made, except it be the loosing of the bands of death” (Alma 11:41). And D&C 19 says “every man must repent or suffer, for I, God, am endless” (verse 4).

For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent; But if they would not repent they must suffer even as I; Which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit—and would that I might not drink the bitter cup, and shrink—Nevertheless, glory be to the Father, and I partook and finished my preparations unto the children of men.

So Christ suffered for all so they don’t have to suffer if they repent. But if they don’t repent, they must suffer. So does Christ still pay for the sins of those people who don’t repent?—else, why do they have to suffer if the price had already been paid? The original price is paid by Christ for all men, and then some still have to suffer if they don’t repent? Is that suffering part of the original price or a new price enforced by God?—does God invent a new and similar price to be paid to punish those who don’t repent, even though their price was already paid by Christ? Or did Christ never even suffer for those sins of which there was no repentance? I still don’t have clarity on this.
2 Nephi 1:10

But behold, when the time cometh that they shall dwindle in unbelief, after they have received so great blessings from the hand of the Lord—having a knowledge of the creation of the earth, and all men, knowing the great and marvelous works of the Lord from the creation of the world; having power given them to do all things by faith; having all the commandments from the beginning, and having been brought by his infinite goodness into this precious land of promise—behold, I say, if the day shall come that they will reject the Holy One of Israel, the true Messiah, their Redeemer and their God, behold, the judgments of him that is just shall rest upon them.
This usage seems to imply the never-ending or abundant definition of the word.
2 Nephi 9:7

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.

This use says that if the atonement were not infinite, basically, the resurrection or plan wouldn’t work; corruption couldn’t be overcome nor could the first judgements upon man be reconciled. Perhaps it was these judgements, which the scriptures say “must needs have remained to an endless duration”, needed an endless atonement. So then, perhaps “endless” is the meaning of “infinite” here.
2 Nephi 25:16

And after they have been scattered, and the Lord God hath scourged them by other nations for the space of many generations, yea, even down from generation to generation until they shall be persuaded to believe in Christ, the Son of God, and the atonement, which is infinite for all mankind—and when that day shall come that they shall believe in Christ, and worship the Father in his name, with pure hearts and clean hands, and look not forward any more for another Messiah, then, at that time, the day will come that it must needs be expedient that they should believe these things.

“Infinite” here is thrown in with reference to Jacob’s sermon, it seems. Or perhaps a teaching that was common among Nephi and him. He says that the atonement is infinite for all mankind. So, this means that the atonement applies to each human individually for endless duration. I suppose that because each of us owed justice, or the judgement of God, being endlessly cut off from His presence, only an endless atonement could remedy that for us. By definition, I don’t know how an endless payment could ever be completed. Perhaps with the gods things are different and being infinite beings who comprehend Eternity, they can use a currency of endless duration. Perhaps all that they are and do is eternal and without time.
Mosiah 5:3
And we, ourselves, also, through the infinite goodness of God, and the manifestations of his Spirit, have great views of that which is to come; and were it expedient, we could prophesy of all things.

This reference is like the first one, mentioned by Nephi, which describes God’s goodness as infinite. There is no limit or bounds to the goodness of God. That’s reassuring to know. This is an important attribute of God. There is no good thing that can be done that God does not do.
Mosiah 28:4

And thus did the Spirit of the Lord work upon them, for they were the very vilest of sinners. And the Lord saw fit in his infinite mercy to spare them; nevertheless they suffered much anguish of soul because of their iniquities, suffering much and fearing that they should be cast off forever.

The sons of Mosiah were spared by God owing to his infinite mercy. This means that there is no case where God withholds mercy, perhaps. God is ever-merciful. I find it useful and interesting how Oxford Languages defines mercy: “compassion or forgiveness shown toward someone whom it is within one's power to punish or harm.” God has power to punish or harm in the highest degree, right? Yet, He shows the greatest compassion and forgiveness unto anyone who simply comes to Him or is open to help and love. God’s mercy is available to me. This is an important attribute of God that I must remember.
Alma 34:10, 12, 14 (10-14 shown below)

For it is expedient that there should be a great and last sacrifice; yea, not a sacrifice of man, neither of beast, neither of any manner of fowl; for it shall not be a human sacrifice; but it must be an infinite and eternal sacrifice.

Now there is not any man that can sacrifice his own blood which will atone for the sins of another. Now, if a man murdereth, behold will our law, which is just, take the life of his brother? I say unto you, Nay.
But the law requireth the life of him who hath murdered; therefore there can be nothing which is short of an infinite atonement which will suffice for the sins of the world.
