A note here is that Isaiah has a lot of references to “mighty men.” Maybe that’s where Nephi and Mormon drew their descriptions. Also, the Old Testament has at least 24 references similar to these which I searched which say “mighty men of valour” (men/man). Most references to “mighty” in the Old Testament are used in a context of war or physical strength.
Moroni 7:3

Wherefore, I would speak unto you that are of the church, that are the peaceable followers of Christ, and that have obtained a sufficient hope by which ye can enter into the rest of the Lord, from this time henceforth until ye shall rest with him in heaven.
Is the rest of the Lord knowing Him and having election made sure? What does it mean? Maybe this is the same hope talked about in Ether 12:4
Moroni 7:39

But behold, my beloved brethren, I judge better things of you, for I judge that ye have faith in Christ because of your meekness; for if ye have not faith in him then ye are not fit to be numbered among the people of his church.
Wow
Moroni 7:40
And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?

Mormon says, “How can you achieve faith unless you shall have hope?” This is a bit ambiguous at first because it seems like it’s saying that unless you already have hope you can’t achieve faith. But on a closer examination I see that the word “shall” is really important because it expresses future tense, as in “You will have hope”. So now the passage instead seems to suggest some incredulity about one who desires and works toward faith but will not at some future point also attain hope.
Moroni 7:41

And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.
We attain a hope through faith in Christ, which, through the power of the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, we can gain a hope of being raised unto life eternal.
Moroni 7:42-44
Wherefore, if a man have faith he must needs have hope; for without faith there cannot be any hope.
And again, behold I say unto you that he cannot have faith and hope, save he shall be meek, and lowly of heart.

If so, his faith and hope is vain, for none is acceptable before God, save the meek and lowly in heart; and if a man be meek and lowly in heart, and confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ, he must needs have charity; for if he have not charity he is nothing; wherefore he must needs have charity.

Even though that first statement can sound like you have to have hope before you have faith—”if a man have faith he must needs have hope”—I believe Mormon is actually saying that if you have faith you really will get a hope through that faith. He’s not saying that hope is the prerequisite. Also, he adds that you can’t have faith and hope unless you are meek and lowly of heart. I don’t know if Mormon is saying that meekness and lowliness of heart come from faith and hope or they are prerequisites. From the way he’s been talking, I would assume that he’s saying they come from faith and hope.
He also says that if you have faith and hope, you not only have meekness and lowliness of heart, but also charity. Maybe they even go in that order when developed.
Side study: When are terms like meekness and lowliness of heart used?
Matthew 11:29
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
This is one of the only verses I could find that says “meek” and “lowly in heart”.
Ephesians 4:2
With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love;
Alma 32:8
I behold that ye are lowly in heart; and if so, blessed are ye.

Preach unto them repentance, and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ; teach them to humble themselves and to be meek and lowly in heart; teach them to withstand every temptation of the devil, with their faith on the Lord Jesus Christ.
Teach them to never be weary of good works, but to be meek and lowly in heart; for such shall find rest to their souls.
Hope in Christ, by President Ballard
Our spiritual identity is enhanced as we understand our many mortal identities, including ethnic, cultural, or national heritage.
This sense of spiritual and cultural identity, love, and belonging can inspire hope and love for Jesus Christ.

I speak of hope in Christ not as wishful thinking. Instead, I speak of hope as an expectation that will be realized. Such hope is essential to overcoming adversity, fostering spiritual resilience and strength, and coming to know that we are loved by our Eternal Father and that we are His children, who belong to His family.
When we have hope in Christ, we come to know that as we need to make and keep sacred covenants, our fondest desires and dreams can be fulfilled through Him.
This is pretty good, although the hope he’s talking about is different I think.
Lexicon & Concordance on Faith
Old Testament
Only two references found in Old Testament. Both come from this word:
† אֵמֻן noun [masculine] trusting, faithfulness (on formation compare Ges§ 84a R. 12).
1. בָּנִים לֹא אֵמֻן בָּם children in whom there is no trusting (poetry)

2. אֱמוּנִים plural abstract faithfulness; צִיר א׳ messenger of faithfulness, trusty messenger; עֵד א׳ faithful witness; compare אִישׁ א׳; שֹׁמֵר א׳ keeping faithfulness, perhaps also נצד א׳ see I. [אָמַן].
This really just tells us that it refers to faith, trust, integrity? Not very helpful.
New Testament
A lot of NT references go to the Greek word (Strong’s G4102) πίστις (pistis). Helpful insight telling how this word is translated elsewhere:
The KJV translates Strong's G4102 in the following manner: (239x), (1x), (1x), (1x), (1x), (1x).
The following scripture has it translated as assurance:

- Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance  unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead.
This suggests God gives faith/assurance, or perhaps a cause for believing, in Christ’s resurrection from the dead.
This scripture translates it as the act of believing (in Jesus):
- To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth  in  Jesus.
One other reference translates it as fidelity, which suggests faithfulness, staying true an loyal.
- Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity;  that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
Here’s an outline of that Greek word from the Blue Letter Bible:

1.conviction of the truth of anything, belief; in the NT of a conviction or belief respecting man's relationship to God and divine things, generally with the included idea of trust and holy fervour born of faith and joined with it
1.relating to God
1.the conviction that God exists and is the creator and ruler of all things, the provider and bestower of eternal salvation through Christ
2.relating to Christ
1.a strong and welcome conviction or belief that Jesus is the Messiah, through whom we obtain eternal salvation in the kingdom of God
3.the religious beliefs of Christians
4.belief with the predominate idea of trust (or confidence) whether in God or in Christ, springing from faith in the same
2.fidelity, faithfulness
1.the character of one who can be relied on

This seems like the Greek word that often translates to “faith” is a belief. So is that the best word to represent its meaning? It’s being loyal and believing and staying true? Well if that is the case then such a conviction must be inspired by something, right? You don’t just become loyal and faithful without cause for intense trust.
Hebrews 11:1 suggests that faith is the confidence in things hoped for. But what supports that confidence? I guess we just infer that it is the assurance of the Spirit.
So how do you get faith?
Faith
13 To some it is given by the Holy Ghost to know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and that he was crucified for the sins of the world.
14 To others it is given to believe on their words, that they also might have eternal life if they continue faithful.

Well, one way, probably not the only way, is to believe on the testimonies of some who actually know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Are we a bit too liberal with our usage of the word “know” in relation to these verses? Because many people get up and say they know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. But often, they probably don’t actually know, they just believe. Belief is still good. It’s not a bad thing to get up in a testimony meeting and say that you believe Christ is the Son of God. In fact, this is really what Jesus Christ commanded us to do, believe and be saved, not know and be saved.
1 John 3:23
And this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ…
So why do people say they know this instead? Perhaps they’re just doing what they’ve heard many do. But speaking of knowledge, let’s read some of the Apostles testimonies and hear what they say.
God Among Us, by Elder Uchtdorf
I bear witness that our Heavenly Father lives, that Jesus Christ leads His Church, that President Russell M. Nelson is His prophet.

I extend to you my love and blessing at this joyful Easter season. Open your hearts to our Savior and Redeemer, no matter your circumstances, trials, sufferings, or mistakes; you can know that He lives, that He loves you, and that because of Him, you will never be alone. God is among us. Of this I testify and bear witness in the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.
Uh… well I guess it is pretty clear there that we “can know that He lives.” I certainly didn’t suggest that we couldn’t, just that perhaps we often don’t even though we say it in our testimonies.
Def: Know
be absolutely certain or sure about something.
This is a serious word to be using. It does NOT mean believe. They are different words.

Maybe when we sing songs like “I Know that My Redeemer Lives” we catch on to this terminology. Where does that song come from? According to , it’s been around for over 200 years and was written by a minister of the Baptist church. The lyrics were inspired by
- For I know  that my redeemer  liveth,  and that he shall stand  at the latter  day upon the earth:
Here’s the
יָדַע yâdaʻ, yaw-dah' Strong’s Definition

יָדַע yâdaʻ, yaw-dah'; a primitive root; to know (properly, to ascertain by seeing); used in a great variety of senses, figuratively, literally, euphemistically and inferentially (including observation, care, recognition; and causatively, instruction, designation, punishment, etc.):—acknowledge, acquaintance(-ted with), advise, answer, appoint, assuredly, be aware, (un-) awares, can(-not), certainly, comprehend, consider, × could they, cunning, declare, be diligent, (can, cause to) discern, discover, endued with, familiar friend, famous, feel, can have, be (ig-) norant, instruct, kinsfolk, kinsman, (cause to let, make) know, (come to give, have, take) knowledge, have (knowledge), (be, make, make to be, make self) known, be learned, lie by man, mark, perceive, privy to, × prognosticator, regard, have respect, skilful, shew, can (man of) skill, be sure, of a surety, teach, (can) tell, understand, have (understanding), × will be, wist, wit, wot.
There certainly are some who know that Jesus is the Christ, as per the gift described above, but others will only believe, at least for a time.
More testimonies:
One by One, by Elder Rasband
I know that Jesus is the living Christ and that He knows each of us individually, or as the scriptures express it, “one by one.”
This sacred assurance is taught compassionately by the Savior Himself in His appearance to the people of Nephi. We read of this in 3 Nephi, chapter 11, verse 15:

“And it came to pass that the multitude went forth, and thrust their hands into his side, and did feel the prints of the nails in his hands and in his feet; and this they did do, going forth one by one until they had all gone forth” (; emphasis added).
To further illustrate the “one by one” nature of our Savior’s ministry, we read in 3 Nephi, chapter 17, verse 9:

“And it came to pass that when he had thus spoken, all the multitude, with one accord, did go forth with their sick and their afflicted, and their lame, and with their blind, and with their dumb, and with all them that were afflicted in any manner; and he did heal them every one as they were brought forth unto him” (; emphasis added).

Elder Rasband even goes to far in his description of his intimate knowledge as to reference the Nephites touching Christ’s hands and side and feet and to personally know Him. This is a person who literally knows that Christ is the Son of God.
The Witness, Elder Boyd K. Packer
Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon recorded the following after a sacred experience:
“And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!
“For we saw him” ().
Their words are my words.

I believe and I am sure that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that He lives. He is the Only Begotten of the Father, and “by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God” ().

I bear my witness that the Savior lives. I know the Lord. I am His witness. I know of His great sacrifice and eternal love for all of Heavenly Father’s children. I bear my special witness in all humility but with absolute certainty, in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

On the subject of sacred and intimate experiences with Jesus, Elder Boyd K. Packer referenced Joseph Smith’s and Sidney Rigdon’s experience personally seeing Jesus Christ. He says their words are his and implies that he has experienced something similar enough to them to testify with their words. He specifically says he is “sure that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that He lives”. Powerful testimony, but does it help us put into perspective what it really means to know that Jesus the Christ?

It’s one thing if we have a bunch of old but nice brethren as our Apostles, which is what the world probably thinks, but their testimonies put them in a place where they are either actual personal witnesses or they are liars. It’s like how the Book of Mormon and it’s claims, as well as the claims made that we are the restored and true Church of Jesus Christ puts our church in a place where we are either true or a lie. It’s right out of the middle ground just like the brethren. There’s no middle ground.
I know that My Redeemer Lives, by Elder Bruce R. McConkie

As members of the church and kingdom of God on earth, we enjoy the gifts of the Spirit—those wonders and glories and miracles that a gracious and benevolent God always has bestowed upon his faithful saints. The first of these gifts listed in our modern revelation on spiritual gifts is the gift of testimony, the gift of revelation, the gift of knowing of the truth and divinity of the work. This gift is elsewhere described as the testimony of Jesus, which is the spirit of prophecy. This is my gift. I know this work is true.

I have a perfect knowledge that Jesus Christ is the Son of the living God and that he was crucified for the sins of the world. I know that Joseph Smith is a prophet of God through whose instrumentality the fullness of the everlasting gospel has been restored again in our day. And I know that this Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is the kingdom of God on earth, and that as now constituted, with President Harold B. Lee at its head, it has the approval and approbation of the Lord, is in the line of its duty, and is preparing a people for the second coming of the Son of Man.

Elder McConkie refines the true meaning of knowing that our Redeemer lives by virtue of this talk while at the same time testifies of his perfect knowledge that Jesus Christ is the Son of the living God. He also talks about the spiritual gifts, especially the gift of knowledge and prophecy and claims these as his own, being given by God. He shares that this gift is a perfect knowledge and it is by this knowledge that he testifies.
These are only a few but you can watch all of the videos in the series called ‘Special Witnesses of Christ’ where each Apostle gives his special witness:

After Christ’s ascension into heaven, the remaining 11 apostles (Judas had killed himself) prayed and chose a new apostle to replace Judas. Peter here mentions that he will be a witness of Jesus’ resurrection.

“So now we must choose a replacement for Judas from among the men who were with us the entire time we were traveling with the Lord Jesus—from the time he was baptized by John until the day he was taken from us. Whoever is chosen will join us as a witness of Jesus’ resurrection.”

FAIR, a church apologetics organization not sponsored by the church has an article on whether apostles really have to literally see Christ and, as sometimes apologists do, they stayed pretty general and simple and were careful not to assert anything for certain. I too must say that I can’t speak for the church or proclaim any certain knowledge here, only that the scriptures and actual testimonies of numerous apostles throughout the latter day give a strong case that these men are literal witnesses of Christ, whether that witness was gained through physical sight or spiritual means, they have perfect knowledge.
Charity
Conference, Elder Dallin H. Oaks

“Charity, ‘the pure love of Christ’ (), is not an act but a condition or state of being. Charity is attained through a succession of acts that result in a conversion. Charity is something one becomes. Thus, as Moroni declared, ‘except men shall have charity they cannot inherit’ the place prepared for them in the mansions of the Father (; italics added)” (in Conference Report, Oct. 2000, 43; or).
Moroni 7:45

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.

Apparently there’s an article where some research shows that Paul’s Hymn to Charity, or 1 Corinthians 13, rather, is not Paul’s own words but dates back to a much earlier time. This could explain why Mormon and Paul share the same words though they presummedly would not have been in contact sharing notes and thoughts.

title: All Things Work Together for Those Who Love God

body.text: I want to start out by making some points:
●Bad things happen to good people and this is not always God’s will
○Those things often are turned into blessings to work toward an even better good through God
●Sometimes what we thought was a bad thing is actually a good thing
●The ideal and normal state for us isn’t happiness or bliss—that’s not the point of this life
○Think of the pioneers or the holy prophets or Jesus Christ
○Reference Jeffrey R. Holland’s talk of the prayer he recites “don’t let anything bad happen to me”
Zen story: The Farmer and the Horse

A farmer had a horse for work and transportation. The horse ran away. His neighbors told him, “such bad luck”. The farmer replied, “May be”. A few days later the horse came back and brought three wild horses back with it. All of the farmer’s neighbors congratulated him saying, “Wow, how fortunate!” The farmer said, “May be”. A few days later the farmer’s son was riding one of the wild horses and he was thrown off and broke his leg. The farmer’s neighbors offered their sympathy saying it was such bad luck. The farmer said, “May be”. The next day, the military officials came through the village to draft young men into the army. Because the farmer’s son had a broken leg they passed him by. The neighbors congratulated the farmer on how well things turned out and told him it was such a good thing. He said, “May be”.
Bad things happen
●WWII
●The Holocaust
●Terrorist attacks
●Earthquakes
●The great depression
●Losing jobs
From a Christian perspective, it makes sense when bad things happen to the wicked:
●Ezekiel 25:17 And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.

●Revelation 21:8 (English Standard Version) But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.
●Deuteronomy 32:43 (NLT) …he will avenge the blood of his children; he will take revenge against his enemies. He will repay those who hate him and cleanse his people’s land.
Scriptures seem to say that sometimes bad things happen because God is smiting the wicked:
●Ether 3:3 Behold, O Lord, thou hast smitten us because of our iniquity, and hast driven us forth, and for these many years we have been in the wilderness;

●Numbers 14:11-12 (NLT) And the Lord said to Moses, How long will these people treat me with contempt? Will they never believe me, even after all the miraculous signs I have done among them? I will disown them and destroy them with a plague. Then I will make you into a nation greater and mightier than they are!
But why do bad things happen to good people?
Every day good, honest people are diagnosed with cancer or terminal diseases. Others are murdered, robbed, injured in car accidents, or have their homes and possessions damaged by natural disasters.
What about the Apostles of Jesus which we assume to have been strict followers and witnesses of Christ?
Peter
Crucified
Andrew
Crucified
James
Killed
Philip
Crucified, stoned, or beheaded ?
Bartholomew
Flayed, crucified, or drowned ?
Matthew
Burned, stoned, or beheaded ?
James
Clubbed or crucified
Jude
Killed with an axe
Simon
Crucified or killed with a saw
Matthias
Stoned or beheaded
Paul
Beheaded
Also, Stephen was stoned (Acts 7).
In Alma 14 we read about women and children who were burned to death along with their scriptures because they were believers. Alma and Ammon had to watch as this happened.
Possible answers
●God is teaching you something
○Does this really hold up? Can you tell a father whose wife and baby die at birth that God’s just teaching him a lesson and he’ll appreciate it later?
●God is punishing you
○This certainly can’t answer every instance

title: A Good Thing From a Bad Thing

body.text: There are many examples and times when God turns something that seems really bad and awful into something better than if the bad thing hadn’t even happened. One example I just read where this happens is when Ammon and King Lamoni journey to the land Middoni to release Ammon’s brothers from prison.

While journeying, they run across King Lamoni’s father who is king over all the land. This king harshly accuses King Lamoni of foolishness for being with a Nephite. He commands King Lamoni to slay Ammon and then, after Ammon defends King Lamoni from the king and also defends himself, finds King Lamoni’s father in his submission offering up to half of his kingdom if Ammon will spare his life. This leads to Ammon asking only for his brethren to be cast out of prison in Middoni and for King Lamoni to retain his kingdom forever without governance from him. Eventually, this father of King Lamoni converts to the gospel all because of this initial episode. What seemed to be horrible at the time ended up being a great blessing.
Talk about that chiasma that I had thought was a mistake. Also mention the garb of secrecy.
Mistakes in The Book of Mormon
Wordy examples

And it came to pass that the angel spake unto me again, saying: Look! And I looked, and I beheld the heavens open again… And he spake unto me again, saying: Look! And I looked, and I beheld the Lamb of God going forth among the children of men… And it came to pass that the angel spake unto me again, saying: Look! And I looked and beheld the Lamb of God, that he was taken by the people; yea, the Son of the everlasting God was judged of the world; and I saw and bear record.
18 Therefore I did obey the voice of the Spirit, and took Laban by the hair of the head, and I smote off his head with his own sword.
19 And after I had smitten off his head with his own sword, I took the garments of Laban and put them upon mine own body; yea, even every whit; and I did gird on his armor about my loins.

20 And after I had done this, I went forth unto the treasury of Laban. And as I went forth towards the treasury of Laban, behold, I saw the servant of Laban who had the keys of the treasury. And I commanded him in the voice of Laban, that he should go with me into the treasury.
1 Nephi 2:8-10
8 And it came to pass that he called the name of the river, Laman, and it emptied into the Red Sea; and the valley was in the borders near the mouth thereof.

9 And when my father saw that the waters of the river emptied into the fountain of the Red Sea, he spake unto Laman, saying: O that thou mightest be like unto this river, continually running into the fountain of all righteousness!
10 And he also spake unto Lemuel: O that thou mightest be like unto this valley, firm and steadfast, and immovable in keeping the commandments of the Lord!
Alma 48:15

And this was their faith, that by so doing God would prosper them in the land, or in other words, if they were faithful in keeping the commandments of God that he would prosper them in the land; yea, warn them to flee, or to prepare for war, according to their danger;
●You’d think that a difficult task of writing on metal plates would result in laconic writing, but this isn’t the case.
○“And it came to pass” at least 1,123 times by my count
●This property isn’t exclusive to the Book of Mormon. It also occurs in the Bible:

○Joshua 24:27: And Joshua said unto all the people, Behold, this stone shall be a witness unto us; for it hath heard all the words of the LORD which he spake unto us: it shall be therefore a witness unto you, lest ye deny your God.

As referenced in this article, Biblical scholar and professor of Jewish Studies, Richard Friedman noted that translations of ancient Hebrew text have certain characteristics, one being redundant formulation:

The formulation "And he said, saying..." occurs fairly often in the Hebrew text. Although it feels redundant and awkward in English, I still prefer to retain the extra word—"saying"—to reflect the original.
Since Egyptian is closely related to Hebrew (), it would follow that a translation of reformed Egyptian, which the Book of Mormon was written in (Mormon 9:32), could have the same characteristic.
Reasons for wordiness
Talk about how words from one language may be short or redundancy is necessary according to their grammar.
Via: by way of
Felix Culpa
Latin for happy fault.
In religious contexts, it refers to the view that Adam’s seemingly disastrous action of partaking of the fruit was actually a good thing because it brought about blessed Redemption.

Here are some thoughts and questions about justice: Why do the seed of Adam, humans, need to be redeemed? They partook of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, whatever that actually represents—I don’t know. That made us fallen man. We became sinners, but not all, right? I mean, infants die who couldn’t have sinned, yet, Christ still had to redeem them. What kind of God enforced this system upon us where Adam and Eve’s transgression leaves a burdensome curse upon us all? I don’t get it. It doesn’t seem fair.

If God created this scenario where humans are imperfect, why does He send forth a punishment upon us which we apparently cannot pay? Is God demanding the punishment? What good does punishment even really do?

I mean, if someone murders, does it really solve anything at all if they are punished by death? The person or people they murdered would still be dead regardless. If it does anything at all it would be that it removes the chance of danger that exists from this person with a history of killing people. That’s reasonable in order to make a safe society. But what about forgiveness and second chances? What if there was a way to not punish the murderer and just separate them from everyone else so they don’t threaten society? Oh yeah, that’s what prison is.

Well, if us limited humans can create a boundary between those deemed dangerous to our society and the rest of us, surely God can do one better. God could make a planet for the dangerous people and another planet for the peaceful people. But what about those dead people who got murdered? Doesn’t seem to work out well for them here does it? No, no, that’s right they’re still dead…

In fact, that’s a big problem—everyone seems to just die and suffer all sorts of difficulties in life. What can we do about that since we’re discussing justice? What can we do about any unfair thing? And who in the world can actually define what is truly fair and unfair? Is that what justice is? But is justice subjective or some objective law proclaimed before or by God?
Let me try to simplify and answer, especially after having watched a couple really great YouTube videos on the subject.
1.Adam and Eve partook of the tree of knowledge of good and evil
a.God had decreed that in the day they did this they would die
i.They then would become mortal
b.No unclean thing can dwell with God, therefore, Adam and Eve, having transgressed His laws, became unclean and were cast out of His presence
i.Being cut off from God, or spiritually dead, leaves us without God’s contagious godly nature and subject to the beings outside His presence, such as Satan, who tempt with carnal desires
2.They, and their seed, were cut off from God’s presence (because of transgressing His laws and becoming unclean) and became mortal.
a.It is not entirely odd that an effect such as mortality would be hereditary
i.It’s not so much that God is punishing innocent children who descend from Adam but that the effect of Adam and Eve’s transgressing simply affects all of Adam’s seed.

3.The effect of Adam and Eve’s transgression leaves them subject to sin, becoming carnal, and mortal, being subject to death. Their curse is death and hell—respective consequences to mortality and subjection to the Devil. This state is a perpetual and eternal one.

a.How could God remedy this? He is the Righteous Judge. Can he rescind His decree that they would die from partaking of the fruit? Okay, let’s say He does this and allows them to partake of the tree of life and live forever in their sins. Wait, but that’s a problem too—He’s got to fix the sin part, right? This may be a big problem. How can God change our natures without conflicting with the laws of agency? He obviously wants to change our natures and commands us to act morally and godly and urges us not to sin, but apparently, He never used the old trick of snapping the change into existence with His sovereign omnipotence. Perhaps this is because doing so would violate laws of free will and such. But what about for those of us who are begging to have this change of nature and become new creatures? He wouldn’t be infringing upon our free will in this case, would He?
i.The mortality problem: God simply told Adam and Eve that they would die if they ate the fruit. They ate the fruit and so they must die or else they would make God a liar.
1.Well why did God say that in the first place? Why didn’t He say, “If you eat the fruit you’ll become mortal but I have a remedy for that.”

ii.The cut-off from God problem: Adam and Eve became mortal because they became unclean because they disobeyed God’s commandment to not partake of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Why did He command them not to eat of that tree in the first place?
Useful Scriptures
●Alma 42:9 The fall brought about physical and spiritual death
●Alma 42:9 We must repent during this probationary period of mortality
●Alma 42:16 The punishment affixed to man was eternal as the life of the soul
●Alma 42:18-21 There was a just law given and reasons why a just law must exist
●Alma 42:25 Mercy cannot rob justice or God would cease to be God
Justice

Justice is fairness, right? There must be a law as Lehi famously taught (2 Nephi 2:13). Lehi taught that if there is no law there is no sin. But if nothing is wrong (sinful) then nothing can be right (righteous). If there is no right or wrong, Lehi argues, there can’t be happiness or misery. Why is that? Why can’t there be happiness and misery even when right and wrong aren’t defined? What kind of world would that be where there is no law? I’m sure people would still be happy and sad. But there would always be an understanding of right and wrong, even without the law. I feel like stealing and murdering are actions that always seem wrong, well in most cases.
Guide to the Scriptures: Justice
Consequences of blessings for righteous thoughts and acts and punishment for unrepented sin.
This is interesting to me. Does it have to be a blessing and punishment system? Punishment makes it sound like its retributive. What if it’s just corrective or practical for the safety of society?
So I get that God, as the judge and executioner, must judge according to the law and

Nephi, in his vision, sees that more scriptures are given in addition to the bible. These extra scriptures are enough to “[convince] the Gentiles and the remnant of the [Lamanites], and also the Jews who were scattered upon all the face of the earth, that the records of the prophets and of the twelve apostles of the Lamb are true.”
What texts are these that will convince such a large group of people that the bible is true? Is it The Book of Mormon or something else?
Reading on through the end of the chapter helps to understand that this is likely The Book of Mormon.
2 Nephi 1:19
…for his are righteousness forever.
2 Nephi 2:6
…he is full of grace and truth.
2 Nephi 2:12

Wherefore, it must needs have been created for a thing of naught; wherefore there would have been no purpose in the end of its creation. Wherefore, this thing must needs destroy the wisdom of God and his eternal purposes, and also the power, and the mercy, and the justice of God.

If something existed that had no purpose and for which righteousness and wickedness were irrelevant, this would destroy the wisdom of God and his purposes. That’s odd. Is God bound to only do things which pertain to the eternal salvation of mankind or can He do other things?
No law → no sin/righteousness → no punishment-misery/happiness → no God → no existence of mankind and earth
What can we derive from this reasoning set forth by Lehi?

title: Managing Priorities and when to Drop Commitments

body.text: 15 And now it came to pass that Alma, having seen the afflictions of the humble followers of God, and the persecutions which were heaped upon them by the remainder of his people, and seeing all their inequality, began to be very sorrowful; nevertheless the Spirit of the Lord did not fail him.

16 And he selected a wise man who was among the elders of the church, and gave him power according to the voice of the people, that he might have power to enact laws according to the laws which had been given, and to put them in force according to the wickedness and the crimes of the people.

It’s important to know when you need to drop commitments in life to serve well in the most important parts. Don’t juggle multiple good things at the cost of not fully serving best in the one most important thing. Alma being chief judge was a good thing but it detracted from his calling to act as high priest and save his people from their wickedness.
Also remember how Moses was advised by his father-in-law to delegate the management of the affairs of the people to others because it was too much for one person.

There’s a common question regarding the garden of Eden that often comes up which is Why does God give Adam and Eve contradicting commandments? He commands them to multiply and replenish the earth yet he also commands them not to partake of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. This question was on my mind and as I thought about the difficulty that often accompanies this question within the church I was surprised at a total lack of any indication of the same conflict in scriptures. I began to think If this was really a contradiction of commandments why didn’t Adam and Eve point that out? Wouldn’t they have complained to God immediately at the glaringly obvious contradiction we get from our understanding of the circumstance? Perhaps they just didn’t understand what multiply and replenish meant? I thought about it more and I began to question the accuracy of our understanding of this supposed conflict. I thought, maybe this is no conflict at all. To give credit to this claim one could also argue that wouldn’t Satan have used this conflict to his advantage in persuading Adam and Eve to eat the fruit if it really was a conflict? I mean, he was desperately trying to get them to fall and surely would have used any poor or contradictory logic to gain this desire. In fact, he even tried to use God’s words to gain his point telling Eve that God told them they would gain knowledge and have their eyes open. He even resorted to lying and telling them that they would not surely die, perhaps tweaking the meaning of “surely die”.

The case becomes very strong that there was actually no contradiction at all in God’s two commandments. The conflict is in our misunderstanding. So what is the correct understanding? I suggest that God’s commandment for them to multiply and replenish the earth was similar to Him commanding the fruit and fish and animals to multiply and replenish. It wasn’t given as a moral code or rule but rather as a decree. God was acting as creator, not law giver. He decreed the design of all living things to procreate and multiply in their own sphere. I designed man via this decree to be capable of procreation and multiplying and replenishing.

To support this claim, look at Abraham where it says God “caused” them to multiply and replenish, not “command”. “Command” becomes an ambiguous word which we mistakenly interpret to always be synonymous with “establish a law of morality of conduct”. Add in the scriptures to support this later. I think it works out nicely and felt that this idea was arrived at by the Spirit in a conversation with Kaylene.

I was reading the second instance where a covenant is made by placing a hand under the thigh. I wondered what significance this had. I found a really interesting article suggesting that “thigh” could also have referred to loins or even testicles. By placing the hand under such, one would be swearing on the seed of the one under whom they placed their hand. Abraham caused his servant to swear by Abraham’s seed. Jacob caused Joseph to swear, by implication, by the same.

However, this isn’t the only interpretation of this practice. Jewish tradition claims that placing a hand under the thigh of someone, or letting them sit on your hand, symbolizes submission to that person.

Is church supposed to be fun or entertaining? I don’t think that’s the actual purpose of it. It’s purpose is to feed us spiritually and allow us to share and bond with our ward family. It’s kind of like asking whether eating is fun or entertaining. That’s somewhat irrelevant.
I found an article about this that’s listed in the references above. Another one that would be worth looking into is:

And let’s not forget the Spencer W. Kimball quote that I struggle with: “What do you do when you find yourself in a boring sacrament meeting?” His answer: “I don’t know. I’ve never been in one.” Ay, really? Is this answer President Kimball being cheeky or was he totally sincere?
Alright, addressing the first article from the Questions & Answers series.
Moroni 6:5-6
5 And the church did meet together oft, to fast and to pray, and to speak one with another concerning the welfare of their souls.
6 And they did meet together oft to partake of bread and wine, in remembrance of the Lord Jesus.

This same purpose applies to us today. It’s not explicitly said that church was for fun or entertainment or laughing. In fact, this reminds me of D&C where it says much laughing is a sin, and certainly so in a sacred context I would imagine.
The article stated: “Remember that you—not the speakers or teachers—control your experience.”
This reminds me, who was it in the last General Conference that talked about us making our own experience at church? It was President Dallin H. Oaks. In his talk he quotes Spencer W. Kimball:

We do not go to Sabbath meetings to be entertained or even solely to be instructed. We go to worship the Lord. It is an individual responsibility, and regardless of what is said from the pulpit, if one wishes to worship the Lord in spirit and in truth, he may do so by attending his meetings, partaking of the sacrament, and contemplating the beauties of the gospel. If the service is a failure to you, you have failed. No one can worship for you; you must do your own waiting upon the Lord. ()

I’ll have to delve more into this talk because how is the sabbath a delight and how is the sabbath for man and not man for the sabbath if it is boring? Perhaps even though it may not be entertaining at times, it doesn’t mean it will be boring. Quietness and stillness are experiences only those who are at peace can enjoy. In our culture I’m afraid that we are dreadfully uncomfortable with these.
Also, what is worship?
Elder Oaks said in :

The Apostle Paul taught that the Lord’s teachings and teachers were given that we may all attain “the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ” (). This process requires far more than acquiring knowledge. It is not even enough for us to be convinced of the gospel; we must act and think so that we are converted by it. In contrast to the institutions of the world, which teach us to know something, the gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to become something.
Now for the question of what worship is, I found an article on a Christian question and answer site titled with the question, ? Here is the content, or at least the parts I found useful.

Worship can be defined as the act of honoring and loving a deity, idol or person in a “selfless” manner. The act of worship involves the total self in giving praise, thanksgiving and reverence to that deity, person or material object…

So, the true worship… comes from the redeemed heart of a man or woman who has been justified before God by faith and who is trusting in the Lord Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness of sins. How can one worship the God of heaven if his sin has not been dealt with?...

Second, true worship of God comes from a heart that desires Him alone. This was precisely where the Samaritan people erred; they sought to worship both God and idols (), and this is reaffirmed by the Lord Jesus Christ when He discourses on the subject of true worship with the Samaritan woman who came to fetch water from the well. “You Samaritans worship what you do not know” (). These people worshiped God “half-heartedly” because their total affection was not set on God. It is possible for even true believers to fall into this second error. We might not assent to having physical idols, like the Samaritans did, but what absorbs our will, our time, our resources most of all? Is it careers, material possessions, money, health, even our families? Let us cry out, like King David in, “My soul will be satisfied as with the richest of foods; with singing lips, my mouth will praise you.” Nothing less than God should satisfy the heart of the regenerate man, and his response to that divine satisfaction, comparable to the best food ever, is the fruit of lips that sing God’s praise ().

Third, true worship of God is the desire to continue to build up our knowledge of God. How we have lost that desire in these days! Apart from the Bible, which we should be reading daily, we need to supplement our knowledge by reading other good books, too. We need to fill our minds constantly with the things of God; God should always be on our mind, and everything we do should be done with reference to Him (;). It is interesting that the Greek word for “worship” in can also mean “service.” So, our daily lives should also be considered as worship. Every day we are to offer ourselves as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God. The church is supposed to be impacting the world by its worship of God. Far too often, it’s the other way around.

Let us purify our hearts if we really want to worship the triune God in spirit and in truth. Our God is holy; He is altogether “Other,” a God who cannot share us with other objects of our affection. Indeed, a God who WILL not share us, for the sake of His holiness. We were made to be creatures who worship, but the Fall has crippled and ruined us. Worship is the most natural thing for man, but until we are restored to God through the sacrifice of His dear Son, then all our worship is but a vain thing. It is as “strange fire” before the altar ().

title: The Late War by Gilbert J. Hunt and The Book of Mormon

body.text: This article is certainly an interesting one. From my understanding, some guys did some textual processing and analysis and compared the text of The Book of Mormon with thousands of books from during or around Joseph Smith’s time. I believe their intention was to find substance to back a claim that Joseph Smith had plagiarized his work in The Book of Mormon. They compared similarities based on, at least one of the metrics was, common and rare 4-grams or phrases. This is common as a practice to discover plagiarism in academic work.

The Late War is a book written by Gilbert J. Hunt which, from what the writers of articles regarding this work purport, was offered as curriculum or supplemental reading material for students during Joseph Smith’s school years. The details start to match up well enough that this book obviously becomes a strong candidate for those doing this work.

Upon further analysis, the authors found many commonalities in the book, The Late War. They found that not only does this book have many common phrases and wording withThe Book of Mormon, but it also exhibits characteristics The Book of Mormon has that many used to back The Book of Mormon’s ancient origin such as Hebraisms, chiasmas, verb/subject order, word choice, etc.
After examining the article fully and the actual text of The Late War, here are my conclusions:
●The Late War has unique and substantial common phrases and terms that are used in The Book of Mormon.
●The Late War demonstrates many characteristics also contained in The Book of Mormon that were thought, and claimed, to be exclusive to texts of ancient origin.
●The Late War has themes or ideas, such as types of war, or “curious” pieces of technology such as ball-like clocks, that are common in The Book of Mormon.

These conclusions do have implications, but none of which I believe to diminish the authenticity of The Book of Mormon as a historical and spiritual text originating from the source Joseph Smith claims. The work discussed here does hint at how The Book of Mormon was translated—seeing the similarities between the two works does suggest The Late War’s influence upon the former. Perhaps Joseph Smith’s translation process was loose in that God was able to pull words and phrases that Joseph would have been accustomed to as part of the translation.

Perhaps Joseph’s translation was based solely or mostly upon phrases and vocabulary that he had read or seen elsewhere. If this were the case, it still wouldn’t suggest fraud or plagiarism in The Book of Mormon. The nature of the commonalities between The Book of Mormon and The Late War are such that it would be difficult even to claim plagiarism according to an academic use of the word. Even if all of the examples given by the authors of the comparison between these two books were sound—which they don’t appear to be and many contain relatively insignificant similarities that you might expect to appear by mere chance—The Book of Mormon would still offer novel plot lines, characters, testimonies, etc. All that these examples could imply is that The Book of Mormon translation into English contains fragments of borrowed wording. The ideas within The Book of Mormon certainly maintain their novelty.

Accusations about Joseph Smith taking ideas such as the Liahona from ideas found within The Late War are not grounded in sufficient information, in my opinion. The similarities between such common ideas could very easily be attributed to chance. We by no means have sufficient significance among the commonalities to assert that Joseph stole this idea from The Late War.

Additionally, similar or exactly matching dates from The Late War found within The Book of Mormon are curious, but what conclusions can be made from such similarities or matches is unsure. Would one claim that Joseph stole such dates from The Late War, as if among all his supposed creative works within The Book of Mormon including novel and multiple intertwining plot lines and characters with their interactions, consistent geography and doctrinal development, etc., that Joseph had to rely upon external or borrowed sources to concoct a date? Dates are not difficult to make up. The frequent occurrence of dates, especially written in the form “____st day of the _____nd month of the ____rd year…”, in both The Late War and The Book of Mormon make the similar or matching dates even less significant.

On the subject of Hebraisms and chiasmas, the finding of such in The Late War does lessen the significance of such in The Book of Mormon. It becomes difficult to defend The Book of Mormon’s authenticity as an ancient record solely upon claims that Joseph couldn’t have stumbled upon such and such practice in writing because it was exclusive to the Hebrews, etc. These claims are strongly refuted by evidence of the same ancient practices demonstrated in The Late War. I think we do have to reexamine such claims and not offer such as sure evidence supporting The Book of Mormon.

On the note of chiasmus, however, I will say that the examples of chiasmus in The Late War seem to be the sort that might appear by accident where the structure and pairs within the chiasma are not very meaningful in their association. Also, the central focus of such chiastic structures are uneventful or meaningful. This makes such examples found within The Late war appear to be accidents—no intentionality. On the other hand, the incredibly prevalent chiasmas found within The Book of Mormon are rich with meaning and focus. Often the center of such chiasmas offers a dramatic shift in thinking or reveals a key doctrine. The pairs within such chiasmas offen tell a progressive story or present a doctrine through a series of introductory steps.

My point here is that the chiasmas I saw from The Late War were very unimpressive and seemed to be accidents rather than a result of intentional rhetorical effort. Conversely, The Book of Mormon chiasma appear to me to be results of direct and intentional effort which offer actual insight and help the reader understand otherwise less apparent details.

I conclude after examining the referenced material that The Book of Mormon’s authenticity as a book of historical and spiritual soundness, accuracy, and merit remains unchallenged. The analysis of The Late War in comparison with The Book of Mormon does not offer anything challenging The Book of Mormon’s authenticity, only that which yields insight and clues as to how the translation of it may have occurred. Even then, I would not conclusively assert that The Late War definitely influenced The Book of Mormon at all. The evidence is strong, but inconclusive. While it seems very likely that Joseph Smith did have access to The Late War and that his translation of The Book of Mormon was influenced by it, we can’t definitively assert that this is the case.
I don’t think that the results of this finding are in disagreement with what The Book of Mormon claims to be.
Note

I think examining critical claims against The Book of Mormon is important when done with a sincere desire to find truth. Often, though, what is termed anti-Mormon material is slanted with a fierce bias against truth, God, and the Spirit. I find that when examining this type of material, I’m accompanied by darkness and a suppressive and lying spirit. Satan of course wants to slander and will use any tactic to lead away truth-seekers from truth. We cannot be fooled. It would be foolish of us to play in the mire and seek truth there, but sometimes you gotta get dirty to find the great reward. Find the balance and bear in mind the intentions of the author and yourself as you examine this sort of stuff. Don’t pursue something that feels dark and dirty that clearly has no intention of yielding truth. It’s like trying to achieve an accurate perception of a political event from the most biased, mainstream news outlets—they cannot offer accuracy, only their biased views.

Are we judged according to our nature or our deeds? Children are “not capable of committing sin” (Moroni 8:8). Is this because of their innocent nature or because they can’t commit the deeds of sin? A child can murder, steal, swear, etc., but these deeds are not counted against them because of their innocence. The behavior may be wicked, but not the heart. This idea has caused me to wonder if Jesus may have appeared to do wrongly in the sight of some but was guiltless because of his divine and pure heart. So what matters, the external behavior or the internal nature or intention?
12 And Amulek hath spoken plainly concerning death, and being raised from this mortality to a state of immortality, and being brought before the bar of God, to be judged according to our works.

13 Then if our hearts have been hardened, yea, if we have hardened our hearts against the word, insomuch that it has not been found in us, then will our state be awful, for then we shall be condemned.

14 For our words will condemn us, yea, all our works will condemn us; we shall not be found spotless; and our thoughts will also condemn us; and in this awful state we shall not dare to look up to our God; and we would fain be glad if we could command the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us to hide us from his presence.
This scripture states that our condemnation will come from our words, works, and thoughts. This seems to correlate strongly with King Benjamin’s counsel in his great and last sermon:
Mosiah 4:30

30 But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds, and observe the commandments of God, and continue in the faith of what ye have heard concerning the coming of our Lord, even unto the end of your lives, ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not.
Here’s another scripture that has relevance to this topic:
Alma 41:11

11 And now, my son, all men that are in a state of nature, or I would say, in a carnal state, are in the gall of bitterness and in the bonds of iniquity; they are without God in the world, and they have gone contrary to the nature of God; therefore, they are in a state contrary to the nature of happiness.
This scripture puts a lot of emphasis on nature. Is the evil thing the deed or the nature? Or are the two inseparable?
Desire is a product of nature. What can be said of one’s desire?
Alma 42:28
28 If he has desired to do evil, and has not repented in his days, behold, evil shall be done unto him, according to the restoration of God.
Here are some examples of righteous converts to Christ who experienced a change of nature:
Mosiah 5:2

2 And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.
There are several aspects to the peoples’ conversion that are notable: 1. Believe in God’s words 2. Knowledge gained from the Spirit of God 3. Experienced a change of nature—becoming new creatures.
This topic has become a crux for some and an interest of superlative magnitude for me. I cannot resist the curious urges of thought that are implied by the processes of evolution as we understand it.
Here’s my rant I had and recorded while out on my walk—mind you, it’s speech to text and I haven’t edited it so forgive any errors:

I was just thinking how weird it is with evolution. Because it is apparent or at least it is very persuasive that evolution is a principal process of life on all levels and forms. It seems to show itself from the smallest forms of life to the largest and even where there is no life. Evolution can apply to inorganic material because the fittest materials and substances within an environment are those which are used and functional. But with life it has shown its course and the imprint of evolution has manifested on multiple levels of our organisms. We can see it in our bone structure shared with other species. We can see the commonalities and the puzzle pieces all start to come together when you compare and analyze like organisms. But the real predicament which drives me crazy because of how curious it is is why does God have a human body. Because the human body is as good an example as any to support evolution. We have borrowed features and even features which seem to be irrelevant or unused by our life form or species yet they still exist within us. Why do these relics of former ancestors exist with us? And if God did use evolution to create us as we are, that's fine. That is a paradigm that works and allows for one to accept evolution as well as Divine creation and god. But when believing that God has a body of flesh and Bones like ours or that we are created in the image of God and in his own likeness. This is the curious part. Why in the world would God have a body such as this which manifests the origin of evolution? Isn't the human body a crude product of evolution? It's one thing to find the fascination and curiosity with how we could have evolved into what we are but why would God have evolved to where he is? Is evolution just the only process for improvements in the universe? But if God evolved, were there others like him? And how did they begin? And where is the beginning of it all? This is the real conundrum that presses on my mind with such weights that it drives me crazy. Maybe it's because I'm a finite being and when I am infinite I will understand it all? Perhaps in some odd way the beginning of it all could be right with us and God could be the product of his own creation. Of course this is paradoxical and seemingly contradictory but alas paradoxes often simply describe the most fundamental truth of reality.

How compelling is evolution? Well, it seems to be VERY compelling. I mean, what scientific facts are as plain to discern as true after a careful and scrupulous examination? The earth’s shape being round, the planets and their orbits, the size and gravitational force of the sun, all these require more assumptions, more mathematics, more learning and study to conclude. Evolution being the product of various life forms and even inorganic material is sensible. According to Ockham’s Razor, a theory suggesting that the most likely event is the one that requires the fewest speculative assumptions—the simplest one. Evolution fits this, I think.
Here’s a website that has some good points in summarizing the strongest arguments for evolution:

They discuss, in this article, how tetrapods, or four-legged animals, all have remarkably similar bone structures. Additionally, the origin of the current shape and structure of each individual tetrapod species becomes apparent when realizing the suboptimality of such species’ bone structure which often causes issues of distress or lack of functionality for such. What explanation can answer this issue? If God individually crafted each creature would He not have done a better job at giving each an optimal body for their function? Or did He purposely neglect this point to allow such creatures to struggle with bodies not perfectly suited for their function? I don’t mean to speak with any disrespect toward God, the holy and supreme creator, I just mean to make a point at what God likely is not, or did not do.

Other arguments include the story told in fossil records that show intermediary species showing transitional changes between some species currently found today. Also, there are the cases of isolated environments such as Hawaii and Madagascar which have exclusive and unique species on the land found nowhere else in the world. Evolution is the most cogent explanation for these phenomena.

I have to make sure I’m clear here, though. I do not know all of the mysteries of God and do not claim sure knowledge. It is possible that evolution is wrong and is not the way God created things. I’m not going to be so arrogant as to assert one way or the other.

In our culture today it’s common to see some writhe in discomfort as they parse through the scriptures that suggest race is a mark set by God in some instances which signifies a curse, God’s disfavor, etc. These people attempt to resolve their dilemma by redefining scriptures, making literal descriptions merely symbolic, writing such scriptures off as being the resulting thought of a racist prophet who was infected by the “social constructs” of his time, or simply ignoring such passages. I don’t believe that any of these are helpful measures. When we have a problem with the scriptures, the problem is not with the scriptures, it is with us. Sure there are minor errors in the bible here and there and our understanding of scriptures is at times miniscule, but we ought not misjudge the holy word of God because of our culture as it stands now.
So what do the scriptures say on this topic?
Helaman 15:4
But behold my brethren, the Lamanites hath he hated because their deeds have been evil continually, and this because of the iniquity of the tradition of their fathers.
Psalm 11:5 (ESV)
The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.
Psalm 5:4–5 (ESV)
For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers.
These scriptures state something most wouldn’t believe is stated in scriptures—God hates sinners.

Wherefore, the word of the Lord was fulfilled which he spake unto me, saying that: Inasmuch as they will not hearken unto thy words they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord. And behold, they were cut off from his presence.

And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity. For behold, they had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint; wherefore, as they were white, and exceedingly fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them.
And thus saith the Lord God: I will cause that they shall be loathsome unto thy people, save they shall repent of their iniquities.
And cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed; for they shall be cursed even with the same cursing. And the Lord spake it, and it was done.
And because of their cursing which was upon them they did become an idle people, full of mischief and subtlety, and did seek in the wilderness for beasts of prey.

And the Lord God said unto me: They shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in remembrance of me; and inasmuch as they will not remember me, and hearken unto my words, they shall scourge them even unto destruction.
Jacob 3:5-9

Behold, the Lamanites your brethren, whom ye hate because of their filthiness and the cursing which hath come upon their skins, are more righteous than you; for they have not forgotten the commandment of the Lord, which was given unto our father—that they should have save it were one wife, and concubines they should have none, and there should not be whoredoms committed among them.

And now, this commandment they observe to keep; wherefore, because of this observance, in keeping this commandment, the Lord God will not destroy them, but will be merciful unto them; and one day they shall become a blessed people.

Behold, their husbands love their wives, and their wives love their husbands; and their husbands and their wives love their children; and their unbelief and their hatred towards you is because of the iniquity of their fathers; wherefore, how much better are you than they, in the sight of your great Creator?
O my brethren, I fear that unless ye shall repent of your sins that their skins will be whiter than yours, when ye shall be brought with them before the throne of God.

Wherefore, a commandment I give unto you, which is the word of God, that ye revile no more against them because of the darkness of their skins; neither shall ye revile against them because of their filthiness; but ye shall remember your own filthiness, and remember that their filthiness came because of their fathers.
Alma 3:6-7

And the skins of the Lamanites were dark, according to the mark which was set upon their fathers, which was a curse upon them because of their transgression and their rebellion against their brethren, who consisted of Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam, who were just and holy men.
And their brethren sought to destroy them, therefore they were cursed; and the Lord God set a mark upon them, yea, upon Laman and Lemuel, and also the sons of Ishmael, and Ishmaelitish women.
Now we will return again to the Amlicites, for they also had a mark set upon them; yea, they set the mark upon themselves, yea, even a mark of red upon their foreheads.

Thus the word of God is fulfilled, for these are the words which he said to Nephi: Behold, the Lamanites have I cursed, and I will set a mark on them that they and their seed may be separated from thee and thy seed, from this time henceforth and forever, except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me that I may have mercy upon them.
And again: I will set a mark upon him that mingleth his seed with thy brethren, that they may be cursed also.
And again: I will set a mark upon him that fighteth against thee and thy seed.

And again, I say he that departeth from thee shall no more be called thy seed; and I will bless thee, and whomsoever shall be called thy seed, henceforth and forever; and these were the promises of the Lord unto Nephi and to his seed.
And it came to pass that those Lamanites who had united with the Nephites were numbered among the Nephites;
And their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white like unto the Nephites;
And their young men and their daughters became exceedingly fair, and they were numbered among the Nephites, and were called Nephites. And thus ended the thirteenth year.

These were all scriptures referring to the curse that God put upon the Lamanites to separate them from the seed of Nephi, Jacob, Joseph, and Zoram. Some things to point out about this curse is that the curse is not a mark of God’s disfavor, necessarily, but a physical sign to distinguish between people. Jacob points out during his day that the Lamanites, although cursed with black skin, were actually more righteous than the Nephites and would be recipients of God’s mercy in the end. He also tells his people not to revile the Lamanites because of the color of their skin—so the Nephites were commanded to not be racist.

Another point is that the mark of this curse need not be skin color, it can be any mark to distinguish one people from another, such as the mark of red in the forehead which the Amlicites put upon themselves.

There is nothing in reference to this curse that implies the Lamanites are disqualified from receiving any blessing that the Nephites are able to receive. In fact, we learn that God still loves the Lamanites and favors them when they are righteous. Late in the Book of Mormon story, the Lamanites join a righteous group of Nephites and mingle with them and also gain white skin.

There does seem to be some sentiment among the Lehites that implies skin whiteness is associated with purity, at least symbolically. Jacob threatens the Nephites that unless they repent, the Lamanites skins will be whiter than theirs at the judgment day. Also, when Jesus ministers to the people, as he blesses them and they receive his countenance, “they [become] as white as the countenance and also the garments of Jesus; and behold the whiteness thereof did exceed all the whiteness, yea, even there could be nothing upon earth so white as the whiteness thereof” (3 Nephi 19:25).

So what can we conclude about this? I think that, first off, we cannot support or justify racism at all using these scriptures from The Book of Mormon. We can, however, state that God has used skin color as a sign of His curse upon a people. We must qualify this, however, by adding that not all people with black skin are cursed—The Book of Mormon states that this curse was exclusive to the people of Lehi and their dealings. We can’t assume this curse still lingers in our culture and dwellings and, in fact, have reason to oppose that idea. But even if it were still a curse, we can’t misinterpret the curse of dark skin to mean that such people who are affected by the curse are less loved or less entitled to any blessing than any other person by virtue of their skin color. God makes it clear that “And he loveth those who will have him to be their God” (1 Nephi 17:40). Further, “...he inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile” (2 Nephi 26:33).

In our culture today where we are hyper-sensitive to racial prejudice, with good intention I’ll add, we are very bad at interpreting the past in context and very quick to jump to false conclusions because we are not careful to examine things within their domain. I see many times where people are so concerned with expunging racism from our society that they overcompensate and create an entirely new prejudice and racism in the opposite direction; they make double-standards where it’s okay to pile high the benefits and special treatment of those whom they seek to protect and make amends to, but find it entirely justified to demean and disrespect those whom they consider to be the offenders of their hated injustice (although they rarely are).

Our culture props up supporting and lifting programs like Black History Month and Women’s History Month, freely disperses grants and funds to black and minority and female students and organizations, applauds instances where any of these groups succeeds and attributes any of their failures to prejudice, racism, or sexism, totally absolving these groups of personal accountability for their own actions in many instances.

Needless to say, this is somewhat of a hot topic these days and I thought it relevant to explore in the scriptures. I also was prompted to study this after hearing a church-member podcaster vehemently express disdain toward those who consider the mark of Cain to be black skin—while I certainly don’t say that this was the mark, we must admit that it could be. And to reject such an idea as a possibility while such a mark was clearly used by God to the people in The Book of Mormon seems very incongruent and inconsistent. I hate dual-standards and inconsistent treatment.
Most compelling scientific evidence for evolution:

●Common skeletal structure—among four-limbed creatures, “tetrapods”, there are only slight variations on the same body plan. It’s like we all share the exact same skeleton but with varying lengths of bones depending on the species.

○Sharing a common skeletal structure for all tetrapods does not seem to be the genius of God’s efficiency in being able to use the same form for so many creatures, but rather the result of evolution from one common ancestor. The reason for concluding this is that our tetrapod skeletal structure is suboptimal for most species using it in some way and this results in inefficiencies—for humans these may be knee or lower back problems. We can conclude that the skeletal structure we have struggles to support an upright creature as the human.

○This also results in vestigial traits, or traits and features that are similar to what other animals have but which no longer seem to function; e.g., tails (or tailbones), wisdom teeth, nictitating membrane, auricular muscles to move ears, palmaris longus muscle present in some wrists of humans but not all.
●Fossil records revealing intermediate species
●Unique species evolved/found-in in isolated environments such as Hawaii and Madagascar

●Study of genetic code for each species shows the shared ancestry we’d expect through examination of other common traits—the genetic code and common traits agree with each other in support of the idea that there is a common ancestor

Some claim the work of Charles Darwin which introduced theories of evolution as Satan’s counter attack against theism and the contemporaneous coming forth of the restoration. I tend to believe, rather, that it is a consequence of the enlightenment of the restoration, along with many other advancements in science, art, and technology.
Are prophets fallible? Yes, of course they are. There was only one man who was sinless—
Hebrews 4:15 (NKJV): 15 For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin.
But what about the words of a prophet? The Bible says a false prophecy is a sign of a false prophet:

Deuteronomy 18:22 (NKJV): 22 when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously; you shall not be afraid of him.

In this case, the prophet must be saying something in the name of the Lord for it to be held to used to condemn him as a false prophet. This is what King Noah and his wicked priests attempted to use on Abinadi:

Mosiah 17:7-8: 7 And he said unto him: Abinadi, we have found an accusation against thee, and thou art worthy of death. 8 For thou hast said that God himself should come down among the children of men; and now, for this cause thou shalt be put to death unless thou wilt recall all the words which thou hast spoken evil concerning me and my people.
In Abinadi’s case, he was condemned not because his prophecy didn’t come to pass, but because it was construed to contradict another prophet who was considered a valid prophet of God.
So how do we know a servant of God from a servant of the devil or someone who is simply crazy?
Matthew 7:15 (NKJV): 15 “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.
Jesus said:
Matthew 7:16 (NKJV): 16 You will know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles?
So it’s okay if someone is wrong as long as they weren’t talking in the name of the Lord and their fruits are good? Well how do we know when someone is talking in the name of the Lord?

And, other related material, Joseph Smith stated that a prophet was only a prophet when he was acting as such, insinuating that a valid prophet of God could perhaps act contrary to his calling when not acting officially:
DHC 5:265 Section Five 1842-43, p.278

Wednesday, Feb. 8.—This morning I read German and visited with a brother and sister from Michigan, who thought that "a prophet is always a prophet;" but I told them that a prophet was a prophet only when he was acting as such.—DHC 5:265.
Accordingly, the First Presidency stated:

The position is not assumed that the men of the New Dispensation —its prophets, apostles, presidencies, and other leaders—are without faults or infallible, rather they are treated as men of like passions with their fellow men.
We can rest assured that “The Lord will never permit [the prophet] or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray.” - Wilford Woodruff.
Brigham Young said:

Can a Prophet or an Apostle be mistaken?
