●using the telephone;
●turning on or off anything which uses electricity, including lights, radios, television, computer, air-conditioners and alarm clocks;
●cooking, baking or kindling a fire;
●gardening and grass-mowing;
●doing laundry;
This article is interesting and suggests that we, as Christians, can keep the Sabbath still but that it’s not necessary.
From the article given as primary reference in this entry, the following comes:

Some work must be done on Sunday. (See Elder Mark E. Petersen, Ensign, May 1975, p. 49.) And it seems clear that we should not take the position that all such work should be left strictly to nonmembers. We need good Latter-day Saints in all honorable occupations, to influence and to bless those they work with and those they serve.

The question of Sabbath work, then, invariably becomes an individual one. Knowing that some Sunday work is not only justified, but also needed, we must ask ourselves, “Is my situation such that Sunday work is unavoidable?”
The article later suggests asking oneself the question:
Am I sure I’m not using my job as an excuse for laziness?

This is a big one. I think many times people don’t even try to avoid working on Sundays. Is there no question as to the Sabbath being holy and a day of rest? It’s like some people don’t even have the desire to avoid employment on the Sabbath.

title: Book of Mormon on Time of Christ’s Death/Resurrection

body.text: The Book of Mormon does a pretty good job at letting the reader know of the approximate chronology within the book. 3 Nephi 8:5 mentions that “in the thirty and fourth year, in the first month, on the fourth day of the month, there arose a great storm, such an one as never had been known in all the land.” This storm included earthquakes and lightnings to such a degree that some cities were burned by fire (verse 8), others sank in the sea (verse 9), and others were covered with earth or mountains (verse 10). These severe natural disasters go on for three hours (verse 19) and are followed by darkness in the land.

If the Nephites used the Hebrew calendar, which I’m not confident of but set forth as a plausible idea, that date given translates to March 22, 33 A.D. I used an online site to convert the dates: . This is also assuming that the sign of Christ’s birth which they reckoned their time after occurred at 0 A.D. This fact is perhaps even less plausible than that the Nephites used the Hebrew calendar, but I think it’s still okay to use in order to derive some approximation.

Going off these assumptions, we can continue approximating the time that Jesus was resurrected, or rather when He visited the Nephites as a resurrected being, by using 3 Nephi 10:9 which says “three days [passed] away” and then Jesus visited them at the temple. This would be to say that March 25th, 33 A.D. is the day Jesus was resurrected. But can we assume that on the same day Jesus was resurrected that He went and visited the Nephites? I don’t know. But the three days after His death matches up with the Bible.
Three is a magic number.
3 Nephi 8:19

And it came to pass that when the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the storm, and the tempest, and the quakings of the earth did cease—for behold, they did last for about the space of three hours; and it was said by some that the time was greater; nevertheless, all these great and terrible things were done in about the space of three hours—and then behold, there was darkness upon the face of the land.
3 Nephi 8:23

And it came to pass that it did last for the space of three days that there was no light seen; and there was great mourning and howling and weeping among all the people continually; yea, great were the groanings of the people, because of the darkness and the great destruction which had come upon them.
3 Nephi 10:9

And it came to pass that thus did the three days pass away. And it was in the morning, and the darkness dispersed from off the face of the land, and the earth did cease to tremble, and the rocks did cease to rend, and the dreadful groanings did cease, and all the tumultuous noises did pass away
3 Nephi 11:1-7

1 And now it came to pass that there were a great multitude gathered together, of the people of Nephi, round about the temple which was in the land Bountiful; and they were marveling and wondering one with another, and were showing one to another the great and marvelous change which had taken place.
2 And they were also conversing about this Jesus Christ, of whom the sign had been given concerning his death.

3 And it came to pass that while they were thus conversing one with another, they heard a voice as if it came out of heaven; and they cast their eyes round about, for they understood not the voice which they heard; and it was not a harsh voice, neither was it a loud voice; nevertheless, and notwithstanding it being a small voice it did pierce them that did hear to the center, insomuch that there was no part of their frame that it did not cause to quake; yea, it did pierce them to the very soul, and did cause their hearts to burn.
4 And it came to pass that again they heard the voice, and they understood it not.

5 And again the third time they did hear the voice, and did open their ears to hear it; and their eyes were towards the sound thereof; and they did look steadfastly towards heaven, from whence the sound came.
6 And behold, the third time they did understand the voice which they heard; and it said unto them:
7 Behold my Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, in whom I have glorified my name—hear ye him.
Three degrees of glory through which to descend. Three members of the Godhead. Three hours of earthquakes and torment. Three days of darkness. Three times of God calling down before being understood.
Some other triplets in this section of scripture:
3 Nephi 9:2

Wo, wo, wo unto this people; wo unto the inhabitants of the whole earth except they shall repent; for the devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice, because of the slain of the fair sons and daughters of my people; and it is because of their iniquity and abominations that they are fallen!
3 Nephi 10:4-5

O ye people of these great cities which have fallen, who are descendants of Jacob, yea, who are of the house of Israel, how oft have I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and have nourished you. And again, how oft would I have gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, yea, O ye people of the house of Israel, who have fallen; yea, O ye people of the house of Israel, ye that dwell at Jerusalem, as ye that have fallen; yea, how oft would I have gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens, and ye would not.
I don’t know why exactly, but Jesus repeats Himself almost verbatim in these verses:
37 And again I say unto you, ye must repent, and become as a little child, and be baptized in my name, or ye can in nowise receive these things.
38 And again I say unto you, ye must repent, and be baptized in my name, and become as a little child, or ye can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God.

In verse 37 He teaches that you are to first become as a little child and then be baptized in order to receive “these things” which I believe refers to the doctrine of Christ that He had been teaching about. Okay, so that’s how you receive the doctrine of Christ, we’ll say; then if you are baptized and then become as a little child you can inherit the kingdom of God?

title: BOM vs NT Sermon on the Mount

body.text: Here are some differences I noticed and my thoughts on why the difference exists based on the Nephite/Israelite backgrounds and contexts. I know John Welch has already compiled much on this topic but I still find it worthwhile to do it myself for my own sake of study.
3 Nephi
Matthew
12:6 And blessed are all they who do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled with the Holy Ghost.
5:6 Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
The Nephites seemed to have a bit more knowledge regarding concepts like the Holy Ghost. These were righteous Nephites at the temple rather than lay people of all walks.
12:8 For verily I say unto you, one jot nor tittle hath not passed away from the law, but in me it hath all been fulfilled.
5:18 For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

I’m not sure why the Jews would need to hear about the heavens and earth passing to have this phrase make sense. Heaven and earth hadn’t passed away during the time that transpired between Christ’s sermon on the mount and His sermon to the Nephites, right? I’m not sure about this one.

Oh, after noticing the verse below—3 Nephi 12:19—I noticed that Christ said that the “law is fulfilled.” Interesting. So had “heaven and earth [passed away]” as foretold? I don’t understand what to make of that part of the prophecy. I know there was a lot of natural disaster among the Nephites before Christ came but would that equate with the heavens and the earth passing away? I would think that means something different.

12:19 And behold, I have given you the law and the commandments of my Father, that ye shall believe in me, and that ye shall repent of your sins, and come unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Behold, ye have the commandments before you, and the law is fulfilled.

5:19 Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

These verses are far different. It seems like Jesus is more concerned with pounding out the idea that mortals are able to earn heaven through their works alone when teaching among the Jews. With the Nephites, His teachings still convey that point but with less weight, it seems. Also, Jesus can be much more overt with His identity and role as the Savior and the one to whom they ought to come to be forgiven.

12:20 Therefore come unto me and be ye saved; for verily I say unto you, that except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.
5:20 For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.
The Nephites didn’t have scribes and Pharisees so this change makes sense.

12:22 But I say unto you, that whosoever is angry with his brother shall be in danger of his judgment. And whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council; and whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

5:22 But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
There’s the minor change that the judge to the Nephites is God (see also 12:21) but the judge in the context of the Jews is the law and the enforcement thereof.

But the absence of “without a cause” in the case of the Temple Sermon makes this law even more difficult. At least in the Sermon among the Jews one could be angry if he had an adequate cause, but not in the case with the Nephites. It seems Jesus was teaching a higher law here.
12:23 Therefore, if ye shall come unto me, or shall desire to come unto me, and rememberest that thy brother hast aught against thee—
12:24 Go thy way unto thy brother, and first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I will receive you.
5:23 Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee;
5:24 Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

The case with the Jews is regarding an offering or sacrifice to God but not so with the Nephites. In their case, they’re not trying to make an offering of animal sacrifice, for these things were done away at this point. They were coming “unto [God]” to be received by Him. This is a much higher ambition. Therefore, instead of animal sacrifice, God requires merely a willing heart in this teaching.
12:28 But I say unto you, that whosoever looketh on a woman, to lust after her, hath committed adultery already in his heart.
5:28 But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
The Book of Mormon sermon suggests that the crime is adultery but doesn’t specify with whom the act is committed.
12:29 Behold, I give unto you a commandment, that ye suffer none of these things to enter into your heart;
12:30 For it is better that ye should deny yourselves of these things, wherein ye will take up your cross, than that ye should be cast into hell.
5:29 And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
5:30 And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
I wonder why Jesus didn’t use the severe language He did to the Jews on this point. This is one of the very strict statements Jesus made to the Jews. Did the Nephites just not need this point made?
13:9 After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.
13:10 Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
13:11 And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
13:12 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
13:13 For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen.
6:9 After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
6:10 Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
6:11 Give us this day our daily bread.
6:12 And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
6:13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
Why leave out the “Thy kingdom come”? Maybe because His kingdom had come among the Nephites.

Why leave out the “Give us this day our daily bread”? This is a good question. I can’t think of any reason why the Nephites would not need to hear this while the Jews did. What difference between the two could explain this omission?

6:25 And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words he looked upon the twelve whom he had chosen, and said unto them: Remember the words which I have spoken. For behold, ye are they whom I have chosen to minister unto this people. Therefore I say unto you, take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

6:25 Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

This verse shows Jesus’ shift of attention during the sermon given to the Nephites. The succeeding verses include the words about fowls of the air and lilies of the field—they are summed up in Jesus’ counsel in the end of verse 25: “Therefore I say unto you, take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?”

Among the Nephites, this counsel is only given to the disciples of Christ who are to minister. This makes sense. For others, they probably should be somewhat concerned with food and shelter as basic needs.

14:1 And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words he turned again to the multitude, and did open his mouth unto them again, saying: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Judge not, that ye be not judged.
7:1 Judge not, that ye be not judged.
Jesus now turns back to the general audience among the Nephites.
Really, the majority of the differences are in the first chapters of the sermon. The second and third chapters contain almost no differences. Pretty interesting.
The elements are the tabernacle of God; yea, man is the tabernacle of God, even temples; and whatsoever temple is defiled, God shall destroy that temple.
The elements are the tabernacle of God
God’s body is made of elements. Okay this isn’t too hard to interpret.
yea, man is the tabernacle of God

Saying this after the previous statement makes me wonder if man and elements are the same? In a verse before this it says man is spirit. But if the elements are the tabernacle of God and man is also the tabernacle of God, we can only interpret that either the elements and man are the same thing or that God is housed by more than one tabernacle, which is certainly plausible. So I’ll say that it’s not fair in this case to take this to mean that man is element, which is the tabernacle of God. I’ll just say that God is housed by more than one tabernacle.

Okay, but how is man the tabernacle of God? Is this because the Holy Ghost, by some accounts, can dwell in us? (although some quotes say this is actually false). Does it mean that a portion of God exists within each of us? I’ve heard some people say that God’s essence is in whatever emulates Him; e.g., if someone demonstrates a characteristic of God, His essence is in them.
But this seems more symbolic, right?
even temples

What? Is this saying that “[temples are] the tabernacle of God” or that “man is [temples]”? It’s ambiguous what “temples” is implicitly synonymous with. I’m thinking it means that man can be a temple for God, where His abode can be. But maybe not? (D&C 130:3 John 14:23—The appearing of the Father and the Son, in that verse, is a personal appearance; and the idea that the Father and the Son dwell in a man's heart is an old sectarian notion, and is false.)

title: Does God Love Everyone? And Should I?

body.text: We are supposed to forgive all men. That much is clear.
For, if ye forgive men their trespasses your heavenly Father will also forgive you; But if ye forgive not men their trespasses neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
And so on unto the second and third time; and as oft as thine enemy repenteth of the trespass wherewith he has trespassed against thee, thou shalt forgive him, until seventy times seven.
But are we supposed to love everyone? Are we supposed to love those that wrong us and despitefully use us?

But I say unto you, love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them who despitefully use you and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father who is in heaven; for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
Jesus teaches exactly that in the Sermon on the Mount. Am I interpreting that correctly? What does “love” mean in that sense? We certainly are commanded to love God.
John 14:23
Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
John 8:42
Jesus said unto them, If God were your Father, ye would love me: for I proceeded forth and came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me.

title: Does God Love Everyone The Same?

body.text: Romans 9:13
As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.
Helaman 15:4

But behold my brethren, the Lamanites hath he hated because their deeds have been evil continually, and this because of the iniquity of the tradition of their fathers. But behold, salvation hath come unto them through the preaching of the Nephites; and for this intent hath the Lord prolonged their days.

title: Was Baptism in BOM Only For Men?

body.text: I was reading in Moroni chapter 6, which speaks about baptism, and realized that Moroni may have revealed something hidden from common understanding about Book of Mormon times—only men were baptized; specifically, “elders, priests, and teachers.” Of course, this isn’t clear enough to state such an idea with confidence, but it’s a compelling theory. Does it fit the rest of the Book of Mormon? If there’s no other verse to counter this implication, perhaps such interpretation is correct. Such an idea would be quite surprising to most members, I think.
Moroni 6:1
And now I speak concerning baptism. Behold, elders, priests, and teachers were baptized; and they were not baptized save they brought forth fruit meet that they were worthy of it.
What scriptures counter the interpretation of this scripture that only such men as elders, priests, and teachers were baptized? Do any scriptures support this interpretation?
Supporting Scriptures
Mosiah 12-15

And now it came to pass that Alma took Helam, he being one of the first, and went and stood forth in the water, and cried, saying: O Lord, pour out thy Spirit upon thy servant, that he may do this work with holiness of heart. And when he had said these words, the Spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he said: Helam, I baptize thee, having authority from the Almighty God, as a testimony that ye have entered into a covenant to serve him until you are dead as to the mortal body; and may the Spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you; and may he grant unto you eternal life, through the redemption of Christ, whom he has prepared from the foundation of the world. And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam were buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the Spirit. And again, Alma took another, and went forth a second time into the water, and baptized him according to the first, only he did not bury himself again in the water.
Opposing Scriptures
Mosiah 18:10-11

Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you? And now when the people had heard these words, they clapped their hands for joy, and exclaimed: This is the desire of our hearts.
Mosiah 18:16 -17

And after this manner he did baptize every one that went forth to the place of Mormon; and they were in number about two hundred and four souls; yea, and they were baptized in the waters of Mormon, and were filled with the grace of God. And they were called the church of God, or the church of Christ, from that time forward. And it came to pass that whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God was added to his church.

This is a pretty strong counter to the interpretation that only men were baptized. If we can assume that the group of about 250 people were not strictly males, this section states that all such were baptized. The idea that these 250 people were not strictly males seems most reasonable to me.
Mosiah 18:21

And he commanded them that there should be no contention one with another, but that they should look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism, having their hearts knit together in unity and in love one towards another. And thus he commanded them to preach. And thus they became the children of God.
The people referred to above are all those that were baptized by Alma.
Mosiah 27:25

And the Lord said unto me: Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state, to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters;
I know “born again” isn’t specifically referring to baptism—Alma had been baptized presumably but hadn’t been born again.
Conclusion

I think baptism was for women and men. The strongest reason for this is probably Mosiah 18 where Alma baptizes all 250 of the souls that followed him out into the waters of Mormon. It’s difficult to assume that all those souls were men and that the whole company was made up merely of men. Later, when Amulon enslaves them, they seem to be composed of families.
Catholicism has the stance that divorce is a sin and this idea is supported by scriptures. Consider the following referenced scriptures with the relevant condemnations against divorce in bold:
Matthew 5:31-32

It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.
Matthew 19:3-12

The Pharisees also came unto him, tempting him, and saying unto him, Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause? And he answered and said unto them, Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder. They say unto him, Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away? He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so. And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery. His disciples say unto him, If the case of the man be so with his wife, it is not good to marry. But he said unto them, All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given. For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.
Luke 16:18
Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery: and whosoever marrieth her that is put away from her husband committeth adultery.
1 Corinthians 7:10-17

And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband: But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife. But to the rest speak I, not the Lord: If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away. And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy. But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace. For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife? But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches.

The teaching is pretty clear that the ideal is that there is never divorce. God joins man and woman in marriage and no one ought to separate what God has joined. Any divorce is a sin in some regard. It’s against God’s will. Those who are married are supposed to stay married. But, there are scenarios where divorce is permitted because of the hardness of the people. For instance, if one of the spouses broke their “one flesh” that God had joined them into; i.e., if a spouse commits adultery then they break the union they had with their spouse. In such a case, the law for the hardened people allows for them to divorce.
Alma 13:3

And this is the manner after which they were ordained—being called and prepared from the foundation of the world according to the foreknowledge of God, on account of their exceeding faith and good works; in the first place being left to choose good or evil; therefore they having chosen good, and exercising exceedingly great faith, are called with a holy calling, yea, with that holy calling which was prepared with, and according to, a preparatory redemption for such.
What does “preparatory redemption” mean in this context?
Context

In the commencement of the tenth year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi…” Alma went to preach in Melek, after which he “traveled three days’ journey on the north of the land of Melek; and he came to a city which was called Ammonihah” (excerpts from Alma 8:3-7).

He is rejected by the people of Ammonihah and when turning back he is told by an angel to return to Ammonihah and preach repentance again to the people. Alma meets Amulek who joins him in his mission to preach to the people.

Alma preaches that the city will be destroyed in one day unless the people repent of their iniquities. He also preaches of the coming of the Son of God and teaches that “he cometh to redeem those who will be baptized unto repentance, through faith on his name” (Alma 9:27).

The Ammonihahites get angry at this message Alma preaches to them and then Amulek begins to preach. He describes his pedigree and reputation and witnesses his belief in Alma’s words. He says the angel who has been visiting people in the land on account of the wickedness of the people appeared to him and told him Alma was a man of God.

At this point, wicked lawyers seek to snare Amulek in his words. Zeezrom approaches and questions Amulek which leads on a discussion of Christ, spiritual deaths, resurrection, and other gospel topics. These words shake Zeezrom and confound him.

Alma begins to preach (Alma 12). He elaborates on Amulek’s teachings about judgment and resurrection. Antionah, “a chief ruler among them”, questions how man can be resurrected since God placed cherubim and a flaming sword at the tree of life lest Adam and Eve and their posterity partake and live forever. This, Antionah suggests, means that God prevented man from living forever.

Alma teaches that man had to die because God said he would if he ate the fruit—and Adam had partaken of the fruit. Else, God would be a liar. Alma teaches about redemption through Christ, the Son of God. He teaches that mankind offended God and became fallen after provoking God to wrath by disobeying His commandments in the Garden. He taught that we ought not offend God a second time with these second sets of commandments, else we will suffer a second death.
Then begins chapter 13. Let’s go verse by verse:
Alma 13:1

And again, my brethren, I would cite your minds forward to the time when the Lord God gave these commandments unto his children; and I would that ye should remember that the Lord God ordained priests, after his holy order, which was after the order of his Son, to teach these things unto the people.

Is “the Lord God” Jehovah or Elohim? I’m guessing that this is one of those instances like Mosiah 15:1-5 where “God” means “Jehovah” and “Son” means “Messiah” or “Jesus”. Otherwise, this might be an interesting case where one could argue that the Father also atoned for worlds because He is “after the order of his Son,” who is a Savior. Of course, any priesthood holder is also after His order, but perhaps not in such a sense. So the support is weak but could yield such an idea.

Also, are we citing our minds forward chronologically or merely adjusting our perspective such that we can imagine God giving these commandments to his children? Who are his children that this verse speaks of? Maybe refer to Mosiah 5 where King Benjamin gives his people the name of the children of Christ.
Moroni 7:5-14
5 For I remember the word of God, which saith by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also.

Does this mean that if their works are evil then they are evil? You’d think so. Can this concept be reduced to such a simplicity where all good people do only good and no evil and all evil people do only evil and no good? These some more like extreme ends of a spectrum. See verse 12 below. It appears that the Devil can only do evil and that God can only do good.
6 For behold, God hath said a man being evil cannot do that which is good; for if he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent it profiteth him nothing.

This clarification is helpful that the intent is a big factor, or the only factor, in determining the goodness of one’s heart. Perhaps only a “good” person can have real intent behind their actions and an “evil” person can only have malice or selfishness as their motive.
7 For behold, it is not counted unto him for righteousness.

A righteous action must be motivated by real intent and not some selfish or malicious desire. That makes sense. That’s why the Pharisees were counted as evil though they followed the law to perfection.
8 For behold, if a man being evil giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God.
The same as I wrote above—the intent and motive behind an action is crucial in determining its moral merit.
9 And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing, for God receiveth none such.
10 Wherefore, a man being evil cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.

And by “being evil” we mean one who doesn’t have real intent. With that explanation it makes sense why he can’t do good—you can’t do actual good without having real intent. Also, this makes me wonder if a fallible person’s foibles and sins can be covered by virtue of one’s real intent and motive behind such actions. It’s a stretch and maybe an inaccuracy to go so far as to think that sin may be absolved because of the intention behind it—I mean, can you really sin with good intention? I can’t think of any examples.

11 For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore, a man being a servant of the devil cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ he cannot be a servant of the devil.

Sometimes people sin because they just made a mistake and acted out of character or fell victim to some vice. Other times, they act with intention to cause harm or to better themselves at the expense of causing others pain, misery, etc. I think these sorts of motives are the truly evil ones.

12 Wherefore, all things which are good cometh of God; and that which is evil cometh of the devil; for the devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually.
13 But behold, that which is of God inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God.

Some sinners love God and hate their sin yet they continue in sin—such is the case with some members of the Church that struggle with lust or addictions. Do these people really love God and are they excused to some degree of their sins? Or is their professed love to God a lie and their sins fully weighted upon themselves? Or does the intention and love of interest resolve around the particular action, i.e., is every action judged based on the intention and love behind that action?
14 Wherefore, take heed, my beloved brethren, that ye do not judge that which is evil to be of God, or that which is good and of God to be of the devil.
So, my evaluation or interpretation of this excerpt from Mormon’s sermon can be summed up as the following:
●Mormon judges the people based on their works
●He teaches that you can tell people’s heart/goodness based on their actions
●If someone does a good thing without real intent it is counted as being evil

○This teaching appears to be at odds with Mormon’s message, which is that only a good person can do good actions. If we are to judge a person based on their fruits, but the fruits are good or bad based on the motive from which they came rather than their superficial appearance, how are we to tell between them?
I feel like I’m missing something in my first run through of these scriptures. I’m going to go through an instead of giving commentary on this I will translate the verses into simplified text.
Moroni 7
Simplified
5 For I remember the word of God, which saith by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also.
God said you know people by their works; if their works are good they are good.
6 For behold, God hath said a man being evil cannot do that which is good; for if he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent it profiteth him nothing.
God said an evil man can’t do good. Unless he has good motive when he prays to God or gives a gift it’s an unprofitable act.
7 For behold, it is not counted unto him for righteousness.
So it’s not considered righteousness.
8 For behold, if a man being evil giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God.
If an evil man gives a gift he does it unwillingly. It’s as if he kept the gift so it’s considered evil to God.
9 And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing, for God receiveth none such.
Similarly, God considers it evil if a man prays without sincere heart—such does no good to the man and God won’t receive him
10 Wherefore, a man being evil cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.
An evil man can’t do good and he won’t give a good gift

11 For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore, a man being a servant of the devil cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ he cannot be a servant of the devil.
A bitter fountain can’t make good water and a good fountain can’t make bitter water; likewise, a servant of the devil can’t follow Christ and a follower of Christ can’t be a servant of the devil

12 Wherefore, all things which are good cometh of God; and that which is evil cometh of the devil; for the devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually.
Good comes from God; evil comes from the devil. The devil is God’s enemy and fights against him continually and tempts others to do evil continually
13 But behold, that which is of God inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God.
But God tempts others to do good continually. God inspires us to do good and to love and serve Him
14 Wherefore, take heed, my beloved brethren, that ye do not judge that which is evil to be of God, or that which is good and of God to be of the devil.
Be careful that you don’t judge the evil to be of God or the good to be of the devil

The main idea I believe Mormon is teaching is that “by their fruits you may know them.” This doesn’t mean that a good person won’t make mistakes or even sin—I believe that a good man is still fallible and will still sin but will confess and forsake them.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

Do prophets sin? Yes. Do prophets commit serious sins such as murdering, commiting adultery, etc.? No*. I put an asterisk by the answer because Moses and Nephi both killed someone but the circumstances justified it. I want to point out on this subject that even Moses sinned against God’s will and didn’t follow His instructions precisely and was prevented from entering the promised land as a consequence.
Deuteronomy 32:51–52

Because ye trespassed against me among the children of Israel at the waters of Meribah-Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin; because ye sanctified me not in the midst of the children of Israel. Yet thou shalt see the land before thee; but thou shalt not go thither unto the land which I give the children of Israel.

This disobedience was serious but was different than a sin of adultery in that it was a transgression of God’s commandment rather than an immorality. This seems akin to Joseph Smith’s pressing God into letting Martin Harris borrow the 116 manuscript pages.

Now, behold, I say unto you, that because you delivered up those writings which you had power given unto you to translate by the means of the Urim and Thummim, into the hands of a wicked man, you have lost them. And you also lost your gift at the same time, and your mind became darkened. Nevertheless, it is now restored unto you again; therefore see that you are faithful and continue on unto the finishing of the remainder of the work of translation as you have begun.
Another time a prophet disobeyed God was with Jonah. God told him to preach to the people of Nineveh and he resisted and it resulted in him being caught in a storm at sea and swallowed by a fish.
Jonah 1:1-3

Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me. But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.

title: Are We Condemned For Not Believing?

body.text: We’re commanded to believe in Jesus Christ and His gospel. People are condemned and, at times, punished because they didn’t believe on the report of the prophets. But is unbelief a sin? And is there a difference between the unbelief of those in the scriptures and the unbelief of an intellectual today? Someone may be a virtuous and upright individual but find it near impossible to believe in the incredulous claims of the Bible—at least taking them literally. Is requiring one to believe in such things as a condition for salvation fair?
Well let’s first see if it really is a commandment to believe and, if it is a commandment, what are we commanded to believe in.
Matthew 21:32

For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him.

After these words are spoken to the people by Jesus He tells them the parable of the householder and the husbandmen. It goes like this: a householder plants a vineyard and dug a winepress in it and a tower and let his husbandmen use and care for it.

When the time for fruit harvest came he sent his servants to go and receive the fruit from the husbandmen. Instead of giving the servants fruit, the husbandmen beat, killed, and stoned the respective servants. The householder sent other servants and the same was done to them.

Lastly, he sent his son thinking that the husbandmen would surely receive him. But the husbandmen colluded together and conspired to seize the son’s inheritance and slew him. Jesus then asked the people what the householder will do to these husbandmen when he comes home and this is their response:
Matthew 21:41
They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.
This parable reinforces the imperative that the people receive and believe in Jesus Christ, or at very least, don’t kill and reject Him.

I find this situation to be different than the situation today where intellectuals may struggle to believe in Jesus Christ. An intellectual today need not be hostile toward the idea of a Christ in order to doubt. In fact, some may be well-intentioned and even hopeful that such an idea could be true, but struggle to intellectually accept the story as fact. Whereas the people who rejected Christ seemed to be directly hostile to Him and reject Him not on a basis of lack of evidence—they had many signs given as proof—but they rejected Him based on what seems to have been a stubbornness and hardness of heart. It’s as if they didn’t want to believe and they gave no room for belief. They were beyond persuasion.

In these modern times I believe this stubbornness and resistance to change or new ideas still occurs. It seems some people are set in their ways and don’t want to believe in some idea, no matter how compelling it may be, simply because it doesn’t fit in their desired paradigm or within their preferred conception of reality. Some examples may be people who reject evolution, the spherical shape of the earth, the reality of distinct sexes and differences between each sex, etc.

Now, I don’t claim that each of these issues is even similar to the cardinality of belief in Jesus or even that these each are necessarily true—at least with the concepts of evolution and spherical shape of the earth. But it seems that the same reactions that led people to reject Christ lead people to reject even considering the validity of these issues.

Why are people hard of heart and stubborn beyond being able to be convinced? Why do they reject something when it’s presented right before their eyes with proof and evidence galore? And is such a state worthy of condemnation in all cases or only/especially when it comes to Jesus Christ?

Additionally, while the people of Jesus’s time appear to be worthy of condemnation for disbelieving on Him, they had much evidence and reason to believe in Him. The scriptures supported His purpose and mission and existence, but the people were hard and wouldn’t consider that He may have been right. His miracles witnessed who He was yet the people were so hard that they would try to explain away the miracles. It got to a point that it seemed like the people simply didn’t want Him and certainly didn’t want Him to exist.

Perhaps this is the distinction between them and some of those who struggle with belief today. If someone struggles to believe today because the historical record is unreliable or they lack evidence, that seems different than the situation of the people alive at the time of Christ.

I think the real sin and egregious error is to reject something when there is evidence merely because you don’t like or want the thing to be true. To reject truth when it bears itself to you is worthy of condemnation.
17 Verily I say unto you, he that is ordained of me and sent forth to preach the word of truth by the Comforter, in the Spirit of truth, doth he preach it by the Spirit of truth or some other way?
18 And if it be by some other way it is not of God.
19 And again, he that receiveth the word of truth, doth he receive it by the Spirit of truth or some other way?
20 If it be some other way it is not of God.
21 Therefore, why is it that ye cannot understand and know, that he that receiveth the word by the Spirit of truth receiveth it as it is preached by the Spirit of truth?
22 Wherefore, he that preacheth and he that receiveth, understand one another, and both are edified and rejoice together.
23 And that which doth not edify is not of God, and is darkness.
24 That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.
25 And again, verily I say unto you, and I say it that you may know the truth, that you may chase darkness from among you;

I believe we are expected to receive light when it is before us and to reject light or truth when it is plain and present before us is worthy of condemnation. Consider the following verses that reinforce this idea:
24 And truth is knowledge of things as they are, and as they were, and as they are to come;
25 And whatsoever is more or less than this is the spirit of that wicked one who was a liar from the beginning.
26 The Spirit of truth is of God. I am the Spirit of truth, and John bore record of me, saying: He received a fulness of truth, yea, even of all truth;
27 And no man receiveth a fulness unless he keepeth his commandments.
28 He that keepeth his commandments receiveth truth and light, until he is glorified in truth and knoweth all things.
29 Man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be.
30 All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it, to act for itself, as all intelligence also; otherwise there is no existence.
31 Behold, here is the agency of man, and here is the condemnation of man; because that which was from the beginning is plainly manifest unto them, and they receive not the light.
32 And every man whose spirit receiveth not the light is under condemnation.

This clarifies that the ones who are worthy of condemnation are those who reject the light or truth when it “is plainly manifest unto them.” This is relieving. I believe that for some of the struggling intellectuals (not all), they sincerely want to believe and are looking for truth but the light may not be plainly manifest unto them. Why? I don’t know. And I cannot judge what is plain and what is not for every person. Only God and that person can know in reality.

But I would urge all to caution that they are being true to the light and evidence they really have before them. Do not reject something on the basis that it doesn’t fit your preference or paradigm. Try to believe. Give place for the truth. Test the truth. Sincerely seek to find light. Don’t be a lazy intellectual—do your research on both sides. Remove bias and receive the truth.
I recently realized that C. S. Lewis touches on this topic in his book, Mere Christianity. Here’s the reference:
Book III. Christian Behavior 11. Faith

I must talk in this chapter about what the Christians call Faith. Roughly speaking, the word Faith seems to be used by Christians in two senses or on two levels, and I will take them in turn. In the first sense it means simply Belief—accepting or regarding as true the doctrines of Christianity.

That is fairly simple. But what does puzzle people—at least it used to puzzle me—is the fact that Christians regard faith in this sense as a virtue. I used to ask how on earth it can be a virtue—what is there moral or immoral about believing or not believing a set of statements? Obviously, I used to say, a sane man accepts or rejects any statement, not because he wants or does not want to, but because the evidence seems to him good or bad. If he were mistaken about the goodness or badness of the evidence that would not mean he was a bad man, but only that he was not very clever. And if he thought the evidence bad but tried to force himself to believe in spite of it, that would be merely stupid.

Well, I think I still take that view. But what I did not see then— and a good many people do not see still—was this. I was assuming that if the human mind once accepts a thing as true it will automatically go on regarding it as true, until some real reason for reconsidering it turns up. In fact, I was assuming that the human mind is completely ruled by reason. But that is not so.

For example, my reason is perfectly convinced by good evidence that anaesthetics do not smother me and that properly trained surgeons do not start operating until I am unconscious. But that does not alter the fact that when they have me down on the table and clap their horrible mask over my face, a mere childish panic begins inside me. I start thinking I am going to choke, and I am afraid they will start cutting me up before I am properly under. In other words, I lose my faith in anaesthetics. It is not reason that is taking away my faith: on the contrary, my faith is based on reason. It is my imagination and emotions. The battle is between faith and reason on one side and emotion and imagination on the other.

When you think of it you will see lots of instances of this. A man knows, on perfectly good evidence, that a pretty girl of his acquaintance is a liar and cannot keep a secret and ought not to be trusted; but when he finds himself with her his mind loses its faith in that bit of knowledge and he starts thinking, "Perhaps she'll be different this time," and once more makes a fool of himself and tells her something he ought not to have told her.

His senses and emotions have destroyed his faith in what he really knows to be true. Or take a boy learning to swim. His reason knows perfectly well that an unsupported human body will not necessarily sink in water: he has seen dozens of people float and swim. But the whole question is whether he will be able to go on believing this when the instructor takes away his hand and leaves him unsupported in the water—or whether he will suddenly cease to believe it and get in a fright and go down.

Now just the same thing happens about Christianity. I am not asking anyone to accept Christianity if his best reasoning tells him that the weight of the evidence is against it. That is not the point at which Faith comes in. But supposing a man's reason once decides that the weight of the evidence is for it. I can tell that man what is going to happen to him in the next few weeks.

There will come a moment when there is bad news, or he is in trouble, or is living among a lot of other people who do not believe it, and all at once his emotions will rise up and carry out a sort of blitz on his belief. Or else there will come a moment when he wants a woman, or wants to tell a lie, or feels very pleased with himself, or sees a chance of making a little money in some way that is not perfectly fair: some moment, in fact, at which it would be very convenient if Christianity were not true. And once again his wishes and desires will carry out a blitz. I am not talking of moments at which any real new reasons against Christianity turn up. Those have to be faced and that is a different matter. I am talking about moments where a mere mood rises up against it.

Now Faith, in the sense in which I am here using the word, is the art of holding on to things your reason has once accepted, in spite of your changing moods. For moods will change, whatever view your reason takes. I know that by experience. Now that I am a Christian I do have moods in which the whole thing looks very improbable: but when I was an atheist I had moods in which Christianity looked terribly probable.

This rebellion of your moods against your real self is going to come anyway. That is why Faith is such a necessary virtue: unless you teach your moods "where they get off," you can never be either a sound Christian or even a sound atheist, but just a creature dithering to and fro, with its beliefs really dependent on the weather and the state of its digestion. Consequently one must train the habit of Faith.

The first step is to recognise the fact that your moods change. The next is to make sure that, if you have once accepted Christianity, then some of its main doctrines shall be deliberately held before your mind for some time every day. That is why daily prayers and religious reading and church going are necessary parts of the Christian life. We have to be continually reminded of what we believe. Neither this belief nor any other will automatically remain alive in the mind. It must be fed. And as a matter of fact, if you examined a hundred people who had lost their faith in Christianity, I wonder how many of them would turn out to have been reasoned out of it by honest argument? Do not most people simply drift away?
I don’t know that his practical advice for solving this problem is very helpful. But at least he identifies the issue at stake here.
Faith & Belief: Nephi vs. Laman & Lemuel

I’ve also been thinking about the example of Nephi and Sam compared to Laman and Lemuel in The Book of Mormon. Consider the difference between the ones who believed and the ones who didn’t and the reasons why for each:
●Lehi is commanded to take his family and depart into the wilderness (1 Nephi 2:2)
●Lehi is obedient and takes his family three days’ journey into the wilderness (1 Nephi 2:3-6)
●Laman and Lemuel are stiffnecked and they murmur against Lehi (1 Nephi 2:11-12)
○Nephi inserts commentary: “And they did murmur because they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them.” (1 Nephi 2:12)
■Why didn’t they know the dealings of God?
■Are they at fault for not knowing the dealings of God?
■How could they have understood the dealings of God?
●Laman and Lemuel don’t believe in the prophecy of their father that Jerusalem would be destroyed—they are like the Jews who sought to kill Lehi (1 Nephi 2:13)
○But they still departed from Jerusalem with the family. If they were already so disbelieving and hostile, what reason did they have to remain with Lehi?
●Lehi confounds Laman and Lemuel, being filled with the Spirit, until they shake before him (1 Nephi 2:14)
●Laman and Lemuel obey Lehi (1 Nephi 2:14)

○Interesting note here that Laman and Lemuel obey and believe but merely out of compulsion. It seems like they don’t want to believe and are being spiritually/intellectually lazy and rejecting truth rather than seeking after it and applying it.
●Nephi desires to know the mysteries of God and cries unto the Lord (1 Nephi 2:16)
●The Lord visits Nephi and softens his heart and he believes all the words of Lehi (1 Nephi 2:16)
●Nephi does not rebel against his father (1 Nephi 2:16)
●Nephi tells Sam the things God had manifested to him through the Spirit (1 Nephi 2:17)
●Sam believes in the words of Nephi (1 Nephi 2:17)
●Laman and Lemuel disbelieve the words of Nephi (1 Nephi 2:18)
●Nephi prays for Laman and Lemuel on account of the hardness of their hearts (1 Nephi 2:18)
●The Lord speaks to Nephi blessing him because of his faith and for seeking God diligently with lowliness of heart (1 Nephi 2:19)
●God tells Nephi that inasmuch as he keeps God’s commandments he will prosper and be led to a land of promise, even a choice land (1 Nephi 2:20)
●Lehi is commanded to send his sons back to Jerusalem to get the Brass Plates
○Laman and Lemuel “murmur, saying it is a hard thing” (1 Nephi 3:5)
○Nephi accepts this commandment and obeys (1 Nephi 5:7)
●All of Lehi’s sons go back to Jerusalem and cast lots to determine who will approach Laban for the brass plates
●Laman is allotted with the task of approaching Laban for the plates.
●Laman requests the plates from Laban
●Laban is angry and casts Laman out of his house and accuses Laman of being a robber and then threatens to slay him
●Laman flees Laban’s presence and reports his failure to obtain the plates
●All of Lehi’s sons are sorrowful
●Nephi’s brothers are about to turn back home
●Nephi declares “As the Lord liveth, and as we live, we will not go down unto our father in the wilderness until we have accomplished the thing which the Lord hath commanded us” (1 Nephi 3:15)
●Nephi comes up with an idea to use his father’s inheritance of gold, silver, and riches to bargain for the plates
○Nephi argues the reason of preserving the language of their fathers and the words of the prophets for obtaining the plates

What I gather from this history of Nephi and his example compared to his brothers is that Nephi was motivated by more knowledge and understanding than his brothers. When the going got tough in the wilderness, Laman and Lemuel complained because they didn’t understand what Nephi did. Nephi, therefore, didn’t complain and he was motivated because he knew why they were there and why it was worth it. When Nephi and his brothers were tasked with obtaining the brass plates from Laban, Laman and Lemuel complained because they didn’t understand the importance of the task and, based on their deficient understanding, questioned whether Lehi was really called of God. Nephi, however, knew much more. He had assurance and convictions that gave him more context and understanding.

Laman and Lemuel, in this history, are guilty of not seeking out knowledge at each step and therefore they didn’t have the convincing evidence that Nephi had obtained by his diligence and desire. We have to work for knowledge and if we are found lacking, it’s our responsibility to obtain it. If we find ourselves tragically deficient of knowledge and understanding and are doubting, we may be guilty of a long history of neglecting to diligently seek truth.

Laman and Lemuel were veering further and further from the truth with each challenge and their skepticism grew deeper and deeper and required an accumulating demand for reassurance. They didn’t diligently seek it, though. They were guilty of lazily relying on the evidence that was available without work. This is the kind of evidence that is transparent and available. There is not much virtue in believing in this sort of evidence. You weren’t the one who earned it and made it transparent. There is not much virtue in accepting what is forcibly convincing. But there is virtue in diligently pursuing the truth and knowledge when you have a chance.

Does Lehi’s journey in the wilderness demonstrate the five covenants of the temple in order?

●Law of Sacrifice
●Law of the Gospel
●Law of Chastity
●Law of Consecration

title: Review of Who Wrote the Book of Mormon?

body.text: The article, , is an excellent read. It’s written by Wayne A. Larsen, a professor of statistics at BYU, and Alvin C. Rencher, a Fellow of the American Statistical Association and author of Linear Models in Statistics and Multivariate Statistical Inference and Applications, probably his dissertation or thesis.

The writers introduce the topic of linguistic aspects of The Book of Mormon and how arguments are used in this category to support and refute the authenticity of it. They describe stylometry, particularly the topic of “linguistic fingerprints”. This type of fingerprint entails relative frequency usage of certain words that are said to indicate a style of writing composed of habits of word use. This fingerprint technique was used to determine the true writers of the Federalist Papers (). It’s shown that this technique is widely established and accepted as a credible method to distinguish different authors.

The authors apply three techniques to determine author fingerprint for the supposed various authors in The Book of Mormon. The authors also apply the technique to a few other works such as the Lectures on Faith. They also include authors outside of The Book of Mormon that are claimed to have written it including Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spaulding.
Multivariate Analysis Of Variance (MANOVA)

The first technique used was MANOVA. They take a corpus of writings ascribed to various authors and then determine a word-print definition including a set of filler words whose relative frequencies will be obtained for each text.

After the initial analysis using a word-print definition of the 10-most-frequent words from their list, the authors found that the differences in word-print frequencies between the authors were “highly significant” to such a degree that they assert, “Differences as large as these simply could not occur if a single author wrote the book. The statistical odds that a single author wrote the book are less than 1 in 100 billion.”

The authors did a second analysis using MANOVA but with 38 frequently occurring words and it resulted in similar outcomes. “Thus”, they conclude, “the 21 authors do not appear to be the same individual.”

The authors then did a third testing including various frequency factors such as letter counts and infrequently occurring words and the results were in line with the previous tests. They also ran some other tests and really seemed to be extensive here. All results were in line with the conclusion that multiple authors certainly contributed to The Book of Mormon’s content.

They also compared results of these against the frequencies for the same word-print definitions of Joseph Smith, W. W. Phelps, Oliver Cowdery, Parley P. Pratt, Sidney Rigdon, and Solomon Spaulding. The results came that contemporary authors in The Book of Mormon have transitional similarities in their style, which is in line with what you’d expect from contemporary authors growing up in the same culture.

Some other results are that the Lord and Jesus’ writing styles are similar, but not so much that it’s implausible to consider them slightly different. Isaiah, however, had no statistically significant difference from the Lord, as quoted by Isaiah. They also concluded that Joseph Smith’s writing style is very different from the Lectures on Faith. I guess those were probably written by Sidney Rigdon. Lastly, “none of the Book of Mormon selections resembled the writing of any of the suggested nineteenth-century authors. The Book of Mormon itself offers the strongest evidence for a clear scientific refutation of the theories that it was written in the nineteenth century.”
The conclusions from this section are two-fold:
1.The 21 major groups of Book of Mormon text we examined were indeed written by several distinct authors, who were individually consistent as suggested in the book itself
2.None of the modern candidates whom we tested for Book of Mormon authorship wrote any of that text
These are huge conclusions.
Cluster Analysis
They do a similar analysis but on 1000-word blocks. The results from this section were very similar to the previous analysis. Nothing appeared noteworthy as compared to the previous section’s report.
Discriminant Analysis

This appears to take the 38-dimensional vector produced through the MANOVA technique and apply some kind of discriminate function to them, such as PCA. I’ve done similar things to this which fall into the dimensionality reduction task. When remaining with two components you can plot them and see apparent spatial disparities between clusters or groups. THe graph included in the report is pretty insightful. Here it is for reference:


Conclusions

1.The wordprint hypothesis appears to be justified. Based on our analysis of known non-Book of Mormon authors, each writer appears to have a unique set of unconscious style characteristics. This profile of usage habits can serve in many cases to identify a piece of writing as belonging to a particular author, just as a fingerprint or voiceprint can be traced to its owner or originator.

2.The results of MANOVA, discriminant analysis, and cluster analysis all strongly support multiple authorship of the Book of Mormon. According to some of the MANOVA results, the odds against the Book of Mormon having a single author are more than a billion to one. Of course the assumptions for MANOVA should be checked. For example, it is unlikely that the data can be considered to have come from a multivariate normal distribution. However, we used the arcsine transformation, which partially compensated for the lack of multivariate normality.

I’m going to make the text green if it’s an important/substantial change or addition from the KVJ.
1 Nephi 21

1 And again: Hearken, O ye house of Israel, all ye that are broken off and are driven out because of the wickedness of the pastors of my people; yea, all ye that are broken off, that are scattered abroad, who are of my people, O house of Israel. Listen, O isles, unto me, and hearken ye people from far; the Lord hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name.

This addition to the KVJ of Isaiah adds in some deeper context that would apply to the Lehites. Nephi obviously felt that Isaiah’s words applied to them because they were broken off from Israel and upon the isles of the sea. They were also broken off “because of the wickedness of the pastors of [God’s] people.”
2 And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;
3 And said unto me: Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified.
4 Then I said, I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for naught and in vain; surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.

5 And now, saith the Lord—that formed me from the womb that I should be his servant, to bring Jacob again to him—though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the Lord, and my God shall be my strength.

6 And he said: It is a light thing that thou shouldst be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel. I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the ends of the earth.

It sounds to me like God is telling Isaiah, “Your calling of ministering to your wicked people in your days is a light, or a small, thing. The real work you will do will be after you die when your words are carried to the Gentiles and bring them salvation.” Maybe God was referring to Isaiah’s words coming forth from the Bible. I think there’s a cross-reference later on that implies that.

7 Thus saith the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nations abhorreth, to servant of rulers: Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the Lord that is faithful.
Who is this person? Is it Isaiah?

8 Thus saith the Lord: In an acceptable time have I heard thee, O isles of the sea, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee; and I will preserve thee, and give thee my servant for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages;

The KJV reads as God telling Israel that He gave Isaiah to them as a token of His covenant to the people. The BOM specifies that God is speaking to the isles of the sea. Did Nephi make the changes so that the words apply directly to his people? I doubt Nephi would change scripture when recording it but maybe so. Maybe this is just how the brass plates read. But this version suggests to the mind a deeper meaning where God isn’t speaking to those Israelites about Isaiah, but to the gentiles and scattered Israel about Joseph Smith (“my servant”).
This also calls to mind the JST in
20 And this is the record of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem, to ask him; Who art thou?
21 And he confessed, and denied not that he was Elias; but confessed, saying; I am not the Christ.
22 And they asked him, saying; How then art thou Elias? And he said, I am not that Elias who was to restore all things. And they asked him, saying, Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No.
23 Then said they unto him, Who art thou? that we may give an answer to them that sent us. What sayest thou of thyself?
24 He said, I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as saith the prophet Esaias.
25 And they who were sent were of the Pharisees.
26 And they asked him, and said unto him; Why baptizest thou then, if thou be not the Christ, nor Elias who was to restore all things, neither that prophet?
27 John answered them, saying; I baptize with water, but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not;

28 He it is of whom I bear record. He is that prophet, even Elias, who, coming after me, is preferred before me, whose shoe’s latchet I am not worthy to unloose, or whose place I am not able to fill; for he shall baptize, not only with water, but with fire, and with the Holy Ghost.
The Book of Mormon has a few cross references that are really good on this verse:
2 Nephi 3:6-15
6 For Joseph truly testified, saying: A seer shall the Lord my God raise up, who shall be a choice seer unto the fruit of my loins.

7 Yea, Joseph truly said: Thus saith the Lord unto me: A choice seer will I raise up out of the fruit of thy loins; and he shall be esteemed highly among the fruit of thy loins. And unto him will I give commandment that he shall do a work for the fruit of thy loins, his brethren, which shall be of great worth unto them, even to the bringing of them to the knowledge of the covenants which I have made with thy fathers.
8 And I will give unto him a commandment that he shall do none other work, save the work which I shall command him. And I will make him great in mine eyes; for he shall do my work.
9 And he shall be great like unto Moses, whom I have said I would raise up unto you, to deliver my people, O house of Israel.
10 And Moses will I raise up, to deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt.

11 But a seer will I raise up out of the fruit of thy loins; and unto him will I give power to bring forth my word unto the seed of thy loins—and not to the bringing forth my word only, saith the Lord, but to the convincing them of my word, which shall have already gone forth among them.

12 Wherefore, the fruit of thy loins shall write; and the fruit of the loins of Judah shall write; and that which shall be written by the fruit of thy loins, and also that which shall be written by the fruit of the loins of Judah, shall grow together, unto the confounding of false doctrines and laying down of contentions, and establishing peace among the fruit of thy loins, and bringing them to the knowledge of their fathers in the latter days, and also to the knowledge of my covenants, saith the Lord.
13 And out of weakness he shall be made strong, in that day when my work shall commence among all my people, unto the restoring thee, O house of Israel, saith the Lord.

14 And thus prophesied Joseph, saying: Behold, that seer will the Lord bless; and they that seek to destroy him shall be confounded; for this promise, which I have obtained of the Lord, of the fruit of my loins, shall be fulfilled. Behold, I am sure of the fulfilling of this promise;

15 And his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father. And he shall be like unto me; for the thing, which the Lord shall bring forth by his hand, by the power of the Lord shall bring my people unto salvation.

Couldn’t be more clear that there is a chosen seer named Joseph to come forth in the last days and Nephi believes, and has good reason for it, that Joseph will restore the knowledge and covenants of the Lord unto his people and to the Gentiles.
8 And when that day shall come, it shall come to pass that kings shall shut their mouths; for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

9 For in that day, for my sake shall the Father work a work, which shall be a great and a marvelous work among them; and there shall be among them those who will not believe it, although a man shall declare it unto them.

10 But behold, the life of my servant shall be in my hand; therefore they shall not hurt him, although he shall be marred because of them. Yet I will heal him, for I will show unto them that my wisdom is greater than the cunning of the devil.

11 Therefore it shall come to pass that whosoever will not believe in my words, who am Jesus Christ, which the Father shall cause him to bring forth unto the Gentiles, and shall give unto him power that he shall bring them forth unto the Gentiles, (it shall be done even as Moses said) they shall be cut off from among my people who are of the covenant.
He will bring the knowledge to the Gentiles in the last days.
Mormon 8:16, 25

16 And blessed be he that shall bring this thing to light; for it shall be brought out of darkness unto light, according to the word of God; yea, it shall be brought out of the earth, and it shall shine forth out of darkness, and come unto the knowledge of the people; and it shall be done by the power of God.
25 And behold, their prayers were also in behalf of him that the Lord should suffer to bring these things forth.
This reference is really good because it uses the word “light” which ties in nicely to verse 6 of Isaiah 49/1 Nephi 21
9 That thou mayest say to the prisoners: Go forth; to them that are sit in darkness: Show yourselves. They shall feed in the ways, and their pastures shall be in all high places.
It sounds more consistent with Isaiah and scriptural language to say “sit in darkness” than “are in darkness”
Psalms 107:10
Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron;
Isaiah 42:7
7 To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.
Micah 7:8
8 Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Luke 1:79
79 To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

I think it really stems from the Psalm 107 reference with “sit in darkness” and “shadow of death”. That seems to be a really influential verse. There are even a few references to it from D&C. It’s very interesting that this one word is changed which just seems more in-line with the Bible and the quotation of the 107th Psalm. But I checked out a few other translations of the Bible and they said “are” instead of “sit”. I like the change the BOM makes.
10 They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither shall the heat nor the sun smite them; for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them.
11 And I will make all my mountains a way, and my highways shall be exalted.
12 And then, O house of Israel, behold, these shall come from far; and lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.

13 Sing, O heavens; and be joyful, O earth; for the feet of those who are in the east shall be established; and break forth into singing, O mountains; for they shall be smitten no more; for the Lord hath comforted his people, and will have mercy upon his afflicted.
14 But, behold, Zion hath said: The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me—but he will show that he hath not.
Unique Chiasmus
The rest didn’t have anything that I felt worth commenting on at this time. Although there is a nice little chiasma at the end:
Isaiah 49:24-25
24 For shall
the prey be taken from the mighty, or
the lawful captives delivered?
25 But thus saith the Lord, even
the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and
the prey of the terrible shall be delivered; for I will contend with him that contendeth with thee, and I will save thy children.
What’s really cool about this structure is that, while the main structure is A-B-B-A, the verbs follow a A-B-A-B structure. I’ve found this happening in The Book of Mormon too.
Moroni 7:11

The eminent Yale professor and Jewish literary scholar Harold Bloom called the Book of Moses and the Book of Abraham two of the “more surprising” and neglected works of Latter-day Saint scripture.
