Apparently, there are a few second-hand accounts from people close to Joseph Smith in the last 5 years of his life that said he expressed the doctrine of Heavenly Mother to them—mainly just affirming that she conceptually exists.
From here on, church members and leaders have reaffirmed this doctrine be making occasional references to this doctrine such as in the following:
●M. Russell Ballard, When Thou Art Converted: Continuing Our Search for Happiness (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 2001), 62
●Harold B. Lee, “The Influence and Responsibility of Women,” Relief Society Magazine 51, no. 2 (Feb. 1964): 85
Personally, I find President Gordon B. Hinkley’s words on this matter satisfying:

Logic and reason would certainly suggest that if we have a Father in Heaven, we have a Mother in Heaven. That doctrine rests well with me. However, in light of the instruction we have received from the Lord Himself, I regard it as inappropriate for anyone in the Church to pray to our Mother in Heaven.

It’s easy to say what we know about Heavenly Mother—reason suggests she exists. That’s really it. We don’t know any of her attributes, physical or otherwise, we don’t know her role. In lieu of the doctrine of polygamy, we don’t even know whether there are one or many of these Heavenly Mothers.

To be fair, we really don’t even know much more about the Father, Elohim. We have descriptions of godly attributes He possesses and we know He has implemented the Plan of Salvation for us and sent His Son to die for us. We notice that He is referred to as Father which indicates a kind of relationship to us in which we are His children. If this relationship can be interpreted with literal application, we can reasonably assume that we may also have a Mother of the same sort.

There’s the question of why we don’t know anything about Heavenly Mother and some have sought to answer this by suggesting that God has refrained from mentioning her out of respect and reverence with the idea that, if He did mention her, it would lead to many profaning her name. I think this is incredibly silly for multiple reasons.

First, we don’t even know Heavenly Father’s name. Heavenly Father, like Eloheim, God, or Lord, are merely descriptive titles and those are really all we have for God. If these sorts of titles are accepted as names then we know just as much a name for Heavenly Mother as we do for the Father—Heavenly Mother would be the equated title.

Secondly, the logic of the action doesn’t make sense. Would mention of Heavenly Mother by God really be so injurious to her as to justify total exclusion of her? I can’t imagine any scenario where this sort of logic could apply and demonstrate the utility of such thinking.
I’m also weary of this concept of praying and worship toward the Mother of Heaven, Queen of Heaven, etc. It sounds eerily similar to the condemned reference to the “Queen of heaven” from Jeremiah:
Jeremiah 44:17-19

17 But we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, as we have done, we, and our fathers, our kings, and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem: for then had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil.
18 But since we left off to burn incense to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, we have wanted all things, and have been consumed by the sword and by the famine.
19 And when we burned incense to the queen of heaven, and poured out drink offerings unto her, did we make her cakes to worship her, and pour out drink offerings unto her, without our men?
I have read that this references the Babylonian goddess Ishtar. But the concept has been present in many forms among the Jews, including Asherah.
| President Nelson

Dear brothers and sisters, my message to you today is that because Jesus Christ overcame this fallen world, and because He atoned for each of us, you too can overcome this sin-saturated, self-centered, and often exhausting world.

Because the Savior, through His infinite Atonement, redeemed each of us from weakness, mistakes, and sin, and because He experienced every pain, worry, and burden you have ever had, then as you truly repent and seek His help, you can rise above this present precarious world.

You can overcome the spiritually and emotionally exhausting plagues of the world, including arrogance, pride, anger, immorality, hatred, greed, jealousy, and fear. Despite the distractions and distortions that swirl around us, you can find true rest—meaning relief and peace—even amid your most vexing problems.
President Nelson said this after referencing some scriptures about Christ talking about overcoming the world and followed it by asking three questions:
1.What is overcoming the world?
2.How do we do it?
3.How are we blessed by it?
What is overcoming the world?
John 16:33
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
For verily I say unto you, I will that ye should overcome the world; wherefore I will have compassion upon you.
In his own words, President Nelson answered this question this way:

It means overcoming the temptation to care more about the things of this world than the things of God. It means trusting the doctrine of Christ more than the philosophies of men. It means delighting in truth, denouncing deception, and becoming “humble followers of Christ.” It means choosing to refrain from anything that drives the Spirit away. It means being willing to “give away” even our favorite sins.

Now, overcoming the world certainly does not mean becoming perfect in this life, nor does it mean that your problems will magically evaporate—because they won’t. And it does not mean that you won’t still make mistakes. But overcoming the world does mean that your resistance to sin will increase. Your heart will soften as your faith in Jesus Christ increases. Overcoming the world means growing to love God and His Beloved Son more than you love anyone or anything else.

It seems that the world’s power lies in its captivation to sin and meaningless distractions. The world persuades with money, entertainment, greed, lust, and power. To overcome the world is to not be persuaded by these things but to change your heart so that you are above them. These things are sinful and appealing to the fallen man. But to rise above them and be concerned more of your love for God and your desires for righteousness, truth, family, fellowship, learning, etc. These pursuits overcome the world.

13 I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one. I write unto you, little children, because ye have known the Father.

14 I have written unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I have written unto you, young men, because ye are strong, and the word of God abideth in you, and ye have overcome the wicked one.
15 Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
16 For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
17 And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.

So it does seem to be overcoming the desires and lusts of the world and loving God more than anything else. This love is an aspect I hadn’t thought of while pursuing the object of overcoming the temptations of the world. How can I become a being not of this world but of heavenly things?
How do I overcome the world?

Going off of King Benjamin’s sermon, President Nelson states, “Each time you seek for and follow the promptings of the Spirit, each time you do anything good—things that “the natural man” would not do—you are overcoming the world.”

So I can seek for and follow the promptings of the Spirit. I can do good, or things that the natural man would not do. This is overcoming the world. Does this lead me to no longer desire things of the world? Merely avoiding something doesn’t make you not want it. I guess seeking for and following the Spirit can help effectuate this change of nature so I will no longer want the things of the world. Also, where will this new and deep love for God come from? If I’m to love Him more than even my own wife this will require true change.

President Nelson says, “As we strive to live the higher laws of Jesus Christ, our hearts and our very natures begin to change.” I feel like I’ve been striving to keep these laws for the last ten years of my life quite sincerely. My nature has changed slightly, but I still feel disappointed at my vulnerability to sin. I turn to sin so quickly. President Nelson also says, "The Savior lifts us above the pull of this fallen world by blessing us with greater charity, humility, generosity, kindness, self-discipline, peace, and rest." This sounds great and it's what I like to hear, but I'm just wondering why I still feel so far from overcoming the world when I have been applying these things already.

President Nelson gives some good advice here: "...take charge of your own testimony of Jesus Christ and His gospel. Work for it. Nurture it so that it will grow. Feed it truth. Don’t pollute it with false philosophies of unbelieving men and women." I think this is important. But, again, I have been doing these things. I feel like the rich young man who comes to Jesus asking what to do to enter the kingdom of heaven. After being told to keep the commandments and claiming that he already has been doing that, Jesus tells him to go and sell all that he has and then follow Jesus. What would that request be equivalent to for me? Would I sell all that I have and follow Jesus? Is there just one thing that I'm hesitant to give up? What's stopping me?
President Nelson gives some counsel I can apply in this segment:

"My plea to you this morning is to find rest from the intensity, uncertainty, and anguish of this world by overcoming the world through your covenants with God. Let Him know through your prayers and your actions that you are serious about overcoming the world. Ask Him to enlighten your mind and send the help you need. Each day, record the thoughts that come to you as you pray; then follow through diligently. Spend more time in the temple, and seek to understand how the temple teaches you to rise above this fallen world."

Pray often and record the thoughts that I get each day. Follow them. Keep a record. Go to the temple and understand how it teaches me to rise above this fallen world. This is what I want so this is what I can do. As President Nelson has said, Let God Prevail.
President Nelson ends by giving an apostolic blessing:

"With the power of the holy apostleship vested in me, I bless you in your quest to overcome this world. I bless you to increase your faith in Jesus Christ and learn better how to draw upon His power. I bless you to be able to discern truth from error. I bless you to care more about the things of God than the things of this world. I bless you to see the needs of those around you and strengthen those you love. Because Jesus Christ overcame this world, you can too. I so testify in the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen."

Some find proxy work for the dead in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints an odd or unfamiliar practice. With only one reference to work for the dead by Paul, referring to baptizing the dead, this is a reasonable reaction. But I think upon closer examination we find that Christianity is replete with the concept of proxy work. From the beginning animal sacrifice symbolically taught the children of God the concept of proxy redemption. This practice suggested that one living thing can suffer in place of another living thing, although this can only practically apply in special circumstances. An animal can't actually pay the debt of the sins of a human. But the concept of this ritual rests on proxy work. This idea is reinforced as Christ suffers as the Lamb of God. He suffers as a proxy for each of us. In light of this Christian doctrine, proxy work isn't as unfamiliar as we may think.

My friend Tom has felt that he's gone through a faith transition where he no longer believes in the faith of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. I've talked with him a few times and we've had some good conversations about his thoughts. But I recently have been reading a paper he's put together and he mentioned a few specific concerns he has. I want to go through them and write down my thoughts for each.

If my salvation is dependent on faith in God and Jesus Christ, why would my faith also be dependent on a story (the restoration) that quite frankly has aspects that are pretty hard to believe once you do a thorough study of it?

The fundamental question here appears to be why would salvation depend on believing something implausible? And to exacerbate the implausibility issue, he suggests, the story becomes only less plausible with further study into the matter. I don't believe the second implication as stated is true—further study into the restoration does not make it less plausible. To refute this idea I cite my own example of increased testimony with further study as well as many scholars and academics who are experts on church history yet hold strong to the faith.

But let me now address the first concern. Why would God require belief in something incredulous? I'm not entirely sure on this one but I have a few thoughts. First off, incredulity is not an exclusive property to the history of Joseph Smith's prophetic role, first vision experience, and the Book of Mormon. It's a characteristic of almost all scriptural history and, fundamentally, the core doctrines of Christianity. How much more incredible is the first vision, bringing forth of the Book of Mormon, and the concept of the restoration of the Gospel than Noah's flood, the city of Enoch being raised into heaven, God creating the earth, prediluvian men living hundreds of years, the existence of human giants, resurrection, and healing the blind, sick, and lame? When considering the totality of scripture, we must admit that any matter of the restoration is as believable, or more, than what Christians already fundamentally believe.
But, one might ask, why would God be so inconspicuous and then require us to believe—even condemn us for not believing?

title: What it Feels Like to be Forgiven

body.text: Mosiah 4:2-3

2 And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.

3 And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.

This simple sequence is valuable to be seen in scriptures. The people recognized their fallen state, believed in God, and prayed for a remission of sins. Following this, they had a spiritual experience with God/The-Holy-Ghost. It sounds a lot like King Lamoni and his father’s experience.

How was their faith “exceeding faith” in this circumstance? What makes faith greater or lesser? Is it the amount of belief relative to the amount of evidence? I want to say no but sometimes this seems to be the case:
Mosiah 26:15
Blessed art thou, Alma, and blessed are they who were baptized in the waters of Mormon. Thou art blessed because of thy exceeding faith in the words alone of my servant Abinadi.
John 20:29
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

It’s reasonable to see why some interpret these types of scriptures to mean that it’s virtuous to believe with less evidence. Well, I find this interpretation to be a problem. I don’t think it’s virtuous to believe in something with little evidence. I think what’s happening here is that the Spirit is speaking and people are taking the evidence of the Spirit as credible. That is the virtue. This is why Christ lauded Peter for such a belief supported by little empirical evidence but much heavenly evidence:
Matthew 16:16-17

And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.
Otherwise, the highest exaltation would be reserved only for the most foolish and gullible. This certainly isn’t the case. Now back to exceeding faith.
I think this scripture is very fitting to the topic and my comments so far:
Alma 13:3-4

And this is the manner after which they were ordained—being called and prepared from the foundation of the world according to the foreknowledge of God, on account of their exceeding faith and good works; in the first place being left to choose good or evil; therefore they having chosen good, and exercising exceedingly great faith, are called with a holy calling, yea, with that holy calling which was prepared with, and according to, a preparatory redemption for such.

And thus they have been called to this holy calling on account of their faith, while others would reject the Spirit of God on account of the hardness of their hearts and blindness of their minds, while, if it had not been for this they might have had as great privilege as their brethren.

The distinction between those who are called and chosen with a holy calling are those that had exceeding faith and good works. If we can take this to mean that those who weren’t called and chosen in such a way had either neither such faith or works—or perhaps they were lacking only one of these if that’s possible; then we can take what is said about these people in verse 4 as indicators of how to have good works and faith. It says of these people that weren’t called and chosen that they rejected the Spirit of God because they had hard hearts and blindness in their minds. This is to say, if my logic is sound, that exceeding faith requires soft hearts and minds that can see. This merges quite well with many scriptural descriptions of people whose hearts and minds were hardened and blind.
Isaiah 6:8-11

Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed. Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate
But I think the point is clear, it is not believing without evidence that is virtuous just as it is not sinful to disbelieve for lack of evidence. But herein lies the sin, as stated in scripture:

Behold, here is the agency of man, and here is the condemnation of man; because that which was from the beginning is plainly manifest unto them, and they receive not the light. And every man whose spirit receiveth not the light is under condemnation.

It is not a sin to doubt when there is not light or truth in a cause, but to reject truth when it is plainly manifest is a great sin and the great obstacle of our eternal progression. I think that receiving light requires not only intellectually believing but acting. It’s as Jordan Peterson often states, “I act as if God exists.” I believe he uses this as evidence for God. I don’t believe that someone acting as if God exists means that God exists or that the person even believes such a thing, but I do believe it would benefit them because it is a true principle.
Men are benefited by living in accordance with the truth, whether or not they believe the truth. But they will be most benefited if they believe in and live according to the truth.

But here’s a question, if receiving truth is so vital to our eternal progression, why make it difficult? Why is the Bible and story of Christianity so incredible? Why not provide evidence to rest all doubts? Why not make the truth so apparent that one can easily receive it rather than be led astray by lies?

Jacob Hansen from Thoughtful Faith describes three levels of theological belief:
1.Is there a God? Yes
2.Which god is God? Jesus
3.Which church is the true church of Jesus?

I’m persuaded that if there is a God, He is the Christian God. And if Christianity is true, it’s either got to be the Catholic church or the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. If I’m believing in God, I’m logically compelled to believe in the LDS church.

In my testimony I feel that I’m most convinced of my answer to question 3 then 2 and then 1. So if I was going to waiver, I think I’d waiver first on whether there was even a God to begin with. I know that’s odd. Because of this, my greatest challenges are not Mormonism challenges, they’re theism challenges. But once I’ve taken the leap of faith to believe in God, it’s not as big a leap to believe in Jesus and even less a leap to believe in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

In my early 20’s I spent a lot of time with the philosophy majors at school and joined clubs and did ethics competitions with them. I was almost persuaded to switch my major to philosophy but I wanted to make enough money to support my family and that major didn’t seem conducive to that objective. But I did learn a lot about the philosophical ideas of many of the great minds from history.

I learned that if God existed, He couldn’t be as simple as Christians make Him out to be. Either they misunderstand Him or He doesn’t exist. For example, If God truly was omnipotent, omniscient, and benevolent, there’s really not a satisfying theodicy.

Also, if you follow basic Christian beliefs about creation and judgment you realize that all sorts of contradictions start appearing. Like if God created everything out of nothing then He is responsible for everything—including the consequences of people’s actions. How could you have free will if God created you with the disposition and in the environment you’re born into? God would have anticipated every choice you’d make over the span of your existence as He formed you, thus He would be the instigator of all your choices.

And why would God go through such great lengths as to sacrifice Himself with great pains and suffering only to undo a problem He could have avoided altogether? Also this sacrifice seems to be an attempt to satisfy some higher law God to which God is beholden. But according to Christians, no such law can exist.

And why would God create men who, if they worked very hard, could attain the status of angels when He could have simply bypassed the man stage and created them as angels? You might offer some kind of soul-building argument saying that these men learn great lessons of temperance and wisdom through their experience as men but you forget that God could have instilled these lessons in them without them having gone through the experience. In short, there’s no benefit to men living mortality before becoming angels that God couldn’t have granted them when creating them. Not to mention all the men that don’t make the cut and are cast into a burning hell.

So my biggest problems are with the simplistic God that Christians worship. And beside this God, world religions don’t provide a better alternative as far as I can tell—or they run into the same problems. So I’m left to wonder whether there really is any supreme God known to our race.

But Mormonism provides a compelling platform of restored Christianity, rituals and theology that give me a second hope. It brings to the table ancient texts, temple rites and ceremonies, claim to divine priesthood authority, prophets, supernatural powers, divine beings, and a God who makes much more sense to me. Basically, it brings the missing elements of Christianity and clarifies God in a magnificent way.

For reference, I think Blake Ostler does a great job hitting on a lot of these philosophical questions from the viewpoint of Mormon theology if anyone wants to check out his books or podcast, Exploring Mormon Thought.

With this process of reasoning behind my belief in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints combined with my interests in the Old Testament, pseudepigrapha, and various ancient texts, my world view and framework of belief is very capable of handling seer stones, fallible church leaders and prophets, conflicting accounts of the first vision, etc. I expect much of it, actually. And as for attempts for slander and disinformation about Joseph Smith and the Church, I expect much of it to exist as I’m sure there was much of the same about Christ and his Church following His death and resurrection. I’m sure there were many lies and half-truths swirling around about Jesus Christ during that time. And probably many were based on some degree of truth that would probably startle us if we knew them today.

We’re often naively living on a fragile testimony built on assumptions that require humans to be infallible and history to be cleaner than it is. Once we overcome this naivety I think our systems of belief become much more mature and robust.

What do you think are the weakest and strongest popular anti arguments you’ve heard?

In the CES Letter there’s a section called “Science”. I think these types of criticisms are probably the strongest but they’re not attacks on Mormonism, they’re attacks on Christianity and God. They criticize the incredulity of the Christian Creation and Bible events such as the Tower of Babel and the Flood.
The weakest would probably be the seer stone or that Joseph Smith had a gun at Carthage.

What would you want to say members of the church who are doubting their faith? What would you want to say to the church leaders on how to help those struggling with their faith and/or leaving the church?

For those who are doubting their faith I’d say read the Book of Mormon every day for at least 30 minutes. Following my philosophical journey of doubts this may seem an odd prescription, but I’ve come to believe that the word of God is food to the soul and the Book of Mormon is the most wholesome form of it that I’ve found. In fact, when my testimony was at its lowest, the thread that held my testimony was my belief that the Book of Mormon was good and that it benefited my life when I read it and applied it.

Additionally, I think it’s crucial to pray a lot. In this era we’re very lazy yet we expect God to reward us despite our meager efforts. If you’re wondering why God doesn’t seem to be answering your prayers or why you can’t feel His presence in your life yet you’re spending more time on entertainment in your life than you are in your pursuit of God then you’re kidding yourself.

But, on a more compassionate note, it’s totally fine to find yourself doubting and wondering. You may be in the process of rebuilding a part of your testimony that’s built on some faulty reasoning or assumptions. Don’t make the egregious mistake of assuming it’s all wrong just because one aspect of your reasoning or understanding was wrong. Maybe you misunderstood the translation process of the Book of Mormon. It doesn’t mean the Book of Mormon is false automatically.

Also, be very careful when reading critics of the Church. Read both sides to every issue. Go on Fair Latter day Saints and read the apologist’s side. I’m not saying you shouldn’t explore issues and criticisms, I’m saying do so with a sound and fair approach. True scholars check every source and look at the context from which each reference is taken. True scholars spot bias. Don’t be sloppy and don’t believe everything you read!

For leaders who are dealing with people in these positions, this can be difficult. A church leader’s role is to promote faith and righteousness. Encourage prayers, scripture reading, etc. Also, seek the Spirit to guide you to know how to help. Don’t try to solve their problems for them but do provide resources and help. I think the “fix it” approach where you try to refute all their concerns at once can be a bit trivializing and patronizing. Try to understand where they’re coming from.

title: The Place Of The Modern Apostles and Whether They Could Apostatize

body.text: Issues like the lifting of the priesthood ban against black members of the Church bring up questions regarding the revelatory process for church leaders and whether they can be led astray and make policy decisions based on bad information or opinions and affect the Church in a negative way because of such. It also brings into question how fallible a church leader can be and whether God would allow leaders to be so wrong on something that it would affect someone’s salvation. You could argue that many black people were turned away from the church because of the priesthood ban which prevented them from being fully involved in the Church and able to receive all of the ordinances for exaltation.

From my reading on the issue of the Priesthood ban it appears that the brethren really did seek revelation and were told by God that the time was not yet for the ban to be lifted until 1978. So, if this is true, there’s not as much cause for questioning how fallible the brethren can be and what place they have in our relationship to God and following and seeking after Him.
I’m sort of surprised by this conclusion, though. I think there’s more to the story that I need to study and find.

title: The Proper Prophetic Successor of Joseph Smith

body.text: After Joseph Smith died in 1844 there was some ambiguity concerning what the Lord’s will was for who would succeed Joseph Smith in his prophetic and leadership role.

Sydney Rigdon claimed to be the proper successor as one of Joseph Smith’s counselors in the First Presidency. When the majority of the Twelve Apostles arrived in Kirtland they decided against Sydney and he made his own sect which dissolved soon after.

Joseph Smith III was another option since he was Joseph’s son and several people recalled quotes from Joseph Smith Jr. that he named his son to be his successor. One problem was that Joseph Smith III was only 11 years old and owing to this young age was unfit to lead the church.
There were some others that claimed to be the rightful successor but it appears that many of these soon failed or dwindled.

It seems reasonable that the majority of the twelve would be the proper channel following the death of the prophet. This follows after the order of the Twelve after Christ’s death. It’s also a good model for today, I believe. If the majority of the twelve have consensus on an issue I believe it’s a good collective support for God’s will being such.

I also think that the current positions of the reorganized LDS church and other sects I’ve heard from veer from the correct doctrine as taught by Joseph Smith including accepting the historicity of the Book of Mormon and the early practice of polygamy (some sects rejected that Joseph Smith ever practiced this which position cannot hold up).

I believe Brigham Young adhered well to the fundamental doctrines taught by Joseph Smith and also demonstrated his prophetic role by fleshing out the temple rites which were still incomplete at the time of Joseph Smith’s death. Brigham Young’s decisions in regards to these rites as well as his doctrinal understanding as exhibited in the architecture and symbols of the Salt Lake Temple are further witnesses to me that he was called of God.

title: Tom’s Podcast with Quinn: An Unfaithful Bias

body.text: I’ve mentioned before that my friend, Tom, has started a podcast. He recently did an interview with someone we knew from high school named Quinn. In the podcast Tom acted differently than he does in our interactions. He appeared to be more bitter toward the Church and biased toward anything against it. Some examples that occurred during the episode that support my claim are these:

●Quinn mentioned that he never really believed in the Church as a young man. He was only going to church from sometime in his childhood to about 11 or 12. But, despite this young age, Tom lauded Quinn for having doubted and been skeptical, saying that such showed Quinn’s logical mind. I don’t think Quinn’s doubts at this time reflected his logical mind but more of his upbringing and the views of his parents. It’s not reasonable to associate, as Tom did, Quinn’s doubts at the age of 11 or 12 with logic. Making such an association would be the response of someone who has doubts themself and is skeptical and quick to praise someone who agrees with them. I think Tom’s claim here could imply that he thinks the more logical position for those raised in the Church is to doubt, be skeptical, and leave the Church. What about those 12-year-olds who don’t doubt? Are they not logical?

●Quinn also mentioned that he would sometimes ask hard questions at Church about the reality of God, etc. Tom laughed as he said, “You’re allowed to ask questions but only the right ones.” His comment suggested that he believes the Church structure avoids hard and critical questions. This is untrue in the classroom, curriculum, Sunday school structure, and any experience I’ve had. I don’t find this conclusion grounded in evidence or reason. But I do find it unsurprising that some Ex-Mormons paint a narrative of the Church that is more negative than a true depiction of the Church. Antagonists often caricaturize their opponents in a form of straw-manning so their beliefs feel more validated and easy to uphold. The mistake here is veering from reality. I believe Tom’s implication of Church teaching is false and paints the Church in a negative light. I expect better of Tom based on our conversations.

●Tom also commented on Quinn’s thoughts on LGBT issues in the Church and how some people leave based on those and Tom said, “The Church is losing its most compassionate and loving members.” This is offensive and false. The people leaving the Church right now are more compassionate and loving than those staying? How could you say that or support it? And in context, we gather that the reason is they support LGBT issues? Are LGBT activists and supporters more compassionate and loving than active Church members or Christians? I was surprised Tom would make this assertion.

title: Sanctified as the Brother of Jared

body.text: Moroni says some amazing stuff in Ether 4. He references the brother of Jared and how we must be cleansed as he was and have faith as he did before we will have more expounded through Jesus Christ.
Ether 4:6-7
6 For the Lord said unto me: They shall not go forth unto the Gentiles until the day that they shall repent of their iniquity, and become clean before the Lord.

7 And in that day that they shall exercise faith in me, saith the Lord, even as the brother of Jared did, that they may become sanctified in me, then will I manifest unto them the things which the brother of Jared saw, even to the unfolding unto them all my revelations, saith Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of the heavens and of the earth, and all things that in them are.

The part that sticks out to me is that we are supposed to repent of our iniquity and become clean by having the kind of faith that the brother of Jared had. Here’s the reference to the brother of Jared’s experience:
Ether 3:7-13
7 And the Lord saw that the brother of Jared had fallen to the earth; and the Lord said unto him: Arise, why hast thou fallen?
8 And he saith unto the Lord: I saw the finger of the Lord, and I feared lest he should smite me; for I knew not that the Lord had flesh and blood.

9 And the Lord said unto him: Because of thy faith thou hast seen that I shall take upon me flesh and blood; and never has man come before me with such exceeding faith as thou hast; for were it not so ye could not have seen my finger. Sawest thou more than this?
10 And he answered: Nay; Lord, show thyself unto me.
11 And the Lord said unto him: Believest thou the words which I shall speak?
12 And he answered: Yea, Lord, I know that thou speakest the truth, for thou art a God of truth, and canst not lie.

13 And when he had said these words, behold, the Lord showed himself unto him, and said: Because thou knowest these things ye are redeemed from the fall; therefore ye are brought back into my presence; therefore I show myself unto you.

How can I have this experience? How can I become redeemed from the fall? Is that the cleansing that Moroni is talking about? Must I see Jesus and believe in Him to the same degree to really be redeemed from the fall in this life? I want to be redeemed. But does it mean what I think it means? Does it mean that the brother of Jared from then on was not carnal or fallen anymore? Was his nature changed? That is what I want. I want to be free from this carnal state.

title: What God is Able to Do

body.text: The New Testament testifies of various miracles which Christ did. They show His power over all sorts of things and I think there’s symbolic meaning behind these. I want to record a few here and talk about how this power demonstrates to me that Christ is able to redeem us from similarly gripping and devastating ailments of the spirit.
Mark 2:5-9
5 When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.
6 But there was certain of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts,
7 Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?
8 And immediately when Jesus perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, he said unto them, Why reason ye these things in your hearts?
9 Whether is it easier to say to the sick of the palsy, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and take up thy bed, and walk?
This story shows that Christ had power to heal and cleanse the spirit as well as the body.
Christ also walked on water symbolizing that He had power over death (water symbolizes death in the ordinance of baptism.
Romans 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.

Christ healed the sick, the maimed, the blind, the dumb, the leoporous, the lame, and even raised the dead. If these miracles showing power over ailments of the flesh from every degree indicate Christ’s power over spiritual ailments, then surely Christ can heal me of my spiritual disease of fallen nature and sinful choices.
He is a God of deliverance.
Alma 5:4
4 And behold, I say unto you, they were delivered out of the hands of the people of king Noah, by the mercy and power of God.
Sister Holland said in this devotional:

As I look back at my life, and if I could live any part of it over again, I would do one thing differently—very differently: simplify! It seems to me that everything is better when it is simplified—our food, our clothing, our furnishings, and our schedules. What I regret most in my youth is that I didn’t see the simple beauty of the gospel; I made even the gospel too complex. I felt it was too overwhelming, too difficult, and sometimes even too mysterious. It seemed to me that even as a young adult I had to climb a mountain of righteousness, go through a fiery furnace of purification, and unravel every doctrinal controversy known to mankind if I were ever to be acceptable before God.

I don’t know if I’m applying the principle the exact same way that she meant it, but I think I sometimes get caught in the branches of the Spiritual subjects and veer too far from the root. I must go back to the root and fundamental branches rather than the limbs far away from the root. To me, this means going back to reading the Book of Mormon and looking for faithful topics and how to apply them to me. It means praying. It means doing the basic things with child-like attitude and humility.

In the New Testament, especially from Paul, we read passages that appear to be saying that all we need to do is believe and we will be saved. At least, it’s said that belief in Jesus will save us. Of course, there is the book of James chapter 2 which rounds this out and states the required effort and works along with faith. But I wonder what is meant by Paul in the passages that I refer to. Here’s one that I want to examine:
Romans 10:5-11 (NIV)

5 Moses writes this about the righteousness that is by the law: “The person who does these things will live by them.” 6 But the righteousness that is by faith says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ ” (that is, to bring Christ down) 7 “or ‘Who will descend into the deep?’ ” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). 8 But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the message concerning faith that we proclaim: 9 If you declare with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and it is with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved.

Paul says here that the law of Moses was a law of actions and that if you live by that law then you are judged by that law, but Christ delivered a new law which justifies us not by our works according to a law, but by our heart believing and our mouth professing faith that “Jesus is Lord.” Isn’t this peculiar in light of the view that you’ve got to be a moral and good person to be saved and that it’s our works that make us good and not our belief in a Being?
James 2:14-25 (NIV)

What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,” but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.
But someone will say, “You have faith; I have deeds.”
Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that there is one God. Good! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.

You foolish person, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is useless? Was not our father Abraham considered righteous for what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith was made complete by what he did. And the scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is considered righteous by what they do and not by faith alone.

In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute considered righteous for what she did when she gave lodging to the spies and sent them off in a different direction? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

This seems to be in disagreement with what Paul said. The way Paul talks makes me think that his view is that works are irrelevant to salvation. Look at the following passage and you’ll see what I mean:
Romans 3:19 - 4:5
3:19 Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
3:20 Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
3:21 But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets;
3:22 Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference:
3:23 For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
3:24 Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
3:25 Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
3:26 To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
3:27 Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith.
3:28 Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
3:29 Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also:
3:30 Seeing it is one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith.
3:31 Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law.
4:1 What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?
4:2 For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.
4:3 For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
4:4 Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
4:5 But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.

By my reading, it seems like Paul is trying to tell us that works of obedience to the law do not justify us, or, at least, they cannot justify us. I guess you could still say that he’s agreeing with James 2 where no one is justified by works of the law but that doesn’t mean that we must have faith alone without works to be saved. It’s just that when we have faith, we must also have works, and when we are saved it will be because of our faith and not our works. But the odd thing is that someone who has faith and no works will not be saved, right?

But LDS members often lean more on the works for salvation side. I've sometimes wondered where this comes from but I was reading the Book of Mormon and found Alma's sermon to the people of Zarahemla to support the salvation by works understanding. In fact, the Book of Mormon in general seems to teach that side more than the salvation by belief or faith alone as Paul sometimes seems to teach.

33 Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you. 34 Yea, he saith: Come unto me and ye shall partake of the fruit of the tree of life; yea, ye shall eat and drink of the bread and the waters of life freely; 35 Yea, come unto me and bring forth works of righteousness, and ye shall not be hewn down and cast into the fire— 36 For behold, the time is at hand that whosoever bringeth forth not good fruit, or whosoever doeth not the works of righteousness, the same have cause to wail and mourn.
Here’s another:

41 Therefore, if a man bringeth forth good works he hearkeneth unto the voice of the good shepherd, and he doth follow him; but whosoever bringeth forth evil works, the same becometh a child of the devil, for he hearkeneth unto his voice, and doth follow him.
42 And whosoever doeth this must receive his wages of him; therefore, for his wages he receiveth death, as to things pertaining unto righteousness, being dead unto all good works.
That one is reminiscent of Romans 6:23, “the wages of sin is death” at the end there.

This entry is the first of several intended articles on the subject of Documentary Hypothesis. Documentary Hypothesis (DH) is the idea that there are multiple sources which contribute to the Bible. This hypothesis is supposedly supported by several characteristics of the text, such as usage of Yahweh vs Elohim, use of repetitions, interpolations, and the appearance of contradictions in repeated stories—which suggests that there may be multiple storytellers involved in the text.
See this article for more details .
The four presuppositions of the DH
1.An evolutionary, unilinear approach to Israelite history
2.The possibility of dividing the Pentateuchal texts on the basis of stylistic criteria
3.A simple conflation of documents by redactors
4.Easy determination of the purposes and methods behind the documents and redactions

The second presupposition has some problems in my mind. First off, the Hebrew that the text was originally in may be a compilation or a summary of earlier discrete texts. To assume that individual sources contributed to such a compilation and summary would retain their distinct literary style despite summarization and possibly translation is not without issue. Also, there’s the assumption that each individual source used merely one name for God and that the source consistently applied this name and no others. There’s also the assumption that such sources are not recapitulated by a commentator or historian scribe who would have arbitrarily applied their own style and words in some places.

The third presupposition also presents some serious problems. The DH suggests that the Bible was produced via practically cutting and snipping parts of sources together in a Frankenstein approach to produce a text that flows relatively well and who’s story is relatively consistent. Such an approach is odd and unprecedented. These snippets might be anywhere from a couple words to whole paragraphs and books. It’s less believable that a compiler or historian would take a few words or one sentence verbatim from one source and interpolate it within another text. Even if such a compiler deliberated such a task, there’s still the difficulty of doing so while maintaining the text narrative and flow.
Further on the fourth presupposition, the linked article above states a very serious issue as follows:

In particular, it was assumed that each writer aimed to produce a single, continuous history but would tolerate no inconsistency, repetition, or narrative digressions. The redactors, on the other hand, were said to be utterly oblivious to every kind of contradiction and repetition.

title: Book of Mormon Support and Projects

body.text: I was just thinking about how I could contribute to the scene of Book of Mormon apologia and discussion. I could build a really good website with textual insights into the Book of Mormon. I could show content that is helpful generally to Book of Mormon study for believers and even non-believers. For instance, I could put a chart up of n-gram references from the Book of Mormon to the Bible. I could also have chiasmus on there and language model representations of the Book of Mormon which are trained on the Bible. I could show charts and graphs of the word distribution in the Book of Mormon and the unique words it has but the Bible and supposed plagiarized sources do/don’t have. I could even put sources in about anything cool or supportive I find about the Book of Mormon. It could become a sort of hub for all kinds of Book of Mormon information. I could show scores for plagiarism against the works that the Book of Mormon is said to borrow from by critics. I could compare the vernacular to Joseph Smith’s sermons and other words.
I could host all of this on a server with a Dash site to display it.
I could also have pages where I replicate studies I’ve found on the Book of Mormon such as the Late War one and the stylometry studies.

I’ve had the claim in my mind of Joseph Smith being the author of the Book of Mormon in my mind lately. I am not wrestling with the idea that this is true, I’m just thinking about what the critics say concerning this.

I was reading Alma 12 and came to the part when Alma is teaching about resurrection and eternal life and Antionah, a chief ruler, asks Alma how it is that they could be resurrected and live forever when the Bible creation story apparently states that “God placed cherubim and a flaming sword on the east of the garden of Eden, lest our first parents should enter and partake of the fruit of the tree of life, and live forever.” Antionah adds “And thus we see that there was no possible chance that they should live forever.”

This interpretation of God’s words after Adam and Eve partake of the fruit is very unique. I’ve never heard anyone use that scripture to suggest that since God placed cherubim around the tree of life to prevent us from eating it that we will never be able to partake of the tree of life and live forever. For Joseph Smith to invent this pretend culture of Book of Mormon people who, in this case, are Nephite dissenters, and to even articulate their misunderstanding of scripture with such a unique Biblical interpretation that I would not have thought of, is pretty impressive in my opinion. For someone to make this up they would have had to think through what doctrines and beliefs the Israelites would have had and where they could have misunderstood, etc. It would have taken some pretty impressive creativity.

title: Stylometry Studies on The Book of Mormon

body.text: Limitations of Stylometry

The authors of the paper referenced above point out that stylometry is more objective than a human’s ability to detect authorship styles but still has its limitations. The authors describe limitations well in this excerpt:

Although a person’s fingerprint and DNA are unchangeably unique to that person, a writer is at liberty to adapt his or her style to a particular topic, audience, and genre; to use artistic license to try new styles or even imitate others’ styles; and to modify his or her own style over time as writing skills increase or falter. Shakespeare, for example, was famously diverse in his writing style—an ability that is one of the hallmarks of a great author and also one of the things that makes stylometry a challenging methodology to apply successfully.

Further, writing style is not singularly specific to a person. Stylometry can assess the similarity of writing styles among authors, but it cannot prove personal identification of an author. Not only is there variation in an author’s word-use patterns, but authors can write sufficiently unlike themselves and sufficiently like each other at times that there are not clear boundaries between them, leaving fuzzy areas where their styles can overlap. So even though an author’s style may be distinctive, it is not distinct enough to be considered unique to that author to the exclusion of all other authors in the world.

I think one point made here is that stylometry via wordprint analysis is better at proving that someone didn’t write a text than that they did. However, stylometry has been used in many legal cases to support convictions of criminals or acquit criminal charges. Some of these can be found under the  section of Wikipedia.

One case of note: “In 1996, stylometric methods were used to compare the Unabomber manifesto with letters written by one of the suspects, Theodore Kaczynski, which resulted in Theodore's apprehension and later conviction.”
Literature Review of Stylometry of the Book of Mormon
The Larsen Study (Who Wrote the Book of Mormon? An Analysis of Wordprints)
Published: July 1, 1980
Authors: Wayne A. Larsen, Alvin C. Rencher, Tim Layton
Publication: BYU Studies Quarterly
Bias: LDS, BYU Faculty
Summary
They divide the Book of Mormon content by alleged authorship (Mormon, Alma, Amulek, Angel, etc.) into 2,000-word blocks.

They first checked for consistency within the blocks of each author and then they compared the major authors of the content of the Book of Mormon against possible 19th century authors (Joseph Smith, W. W. Phelps, Oliver Cowdery, Parley Pratt, Sidney Rigdon, Solomon Spaulding, etc.). Basically they checked the frequencies of non-contextual words:
And, the, of, that, to, unto, in, it, for, be, which, a, not, came, pass, behold, all, this, now
They actually tried using frequently appearing non-contextual words and infrequently appearing non-contextual words in their study. They were pretty thorough.
The conclusions of this study were:
1.Wordprint analysis shows distinct results for each supposed author in the Book of Mormon
2.The three methods they applied—MANOVA, discriminant analysis, and cluster analysis—all support multiple authorship of the Book of Mormon.
a.It doesn’t seem possible that Joseph Smith or any writer could have fabricated a work with 24 or more discernible authorship styles

b.“The implications for translation are that the process was both direct and literal and that each individual author’s style was preserved. Possibly it was given to Joseph Smith word for word. If not then he was required to render it in a rather precise format with minimum deviations from the original word print. The demonstrated presence of distinguishable authorship word prints in the book of mormon argues for a formal translation in which information was transferred but the imprint of the original language remained”
c.The Book of Mormon authors don’t resemble any of the selected 19th century authors.

Another result I found interesting was that the wordprint results suggest a time trend within Book of Mormon authors; i.e. Nephi is similar to Jacob, and Jacob to Alma, and Alma to 3 Nephi, but Mormon is very different from Nephi. But one anomaly is Moroni who appears to be in the middle somewhere.

Also, the authors state that the results show that Lectures on Faith does not appear to be written by Joseph Smith but resembles more closely Sidney Rigdon. This isn’t a claim that the authors probably would have wanted to make which supports their level of objectivity.
The Hilton Study (On Verifying Wordprint Studies: Book of Mormon Authorship)
Published: 1982
Authors: John Hilton
Publication: BYU Studies Quarterly
Bias: LDS

Hilton used noncontextual word patterns instead of individual words such as “The [word]” at the beginning of a sentence, or “and [adjective]”. The idea is that this may be a better metric for author wordprints than individual noncontextual word frequencies. When he found a frequency that stood out among two authors’ texts, he called it a rejection and it was used as a distinguishing characteristic between the authors. The more rejections, the more dissimilar the authors’ texts.
Limitation, the author only used text of Nephi, Alma, Joseph Smith, Oliver Cowdery, and Solomon Spaulding, which leaves out Sidney Rigdon, Gilbert J. Hunt (The Late War), etc.
Conclusions:

1.“It is statistically indefensible to propose Joseph Smith or Oliver Cowdery or Solomon Spaulding as author of the 30,000 words from the Book of Mormon manuscript texts attributed to Nephi and Alma. …Therefore, the Book of Mormon measures [as being] multiauthored, with authorship consistent to its own internal claims.”

The authors of the literature review of the initial article point out aptly that “The most important result was that all of the Nephi, Alma, Smith, Cowdery, and Spalding texts are each consistent within themselves but distinctly different from one another.”
The Holmes Study (A Stylometric Analysis of Mormon Scripture and Related Texts)
Published: 1992
Authors: David I. Holmes
Publication: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society
Bias: non-member / antagonistic?

He measured vocabulary richness by measuring words only found once in the text, twice in the text, etc. How many words or nouns apply in each category. He felt that this was an “effective measure for discrimination between writers.” He relies on a study by himself, Holmes (1985), to support this assertion. I’ll add that while vocabulary richness could distinguish between authors, it doesn’t prove authorship, in my opinion.

Because we’re not measuring which words, but how many in each category. If two texts have similar scores it just means that we can’t prove that they’re different authors by this method but what does it say further? Have there been studies to show how many texts from different authors can give similar results according to this metric and what the distribution of scores would be?

That the “prophetic voice” of Joseph as captured in D&C and Book of Mormon and Book of Abraham are clustered together while the other texts of Joseph Smith are separate does not indicate to me that the author of any of the “prophetic voice” texts are assumed to be the same author.
Conclusions:
The formation of the clustering… runs counter to Ropp’s assertion that the Book of Mormon was written in the King James Bible style (116-117).
This is an odd conclusion and one that even many exmos would disagree with.
Another odd excerpt in the conclusions of this paper in criticism of the Larsen study:

The Brigham Young team did admit (Larsen et a/. (1980), p. 242) that they found Moroni 'consistently hard to classify', unlike other prophets. The plots in this study show the two Moroni samples to be in the middle of the prophets cluster, yet they are not close in terms of similarity. This study has therefore not found any evidence of multiple authorship within the Book of Mormon itself.

This is a flawed statement and makes me skeptical of this publication. Just because one of the many Book of Mormon authors isn’t separable from the other authors, which are very distinct, it doesn’t mean that multiple authorship is disproved. That just doesn’t make sense. It’s like saying that if there exists some fruit that is difficult to distinguish from both apples and oranges then apples and oranges aren’t different from each other.
He states that the richness of vocabulary as measured in his study for the Book of Abraham matches Joseph Smith’s results.
His bias appear clear to me here:

It is my conclusion, from the results of this research and the supporting historical evidence, that the Book of Mormon sprang from the prophetic voice of Joseph Smith himself, as did his revelations and the text of the Book of Abraham. There is little doubt that Joseph Smith was capable of speaking and dictating with a prophetic voice.

What supporting historical evidence is there that Joseph Smith wrote the Book of Mormon? This guy seems to have an antagonistic bias. He also references Fawn Brodie after that quote. He also refers to the prophetic voice of Joseph Smith even though that voice, which he supposedly captures in D&C texts, doesn’t match the Book of Mormon results in his own study.

Also, the PCA charts in his study do show distinct clusters for Joseph Smith apart from D&C and Book of Mormon authors. But this doesn’t seem to be accounted for in his conclusions. The D&C points to land near the Book of Mormon ones though, to his credit.

Other concerns I have are how well the sections of text were separated by author for this research. I think I read in another article which commented on this work that the chapter headings were left in the text. That is a bad choice in my opinion because that doesn't match the original manuscript of the Book of Mormon. I'm not confident that this guy knew the Book of Mormon well enough to know what sections were by particular authors such as Moroni and Mormon etc. I have more confidence in someone who is more familiar with the Book of Mormon such a as the BYU faculty. This isn't to say no one else can understand the Book of Mormon well enough to do this kind of study, but this guy in particular doesn't win my confidence in that.

title: Plurality of Gods in The Book of Mormon

body.text: One criticism of the Book of Mormon is that it teaches 19th century Christianity in its sermons. I think it only does this insofar as 19th century Christianity aligns with truth as proclaimed in Mormonism. But there are a couple places where the Book of Mormon varies from the traditional Christian thought. One place is here:
Alma 12:31

Wherefore, he gave commandments unto men, they having first transgressed the first commandments as to things which were temporal, and becoming as Gods, knowing good from evil, placing themselves in a state to act, or being placed in a state to act according to their wills and pleasures, whether to do evil or to do good

This mentioning of Gods is a critical variance from the traditional 19th century Christianity. However, it does align well with Mormon doctrine concerning gods even though that wasn’t elaborated on until much later. To be fair, though, one could argue that this verse is just quoting the Serpent who said, “Ye shall not surely die: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:4-5)

title: What are the Two Provocations in Alma 12:36?

body.text: 35 And whosoever will harden his heart and will do iniquity, behold, I swear in my wrath that he shall not enter into my rest.

36 And now, my brethren, behold I say unto you, that if ye will harden your hearts ye shall not enter into the rest of the Lord; therefore your iniquity provoketh him that he sendeth down his wrath upon you as in the first provocation, yea, according to his word in the last provocation as well as the first, to the everlasting destruction of your souls; therefore, according to his word, unto the last death, as well as the first.

37 And now, my brethren, seeing we know these things, and they are true, let us repent, and harden not our hearts, that we provoke not the Lord our God to pull down his wrath upon us in these his second commandments which he has given unto us; but let us enter into the rest of God, which is prepared according to his word.

This part of Alma’s sermon correlates with Hebrews 3 where similar concepts are discussed. The author of Hebrews references the provocation of the children of Israel where God says in His wrath that not one of the original generation of Israel will enter the promised land except Caleb since he believed.
Exodus 1:32-37
32 Yet in this thing ye did not believe the LORD your God,
33 Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents in, in fire by night, to shew you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day.
34 And the LORD heard the voice of your words, and was wroth, and sware, saying,
35 Surely there shall not one of these men of this evil generation see that good land, which I sware to give unto your fathers.
36 Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh; he shall see it, and to him will I give the land that he hath trodden upon, and to his children, because he hath wholly followed the LORD.
37 Also the LORD was angry with me for your sakes, saying, Thou also shalt not go in thither.
This is the provocation in the wilderness that is referred to in Alma 12. To clarify, here’s the reference from Hebrews:
8 Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
9 When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works forty years.
11 So I sware in my wrath, They shall not enter into my rest.)
15 While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.
16 For some, when they had heard, did provoke: howbeit not all that came out of Egypt by Moses.
17 But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness?
18 And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not?
19 So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief.

So what is the first provocation and what is the second? And what is the first set of commandments and what is the second? Also, it seems relevant to point out how Alma touches on the first death and the second. A lot of first and second phases mentioned here.
The second commandments could be the Law of Moses as opposed to the first commandments which would have been whatever preceded that. Or it could be the second set of tablets that God wrote for Moses:
Exodus 34:1-4
1 And the LORD said unto Moses, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest.
2 And be ready in the morning, and come up in the morning unto mount Sinai, and present thyself there to me in the top of the mount.
3 And no man shall come up with thee, neither let any man be seen throughout all the mount; neither let the flocks nor herds feed before that mount.

4 And he hewed two tables of stone like unto the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up unto mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand the two tables of stone.

title: Alma's Sermon to the Ammonihahites and The Book of Hebrews

body.text: I’ve noticed several places in the Book of Mormon that seem to be heavily referencing New Testament sources. Of course there’s the time Mormon quotes, almost verbatim, Corinthians on charity. There are plenty others but I just noticed one that really stuck out to me. It’s Alma 12-13 referencing Hebrews 3-5. There are a lot of common themes like coming into the rest of God and not hardening your heart and also the reference to Melchizedek.

It may be coincidental, but there’s another reference to Hebrews which is Ether 12 and Hebrews 11. I wonder if the Biblical references have any pattern. For instance, if you called out all the Biblical references in the Book of Mormon and laid them out, would the order show any pattern or sequence? This would be interesting to find.
Anyway, here are some common terms found in both Alma 12-13 and Hebrews 3-5; for example:
●Foundation of the world
●Thoughts and intents of the heart
●According to
●Enter into my rest / the rest of God
●High priest
●After the order of Melchizedek
●Resurrection of the dead
The Bible

There are flaws and contradictions in the Bible. Some of these can be resolved and others are more difficult. But one question that is encountered in light of the existence of these flaws is whether such flaws affect the integrity of the book. If this book is false in the historical details and consistency of its contents, is it also false in its claims regarding God and morality?
Here are some of the flaws in question:
●The flood

○The Bible teaches that there was a global flood sometime after 4000 B.C. This is verifiably false. The fossil record and geological record bear no such mark of a worldwide flood. Also, there’s the glaring problem of Noah not being able to access or fit every animal in existence today inside the ark. There are hundreds of thousands of species of animals on the earth today and no place in the world, certainly not Noah’s land, contains all such variety. Also, it appears to be just as doubtful that the variety of races of humans that exist today could have derived from Noah and his three sons in just 5 or 6 thousand years.
●The creation

○The creation accounts, if taken literally, tell a view of the world that doesn’t match what we observe. The view portrayed is one where we are inside an air pocket that God put in the waters and land is the place where God moved some of the lower waters. Also, this account suggests that the sun, moon, and stars are inside this air pocket, or firmament. To me, this account seems to be more of a primitive tradition than a true revelation regarding the truth of reality.
Here are some of the supporting evidences:
●Messianic symbolism in the Old Testament

○Is the story of Jesus retrofitted into the prophecies and types of the Bible? If so, you’d expect such instances of fitting to have attention called to them as support for Christ by whomever was doing the retrofitting. The disciples who promoted Christ after His death did call attention to many Jewish prophecies He fulfilled. This is especially true in the case of the Gospel of Matthew. But they didn’t call attention to some Old Testament symbols or references to Christ which leaves us to wonder if Christ truly was the Messiah the Old Testament points to and His disciples didn’t catch every Old Testament reference, or if they did notice such references and retrofitted Christ’s historical narrative to fit them but either didn’t call attention to such instances or such instances are left untold in the writings we have. Below are some of those symbols and references I refer to.
■Joseph of Egypt
■Moses
■Abraham

title: Aaronic Priesthood Leadership Training: The Work of Salvation and Exaltation

body.text: The  breaks down the work of salvation and exaltation into four categories:
1.Living the gospel of Jesus Christ
2.Caring for those in need
3.Inviting all to receive the gospel
4.Uniting families for eternity
Template to guide the discussion:
Moroni 10:32

Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
Ephesians 4:11-13
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:
D&C 20:59 (Deacons and Teachers)
They are, however, to warn, expound, exhort, and teach, and invite all to come unto Christ.
What is salvation?
2 Nephi 9:10

O how great the goodness of our God, who prepareth a way for our escape from the grasp of this awful monster; yea, that monster, death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit.
What is exaltation?

…and they shall pass by the angels, and the gods, which are set there, to their exaltation and glory in all things, as hath been sealed upon their heads, which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever.

Then shall they be gods, because they have no end; therefore shall they be from everlasting to everlasting, because they continue; then shall they be above all, because all things are subject unto them. Then shall they be gods, because they have all power, and the angels are subject unto them.
How are we already living the gospel?
What are we doing to help people have salvation and exaltation?
How can we help our quorums actively do family history and temple work?
Matthew 18:2-4

And Jesus called a little child unto him, and set him in the midst of them, And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

I was just listening to Ella say the prayer for breakfast as I was studying upstairs. Kaylene has a couple kids over that she’s babysitting and the boy who’s Ella’s age is picky. Ella said in her prayer, “Please help Ben to like eggs and toast…” and carried on with the rest of her prayer. After the prayer she had Ben try the eggs and when he ate them she said with excitement, “Hey I made Ben like eggs with my prayer!” Kaylene corrected her that it was God. But it made me ponder about how simple a child’s mind and faith is. They simply ask and when it is given they don’t doubt that it was an answer to their prayer from God.
Mosiah 3:19

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.
The punctuation in this verse from Mosiah isn’t to my liking. I’d suggest it this way:
…becometh as a child: submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him—even as a child doth submit to his father.
I would make this change because it appears that these characteristics are such of a child. These are the attributes that God wants us to follow in becoming as a child.

Many biblical scholars believe that, while Isaiah chapters 1-39 were written by Isaiah, chapters 40 and onward were written by another person or even multiple people. This theory stems mainly from a difference in writing style—apparently these latter chapters don’t offer personal insight into Isaiah’s life—and the mention of King Cyrus, who’s name wouldn’t have been known to Isaiah because it was during the exile of Israel after 586 B.C.

This theory challenges the Book of Mormon’s authenticity because the Book of Mormon quotes from these latter chapters, called the Deutero-Isaiah chapters, attributing them to Isaiah and dating them to the time before Israel’s exile into Babylon. Many see this conflict as anachronistic material in the Book of Mormon and use it as evidence that the Book of Mormon is 19th-century material rather than an authentic translation of an ancient record.

From my understanding, bible scholars take this Deutero-Isaiah theory pretty seriously although I don’t know what level of consensus there is.  as it threatens the idea that the bible is the inspired word of God; e.g., if what the bible presents as prophecies are actually historical references retrofitted to appear as prophecies, this would challenge the legitimacy of many or all other prophecies in the bible as well as the accuracy of attributed authorship as presented in the bible.

I am wary of accepting the full extent of this Deutero-Isaiah theory as a response to the Isaiah problem. As with other authorship problems identified in bible analysis, such as Documentary Hypothesis, this criticism threatens the inspired origin of the bible. To accept even some of these criticisms is to tread a path that leaves one with a view that the bible is not inspired or prophetic but is a biased portrayal of history that rewrites historic events and tricks readers into believing false ideas such as in prophecy.
I question the accuracy of this Deutero-Isaiah theory. Admittedly, I haven’t studied this subject extensively and owe it more time before offering further conclusions and assessments.
I was listening to this scripture in the car the other day after having a day where I had fallen short. As I heard this scripture I felt that it applied to me in my oblations toward God.
Malachi 1:6-8 (NIV)

“A son honors his father, and a slave his master. If I am a father, where is the honor due me? If I am a master, where is the respect due me?” says the Lord Almighty. “It is you priests who show contempt for my name. “But you ask, ‘How have we shown contempt for your name?’ “By offering defiled food on my altar. “But you ask, ‘How have we defiled you?’ “By saying that the Lord ’s table is contemptible. When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is that not wrong? When you sacrifice lame or diseased animals, is that not wrong? Try offering them to your governor! Would he be pleased with you? Would he accept you?” says the Lord Almighty.

I felt this applied to me in the way my oblations to God had been more like leftovers rather than suitable offerings.
