Instead of dedicating the first part of my day to prayer and scriptures everyday, sometimes I just listened to a bit of scriptures in the car or said a little prayer in my head. Instead of praying to God with all my heart, might, mind, and strength, I would just say a quick one with little thought or effort. And with these meager efforts, I expect God to respond to me and reward me with great rewards. I can offer much better than this! I felt humbled in the chastisement from these verses.
Mosiah 5:2

And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.

Because the people believed on the word of God which was preached to them, the Spirit was about to work a mighty change in their hearts which led them to have a disposition to do good continually and not evil.

This example always sounds so nice to me. It makes me wish that I could have such a conversion where the Spirit just does all the work for me—I believe, now change me into a saint who no longer struggles with sin. I think this view of this event of change for these people over-simplifies the process of change and their experience following this. I had thought, previously, that these people just had easy lives after this experience and no longer struggled with sin. But perhaps it was just in that moment that they experienced such change and maintaining it took constant effort of bringing the Spirit back into their lives.

Such rigorous effort is prescribed by King Benjamin in the sermon preceding this conversion (Mosiah 3:19). Another example where great effort is taken to bring about a long-term conversion is the sons of Mosiah. Although they had a dramatic wake-up call by an angel of the Lord, they had much work to do after this visitation. It wasn’t a passive, but active process required of them.
Mosiah 27:33-35
But notwithstanding all this, they did impart much consolation to the church, confirming their faith, and exhorting them with long-suffering and much travail to keep the commandments of God.
And four of them were the sons of Mosiah; and their names were Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and Himni; these were the names of the sons of Mosiah.

And they traveled throughout all the land of Zarahemla, and among all the people who were under the reign of king Mosiah, zealously striving to repair all the injuries which they had done to the church, confessing all their sins, and publishing all the things which they had seen, and explaining the prophecies and the scriptures to all who desired to hear them.

They were heavily involved in evangelical ministry and missionary work for the rest of their lives, as far as I can tell. They must have spent a lot of time serving and reading prophecies and scriptures and traveling with great hunger and pains and facing persecution, all in the name of repairing the wrongs they had done and in bringing souls to Christ.
King Lamoni’s father was willing to give up everything—which was a lot coming from the King of the Lamanites—in order to have the “wicked spirit rooted out of [his] breast.”

And it came to pass that after Aaron had expounded these things unto him, the king said: What shall I do that I may have this eternal life of which thou hast spoken? Yea, what shall I do that I may be born of God, having this wicked spirit rooted out of my breast, and receive his Spirit, that I may be filled with joy, that I may not be cast off at the last day? Behold, said he, I will give up all that I possess, yea, I will forsake my kingdom, that I may receive this great joy.

But Aaron said unto him: If thou desirest this thing, if thou wilt bow down before God, yea, if thou wilt repent of all thy sins, and will bow down before God, and call on his name in faith, believing that ye shall receive, then shalt thou receive the hope which thou desirest.
And it came to pass that when Aaron had said these words, the king did bow down before the Lord, upon his knees; yea, even he did prostrate himself upon the earth, and cried mightily, saying:

O God, Aaron hath told me that there is a God; and if there is a God, and if thou art God, wilt thou make thyself known unto me, and I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead, and be saved at the last day. And now when the king had said these words, he was struck as if he were dead.

It stands out to me how the King pleads for that which we, perhaps naively and arrogantly, take for granted—eternal life and resurrection. We are taught that all will be resurrected and saved from death and hell. Not all will remain in that saved state from hell, but we will be redeemed from death forever. Perhaps we ought to plead more like the King instead of assuming it will so easily be given us. Or, at least, we can plead for salvation from hell and pray that we will not be found among those dying the second death.

The King really did believe that damnation was real as well as eternal life and he sought it with all his heart. Who wouldn’t desire such a thing? What about the wicked and those who kill Christ? Would they not like eternal life? Maybe they don’t want to live with God and the saints in love and harmony. Maybe they just don’t believe it.
Ether 3:15-16

And never have I showed myself unto man whom I have created, for never has man believed in me as thou hast. Seest thou that ye are created after mine own image? Yea, even all men were created in the beginning after mine own image.

Behold, this body, which ye now behold, is the body of my spirit; and man have I created after the body of my spirit; and even as I appear unto thee to be in the spirit will I appear unto my people in the flesh.

I take this to mean that Jehovah created mankind—Adam and Eve—even though He was a spirit at the time. And He created them after the image of His spirit. It’s sort of odd though. Where does Elohim enter the scene here? Where is Elohim in the Book of Mormon? And if anyone would try to argue that in this verse there’s some kind of divine investiture going on where this is Jehovah speaking on behalf of Elohim, such would easily be refuted by verse 14 where Jesus states: “Behold, I am Jesus Christ. I am the Father and the Son.”

The stories of a powerful man being seduced by a daughter of someone dancing before them who then requests for someone to be beheaded occur in both the Book of Mormon and the Bible. In the Book of Mormon you have the story of Jared’s daughter dancing before Akish and requesting that Omer be beheaded. In the Bible you have the story of the daughter of Herodias dancing before Herod and requesting that John the Baptist be beheaded. Isn’t it interesting that this similar story happens in both sources?
Jared’s Daughter & Akish Conspire to Kill King Omer (Ether 8:8-12)
Now the daughter of Jared being exceedingly expert, and seeing the sorrows of her father, thought to devise a plan whereby she could redeem the kingdom unto her father.

Now the daughter of Jared was exceedingly fair. And it came to pass that she did talk with her father, and said unto him: Whereby hath my father so much sorrow? Hath he not read the record which our fathers brought across the great deep? Behold, is there not an account concerning them of old, that they by their secret plans did obtain kingdoms and great glory?

And now, therefore, let my father send for Akish, the son of Kimnor; and behold, I am fair, and I will dance before him, and I will please him, that he will desire me to wife; wherefore if he shall desire of thee that ye shall give unto him me to wife, then shall ye say: I will give her if ye will bring unto me the head of my father, the king.
And now Omer was a friend to Akish; wherefore, when Jared had sent for Akish, the daughter of Jared danced before him that she pleased him, insomuch that he desired her to wife.
And it came to pass that he said unto Jared: Give her unto me to wife. And Jared said unto him: I will give her unto you, if ye will bring unto me the head of my father, the king.
The Daughter of Herodias & Herod Conspire and Kill John the Baptist (Mark 6:17-28)

For Herod himself had sent forth and laid hold upon John, and bound him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife: for he had married her.  For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.

Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not:  For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.

And when a convenient day was come, that Herod on his birthday made a supper to his lords, high captains, and chief estates of Galilee;  And when the daughter of the said Herodias came in, and danced, and pleased Herod and them that sat with him, the king said unto the damsel, Ask of me whatsoever thou wilt, and I will give it thee.

And he sware unto her, Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, I will give it thee, unto the half of my kingdom.  And she went forth, and said unto her mother, What shall I ask? And she said, The head of John the Baptist.

And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist.  And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath’s sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her.

And immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison,  And brought his head in a charger, and gave it to the damsel: and the damsel gave it to her mother.

There are some differences between the stories, for instance, in the Book of Mormon, Omer, the king, isn’t beheaded because the Lord warns him in a dream to flee the land. Also, the relationships of the people in the stories differ; Jared is son to king Omer and Akish is a friend of Jared, not a relative. Jared’s daughter is granddaughter to the king and has no relationship to Akish.

title: Theory: Mormon and Moroni Read the New Testament

body.text: The Book of Mormon is saturated with references to the New Testament, and not just after Christ personally visited the Nephites. This has been an issue critics bring up that challenges the internal claim of the Book of Mormon and suggests that perhaps a 19th century writer, Joseph Smith or otherwise, crafted the Book of Mormon and fraudulently characterized it as an ancient document.

Some try to brush off these references as just a few coincidences which likely spur from common theological similarities between the Nephites and the New-Testament-era Christians. But this claim is weak in the aspect that it implies that these New Testament references are sparse and secondly that they are just common wording from shared doctrinal belief. The references are not sparse at all, there are hundreds of significant and exact quotes from the New Testament that are 8 or more words long.
For example:
Jeremiah 28:1; 49:34
(of, the, reign, of, zedekiah, king, of, judah)
1 Nephi 1:11; Ether 9:35
Jeremiah 25:26
(upon, the, face, of, the, earth, and, the)
1 Nephi 4:14
Joshua 24:27; Jeremiah 37:2
(the, words, of, the, lord, which, he, spake)
And this is just in the first few chapters of 1 Nephi. There are plenty more. And the quotes get lengthy and very specific making the coincidence theory untenable.

But another explanation is that Mormon and Moroni had the New Testament scriptures and were familiar with them. This led to them adding all the references throughout the Book of Mormon as they were transcribing the records. When they read something that sounded familiar to them perhaps they intentionally wrote it referencing the New Testament verse.

Evidence that Mormon and Moroni were well acquainted with the New Testament is that, firstly, they said that the three disciples who couldn’t die had ministered to them and it’s not unreasonable to assume that these disciples had visited Jerusalem by that time. Also, Mormon and Moroni blatantly reference the New Testament all over in their own writings (see Moroni 7 referencing Paul’s writings on charity and Ehther 12 referencing Hebrews 11 on faith).
Lastly, a strong evidence to support this claim is found in Ether 12 from Moroni’s pen:
Ether 12:33

And again, I remember that thou hast said that thou hast loved the world, even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again to prepare a place for the children of men.
Moroni said that he remembers Christ saying he loves the world even unto the laying down of his life?
Sounds a lot like the writings of St. John:
John 3:16
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep. And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.

With the John 10 reference it’s interesting because this scripture is very poignant to the Nephites since it references them—the “other sheep.” This is one particular scripture they would have liked if they read the New Testament.

One could also say that if the 3 Nephite disciples could travel to the Holy Land then why not John the Beloved to the New World if he also was privileged to never taste of death. The John 10 reference Moroni makes seems almost unmistakable to me, but perhaps I’m biased and seeing things where there is nothing? Judge for yourself.

I find this incredible reference to yield strong support to the idea that Mormon and Moroni knew at least parts of the New Testament and that explains the numerous quotes made of the New Testament found in the Book of Mormon.
Another example that demonstrates this is from a sermon of Mormon:
Moroni 7:5, 11
For I remember the word of God which saith by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also.

For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore, a man being a servant of the devil cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ he cannot be a servant of the devil.
Matthew 7:16-20

Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

This reference is a bit modified. Maybe Mormon received a version of this from Christ or an angel that was modified to fit his culture by replacing the tree in Matthew with a fountain. Perhaps that was a more relevant object to demonstrate the principle for Mormon and his people. Also, this modification could have been one made by Mormon while he received the scripture first in its original form.
Also note the Mormon refers to this scripture, or word of God, by saying “I remember the word of God…” whereas Moroni said “I remember that thou hast said…” The similarity is striking.
I’ve noticed several things that Nephi says exclusively in the Book of Mormon. It’s interesting to find these as it may imply authorship signature. Here are some examples:
Bade
●1 Nephi 1:11 And they came down and went forth upon the face of the earth; and the first came and stood before my father, and gave unto him a book, and bade him that he should read.
●1 Nephi 4:25 And I also bade him that he should follow me.
●1 Nephi 8:6 And it came to pass that he spake unto me, and bade me follow him.
●1 Nephi 8:38 And after he had preached unto them, and also prophesied unto them of many things, he bade them to keep the commandments of the Lord; and he did cease speaking unto them.
●*3 Nephi 17:19 And it came to pass that Jesus spake unto them, and bade them arise.
Note that the last reference is the only usage in the Book of Mormon not used by Nephi1
After this manner of language
●1 Nephi 3:21 And it came to pass that after this manner of language did I persuade my brethren, that they might be faithful in keeping the commandments of God.
●1 Nephi 5:3 And after this manner of language had my mother complained against my father.

●1 Nephi 5:6 And after this manner of language did my father, Lehi, comfort my mother, Sariah, concerning us, while we journeyed in the wilderness up to the land of Jerusalem, to obtain the record of the Jews.

●1 Nephi 5:8 And she spake, saying: Now I know of a surety that the Lord hath commanded my husband to flee into the wilderness; yea, and I also know of a surety that the Lord hath protected my sons, and delivered them out of the hands of Laban, and given them power whereby they could accomplish the thing which the Lord hath commanded them. And after this manner of language did she speak.

●1 Nephi 10:15 And after this manner of language did my father prophesy and speak unto my brethren, and also many more things which I do not write in this book; for I have written as many of them as were expedient for me in mine other book.

●1 Nephi 17:22 And we know that the people who were in the land of Jerusalem were a righteous people; for they kept the statutes and judgments of the Lord, and all his commandments, according to the law of Moses; wherefore, we know that they are a righteous people; and our father hath judged them, and hath led us away because we would hearken unto his words; yea, and our brother is like unto him. And after this manner of language did my brethren murmur and complain against us.

title: Is The Book of Mormon Racist?

body.text: An LDS YouTuber I like who makes videos on church doctrine is Stephen Murph. His channel is called Mormonism with the Murph. He’s done some excellent videos. His recent one, however, hit on a topic which seems to stir a reaction in many that is confusing to me. Apparently, some are so bothered by the implications of literal interpretation that the Lamanites had a mark of the curse put upon them, which mark was black/dark skin that they are willing to accept incredibly weak and senseless arguments whose credulity would make a child laugh. I want to compile a list of the references that are relevant to this discussion in the Book of Mormon. I hope it can clarify whether the Book of Mormon is as clear as I’m suggesting it is or whether there might be some weight to the alternative interpretations. Also, I’ll bring up the changes Joseph Smith made of “white” to “pure and delightsome”.
1 Nephi 5:21-25 (The Lord’s curse upon the Lamanites)

And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity. For behold, they had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint; wherefore, as they were white, and exceedingly fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them.

We see here that the skin of blackness came upon them so “they might not be enticing to [the Nephites]”. How would this passage make sense if it were a figurative blackness of skin? Yet it makes perfect sense if you accept the literal interpretation.
And thus saith the Lord God: I will cause that they shall be loathsome unto thy people, save they shall repent of their iniquities.
And cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed; for they shall be cursed even with the same cursing. And the Lord spake it, and it was done.
Genetic passing of the curse; the seed of those who mix are cursed with the same mark.
And because of their cursing which was upon them they did become an idle people, full of mischief and subtlety, and did seek in the wilderness for beasts of prey.

And the Lord God said unto me: They shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in remembrance of me; and inasmuch as they will not remember me, and hearken unto my words, they shall scourge them even unto destruction.
1 Nephi 11:13-15 (Nephi notes that Mary is white)

And it came to pass that I looked and beheld the great city of Jerusalem, and also other cities. And I beheld the city of Nazareth; and in the city of Nazareth I beheld a virgin, and she was exceedingly fair and white.
And it came to pass that I saw the heavens open; and an angel came down and stood before me; and he said unto me: Nephi, what beholdest thou?
And I said unto him: A virgin, most beautiful and fair above all other virgins.

Nephi sees the Virgin Mary in a vision and describes her as being “fair and white” and, later, “beautiful and fair”. The description of “fair and white” has no contextual clues to lead the reader to believe that this is anything other than a literal description.
1 Nephi 13:15 (The Gentiles have white skin, like the Nephites)

And I beheld the Spirit of the Lord, that it was upon the Gentiles, and they did prosper and obtain the land for their inheritance; and I beheld that they were white, and exceedingly fair and beautiful, like unto my people before they were slain.

It appears that Nephi not only describes the Gentiles, which are Europeans in this instance, as having white skin like his people, but he calls them fair and beautiful. It appears that Nephi may associate white skin with being fair and beautiful. This association could be argued to be perpetuated throughout the Book of Mormon. Inherently, this is not a racist idea that one skin color is more attractive than another. This is a subjective preference that likely has existed through most cultures. If Nephi, and other Book of Mormon contributors, thought white skin was “fair and beautiful” while dark skin was not, that’s their prerogative. They’re not suggesting one race is better than another, only that they find one race more attractive than another.

Another note on this, Nephi does appear to be describing skin color here, though it is white skin not dark in this instance. If Nephi cares to describe skin tone here, why would his words in describing the mark of the curse not also be describing skin tone? If we’re to accept the consistency of his descriptions and language, the literal interpretation makes most sense here.
Jacob 3:5-9 (Jacob says the Lamanites are more righteous than the Nephites)

Behold, the Lamanites your brethren, whom ye hate because of their filthiness and the cursing which hath come upon their skins, are more righteous than you; for they have not forgotten the commandment of the Lord, which was given unto our father—that they should have save it were one wife, and concubines they should have none, and there should not be whoredoms committed among them.

This reference shows that there was a mark or curse set upon the Lamanites’ skins. What curse would the figurative interpretation suggest is being referred to here? The literal interpretation makes most sense here.

And now, this commandment they observe to keep; wherefore, because of this observance, in keeping this commandment, the Lord God will not destroy them, but will be merciful unto them; and one day they shall become a blessed people.

Behold, their husbands love their wives, and their wives love their husbands; and their husbands and their wives love their children; and their unbelief and their hatred towards you is because of the iniquity of their fathers; wherefore, how much better are you than they, in the sight of your great Creator?
O my brethren, I fear that unless ye shall repent of your sins that their skins will be whiter than yours, when ye shall be brought with them before the throne of God.

This reference uses skin color as a marker for righteousness before God in judgment. I admit that this reference would make sense with the figurative interpretation in that we believe God will judge us based on whether we are cleansed from the stain of sin. We believe that sin does not cause dark skin, but the imagery of stained clothes, or skins in this instance, has been applied (see Isaiah 1:18, “though your sins be as scarlet… though they be red like crimson…”).

The literal interpretation here doesn’t make as much sense. One might be confused why it would matter if our skins are darker or whiter on judgment day. Unless we’re accepting the doctrine that black and white skin tones reflect our sinfulness such that God will judge based on their color, but I don’t think (hope) anyone believes that.

Wherefore, a commandment I give unto you, which is the word of God, that ye revile no more against them because of the darkness of their skins; neither shall ye revile against them because of their filthiness; but ye shall remember your own filthiness, and remember that their filthiness came because of their fathers.

Here I want to point out to those who feel that the portrayal of this curse has racist implications that God, though using skin color to mark those cursed in this culture, commands people not to be racist—don’t relive against people based on the darkness of their skins. Does this match the 19th-century views on blacks which people often point out? No. In fact, not only does the Book of Mormon urge against treating those with dark skins with prejudice, but, it also is anti-slavery (Alma 27:9 “It is against the law… that there should be any slaves”). Critics want to claim that Joseph Smith was just copying the modern political views of slavery and racism into the Book of Mormon yet these two instances go against such views.
Alma 3:4-10 (The Amlicites’ red mark on their forehead also serves as a mark of the same curse the Lamanites have)

And the Amlicites were distinguished from the Nephites, for they had marked themselves with red in their foreheads after the manner of the Lamanites; nevertheless they had not shorn their heads like unto the Lamanites.

Here it’s clear that the mark of the curse here is a visible sign that distinguishes one group of people from another. It’s not a figurative mark. The Amlicites put a red mark on their foreheads, which, apparently, the Lamanites also did.

Now the heads of the Lamanites were shorn; and they were naked, save it were skin which was girded about their loins, and also their armor, which was girded about them, and their bows, and their arrows, and their stones, and their slings, and so forth.

And the skins of the Lamanites were dark, according to the mark which was set upon their fathers, which was a curse upon them because of their transgression and their rebellion against their brethren, who consisted of Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam, who were just and holy men.

This wording “the skins… were dark” is so clear in this context that it’s difficult to see how someone could think this reference were referring to a figurative darkness. The literal interpretation best fits here.
And their brethren sought to destroy them, therefore they were cursed; and the Lord God set a mark upon them, yea, upon Laman and Lemuel, and also the sons of Ishmael, and Ishmaelitish women.

And this was done that their seed might be distinguished from the seed of their brethren, that thereby the Lord God might preserve his people, that they might not mix and believe in incorrect traditions which would prove their destruction.
And it came to pass that whosoever did mingle his seed with that of the Lamanites did bring the same curse upon his seed.
Therefore, whosoever suffered himself to be led away by the Lamanites was called under that head, and there was a mark set upon him.

This clarifies the purpose and mark of the curse. The purpose is to prevent intermarrying between the Nephites and Lamanites so as to avoid the Nephites adopting the incorrect traditions of the Lamanites. This concept of God condemning intermarriage with heathen nations is prevalent all throughout the Old Testament from Noah to the Israelites to King Solomon. The mark of the curse is a visible distinguishing characteristic that was passed genetically—“whosoever did mingle his seed with that of the Lamanites did bring the same curse upon his seed”. We see that those who intermarried did not bring the mark upon themselves, but upon their seed. This goes perfectly in line with the dark skin being literal but doesn’t make much sense with it being figurative.
3 Nephi 2:14-15 (The Lamanites unite with the Nephites and their curse is taken and their skin becomes white)
And it came to pass that those Lamanites who had united with the Nephites were numbered among the Nephites;
And their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white like unto the Nephites;
And their young men and their daughters became exceedingly fair, and they were numbered among the Nephites, and were called Nephites. And thus ended the thirteenth year.

When the Lamanites become righteous and join the Nephites, their skin becomes white like the Nephites’ skin. It appears, again, that the mark of the curse is taken from the seed and not those who may be intermarrying.
Joseph changing “white” to “pure and delightsome”

The 1840 edition of the Book of Mormon changed a few phrases of “...they shall be a white and a delightsome people”, such as in 2 Nephi 30:6, to “...they shall be a pure and a delightsome people.” This change, which was likely made by Joseph Smith, suggests that, for at least these instances, “white” can be substituted for “pure”, which reflects a more figurative than literal meaning.

I admit that this change does offer a more figurative meaning, but “pure” seems quite synonymous with both the literal and figurative interpretations in this context. Here are some examples where similar points are being made as in this scripture.
2 Nephi 5:21

And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity. For behold, they had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint; wherefore, as they were white, and exceedingly fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them.
This is clearly describing a visible marker and characteristic such that it leads the Nephites to be less enticed by the Lamanites.
2 Nephi 30:6

And then shall they rejoice; for they shall know that it is a blessing unto them from the hand of God; and their scales of darkness shall begin to fall from their eyes; and many generations shall not pass away among them, save they shall be a pure and delightsome people.

Is this describing the physical appearance of the Lamanites or their spiritual state? I don’t know. I could see it both ways. If it said “white” instead of “pure” then I would say it sounded more like a physical description but when “pure” is used it sounds more figurative.
4 Nephi 1:10
And now, behold, it came to pass that the people of Nephi did wax strong, and did multiply exceedingly fast, and became an exceedingly fair and delightsome people.
Probably just describing the people as being visibly and behaviorally attractive and pleasant.

I don’t see how the change of “white” to “pure” in the named instance would give us logical permission to apply a literal-to-figurative meaning transformation to all instances of not only the word “white”, but “black” and “dark”, especially when such descriptors are clearly being applied to skin tone.

title: What do the scriptures teach about how to pray?

body.text: If a person wanted to learn about praying to God and knew nothing about the topic, what would they learn from reading the scriptures? How would the scriptures teach such a person to pray?
Genesis 4:26
And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the Lord.
From this scripture we learn that the ancients of the human race called upon the name of the Lord. This isn’t very descriptive but it does give an idea that one could call upon God to talk.
Genesis 13:4
Unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first: and there Abram called on the name of the Lord.
The example is given of, again, calling upon the name of the Lord, but this time in the context of sacrificing in conjunction with calling upon God’s name.
1 Samuel 12:23
Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way:

Samuel, a prophet, sets an example of the good and right way by not ceasing to pray for Israel. Here we get the mention of prayer but are not instructed in this reference how to pray, only that one can pray for another person or group of people.

title: What’s Spiritual Death and am I Spiritually Dead?

body.text: And because of the way of deliverance of our God, the Holy One of Israel, this death, of which I have spoken, which is the temporal, shall deliver up its dead; which death is the grave.

And this death of which I have spoken, which is the spiritual death, shall deliver up its dead; which spiritual death is hell; wherefore, death and hell must deliver up their dead, and hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies, and the bodies and the spirits of men will be restored one to the other; and it is by the power of the resurrection of the Holy One of Israel.
According to this verse, physical death is when our bodies die and our spirits leave our bodies; and spiritual death is hell.
What is this hell referred to? The answer seems to lie in a preceding excerpt:
2 Nephi 9:8-9

O the wisdom of God, his mercy and grace! For behold, if the flesh should rise no more our spirits must become subject to that angel who fell from before the presence of the Eternal God, and became the devil, to rise no more.

And our spirits must have become like unto him, and we become devils, angels to a devil, to be shut out from the presence of our God, and to remain with the father of lies, in misery, like unto himself…
Guide to the Scriptures: Death, Spiritual

Separation from God and His influences; to die as to things pertaining to righteousness. Lucifer and a third part of the hosts of heaven suffered a spiritual death when they were cast out of heaven (D&C 29:36–37).

Spiritual death was introduced into the world by the Fall of Adam (Moses 6:48). Mortals with evil thoughts, words, and works are spiritually dead while still alive on earth (1 Tim. 5:6). Through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and by obedience to the principles and ordinances of the gospel, men and women can become clean from sin and overcome spiritual death.

Spiritual death also occurs following the death of the mortal body. Both resurrected beings and the devil and his angels will be judged. Those who have willfully rebelled against the light and truth of the gospel will suffer spiritual death. This death is often called the second death (Alma 12:16; Hel. 14:16–19; D&C 76:36–38).

The separation from God and his light, righteousness, etc., is what I’ve thought of as spiritual death. When we’re cut off from God and His virtue then we’re dead and can’t produce good of ourselves. We’re left to carnal and sensual natural desires and overcome by them. We’re to live out in misery and sin.

But what does it mean to be cut off from God? As far as I know, Adam and Eve were cut off from God’s presence when they partook of the forbidden fruit. That was a spiritual death for them then, right? They were no longer physically in God’s presence. But they didn’t immediately become totally depraved and wicked. Adam and Eve were still good and sought after righteousness through obedience to God who spoke to them through angels (Alma 12:29 “Therefore he sent angels to converse with them, who caused men to behold of his glory.”).

This is where it gets a bit confusing. Is spiritual death something that happens based on one’s physical proximity to God? Are all of Adam’s and Eve’s seed born spiritually dead, just as their parents, being physically cut off from God’s presence? This following scripture sheds some light on the topic:

6 But behold, it was appointed unto man to die—therefore, as they were cut off from the tree of life they should be cut off from the face of the earth—and man became lost forever, yea, they became fallen man.
7 And now, ye see by this that our first parents were cut off both temporally and spiritually from the presence of the Lord; and thus we see they became subjects to follow after their own will.
8 Now behold, it was not expedient that man should be reclaimed from this temporal death, for that would destroy the great plan of happiness.

9 Therefore, as the soul could never die, and the fall had brought upon all mankind a spiritual death as well as a temporal, that is, they were cut off from the presence of the Lord, it was expedient that mankind should be reclaimed from this spiritual death.
10 Therefore, as they had become carnal, sensual, and devilish, by nature, this probationary state became a state for them to prepare; it became a preparatory state.
11 And now remember, my son, if it were not for the plan of redemption, (laying it aside) as soon as they were dead their souls were miserable, being cut off from the presence of the Lord.

This lays out the doctrine as initially described: Spiritual death is being physically cut off from the presence of the Lord. Adam and Eve, after they partook of the forbidden fruit, brought upon themselves physical and spiritual death. Now, just as physical death didn’t come immediately but was prolonged that Adam and Eve might have a probationary period, perhaps the spiritual death didn’t occur immediately either but as spiritual life slowly faded as God’s presence was removed. One could also argue, though, in a strict sense, physical death is clearly defined as the separation of body and spirit and spiritual death is clearly defined as the separation of God and the soul. By this definition, Adam and Eve, and all their posterity, spiritually fell the moment God’s presence removed from them and it was not done gradually.
And thus we see, that there was a time granted unto man to repent, yea, a probationary time, a time to repent and serve God.

Therefore, according to justice, the plan of redemption could not be brought about, only on conditions of repentance of men in this probationary state, yea, this preparatory state; for except it were for these conditions, mercy could not take effect except it should destroy the work of justice. Now the work of justice could not be destroyed; if so, God would cease to be God.
Doctrine and Covenants has some elaboration on this discussion:

Wherefore, it came to pass that the devil tempted Adam, and he partook of the forbidden fruit and transgressed the commandment, wherein he became subject to the will of the devil, because he yielded unto temptation.

Wherefore, I, the Lord God, caused that he should be cast out from the Garden of Eden, from my presence, because of his transgression, wherein he became spiritually dead, which is the first death, even that same death which is the last death, which is spiritual, which shall be pronounced upon the wicked when I shall say: Depart, ye cursed.
And they that believe not unto eternal damnation; for they cannot be redeemed from their spiritual fall, because they repent not;

According to the scriptures that I’ve included, it appears that mankind, while living in mortality, and by being of the seed of Adam, are physically cut off from the presence of God and are therefore spiritually dead. I believe this applies to all humans who are the seed of Adam from the moment they are born to the time of their resurrection when they are reconciled back to the presence of God by Christ (1 Colossians 1:22).
So, can we have spiritual life restored unto us while in this earthly life? How could we unless we were restored back in the presence of this life?
Paul said:
Romans 8:6
For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.

Does he mean that to be spiritually minded makes us spiritually alive again? I don’t think so. I think he’s just saying that if we’re spiritually minded it will lead us to life and peace. Just as to be carnally minded doesn’t make one immediately dead but, instead, leads one to death.
Samuel, from the Book of Mormon, teaches that the first spiritual death is not resolved to spiritual life until the resurrection when we are brought back into the presence of God:
Helaman 14:15-19

15 For behold, he surely must die that salvation may come; yea, it behooveth him and becometh expedient that he dieth, to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, that thereby men may be brought into the presence of the Lord.

16 Yea, behold, this death bringeth to pass the resurrection, and redeemeth all mankind from the first death—that spiritual death; for all mankind, by the fall of Adam being cut off from the presence of the Lord, are considered as dead, both as to things temporal and to things spiritual.
17 But behold, the resurrection of Christ redeemeth mankind, yea, even all mankind, and bringeth them back into the presence of the Lord.

18 Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
19 Therefore repent ye, repent ye, lest by knowing these things and not doing them ye shall suffer yourselves to come under condemnation, and ye are brought down unto this second death.

It seems pretty clear that spiritual life is not restored until we are resurrected and brought back into the presence of God. There do appear to be possible exceptions to this rule, however. Consider the Brother of Jared:
Ether 3:13

And when he had said these words, behold, the Lord showed himself unto him, and said: Because thou knowest these things ye are redeemed from the fall; therefore ye are brought back into my presence; therefore I show myself unto you.

This suggests that man, at least temporarily—if not permanently—can be redeemed from the first spiritual death while being mortal and living in this fallen world. I would say that these types of exceptions are rare. Perhaps there are saintly beings who have become spiritually alive while in this life. But to do so, such persons must literally come back into the presence of God. I suppose it’s after that instance that God may or may not leave them but they remain spiritually alive. This aspect isn’t clear to me. Perhaps this is how Christ lived, having never sinned and not being the seed of Adam, he was exempt from the curse of the fall and was not subject to spiritual death.

I had a friend yesterday with whom I spoke on the phone and we were talking about progressing in life with regards to spirituality. He challenged me on the idea that sin was the problem of spiritual progression. What he meant was that he thought our fallen nature was the problem more so than our actions. I concurred with this idea when it was formulated, but when he first expressed it he merely challenged the idea that Jesus condemned sin. If that is the question, whether Jesus condemns sin, here’s a good response. I got this response from Google’s AI bot, Bard:
[question]
A friend challenged me on the idea that Jesus condemned sin. What scriptural support is there for that idea that Jesus condemned sin?
[response]
Sure, there is a lot of scriptural support for the idea that Jesus condemned sin. Here are a few examples:
Matthew 15:19-20
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person.

For it is from within, out of a person's heart, that evil thoughts come—sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, malice, deceit, lewdness, envy, slander, arrogance, and folly. All these evils come from inside and defile a person.

The Pharisee stood up and prayed about himself: 'God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.'
John 8:1-11

But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them. The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery. They made her stand before the group and said to Jesus, 'Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?'

In these passages, Jesus clearly condemns sin. He calls out the evil thoughts and actions that come from people's hearts. He also condemns the religious leaders who were more concerned with their own self-righteousness than with helping others.

Jesus' condemnation of sin is not meant to make us feel guilty or ashamed. It is meant to help us understand the destructive power of sin and to turn away from it. When we sin, we are not only hurting ourselves, but we are also hurting others and separating ourselves from God.

Jesus' condemnation of sin is also a reminder of his love for us. He knows that we are capable of sinning, but he loves us anyway. He came to earth to die for our sins, so that we could be forgiven and have a relationship with him.
If you are struggling with sin, I encourage you to turn to Jesus for help. He is the only one who can truly set you free from its power.

title: Do Actions Matter or Only Heart?

body.text: Do our actions matter or only our heart acting behind such actions? Here are a few scriptures that support the idea that God looks upon our heart:
1 Samuel 16:7
…The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.
Hebrews 4:12
For the word of God is alive and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it penetrates even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow; it judges the thoughts and attitudes of the heart.
For I, the Lord, will judge all men according to their works, according to the desire of their hearts.
But then you also have scriptures like these which leave me questioning whether we can really say our actions don’t matter, only our heart:
Alma 5:15

Do ye exercise faith in the redemption of him who created you? Do you look forward with an eye of faith, and view this mortal body raised in immortality, and this corruption raised in incorruption, to stand before God to be judged according to the deeds which have been done in the mortal body?
Helaman 15:4

But behold my brethren, the Lamanites hath he hated because their deeds have been evil continually, and this because of the iniquity of the tradition of their fathers. But behold, salvation hath come unto them through the preaching of the Nephites; and for this intent hath the Lord prolonged their days.
3 Nephi 26:4-5

And even unto the great and last day, when all people, and all kindreds, and all nations and tongues shall stand before God, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil—If they be good, to the resurrection of everlasting life; and if they be evil, to the resurrection of damnation; being on a parallel, the one on the one hand and the other on the other hand, according to the mercy, and the justice, and the holiness which is in Christ, who was before the world began.
One section that talks about this subject a lot is Moroni 7 where there is a sermon recorded from Mormon.
Moroni 7:5-13

For I remember the word of God, which saith by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also. For behold, God hath said a man being evil cannot do that which is good; for if he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent it profiteth him nothing. For behold, it is not counted unto him for righteousness.

For behold, if a man being evil giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God. And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing, for God receiveth none such.

Wherefore, a man being evil cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift. For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore, a man being a servant of the devil cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ he cannot be a servant of the devil.

Wherefore, all things which are good cometh of God; and that which is evil cometh of the devil; for the devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually. But behold, that which is of God inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God.

Mormon is saying that you can know the inner virtue of a person based on their actions—only those with a good and pure heart can do good. The odd part is that he acknowledges that an evil man can give a gift, but when he does so he does it grudgingly and it’s not acceptable before God. He also notes that a man can pray and not with real intent and it’s unprofitable and unacceptable before God.

This leaves me wondering whether Mormon is saying that the actions of a person perfectly reflect their heart or that the heart is what matters, not the action. If both an evil and good person can give a gift and pray, which would both be considered fruits in the sense used here, then how can we discern these two apart?

title: Is There a Devil and Who is He?

body.text: I was just realizing this morning as I was reading the Isaiah sections from the Book of Mormon that the concept of the devil is vastly different in the Old Testament than in the New Testament and the Book of Mormon. title: What Does it Mean to Worship God?

body.text: 2 Nephi 25:29
…wherefore ye must bow down before him, and worship him with all your might, mind, and strength, and your whole soul; and if ye do this ye shall in nowise be cast out.
Moses 1:15

Blessed be the name of my God, for his Spirit hath not altogether withdrawn from me, or else where is thy glory, for it is darkness unto me? And I can judge between thee and God; for God said unto me: Worship God, for him only shalt thou serve.
Exodus 34:14
For thou shalt worship no other god: for the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
1 Chronicles 16:29
Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name: bring an offering, and come before him: worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness.
John 9:38
And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him.
Revelation 19:10

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
Revelation 22:9
Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.
These are a few instances where God commands His followers to worship Him or to not worship idols or any others beside Him.
Is there progression between the kingdoms after final judgment? What do the scriptures say about final judgment?
Alma 41:3

And it is requisite with the justice of God that men should be judged according to their works; and if their works were good in this life, and the desires of their hearts were good, that they should also, at the last day, be restored unto that which is good.
So there is a time when each man will be judged according to his works and desires of his heart.
Mosiah 2:38-39

Therefore if that man repenteth not, and remaineth and dieth an enemy to God, the demands of divine justice do awaken his immortal soul to a lively sense of his own guilt, which doth cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord, and doth fill his breast with guilt, and pain, and anguish, which is like an unquenchable fire, whose flame ascendeth up forever and ever.
And now I say unto you, that mercy hath no claim on that man; therefore his final doom is to endure a never-ending torment.
King Benjamin says that he who does not repent will have to endure a final doom of never-ending torment.
But wait, what about D&C 19 where Joseph Smith receives revelation about what this endless torment is?
4 And surely every man must repent or suffer, for I, God, am endless.
5 Wherefore, I revoke not the judgments which I shall pass, but woes shall go forth, weeping, wailing and gnashing of teeth, yea, to those who are found on my left hand.
6 Nevertheless, it is not written that there shall be no end to this torment, but it is written endless torment.
7 Again, it is written eternal damnation; wherefore it is more express than other scriptures, that it might work upon the hearts of the children of men, altogether for my name's glory.
8 Wherefore, I will explain unto you this mystery, for it is meet unto you to know even as mine apostles.
9 I speak unto you that are chosen in this thing, even as one, that you may enter into my rest.
10 For, behold, the mystery of godliness, how great is it! For, behold, I am endless, and the punishment which is given from my hand is endless punishment, for Endless is my name. Wherefore--
11 Eternal punishment is God's punishment.
12 Endless punishment is God's punishment.
13 Wherefore, I command you to repent, and keep the commandments which you have received by the hand of my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., in my name;
14 And it is by my almighty power that you have received them;

15 Therefore I command you to repent--repent, lest I smite you by the rod of my mouth, and by my wrath, and by my anger, and your sufferings be sore--how sore you know not, how exquisite you know not, yea, how hard to bear you know not.
16 For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent;
17 But if they would not repent they must suffer even as I;

This changes things. Now when we hear “Endless torment” or “Endless damnation” we’re to think not that such torment or damnation is without end but is simply God’s torment and damnation because “Endless” is God’s name. What about King Benjamin’s sermon where he says never-ending torment? Well in Mosiah 5:5 King Benjamin clarifies that when he says “never-ending torment” he’s referring to drinking out of the “cup of the wrath of God.”
Mosiah 5:5

And we are willing to enter into a covenant with our God to do his will, and to be obedient to his commandments in all things that he shall command us, all the remainder of our days, that we may not bring upon ourselves a never-ending torment, as has been spoken by the angel, that we may not drink out of the cup of the wrath of God.

This language of “cup of the wrath of God” means that, again, this is God’s punishment, Endless punishment, not punishment without end. So where does this leave us? We no longer can use scriptures that say “Endless punishment” or “Endless damnation” or even King Benjamin’s “never-ending torment” because all such references have been described by the revelation of D&C 19 to mean God’s punishment and not punishment without end.
Here I want to comment on such references describing torment or suffering as endless. I think all of them may be referring to suffering had before the resurrection. Let me clarify this point.
There are 12 references in our cannon of the type described other than the references in D&C 19 which are describing what type of suffering this is. What time frame does such suffering take place?
I highlighted the references before judgment and resurrection in yellow and the ones after in red. The purple highlights are unclear.
●2 Nephi 9:19: This is referring to the lake of fire and brimstone before which we can be redeemed from, meaning this is not the second death, only the first.
●2 Nephi 9:26: Same as the above reference.
●2 Nephi 28:23: This reference refers to the second death after judgment and calls that lake of fire and brimstone “endless torment”.
●Jacob 6:10: Referring to the lake of fire and brimstone after resurrection and judgment.

●Mosiah 2:39: It’s not clear to me whether this reference is before or after resurrection and judgment because a few verses after this one it opposes this suffering to those who are righteous and blessed to “dwell with God in a state of never-ending happiness” (Mosiah 2:41)
●Mosiah 2:41: Same as the above reference.
●Mosiah 3:25: After judgment.
●Mosiah 5:5: After judgment, probably.
●Mosiah 16:11: After resurrection and judgment.
●Alma 28:3: After resurrection and judgment.
●Alma 28:12: After resurrection and judgment.
●Moroni 8:21: Probably after resurrection and judgment.
109 But behold, and lo, we saw the glory and the inhabitants of the telestial world, that they were as innumerable as the stars in the firmament of heaven, or as the sand upon the seashore;
110 And heard the voice of the Lord saying: These all shall bow the knee, and every tongue shall confess to him who sits upon the throne forever and ever;
111 For they shall be judged according to their works, and every man shall receive according to his own works, his own dominion, in the mansions which are prepared;
112 And they shall be servants of the Most High; but where God and Christ dwell they cannot come, worlds without end.

This scripture says that those of the telestial world "cannot come" to the celestial kingdom "worlds without end", meaning forever. George Albert Smith, Spencer W. Kimball, and Bruce R. McConkie speak to this point:
Conference Report, Oct 1945, p 172; George Albert Smith

There are some people who have supposed that if we are quickened telestial bodies that eventually, throughout the ages of eternity, we will continue to progress until we will find our place in the celestial kingdom, but the Scriptures and the revelations of God have said that those who are quickened telestial bodies cannot come where God and Christ Dwell, worlds without end.
Miracle of Forgiveness pp 243-244; Spencer W. Kimball

After a person has been assigned to this place in the kingdom, either in the telestial, the terrestrial or the celestial, or to his exaltation, he will never advance from the assigned glory to another glory.  That is eternal!
Doctrinal New Testament Commentary 1: 196; Bruce R. McConkie

It is from these revelations which recite that resurrected beings come forth with different kinds of bodies [D&C  76; D&C 88:16-33; 1 Cor 15:35-58] that we learn a few of the many revealed reasons why there is not and cannot be progression from one degree of glory to another after the resurrection.

An explanation for why such progression between kingdoms after the resurrection cannot occur is that in the resurrection we are resurrected with bodies that are suited for the kingdom to which we will go.
1 Corinthians 15:39-42
39 All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
40 There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
41 There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
42 So also is the resurrection of the dead...
This concept is reiterated in D&C:
96 And the glory of the celestial is one, even as the glory of the sun is one.
97 And the glory of the terrestrial is one, even as the glory of the moon is one.
98 And the glory of the telestial is one, even as the glory of the stars is one; for as one star differs from another star in glory, even so differs one from another in glory in the telestial world;

Now, in contrast to the point I've made which has been supported by my interpretation of the scriptures cited and which also has been supported by the selected quotes, here are several quotes I gathered from a discussion forum from individuals arguing in opposition to this conclusion:

“The brethren direct me to say that the Church has never announced a definite doctrine upon this point. Some of the brethren have held the view that it was possible in the course of progression to advance from one glory to another, invoking the principle of eternal progression; others of the brethren have taken the opposite view. But as stated, the Church has never announced a definite doctrine on this point.”
-Secretary to the First Presidency in a 1952 letter; and again in 1965

“None would inherit this earth when it became celestial and translated into the presence of God but those who would be crowned as Gods — all others would have to inherit another kingdom — they would eventually have the privilege of proving themselves worthy and advancing to a celestial kingdom but it would be a slow process [progress?].”
-Brigham Young, in Wilford Woodruff Journal, 5 Aug 1855

“Once a person enters these glories there will be eternal progress in the line of each of these particular glories, but the privilege of passing from one to another (though this may be possible for especially gifted and faithful characters) is not provided for.”
-Joseph F. Smith, Improvement Era 14:87 [November 1910]

“I am not a strict constructionalist, believing that we seal our eternal progress by what we do here. It is my belief that God will save all of His children that he can: and while, if we live unrighteously here, we shall not go to the other side in the same status, so to speak, as those who lived righteously; nevertheless, the unrighteous will have their chance, and in the eons of the eternities that are to follow, they, too, may climb to the destinies to which they who are righteous and serve God, have climbed to those eternities that are to come.”
-J. Reuben Clark, Church News, 23 April 1960, p. 3

“It is reasonable to believe, in the absence of direct revelation by which alone absolute knowledge of the matter could be acquired, that, in accordance with God’s plan of eternal progression, advancement from grade to grade within any kingdom, and from kingdom to kingdom, will be provided for. But if the recipients of a lower glory be enabled to advance, surely the intelligences of higher rank will not be stopped in their progress; and thus we may conclude, that degrees and grades will ever characterize the kingdoms of our God. Eternity is progressive; perfection is relative; the essential feature of God’s living purpose is its associated power of eternal increase.”
-James E. Talmage, The Articles of Faith [1899 edition] pp. 420-421

You that are mourning about your children straying away will have your sons and your daughters. If you succeed in passing through these trials and afflictions and receive a resurrection, you will, by the power of the Priesthood, work and labor, as the Son of God has, until you get all your sons and daughters in the path of exaltation and glory. This is just as sure as that the sun rose this morning over yonder mountains. Therefore, mourn not because all your sons and daughters do not follow in the path that you have marked out to them, or give heed to your counsels. Inasmuch as we succeed in securing eternal glory, and stand as saviors, and as kings and priests to our God, we will save our posterity. When Jesus went through that terrible torture on the cross, He saw what would be accomplished by it; He saw that His brethren and sisters the sons and daughters of God would be gathered in, with but few exceptions those who committed the unpardonable sin. That sacrifice of the divine Being was effectual to destroy the powers of Satan. I believe that every man and woman who comes into this life and passes through it, that life will be a success in the end. It may not be in this life. It was not with the antediluvians. They passed through troubles and afflictions; 2,500 years after that, when Jesus went to preach to them, the dead heard the voice of the Son of God and they lived. They found after all that it was a very good thing that they had conformed to the will of God in leaving the spiritual life and passing through this world.
Lorenzo Snow, MS 56:49-53; Collected Discourses 3:364-65.

The question of advancement within the great divisions of glory celestial, terrestrial, and telestial; as also the question of advancement from one sphere of glory to another remains to be considered. In the revelation from which we have summarized what has been written here, in respect to the different degrees of glory, it is said that those of the terrestrial glory will be ministered unto by those of the celestial; and those of the telestial will be ministered unto by those of the terrestrial ”that is, those of the higher glory minister to those of a lesser glory. I can conceive of no reason for all this administration of the higher to the lower, unless it be for the purpose of advancing our Father’s children along the lines of eternal progression. Whether or not in the great future, full of so many possibilities now hidden from us, they of the lesser glories after education and advancement within those spheres may at last emerge from them and make their way to the higher degrees of glory until at last they attain to the highest, is not revealed in the revelations of God, and any statement made on the subject must partake more or less of the nature of conjecture. But if it be granted that such a thing is possible, they who at the first entered into the celestial gloryâ€”having before them the privilege also of eternal progress ”have been moving onward, so that the relative distance between them and those who have fought their way up from the lesser glories may be as great when the latter have come into the degrees of celestial glory in which the righteous at first stood, as it was at the commencement. Thus: Those whose faith and works are such only as to enable them to inherit a telestial glory, may arrive at last where those whose works in this life were such as to enable them to entrance into the celestial kingdom ”they may arrive where these were, but never where they are.”
B. H. Roberts, New Witnesses for God 1:391-392.

Some years ago I was in Washington, D.C., with President Harold B. Lee. Early one morning he called me to come into his hotel room. He was sitting in his robe reading Gospel Doctrine, by President Joseph F. Smith, and he said, “Listen to this!”

“Jesus had not finished his work when his body was slain, neither did he finish it after his resurrection from the dead; although he had accomplished the purpose for which he then came to the earth, he had not fulfilled all his work. And when will he? Not until he has redeemed and saved every son and daughter of our father Adam that have been or ever will be born upon this earth to the end of time, except the sons of perdition. That is his mission. We will not finish our work until we have saved ourselves, and then not until we shall have saved all depending upon us; for we are to become saviors upon Mount Zion, as well as Christ. We are called to this mission.”
“There is never a time,” the Prophet Joseph Smith taught, “when the spirit is too old to approach God. All are within the reach of pardoning mercy, who have not committed the unpardonable sin.”
Boyd K. Packer, “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” Ensign, Nov. 1995, 18
Final Thoughts

If all these excerpts are accurate, the case can be made that there is no official stance or decision as to whether this doctrine is one way or another. In my opinion, I find it prudent to believe that final judgment is final and that we must act as if such is the truth, for it may well be. I find absolutely no advantage to believing otherwise except as it may placate the emotional distress of some who find celestial kingdom requirements unattainable for themselves or loved ones and are driven to the contemplation of alternatives. They are driven by a denial of truth and an attempt to bargain or amend truth to fit their desires rather than a loyalty and sincerity to the truth of the scriptures and reason. I would urge to believe that judgment and resurrection is final and eternal because I feel that reason and scriptures suggest that it is more in-line with the truth, even if there are actual differing possibilities. If there were a cliff whose foundation was known to be compromised, it could be argued that while there are many reasons why the cliff edge would crumble under the weight of an individual leading to their fall and death, it may also be possible that it could withstand their weight. Even though this fact may be true, only a fool would venture to set foot on this cliff and test the probability. Likewise, only a fool would put their trust in the idea of eternal progression holding on to a hope and motive which at most may offer a glimmer of hope for a distant future but at worst lead one to destructive ways and beliefs led by foolish and vain hopes.

To briefly summarize what was pertinent, we start with mention of the famous Greek philosopher Plato (ca. 429-347 B.C.). He believed in a divine triad of "God, the ideas, [and] the World-Spirit," though he "nowhere explained or harmonized this triad" (Charles Bigg, Christian Platonists of Alexandria, 1886, p. 249).

Later Greek thinkers refined Plato's concepts into what they referred to as three "substances"—the supreme God or "the One," from which came "mind" or "thought" and a "spirit" or "soul." In their thinking, all were different divine "substances" or aspects of the same God. Another way of expressing this was as "good," the personification of that good, and the agent by which that good is carried out. Again, these were different divine aspects of that same supreme good—distinct and yet unified as one.

Such metaphysical thinking was common among the intelligentsia of the Greek world and carried over into the thinking of the Roman world of the New Testament period and succeeding centuries. As the last of the apostles began to die off, some of this metaphysical thinking began to affect and infiltrate the early Church—primarily through those who had already begun to compromise with paganism.

Many of the church leaders who formulated the doctrine of the Trinity were steeped in Greek and Platonic philosophy, and this influenced their religious views and teaching. The language they used in describing and defining the Trinity is, in fact, taken directly from Platonic and Greek philosophy. The word trinity itself is neither biblical nor Christian. Rather, the Platonic term trias, from the word for three, was Latinized as trinitas—the latter giving us the English word trinity.
Cyclopaedia of Biblical, Theological, and Ecclesiastical Literature, 1891, Vol. 10, "Trinity," p. 553

Towards the end of the 1st century, and during the 2d, many learned men came over both from Judaism and paganism to Christianity. These brought with them into the Christian schools of theology their Platonic ideas and phraseology.
The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge, Samuel Macauley Jackson, editor, 1911, Vol. 9, p. 91

The doctrines of the Logos [i.e., the "Word," a designation for Christ in John 1] and the Trinity received their shape from Greek Fathers, who . . . were much influenced, directly or indirectly, by the Platonic philosophy …That errors and corruptions crept into the Church from this source can not be denied.

It seems to be accepted that Greek and pagan ideas largely influenced early Christians and even made their way into creeds such as the which articulate definitions of God in a way similar to Plato’s descriptions of God ().

Understanding that the concept of the Trinity comes not from Biblical interpretation but Greek philosophy and was contorted or retrofitted into the Biblical interpretation of God challenges the validity of such concept. One might have expected that this view was always had and was plain for all Bible readers to interpret or that such an idea might have been elaborated by prophets through mystical experiences or revelation but such is not the case. Unless one accepts Greek philosophy or Egyptian occultism as valid sources of truth, such origins for ideas like the Trinity are challenging.
Well, if this origin story of the Trinity makes it an incredulous doctrine, would a similar origin story for other Christian doctrines compromise them in the same way?

Well there’s a good case that the modern Christian conception of the devil came from, or was influenced by, the Greek god, . Even the pagan, witches, and occultists accept this similarity as less than accident:
The Satanic Bible 1969, Antone LaVey

Many pleasures revered before the advent of Christianity were condemned by the new religion. It required little change-over to transform the horns and cloven hooves of Pan into a most convincing devil! Pan’s attributes could neatly be changed into charged-with-punishment sins, and so the metamorphosis was complete.
Pan has horns, goat legs, and loves sex. He’s often correlated with evil, corruptness, etc.

The latin word Lucifer, light bringer, has a Greek equivalent of Phosphorus, which happens to be a Greek god who is known as god of Venus. This word was intentionally used because of its known meaning when St. Gerome translated the vulgate in the instance of Isaiah 14:12-13, making what seemed to be a comment on the king of Babylon into a verse that has obvious reference to this Greek idea—Phosphorus.
Isaiah 14:12-13 KJV
Isaiah 14:12-13 NIV
How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
How you have fallen from heaven,
morning star, son of the dawn!
You have been cast down to the earth,
you who once laid low the nations!
For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:
You said in your heart,
“I will ascend to the heavens;
I will raise my throne
above the stars of God;
I will sit enthroned on the mount of assembly,
on the utmost heights of Mount Zaphon.
Many bible commentators believe this reference of morning star, day star, or Lucifer, to be referring to the king of Babylon.
Even the Apocalypse of Paul, or the Vision of Hell, a fourth-century pseudepigraphal work conveys a consistent version of the devil where he has horns, red skin, forked tail, etc.
Conclusion, the modern conception of the devil, or even a devil, appears to be a New-Testament-era development. However, a reference to the devil appears as early as 600 B.C. in the Book of Mormon:
1 Nephi 12:17

And the mists of darkness are the temptations of the devil, which blindeth the eyes, and hardeneth the hearts of the children of men, and leadeth them away into broad roads, that they perish and are lost.

I should note that it is possible that Lehi developed his conception of the devil from Zoroastrianism, a religion that is believed to have developed around the 6th or 7th centuries B.C. This lines up precisely with Lehi. Zoroastrianism's concept of the devil, interestingly, has uncanny similarities to the Greek Pan, or Phosphorus, having horns, wings, a tail, and being evil and corrupt, even rebelling against Ahura Mazda, their conception of the great creator god.
Some interesting descriptors of Angra Mainyu, this Zoroastrianism’s devil, given by Bard are:
●He is often depicted as a hideous creature with horns, wings, and a tail.
●He is said to be able to control the forces of nature, such as storms, earthquakes, and disease.
●He is also said to be able to possess people and make them do evil things.
●He is ultimately doomed to be defeated by Ahura Mazda and the forces of good.
●He is said to have been created by Ahura Mazda as a test of humanity's free will. Ahura Mazda wanted to see if humans would choose to follow the path of good or the path of evil.
And how would Lehi have had familiarity with Zoroastrianism? Well he’s known to be a somewhat wealthy merchant who could have traveled.

There seem to be many who claim that the Book of Mormon gives hints that the Nephites were among other civilizations in America other than the Lamanites. Of course, they eventually found and joined with the Mulekites, but I always meet this idea with incredulity and skepticism because I haven’t seen any scriptures that give such hints. People on podcasts and videos will often just make that statement and give no support as if it’s tacit. It’s frustrating to me because I’ve searched for such support and found almost none. What I have found to be possible support is really just a huge stretch of interpretation and speculation around the Nephites living near, but not finding, the Mulekites for nearly 450 years.
But this verse in Jacob makes the case of extra-Lehite people among the Lehites very unlikely in my opinion.
Jacob 7:26

And it came to pass that I, Jacob, began to be old; and the record of this people being kept on the other plates of Nephi, wherefore, I conclude this record, declaring that I have written according to the best of my knowledge, by saying that the time passed away with us, and also our lives passed away like as it were unto us a dream, we being a lonesome and a solemn people, wanderers, cast out from Jerusalem, born in tribulation, in a wilderness, and hated of our brethren, which caused wars and contentions; wherefore, we did mourn out our days.

Jacob identifies his people as lonesome and solemn. Well isn’t that pretty clear that they didn’t have any other company to affiliate with other than the Lamanites, at least at this point in their history?

I’ve certainly heard the teaching in the Church that Christ’s atonement applies to all the inhabitants and life on other planets, not just this one, though Christ only had one mortal ministry and it was on this earth because only this earth would have people so wicked that they would crucify their God.
Is this true? Is this backed up by scripture? Why do we even believe this in the first place?

The  referenced in the subtext of the heading for this entry is from AskGramps and argues to the affirmative—that Christ’s atonement applies to the whole universe. His evidence for this answer is based on the following points:
●Christ descended below all things (D&C 88:6), all things broadening scope beyond this earth.
●“There has not been so great wickedness as among thy brethren” (Moses 7:36), supporting the idea that only this earth was wicked enough to crucify their God.
●The parable in D&C 88:46-61 is interpreted as referencing planets, or kingdoms, and says Christ visits each of the 12 in their time, first to last, last to first, and first to last.
There was an article on this topic in the April 1976 Ensign ().
I like how in the article it brings up the revelation of Moses where we learn that Moses was only allowed to have a knowledge of this earth.
Moses 1:33-35

And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten.
