And the first man of all men have I called Adam, which is many. But only an account of this earth, and the inhabitants thereof, give I unto you. For behold, there are many worlds that have passed away by the word of my power. And there are many that now stand, and innumerable are they unto man; but all things are numbered unto me, for they are mine and I know them.

Moses got this answer in response to asking why everything was created. It’s relevant that God tells him only what concerns this earth and the inhabitants thereof. Moses wasn’t privileged to learn of other earths or of inhabitants from other spheres. Maybe we’re not allowed to have detailed knowledge for these other spheres and it’s best that we know only concerning our sphere.
In this encounter with God, Moses learns that Christ created other worlds:
Moses 1:33
And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten.
Although we aren’t told here explicitly that Christ is also the savior of these worlds, it makes sense logically that the creator must assume the role of savior.
That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
This tells us that the worlds created which have inhabitants are also sons and daughters of God, at least the “worlds” referred to here.
The Prophet Joseph Smith apparently believed in the idea of Christ being the savior of other worlds. It’s said here in a poem he wrote:
A Poem by Joseph Smith, Times and Seasons 4:82–85
For the Lord he is God, and his life never ends,
And besides him there ne’er was a Saviour of men. …
He’s the Saviour, and only begotten of God—
By him, of him, and through him, the worlds were all made,
Even all that career in the heavens so broad,
Whose inhabitants, too, from the first to the last,
Are sav’d by the very same Saviour of ours;
And, of course, are begotten God’s daughters and sons,
By the very same truths, and the very same pow’rs.”
Bruce R. McConkie, Mormon Doctrine

Now our Lord’s jurisdiction and power extend far beyond the limits of this one small earth on which we dwell. He is, under the Father, the Creator of worlds without number. (Moses 1:33.) And … the atonement of Christ, being literally and truly infinite, applies to an infinite number of earths.

Just as the creative and redemptive powers of Christ extend to the earth and all things thereon, as also to the infinite expanse of worlds in immensity, so the power of the resurrection is universal in scope. Man, the earth, and all life thereon will come forth in the resurrection. And the resurrection applies to and is going on in other worlds and other galaxies.
But there are serious questions one might ask when considering the ramifications of this being true:

If the one atonement has infinite influence across all worlds in all universes, why hadn't such an atonement already been arranged and completed many generations of gods ago? And, if Jesus suffered and died and resurrected to save all worlds, does that mean that the disobedience and fall of this earth's Adam cursed all worlds? And, does Lucifer and his gang tempt all worlds?

I find a lot of authenticity shown in the Book of Mormon where subtle details suggest real and not fabricated history—only really good story tellers can add in details like these. Some examples of this lie in the names of people. I’ll give some examples that come to mind:
King Benjamin names his youngest Helaman
Mosiah 7:3-6

And it came to pass that on the morrow they started to go up, having with them one Ammon, he being a strong and mighty man, and a descendant of Zarahemla; and he was also their leader. And now, they knew not the course they should travel in the wilderness to go up to the land of Lehi-Nephi; therefore they wandered many days in the wilderness, even forty days did they wander. And when they had wandered forty days they came to a hill, which is north of the land of Shilom, and there they pitched their tents. And Ammon took three of his brethren, and their names were Amaleki, Helem, and Hem, and they went down into the land of Nephi.

King Mosiah I chose Ammon to lead the important expedition to the land of Nephi to recover the Nephites who had journeyed there two generations prior. This King Mosiah I has three sons: “Mosiah, and Helorum, and Helaman” (Mosiah 1:2). He names his firstborn after himself, a common practice among them it seems, and the second and third name appear to be unique.

It may be that these unique names are Zarahemlite names. Support for this comes from the referenced verses above from Mosiah 7—Ammon was a descendant of Zarahemla and his three brethren, most likely also descendents of Zarahemla, were named Amaleki, Helem, and Hem. There's a similarity between the name Helem and Mosiah’s grandson’s name, Helaman. Perhaps King Benjamin was attempting to integrate the people of Zarahemla with his people and either intermarried with them or at least started naming some of his children after people of Zarahemla. This would be politically tactful in his case.

However, there is an issue with this theory. While Helaman is similar sounding to Helem, we can’t assert that they are related or even that Helem is a name from the people of Zarahemla. Why? Because the same name with different spelling is found among the Nephites in the land of Nephi in the account of Alma when baptizing Helam:
Mosiah 18:12-14

And now it came to pass that Alma took Helam, he being one of the first, and went and stood forth in the water, and cried, saying: O Lord, pour out thy Spirit upon thy servant, that he may do this work with holiness of heart. And when he had said these words, the Spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he said: Helam, I baptize thee, having authority from the Almighty God, as a testimony that ye have entered into a covenant to serve him until you are dead as to the mortal body; and may the Spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you; and may he grant unto you eternal life, through the redemption of Christ, whom he has prepared from the foundation of the world. And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam were buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the Spirit.
Mosiah II names his son Ammon

Then King Benjamin’s son Mosiah goes on to name his sons Ammon, Aaron, Omner, and Himni. There's a clear motive for why he would revere the explorer Ammon enough to name his own son after him. Of course, it could have just been a beloved and popular name, but I like the idea that he was naming him after the explorer Ammon.
Alma the Younger names his son Helaman
Perhaps Helaman is a variant of Helam and he was naming his son after Helam, who would have been like an uncle to Alma in that Helam and Alma the Elder were well acquainted as shown in Mosiah 18.

title: Patterns in Christ; What’s the Extent?

body.text: It appears that God has designed symbols and patterns throughout history that have significance in demonstrating Messianic symbols or manifesting gospel truths. There are many Messianic types throughout the scriptures such as Joseph of Egypt, the rock of Horeb, the manna from heaven that fed the Israelites. Jesus Christ’s miracle of turning water to wine hints at his power to turn death unto life via common symbols of death and life, i.e., water and wine. Also his walking on water can be understood as his power over death.

But what is the extent of these types of design throughout scriptural history? Are they interwoven through everything? Are the numbers and patterns found in nature which often align with Fibonacci sequences or the Golden Ratio equally intentioned? Is human history similarly entrenched in such patterns or is that taking it too far?

I’ve seen some enthusiastic members take an idea such as chiasmus in the Book of Mormon and run too far with it, thinking that chiasmus are everywhere and they attempt to forcefully apply the pattern into everything, even the Book of Mormon as a whole. In my opinion, this is the result of wishful thinking and bad reasoning or application. Such people begin to see not what reality is but what they want it to be.

title: Belief and Faith For Change and Prophecy

body.text: King Benjamin gives a powerful sermon that leads his people to drastic results. After this sermon, King Benjamin asks them whether they believe his words. They answer:
Mosiah 5:2-5

2 And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.

3 And we, ourselves, also, through the infinite goodness of God, and the manifestations of his Spirit, have great views of that which is to come; and were it expedient, we could prophesy of all things.
4 And it is the faith which we have had on the things which our king has spoken unto us that has brought us to this great knowledge, whereby we do rejoice with such exceedingly great joy.

5 And we are willing to enter into a covenant with our God to do his will, and to be obedient to his commandments in all things that he shall command us, all the remainder of our days, that we may not bring upon ourselves a never-ending torment, as has been spoken by the angel, that we may not drink out of the cup of the wrath of God.

I find the connections made in these verses interesting. They know because of the Spirit which brought about a change in them as well as filling them with prophecy and knowledge. If it’s the Spirit which can bring such great effects, how does one receive the Spirit? What did they do to have the Spirit come and bring such great effects? If it were clear and formulaic I would love to receive such gifts.

title: Only Prophets Receive Revelation for the Church?

body.text: …no one shall be appointed to receive commandments and revelations in this church excepting my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., for he receiveth them even as Moses.
If this pattern applies to all dispensations, does it present a conflict for scenarios like Abinadi’s where he begins to preach unto the people on behalf of the Lord?
Mosiah 11:20-25

…Behold, thus saith the Lord, and thus hath he commanded me, saying, Go forth, and say unto this people, thus saith the Lord—Wo be unto this people, for I have seen their abominations, and their wickedness, and their whoredoms; and except they repent I will visit them in mine anger.

And except they repent and turn to the Lord their God, behold, I will deliver them into the hands of their enemies; yea, and they shall be brought into bondage; and they shall be afflicted by the hand of their enemies.
And it shall come to pass that they shall know that I am the Lord their God, and am a jealous God, visiting the iniquities of my people.
And it shall come to pass that except this people repent and turn unto the Lord their God, they shall be brought into bondage; and none shall deliver them, except it be the Lord the Almighty God.
Yea, and it shall come to pass that when they shall cry unto me I will be slow to hear their cries; yea, and I will suffer them that they be smitten by their enemies.

And except they repent in sackcloth and ashes, and cry mightily to the Lord their God, I will not hear their prayers, neither will I deliver them out of their afflictions; and thus saith the Lord, and thus hath he commanded me.

I suppose there’s not a contradiction of line of authority since the church leadership wasn’t ecclesiastic or well established in the land at this point, or rather, King Noah, the presiding monarch authority, and his priests, were entrenched in wickedness and needed to be rebuked.

But does this paint an exception to the rule that only the prophet receives revelation for the whole church? There are many times in the Old Testament where prophets came and rebuked the people warning them of punishments to come unless they repented, see Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, etc.
If the church fell into apostasy, would God work through channels outside of the church to rebuke the church?
Joseph Smith, Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, p. 370
The keys of the kingdom of God will never be taken from this people, neither shall the church be left to perish; but it shall be built up to the glory of God.
I suppose there is this quote and several others that support the idea that the church will not ever fall into apostasy, though.
Matthew 19:17 NIV
…If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.
Jesus gave these words to the rich young man wanting eternal life. When answering that he had already been keeping the commandments Jesus had elaborated, Jesus answered the following.
Matthew 19:21 NIV
If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.

In both of these answers for how to obtain life, or eternal life and salvation, Jesus doesn’t mention faith or belief on his name, albeit, the latter case might require faith and belief on Jesus’ name. But both answers do require work. Obviously, obedience to God almost always requires faith. But it is interesting how much this answer concerns works when so many profess that works are meaningless in Christian circles.
Mosiah 12:4
And it shall come to pass that I will smite this my people with sore afflictions, yea, with famine and with pestilence; and I will cause that they shall howl all the day long.

Abinadi first warns the people at the request of the Lord to repent. After two years, the people had not repented and God gave Abinadi more to say. This scripture is a portion of the message. Part of the prophecy of what will happen to the people since they had not repented is that pestilence will come upon them. As far as I can tell, this portion of the prophecy is not fulfilled, or at least recorded, in the Book of Mormon. Is that important?
Jesus was concerned when the Nephites hadn’t recorded the fulfillment of Samuel the Lamanites’ words about the resurrection of the righteous after Christ’s resurrection and
commanded that it should be written. This suggests that it’s very important that fulfillment of prophecy is important.

I was watching the YouTube channel HelloSaints the other day where Pastor Jeff reads and gives his thoughts on the book of Heleman. After reviewing the story of Nephi and Lehi in the prison engulfed in fire, he said that the Holy Ghost manifesting in tongues in such a way is anachronistic with the Bible where such things only occurred on and following the Day of Pentecost.
Heleman 5:45
And behold, the Holy Spirit of God did come down from heaven, and did enter into their hearts, and they were filled as if with fire, and they could speak forth marvelous words.
Is this really so anachronistic? Did the Holy Ghost not operate before the Day of Pentecost?
Exodus 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship.

And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the LORD. And, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake:
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.

There really isn’t much showing the Holy Ghost operating before the day of Pentecost in the Bible. The Book of Mormon does have a lot of it, though. Is this a problem? We also have the Pearl of Great Price mentioning the Holy Ghost.
Moses 6:65-66
And thus he was baptized, and the Spirit of God descended upon him, and thus he was born of the Spirit, and became quickened in the inner man.
And he heard a voice out of heaven, saying: Thou art baptized with fire, and with the Holy Ghost. This is the record of the Father, and the Son, from henceforth and forever;

As an individual born and raised in the Church, I never saw the issue with the Holy Ghost operating prior to the day of Pentecost, but I can see why this would be a problem for some. I still don’t know how we can explain this. The gift of tongues before the Day of Pentecost, and before Christ’s mortal ministry in Jerusalem, is unprecedented in scripture.

title: Is The Book of Mormon Racist? v2

body.text: I want to continue on this subject in order to clarify my thoughts and be able to present them in discussion.
Merriam Webster Dictionary: Racist
A.: having, reflecting, or fostering the belief that race is a fundamental determinant of human traits and capacities and that racial differences produce an inherent superiority of a particular race
B.: of, relating to, or characterized by the systemic oppression of a racial group to the social, economic, and political advantage of another
Dictionary.com: Racist
a person who believes in racism, the doctrine that one's own racial group is superior or that a particular racial group is inferior to the others.

It’s difficult to find a traditional definition. Those in the liberal arts are quick to adopt definition changes that are exclusively used by a minority of the population but match their political interests. Here we see how Merriam Webster is attempting to redefine “racist” in order to placate their political sensitivities. They do the same with words like “female” for which they offer a definition of “having a gender identity that is the opposite of male.” These definitions are less sensical than traditional ones and offer more confusion than clarification, but such is their industry.
Anyway, let’s go with the definition of “racist” which is that racism is a belief that one race is superior to another. That will make the conversation more productive.

First off, ever since humans have existed there have been groups, hierarchies, tribes, and systems of some sort. Within each of these there has existed nationalism or tribalism in almost every case. Humans have a sense of pride for their team, their group, and their race. Humans have segregated themselves in almost every society and made it a point to note differences between any and every group.

Whether we’re talking about individual distinctions made between native American tribes, African tribes, European villagers, it has been a ubiquitous characteristic for such groups to hold a level of pride and identity within their subgroups and subcultures.

To look back in history and expect to find a tribe or group who believed that their clan were no different in any way than any other humans or that they were more or less entitled to their land, beliefs, customs, language, etc. is asinine. If we look in the Bible we’re going to find that the Israelites had a huge sense of pride in their identity as the covenant people of God and they conquered many other people. They believed their lineage was blessed, chosen, and special.
If we examine the historical cast system of India we’ll see their deeply embedded distinctions of superiority between members of their own race.

It is not odd to find ideas that we now call prejudiced or racist throughout history. In fact, these ideas were the norm and the distinctions that were based on such ideas were not always rooted in unsupported ideologies. Neighboring cultures identified stereotypes that were sometimes based in logic and were statistically supported. The human ability to identify correlations and predictions based on historic interactions and events is impressive to say at the least.

If two cultures were geographically juxtaposed and each acquired the ability to discern between a local of their land and a foreigner, they would be aided in their ability to deduce a stranger’s language, education, background, political views, and more. It’s not prejudiced to have this discerning ability. It’s genius.

The culture we now live in is unprecedented and poses a scenario so different from what we see in history that what once may have been somewhat accurate stereotypes and valid assumptions may very well be wrong and unfair to impose on individuals. It was once true in our country that the color of one’s skin could almost definitely identify that person’s dialect of language, education, and, further, their clothes, accent, and other characteristics could naturally identify their salary, expertise, background, etc. But now, such markers are likely not indicative in nearly any of these cases.

Where problems arise, especially in our culturally mixed, melting-pot-of-a-country, is when individuals are unfairly treated, degraded, or abused because they are viewed as less worthy, capable, or human. In human history, some groups have treated other humans in such ways, justifying their actions by identifying their victims as less worthy, capable, or human, and concluding such based on their victims nationality, skin color, or birth lineage.

These atrocities have not been limited to racist ideas but have stemmed from various illogical ways of thinking. Of course, all humans deserve to be treated with the same level of dignity, respect, and love.

The reason I spend the time ranting about this topic is because some read through history and are guilty of the worst presentism possible by condemning our ancient ancestors for doing or believing what, in many cases, was not only natural and intelligent, but the same thing any human would have done or believed given the same upbringing, culture, and context.

If we read of an ancient tribe that describes an adjacent tribe by saying, “They speak with an odd accent—they can’t make the “f” sound. They also often have long fingernails and hum sons while they walk. They don’t ever shower so they often stink. They also have hair on their feet and don’t wear shoes and their feet look ugly because of it.” Such a description could be wrong, but it could also be spot on.

Likewise, when we read any ancient text where the tribe, group, or whomever it may be writing the text, is describing their neighboring tribes or foes, it should be expected to find some level of distinction made between the two. In the case of the Book of Mormon, we have the Nephite authors writing the record. The descriptions noting the differences between the Nephites and the Lamanites are not inherently racist just because they involve physical appearance distinctions. Likewise they are not inherently rude or wrong because they call the Lamanites lazy and filthy. That may have been wrong, but it also may have been accurate.

The fact that Nephi calls the Lamanites both dark and loathsome does not mean “dark because they’re loathsome” or “loathsome because they’re dark”. He’s simply naming two characteristics. It’s annoying to me how so many readers have such a high sensitivity to drawing distinctions between races that they think the mere belief that different races could have different predispositions or characteristics is racist. That idea is absurd.
Nephi’s encounter with a divine being preceding his vision is somewhat perplexing. Who is this being?

Nephi first mentions that he was “caught away in the Spirit of the Lord” (v. 1) into a mountain. Once Nephi is there, “the Spirit” says “Behold, what desirest thou?” (v. 2). Who is this being that had taken Nephi up to a high mountain and then begins to speak to him? I think it’s fair to interpret the being who took him up to the mountain and the being who then speaks to him as the same person. I’m just going to paste the content of this section here and analyze it line by line.

11:1 For it came to pass after I had desired to know the things that my father had seen, and believing that the Lord was able to make them known unto me, as I sat pondering in mine heart I was caught away in the Spirit of the Lord, yea, into an exceedingly high mountain, which I never had before seen, and upon which I never had before set my foot.
This verse reminds of several scriptures:
Matthew 4:8
Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;
I suppose I ought to include too the JST of this verse making it more similar.
Matthew 4:8 JST
8 And again, Jesus was in the Spirit, and it taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and showeth him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them.
Revelation 21:10
And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God

The similarities between Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness and John’s vision of the Lamb’s wife are interesting. Of course, there are many other parallels between Nephi’s vision of the tree of life and John’s vision. Nephi even mentions that John also would see this vision and that his portion (Nephi’s) was only partial.
11:2 And the Spirit said unto me: Behold, what desirest thou?

Now instead of being called “the Spirit of the Lord” this Being is referred to as “the Spirit”. Most people would associate this label with the Holy Ghost. Is this label ever applied in scripture to another? Not that I know of.
11:3 And I said: I desire to behold the things which my father saw.
11:4 And the Spirit said unto me: Believest thou that thy father saw the tree of which he hath spoken?
11:5 And I said: Yea, thou knowest that I believe all the words of my father.

11:6 And when I had spoken these words, the Spirit cried with a loud voice, saying: Hosanna to the Lord, the most high God; for he is God over all the earth, yea, even above all. And blessed art thou, Nephi, because thou believest in the Son of the most high God; wherefore, thou shalt behold the things which thou hast desired.

This verse is odd if we’re to think that the Being shouting this Hosanna is Jehovah. Would He be referencing Himself in such a way? Wouldn’t He have worded it differently such as “blessed art thou because thou believest in Me”? And I can’t imagine that Jehovah would be shouting that Hosanna to the Lord, which most likely would be referring to Himself anyway.

11:7 And behold this thing shall be given unto thee for a sign, that after thou hast beheld the tree which bore the fruit which thy father tasted, thou shalt also behold a man descending out of heaven, and him shall ye witness; and after ye have witnessed him ye shall bear record that it is the Son of God.

If this were Jesus, wouldn’t he say “after ye have witnessed Me ye shall bear record that I am the Son of God”? I’ve got to say, I’m more persuaded that this individual who speaks to Nephi must be the Holy Ghost or an angel.

11:8 And it came to pass that the Spirit said unto me: Look! And I looked and beheld a tree; and it was like unto the tree which my father had seen; and the beauty thereof was far beyond, yea, exceeding of all beauty; and the whiteness thereof did exceed the whiteness of the driven snow.
11:9 And it came to pass after I had seen the tree, I said unto the Spirit: I behold thou hast shown unto me the tree which is precious above all.
11:10 And he said unto me: What desirest thou?

11:11 And I said unto him: To know the interpretation thereof—for I spake unto him as a man speaketh; for I beheld that he was in the form of a man; yet nevertheless, I knew that it was the Spirit of the Lord; and he spake unto me as a man speaketh with another.

If it weren’t for this verse, I don’t think anyone would really question whether this was the Holy Ghost. Up until this point it seems pretty clear that this is the Holy Ghost. But does the Holy Ghost appear in the form of a personage to anyone? I’ve never noticed that in scripture. Does the Holy Ghost speak verbally to people? Maybe. At this point, the idea that this is the Holy Ghost becomes difficult, perhaps as challenging as it would be to identify the individual as Jehovah.
The Spirit of the Lord—who does that refer to, the Holy Ghost or Jehovah? It all becomes somewhat unclear at this point.
11:12 And it came to pass that he said unto me: Look! And I looked as if to look upon him, and I saw him not; for he had gone from before my presence.

11:13 And it came to pass that I looked and beheld the great city of Jerusalem, and also other cities. And I beheld the city of Nazareth; and in the city of Nazareth I beheld a virgin, and she was exceedingly fair and white.
11:14 And it came to pass that I saw the heavens open; and an angel came down and stood before me; and he said unto me: Nephi, what beholdest thou?

It’s at this point that I wonder if the Being was actually Jesus. Because at the point in the vision when Nephi sees Mary and is about to see the nativity, the Being disappears and an angel proceeds to guide Nephi through the vision. Why doesn’t the initial guide remain with Nephi? Is there some necessity for why they would leave him and an angel take their place? Maybe the Holy Ghost was the initial guide and couldn’t be present while Jesus, the baby, was present in the vision. Maybe the same was true but for Jesus—Jesus couldn’t be showing Nephi the vision of His own nativity and birth. Is it like sci-fi plots where you can’t go back in time and see yourself sort of thing?
Anyway, it gets confusing and I know there’s some controversy among church leaders and has been for some time.

title: Who Was With Alma When The Angel Appeared?

body.text: The popular interpretation is that Alma and four sons of Mosiah were present when the angel appeared to them and spoke to Alma against his wicked and rebellious ways. In fact, the chapter heading for Mosiah 27 says “Alma the younger and the four sons of Mosiah seek to destroy the Church” and “Alma and the sons of Mosiah declare glad tidings”.
I want to present an alternative view which is that more than four others were with Alma during this encounter. Here’s my evidence:
●Mosiah 27:8 says “the sons of Mosiah were numbered among the unbelievers” and verse 10 says “[Alma] did go about secretly with the sons of Mosiah seeking to destroy the church.”
○It’s important to note that it doesn’t say here that there were four of the sons of Mosiah or that Alma was going about only with the sons of Mosiah.

●After Alma is revived from his weakened state, Mosiah 27:32 says “Alma began from this time forward to teach the people, and those who were with Alma at the time the angel appeared unto them”. It doesn’t say “four” and it doesn’t say “sons of Mosiah”.

○Mosiah 27:34 says, referring to “those who were with Alma”, “And four of them were the sons of Mosiah; and their names were Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and Himni; these were the names of the sons of Mosiah.”

■The first part of the verse saying “And four of them were the sons of Mosiah” strongly suggests that there were more than four total with him, or else it would have likely said, “The four who were with him were the sons of Mosiah.”

■The last part of the verse saying these were the names of the sons of Mosiah does make it sound like these probably were all of Mosiah’s sons but it’s possible that it’s instead saying something like, “these are the names of the sons of Mosiah who were with Alma during the encounter but are not the names of all of the sons of Mosiah”
I’m led to believe that Alma, four of the sons of Mosiah, and at least two others, probably more, were present during this encounter.
Next comes the mission to the Lamanites by the sons of Mosiah and some select individuals.
Mosiah 28:1

Now it came to pass that after the sons of Mosiah had done all these things, they took a small number with them and returned to their father, the king, and desired of him that he would grant unto them that they might, with these whom they had selected, go up to the land of Nephi that they might preach the things which they had heard, and that they might impart the word of God to their brethren, the Lamanites

The fact that the sons of Mosiah take a few brethren with them on their mission makes me wonder who these individuals are—were they present at the encounter with the angel? Are they merely converts resulting from the reparations made by the sons of Mosiah?
We later learn two of the names of these selected individuals although it sounds like there are more than two of them.
Alma 20:2

And the voice of the Lord came to Ammon saying: Thou shalt not go up to the land of Nephi, for behold, the king will seek thy life; but thou shalt go to the land of Middoni; for behold, thy brother Aaron, and also Muloki and Ammah are in prison.

Aaron is here grouped with two men, Muloki and Ammah. Aaron had first gone to the land of Jerusalem (Alma 21:4) but had no success. Then he went to a village called Ani-Anti (Alma 21:11) where he found “Muloki preaching the word unto them; and also Ammah and his brethren”. This definitely identifies that there were more than just Ammah and Muloki along with the sons of Mosiah on this mission.

It appears that this whole group—Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah and his brethren—had no success and then “came over into the land of Middoni” (Alma 21:12) where “few believed on the words which they taught.” At this point, “Aaron and a certain number of his brethren were taken and cast into prison, and the remainder of them fled out of the land of Middoni unto the regions round about” (Alma 21:13).

If we link this account with the Alma 20:2, which is cited above, we find that it is Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah who are in prison. So Alma 21:13 saying “Aaron and a certain number of his brethren were taken and cast into prison” is referring to those three.
Alma 22:1-2

1 Now, as Ammon was thus teaching the people of Lamoni continually, we will return to the account of Aaron and his brethren; for after he departed from the land of Middoni he was led by the Spirit to the land of Nephi, even to the house of the king which was over all the land save it were the land of Ishmael; and he was the father of Lamoni.

2 And it came to pass that he went in unto him into the king’s palace, with his brethren, and bowed himself before the king, and said unto him: Behold, O king, we are the brethren of Ammon, whom thou hast delivered out of prison.

Most people don’t realize this, but it was not merely Aaron who taught the father of King Lamoni. It was Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah, from what I can gather. Even the chapter heading to Alma 22 says “Aaron teaches Lamoni’s father about the Creation” and doesn’t mention Muloki and Ammah. Perhaps this is only because we only have the words of Aaron to the king and Muloki and Ammah aren’t doing the preaching. But I still think it’s important to point it out.
Anyway, my conclusion is that it is most likely that Muloki and Ammah, and perhaps others, were present at the encounter with the angel when Alma and the sons of Mosiah were going about rebelling.

title: Did Christ or the Father Create Adam and Eve?

body.text: Here are the relevant scriptures telling of the creation of man.
Genesis 1:26-27

26 And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Genesis 2:7-8
7 And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
8 And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
Genesis 2:18, 21-23
18 And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
21 And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
22 And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
23 And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.
We see that the descriptions include “formed”, “created”, “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life”. Is this how man was created?
Joseph Smith taught that God breathed into Adam his spirit (Adam’s spirit).
Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, pg. 301

The 7th verse of 2nd chapter of Genesis ought to read—God breathed into Adam his spirit [i.e., Adam’s spirit] or breath of life; but when the word “ruach” applies to Eve, it should be translated lives.
JD 6:1, Joseph Smith, Jr., Character and Being of God, Etc.

title: Anachronistic Biblical References in the Book of Mormon

body.text: There are many scriptures referenced in the Book of Mormon which appear to be anachronistic. I won’t begin giving examples quite yet, I’ll try to do that somewhat exhaustively later on. Questions and concerns are raised wondering how Nephites in America during 587 and later periods before Christ’s birth in the Middle-East could have been familiar enough with scriptures that were written after their time and on the opposite side of the globe that they could have quoted them verbatim. The concern is warranted. The examples are apparent enough that one cannot dismiss them as a stretch of application.
How do we reconcile these? I’ll first dig into the claims and accusations to make clear the issue and then I’ll offer a response.
The Issues
Deutero-Isaiah Theory

In an  the Deutero-Isaiah theory is described. Basically, there’s a consensus among Jewish and Christian Biblical scholars that the book of Isaiah in the Old Testament is written not by one author, but likely three different authors who are referred to by proponents of this theory as Proto-, Deutero-, and Trito-Isaiah. Here is how the chapters of Isaiah are theorized to be associated which each:
Proto-Isaiah: Isaiah 1 - 39
Deutero-Isaiah: Isaiah 40 - 55
Trito-Isaiah: Isaiah 56 - 66

The support for this theory lies in differences in speaking patterns, vocabulary, and in style and purpose of writing. Additionally, Trito-Isaiah references king Cyrus by name, who was thought to have been born around 590 - 580 B.C. (). This is some time after the range of “between 740 BC and c. 686 BC” which is when Isaiah is purported to have lived ().

Of the ~18 Isaiah chapters quoted in the Book of Mormon before the coming of Christ, five are Deutero-Isaiah chapters while the rest are Proto-Isaiah, but we’ll ignore those since they pose no anachronistic problem.

So, the mentioning of Cyrus in Isaiah 44 and 45 is a big deal. Mentioning a future king by name in a way which doesn’t have relevance to the people who receive this prophecy doesn’t seem consistent with scriptures. Unless maybe you refer to how Jesus Christ’s name is known via prophecy among the Nephites hundreds of years before His birth as well as perhaps Joseph Smith’s name (2 Nephi 5).
Note, though, that the Book of Mormon does not contain Isaiah 44 or 45. This is important for one theory that seeks to resolve the dilemma proposed here.

…what appears to have happened is this: when the Jews returned from exile in Babylon, they read what Isaiah wrote, and because there were references to Babylon, assumed that he was talking about events in their day. While this might technically have been correct, they missed the point that Isaiah’s prophecies were primarily concerned with the latter days. In editing the book as they passed it down, they substituted the name “Cyrus,” which by that point did make sense to them, as he was an historical figure, for what was there originally. We don’t know, of course, what “Cyrus” might have replaced, but from the context it appears as if it was a messianic type meant to refer to the 2nd coming of Christ.

The author of this article also points out how ancient manuscripts of the Bible always treat the book of Isaiah as one book and does not distinguish between Proto- or Deutero-Isaiahs. This is an oddity why the book of Isaiah would have exclusively been a conglomerate of multiple prophets combined into one.

So perhaps the Deutero-Isaiah theory is wrong. It does have some inconsistencies and relies quite heavily upon the mentioning of the name of Cyrus, which issue can be resolved by the theory of the author as shown in the quote given. Besides the mentioning of Cyrus, they’re left with differences of speaking style and prophetic style but these differences haven’t been demonstrably proven. In fact, it appears that linguistic analysis has not differentiated between the proposed Isaiahs ().
NT references in OT Book of Mormon
Okay, so that may resolve the Isaiah problem, but what about other anachronistic references such as New Testament passages in the Book of Mormon?

A topic that has been more relevant over the past decade is whether Christians should attend gay weddings. Homosexual weddings are becoming more popular. Personally, my own sister has had two gay weddings so this question is one I’ve had to consider.

After digging into the topic and doing some praying, I concluded that it was not right for me to attend my sister’s wedding or reception. The reason for my conclusion was that both of these activities are celebrations of a sinful union. Attending these ceremonies and celebrations, even if done with the expressed stance that one does not agree that the union is moral, cannot escape the express condoning of the action. You do not support sin, especially one of this magnitude.
The article shared as a reference expresses my views quite accurately. I think my conclusion is best supported by scripture of the alternative stances.
I’m going to quote a huge chunk of the article just in case it isn’t hosted in the future:
Not “a Romans 14 Issue” as the Analogue of Incest in 1 Corinthians 5 Shows

Attending a “gay wedding” is not “a Romans 14 issue” where believers can agree to disagree over matters of indifference like eating meat or not, which do not determine entrance into the kingdom of God (Rom. 14:17). Those who think otherwise either have difficulty reasoning analogically on this matter or else have departed in some way from the scriptural view of homosexual practice. They use arguments like wanting to stay in relationship with a “gay” family member or friend; imitating Jesus’ practice of eating with sinners; or comparing attending a “gay wedding” to attending a wedding of a divorced believer.

All these arguments can easily be seen as wanting if one compares attending a “gay wedding” to its most appropriate analogue: Attending an incestuous wedding between consenting adults “committed” to one another—for example, a man and his mother, or a woman and her brother. There may even be a “genetic sexual attraction” between close kin who are reunited late in life (see also this, this, this, and this). Incestuous unions are comparable to homosexual unions in terms of degree of severity (though from a biblical perspective homosexual practice is even worse) and problematic aspect (sex with another who is too much of an embodied same, whether as regards kinship or gender).

Paul’s response to the incestuous man in 1 Corinthians 5 gives us a good indication of what Paul’s response to attending a “gay wedding” would have been. True, Paul doesn’t mention that the self-professed Christian man who is in a sexual relationship with his stepmother is getting married to his stepmother. Yet, given Paul’s overall reaction to the situation, it is historically absurd to contend that Paul would have given his consent to their attendance of such an incestuous wedding, had it been requested.

The Corinthian response of being “puffed up,” inflated with pride, at their ability to tolerate an incestuous relationship, certainly made matters worse. That does not mean, though, that had they made clear to the incestuous man their disapproval of the relationship, Paul would have approved their attendance of a wedding between the two.

Paul insists rather that the Corinthian believers should “mourn” his actions, because it puts the offender at high risk of exclusion from God’s kingdom (1 Cor. 6:9–10). One mourns at a funeral. A person cannot go to a wedding mourning, since the entire point of the event is to celebrate the rendering permanent of the union. Marriage involves a commitment to stay in the union permanently. In this case, the parties would be declaring their intent to sin egregiously as long as they live, and celebrating that declaration. A believer can’t attend such a ceremony.

Indeed, Paul recommends that the Corinthians put the incestuous man, who “calls himself a brother [i.e. a believer],” out of the community (“remove from your midst the one who did/does this deed”), to cease “associating with” him, “not even to eat with such a one” (1 Cor. 5:2, 11). Obviously, such injunctions preclude something much worse: Going to the wedding of a man celebrating the grave immorality of incest. Going to a wedding that celebrates a gravely immoral union would be comparable to going to a ritual celebrating a person’s suicide or self-immolation.
Paul’s Act of Love in The Face of Today’s Excuse to Stay in Relationship

Paul’s actions may seem harsh, but Paul’s hope was to yet save the offender’s “spirit . . . on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:5). Paul’s actions are remedial, not punitive. The offender needs a massive wake-up call; otherwise, he is heading to hell in a hand basket. He does not need further accommodations to his death-inducing immorality by the church. Paul wants the incest to have stopped yesterday, for the sake of the offender (whom he seeks to reclaim), for the sake of the community (whose accommodations to immorality are threatening their existence), and for the sake of God (who expended the ultimate cost to redeem them, the atoning death of his Son).

We should bear in mind that this is the same Paul who wrote in marvelous praise of love just eight chapters later in the same letter. Paul did not violate that praise in the actions that he took toward the incestuous man.

To claim that Paul gives us no advice as to whether a believer can attend an incestuous wedding, making it “a Romans 14 issue,” would be historically ridiculous. Paul’s remarks in 1 Corinthians 5 make crystal clear that there is no way that he would have condoned attendance at such a celebration of immorality. Try any of the arguments that some Christians use to justify attendance at a “gay wedding” and see if they work well for an incestuous “wedding.” For example:

“It is better to go to an incestuous wedding and stay in a relationship with a person who wants to marry a parent or sibling than it is to not go and thereby cut oneself off from future opportunities to witness to Christ.” Do you think such an argument would pass muster for Paul, much less for Jesus? Attending an incestuous wedding communicates acceptance even if you tell your incestuous friend that you do not approve of incestuous unions.

You may say that you are opposed, but your coming communicates at best that your moral stance is no big deal. Otherwise, you would be weeping for the offending family member or friend at the service, and not making merry at the reception. By going to such a wedding, you would not be witnessing to them of Christ’s love, but rather of Christ’s tacit acceptance of the incest. There are other ways of showing love without attending such a wedding.

By its very nature, a wedding is a public celebration of a sexual union. when we attend a wedding, we are there to serve as witnesses of the vows. Even if there is no statement like “speak now or forever hold your peace” (and if there were, your failure to speak would count against you on the day of judgment), the attendees are still summoned to assist in holding the parties accountable to the vow of matrimony. Attendees are often expected to applaud, and certainly to smile, at the ritual, not to cry tears of anguish.

Attendance conveys joint celebration: “I’m happy for you. I’m here to celebrate with you this sexual union, and to work for its longevity.” A faithful Christian, however, cannot be happy at a ritual that celebrates the offense of incest; nor can a Christian congratulate those entering the union (e.g., in a receiving line at the end of the service). There is no doubt as to what Paul’s response to an invitation to an incestuous wedding would have been, even if it were an incestuous wedding of a friend who was an unbeliever.

If your family member or friend made attendance at their incestuous “wedding” a precondition for continuing to be in relationship, you would (hopefully) balk. That precondition would be a form of manipulation, even extortion, setting the parameters for future relationship that would lead to further future demands, requiring you to violate conscience and compromise God’s standards for sexual purity. When Paul tells the Corinthians to “flee sexual immorality (porneia)” (1 Cor. 6:18), he certainly did not have in mind that they attend the ritual celebration of a grossly immoral sexual union.
Other Excuses for Attending an Immoral Wedding, Debunked by Jesus and Paul
“Jesus Ate with Sinners, and So Should I”

“But didn’t Jesus eat with sexual sinners? Wouldn’t that suggest that he would approve of attendance at an incestuous wedding?” Obviously, Jesus’ eating with sexual sinners did not involve attending a ritual that celebrated the immoral sexual activity (least of all, incest and homosexual practice) of those whom he was trying to reclaim for the Kingdom of God that he was proclaiming. The same applies to his eating with exploitative tax collectors: Jesus would not have attended a ritual celebrating their financial exploitation of the poor, even if he first made clear his disapproval of such exploitation. That would be an abomination to God.
“Attending the Wedding of Someone Divorced is Almost the Same Thing!”

“You are being inconsistent: If you are willing to go to a wedding of a divorced person, you should be able to go to a wedding of two siblings or of an adult and his or her parent.” Really? Do you not realize that incest is far worse, and that, logically speaking, one cannot move from permission in a lesser offense to permission in a far greater offense? Arguably, given Jesus’ teaching on divorce-and-remarriage, the church should disapprove of Christians attending the wedding of a divorced person (which Jesus would have done), at least of a person who divorced a spouse on invalid grounds or was the cause of divorce through adultery.

Regardless, there is no morality in a premise that finds virtue in being more consistently disobedient to the will of God, and that as pertains to ever-worse offenses. The same applies to those who argue from willingness to attend the wedding of a divorced person to a willingness to attend a “gay wedding.” The closest analogue to a “gay wedding” is an incestuous wedding, not the wedding of someone divorced.
“I’ll Only Attend the Reception, Not the Ceremony”

“Well, I should at least be allowed to attend the wedding reception of an incestuous couple.” No, you should not. A reception continues the celebration of the sexual union, often even more so. One is expected to express congratulations to the couple, to lift up one’s glass in response to toasting the union, to dance, and to share in a festive meal. It is a continuation of the ritual of the wedding ceremony.
What Applies to Incestuous Marriage Applies to Homosexual Marriage

If these excuses would be unacceptable grounds for attending an incestuous “wedding,” they would be just as unacceptable in the case of a “gay wedding.” A “gay wedding” is a parallel union to an incestuous union. In fact, as noted above, a “gay wedding” is even worse than an incestuous “wedding” from Paul’s perspective, and the perspective of Jesus, since homosexual unions challenge the very foundation of human sexual ethics, the male-female prerequisite ensconced since creation (Gen. 1:27; 2:24; so Mark 10:6–9; parallel in Matt. 19:4–6, 8). It is from this foundation that Jesus extrapolated other standards, like a limitation of two persons to a sexual union, whether concurrent (no polygamy) or serial (no remarriage after [invalid?] divorce).

Yes, Scripture (including Jesus) views homosexual practice as a worse offense than even incest. Many Christians today do not grasp that point because “gay” sexuality is celebrated in the culture, whereas incest is still largely regarded with revulsion. The prohibition of incest is extrapolated secondarily from the prohibition of homosexual practice: One cannot have as a sexual partner someone who is already too much of a structural same. Unlike the prohibition of homosexual practice, the prohibition of incest is not grounded in creation. Loopholes to some forms of incest are not closed off till the period of Levitical legislation (Lev. 18 and 20). There never were any loopholes for some forms of homosexual practice, indicating the greater severity of the offense.

Evangelical and conservative Catholic leaders who acknowledge homosexual practice to be immoral but still seek to persuade fellow believers that it is permissible to attend a “gay wedding” should be ashamed of themselves. They are not thinking scripturally. They are informed more by their culture than by Jesus and the word of God. They are lying to themselves and to others if they think that Paul would ever have permitted believers to attend a “wedding” between an arsenokoites (a man lying with a male; 1 Cor. 6:9) and his malakos (a male who feminized his appearance to attract a male sex partner; 1 Cor. 6:9).[1]
1. These are the two Greek terms that are often translated “homosexuals” or “men who practice homosexuality” in many English translations of the Bible.

Presumably (one can only hope), these same Evangelical and conservative Catholic leaders would never think of attending an incestuous “wedding.” Why not? Well, because such a “wedding” would still be roundly disapproved even by today’s dissolute society (indeed, it is illegal, though perhaps not prosecuted in some places). They would have society’s approval for their own decision to decline attendance for this “really bad” sexual union; but they would have society’s strong disapproval for declining to attend a “gay wedding.”

It is secular society, not Scripture, not Jesus, that determines their thinking. Because of society’s strong push for normalizing homosexual practice (and even transgenderism), these leaders have allowed themselves to be brainwashed into thinking that homosexual practice is not as bad as incest, let alone worse.
Does the Situation Change If the Participants Are Unbelievers?

What about attending the “gay wedding” of an unbeliever? Would that be okay? Think again of the analogy of an incestuous wedding. Do you think Jesus or Paul would permit attending such a wedding if the participants were unbelievers? Of course not.

To be sure, Paul in 1 Corinthians 5 applies his strictures to the case of an incestuous offender who is a self-professed believer, and adds that believers cannot disassociate completely with unbelievers (“since otherwise you would need to come out of world,” 1 Cor. 5:10). That, however, is not the same thing as making attendance at a wedding that celebrates a grossly immoral sexual union optional. Note that Paul also warns the Corinthians not to be “unevenly yoked (i.e., harnessed or bound, tied up as partners, mismatched) with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:14). Attendance at such a ceremony would convey tacit acceptance, no matter what the attendee says about disapproval.

As it happens, when it comes to discussing relations with unbelievers, we have an excellent parallel to the way Paul treated the problem of invitations that believers might receive to celebrate an occasion at an idol’s temple. Association with unbelievers in idolatrous or immoral rituals was forbidden.

Paul closely associated idolatry and sexual immorality. Paul’s vice or offender lists nearly always lead off with idolatry and sexual immorality (in either order) because of the severity of these common Gentile offenses (e.g., 1 Cor. 6:9–10; Gal. 5:19–21; Rom. 1:18–32; compare 1 Thess. 1:9 with 1 Thess. 4:3–8). Paul has two “flee” statements in 1 Corinthians: “Flee sexual immorality (porneia)” (1 Cor. 6:18) and “Flee from idolatry” (1 Cor. 10:14). His “midrash” (exposition) on Israel’s wilderness sojourn in 1 Cor. 10:1–11 focused on the twin reasons why nearly all who escaped from Egypt never made it to the Promised Land: idolatry and sexual immorality.

Thus, Paul in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10 absolutely forbade dining in an idol’s temple, and did so on two grounds. First, such actions could “stumble” (i.e., precipitate the spiritual downfall of) others with a weak conscience by sending the message that idol worship wasn’t such a big deal (ch. 8). Second, those attending such rituals, at which sacrifices would be made to an idol, were actually offending God by aligning themselves unknowingly with demonic powers (1 Cor. 10:14–22). Going to a “gay wedding”—which centers around the ritual celebration of a sexual union offensive enough to have become a byword for God’s cataclysmic judgment (Sodom)—is not much different from going to an idol’s temple to celebrate a friend’s or business partner’s marriage, birth, or job success.

Those Christians who say it is okay to attend a “gay wedding” are adopting a position that would be comparable to the Corinthians responding to Paul’s remarks in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10 in the following way:

We understand your position, Paul; but we have seen good fruit borne from attending functions held at an idol’s temple. So, we are going to pray about things and decide on a case-by-case basis whether we should continue attending because we feel that by maintaining socializing contacts with our pagan friends at these events we will have a better chance of winning them over to the Lord.

There is no way that Paul would have accepted such a missionizing self-justification—not for attending an unbeliever’s ceremony at an idol’s temple and not for attending an incestuous or homosexual wedding. Those peddling such a view have become partners (koinonoi, 2 Cor. 6:14) to evil, compromised Christian morality, offended God, and stumbled the weak.

Anyone who cites Paul’s Mars Hill episode in Acts 17 as a counterexample would miss the point. At Mars Hill Paul was not attending a religious ritual in a temple. He was attending a meeting of Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debating various ideas. He then proclaimed the gospel to them, calling on them to repent or be destroyed. There is no parallel in Acts 17 to attending a ritual celebrating a “gay wedding” that brings God’s judgment on the heads of the participants. So far as all the other guests at this event are concerned, you approve—even if you’ve made a private mild communication of disapproval to one of the persons involved but otherwise remain publicly silent.
Orientation and Conclusion

The fact that some persons have an exclusive homosexual “orientation” does not change the moral equation. Homosexual practice remains repugnant to God, a violation of God’s intentional creation of sexual counterparts, even when it meets needs for sexual companionship. A person in a sexual union with the same sex is devaluing God’s stamp of gender on the body, treating maleness or femaleness as only half intact in relation to one’s own sex.

God did not design half-males and half-females who need to unite sexually with someone of their own sex in order to feel whole as a male or female. We are each half of a whole sexual spectrum made of “male and female” as designed by God. Same-sex sexual unions are intrinsically “dishonoring” to the participants (the term Paul uses in Rom. 1:24–27), whether or not they admit to it, and “something abhorrent” (to’evah) to God (Lev. 18:22; 20:13).

Christians who attend a “gay wedding” should be honest with themselves and announce publicly that they have changed their mind about homosexual practice in key ways that deviate from the only witness of Scripture. They will eventually come to that realization in the not-too-distant-future if they aren’t already putting on a fake mask now.

title: Should Christian Women Pray With Their Heads Covered

body.text: 1 Cor 11:5-6 (NIV)

But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head—it is the same as having her head shaved. For if a woman does not cover her head, she might as well have her hair cut off; but if it is a disgrace for a woman to have her hair cut off or her head shaved, then she should cover her head.

If you read 1 Corinthians 11, you’ll find that Paul is quite clear that he believes a woman should cover her head when she prays or else she dishonors her husband, he being the authority over her. He also says that a man ought not to cover his head when he prays or he dishonors Christ, being his head and authority. There’s not much explanation given for why women show their subjugation to their husbands by wearing a covering but men don’t have the same physical symbol of their subjugation to Christ who is their authority.
Some people seem to think that 1 Cor 11:15 means that women having long hair is sufficient as a covering.
1 Cor 11:15 (NIV)

But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head—it is the same as having her head shaved. For if a woman does not cover her head, she might as well have her hair cut off; but if it is a disgrace for a woman to have her hair cut off or her head shaved, then she should cover her head. but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering.

But taking this without considering Paul’s earlier words of “For if a woman does not cover her head, she might as well have her hair cut off” is sloppy. I mean, that’s a direct contradiction of what Paul says. It seems that he’s saying that while nature itself seeks to cover women’s heads with hair, a covering is additionally necessary.

Also, interestingly, the translations of this section (1 Cor. 11) vary drastically, which reflects the liberty and bias that given translations have. For example, read the MSG paraphrasing of these verses and you’ll find huge differences between more traditional translations in the interpreted meaning.
1 Corinthians 11:3-16 (MSG)

In a marriage relationship, there is authority from Christ to husband, and from husband to wife. The authority of Christ is the authority of God. Any man who speaks with God or about God in a way that shows a lack of respect for the authority of Christ, dishonors Christ. In the same way, a wife who speaks with God in a way that shows a lack of respect for the authority of her husband, dishonors her husband. Worse, she dishonors herself—an ugly sight, like a woman with her head shaved. This is basically the origin of these customs we have of women wearing head coverings in worship, while men take their hats off. By these symbolic acts, men and women, who far too often butt heads with each other, submit their “heads” to the Head: God.

Don’t, by the way, read too much into the differences here between men and women. Neither man nor woman can go it alone or claim priority. Man was created first, as a beautiful shining reflection of God—that is true. But the head on a woman’s body clearly outshines in beauty the head of her “head,” her husband. The first woman came from man, true—but ever since then, every man comes from a woman! And since virtually everything comes from God anyway, let’s quit going through these “who’s first” routines.

Don’t you agree there is something naturally powerful in the symbolism—a woman, her beautiful hair reminiscent of angels, praying in adoration; a man, his head bared in reverence, praying in submission? I hope you’re not going to be argumentative about this. All God’s churches see it this way; I don’t want you standing out as an exception.

When I read this I thought, “Well they took some major liberty to insert their particular interpretation in this section.” The meaning they portray here is not in the text but beyond it—in fact, the meaning they portray lies not in the text itself but in their interpretation of the text. I know the MSG version of the Bible is a paraphrasing, but I still expected a more true-to-the-text paraphrasing.

title: Nephi’s Abundance of Precious Things Contradiction

body.text: And I did teach my people to build buildings, and to work in all manner of wood, and of iron, and of copper, and of brass, and of steel, and of gold, and of silver, and of precious ores, which were in great abundance.

And I, Nephi, did build a temple; and I did construct it after the manner of the temple of Solomon save it were not built of so many precious things; for they were not to be found upon the land, wherefore, it could not be built like unto Solomon’s temple. But the manner of the construction was like unto the temple of Solomon; and the workmanship thereof was exceedingly fine.

Many identify a contradiction here between Nephi saying that all these precious metals can be found in great abundance but in the next verse saying that the “precious things” required to build a temple just like Solomon’s “were not to be found upon the land.”
For , this is an issue so serious that it alone threatens the internal integrity of the Book of Mormon. I think I can resolve the issue sufficiently. Here’s what I think of it:

It’s important to note that verse 15 is talking about precious metals. While Nephi does say that his people began “to work in all manner of wood” as well as with precious metals. It seems that when he says “which were in great abundance” he’s referring to the “precious ores” and not the wood.

Verse 16 says only that Nephi’s people couldn’t have the same amount of “precious things” as Solomon’s temple because that amount could “[not] be found upon the land”. This is believable since Solomon’s temple consisted of an incredibly large amount of precious cedars, stones, bronze, gold, and silver.

When Nephi said that there weren’t enough precious things in the land to mimic Solomon’s temple fully, he probably was referring to the lack of cedars, stones, and supply of precious metals—for while there may have been an abundance of precious metals in the land, Solomon’s temple required an even greater abundance that exceeded the abundance available in the Lehites’ promised land.
John W. Welch also has a response to this query and I’ll put it here for reference:
John W. Welch, “The Temple in the Book of Mormon,” in Temples of the Ancient World, p. 325]

According to John Welch, when Nephi says his temple was “not built of so many precious things” (2 Nephi 5:16), he probably is not speaking of gold or silver, which were found in the land of Nephi. The common Book of Mormon phrase “gold, silver, and precious things” appears to parallel the Near Eastern formulaic expression in which “precious things” commonly referred to precious gems. Thus, while Nephi mentions an abundance of metallic ores (gold, silver, and copper) in his description of the new promised land (see 1 Nephi 18:25), he conspicuously fails to mention gems or “precious things,” such as carbuncle, emerald, sapphire, and diamond, which Solomon used extensively in constructing his temple (see 2 Chronicles 3:6; also Exodus 39:10-13). Accordingly, the Book of Mormon is consistent; Nephi could not decorate his temple with the same kinds of precious things as were used in Solomon’s temple.

title: The Long Ending of Mark Problem & The Book of Mormon

body.text: Biblical scholars mostly agree that verses 9-20 of Mark 16 were added in later and are not part of the authentic text. The main reason they argue this is that the two earliest sources of the text, which I believe are the Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. These two texts have the book ending with Mary being astounded at the appearance of Christ at the tomb.
However, it’s interesting to note that …

Another entry to put in here is the dispute of the lung ending of Mark existing in the book of mormon. This argument comes from a consensus of biblical scholars and relies upon mostly the long ending of Mark missing from the two earliest codexes of the new testament. Seem to be a compelling case there are some extra details that I find of interest. For example these two codexes are missing other parts of the scripture such as the story of the woman Continental tree and some wording in the transfiguration on the mount and stuff. One very interesting thing to me was that at least Bard told me this the wording from The sermon on the Mount of without cause is not found in these codexes. I think I remember that wording also being taken out of The sermon on the Mount found in the book of Mormon which is an interesting parallel if that is true. Here is my conversation with bard. Check it and verify it and turn this into a entry
Sure. Here are some other scriptures that are missing from one or both of the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus:
* **The story of the woman caught in adultery** (John 7:53-8:11) is missing from the Codex Vaticanus.
* **The ending of Mark's Gospel** (Mark 16:9-20) is missing from the Codex Sinaiticus.
* **The doxology at the end of the Lord's Prayer** (Matthew 6:13) is missing from the Codex Vaticanus.
* **The phrase "without cause"** in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:22) is missing from both codices.
* **The story of the woman with the issue of blood** (Mark 5:25-34) is missing from the Codex Vaticanus.
* **The story of the raising of Jairus' daughter** (Mark 5:21-43) is missing from the Codex Sinaiticus.
* **The story of the Transfiguration** (Matthew 17:1-13; Mark 9:2-13; Luke 9:28-36) is shorter in the Codex Sinaiticus than in other manuscripts.
* **The story of the cursing of the fig tree** (Matthew 21:18-22) is missing from the Codex Vaticanus.

It is important to note that the absence of these scriptures from the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus does not necessarily mean that they were not part of the original text of the Bible. It is possible that these scriptures were omitted by the scribes who copied these codices, or that they were lost due to damage or scribal error.

The study of the differences between different manuscripts of the Bible is a complex and ongoing field of research. Scholars continue to debate the significance of the omissions and discrepancies that are found in these manuscripts. However, the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus are still considered to be two of the most important and reliable manuscripts of the Bible, and they provide valuable insights into the transmission of the text of the Bible over time.

You are correct. The Book of Mormon does not include the phrase "without cause" in the Sermon on the Mount. This is one of the many similarities between the Book of Mormon and the earliest manuscripts of the Bible.
The phrase "without cause" is found in the following versions of the Sermon on the Mount:
* The King James Version (Matthew 5:22)
* The New International Version (Matthew 5:22)
* The New Revised Standard Version (Matthew 5:22)
* The Revised Standard Version (Matthew 5:22)
* The Douay-Rheims Bible (Matthew 5:22)
However, the phrase is not found in the following manuscripts:
* The Codex Sinaiticus (Matthew 5:22)
* The Codex Vaticanus (Matthew 5:22)
* The Codex Bezae (Matthew 5:22)
* The Codex Washingtonianus (Matthew 5:22)
* The Ephraemi Rescriptus (Matthew 5:22)

The omission of the phrase "without cause" from the Book of Mormon is consistent with the omission of this phrase from the earliest manuscripts of the Bible. This suggests that the Book of Mormon may be based on an earlier version of the Sermon on the Mount than the versions that are found in the King James Version and other modern translations.

However, it is important to note that the absence of the phrase "without cause" from the Book of Mormon does not necessarily mean that it was not part of the original Sermon on the Mount. It is possible that the phrase was omitted from the Book of Mormon by the scribes who copied it, or that it was lost due to damage or scribal error.

Ultimately, the question of whether the phrase "without cause" was part of the original Sermon on the Mount is a matter of scholarly debate. There is no definitive answer, and scholars will continue to discuss this issue for many years to come.

The similarities between the Book of Mormon and the earliest manuscripts of the Bible are one of the arguments that are used by some people to support the authenticity of the Book of Mormon. However, it is important to note that these similarities do not prove that the Book of Mormon is authentic. There are many other possible explanations for these similarities, such as the possibility that the Book of Mormon was influenced by the Bible.

The question of whether the Book of Mormon is authentic is a matter of faith. There is no scientific or historical evidence that can definitively prove or disprove the Book of Mormon. Ultimately, each individual must decide for themselves whether or not they believe the Book of Mormon is true.
Gospel Topics: Death, Spiritual

Spiritual death is separation from God. The scriptures teach of two sources of spiritual death. The first source is the Fall, and the second is our own disobedience. Spiritual death can be overcome through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and by obedience to His gospel.

The Gospel Topics manual for this topic elaborates further giving me the impression that spiritual death is overcome via the resurrection when we are brought back into the presence of God, which aligns with the words of Samuel the Lamanite.
Helaman 14:16-17

Yea, behold, this death bringeth to pass the resurrection, and redeemeth all mankind from the first death—that spiritual death; for all mankind, by the fall of Adam being cut off from the presence of the Lord, are considered as dead, both as to things temporal and to things spiritual.
But behold, the resurrection of Christ redeemeth mankind, yea, even all mankind, and bringeth them back into the presence of the Lord.
Gospel Topics: Death, Spiritual

Further spiritual death comes as a result of our own disobedience. Our sins make us unclean and unable to dwell in the presence of God (see Romans 3:23; Alma 12:12–16, 32; Helaman 14:18; Moses 6:57). Through the Atonement, Jesus Christ offers redemption from this spiritual death, but only when we exercise faith in Him, repent of our sins, and obey the principles and ordinances of the gospel (see Alma 13:27–30; Helaman 14:19; Articles of Faith 1:3).

The referenced scriptures appear to me to only indicate that spiritual death may be overcome in the resurrection when we are brought back into the presence of God after which we may suffer a second spiritual death.
Guide to the Scriptures: Death, Spiritual
Separation from God and His influences; to die as to things pertaining to righteousness.

The Guide to the Scriptures resource references 1 Timothy 5:6 as support when asserting, "Mortals with evil thoughts, words, and works are spiritually dead while still alive on earth." While it ought to be true that sinful works will lead to spiritual death, what's not clear is whether any of us might otherwise be spiritually alive during this life. Can we have spiritual life while living in this corruptible tabernacle being cut off from the presence of God? Paul's words here quoted might lead one to think that if only sinners are spiritually dead then the rest of us might be spiritually alive. But that's a jump that's not logically explicit from the statement. I'm unsure if this can be the case. My hesitation to accept that mortals can have spiritual life during this probation comes from the doctrine of the second death. The second death occurs after spiritual life has been restored following the first spiritual death—that one imposed upon us from the fall immediately when we are born into this realm.
Christ’s Atonement overcomes physical and spiritual death so we can reenter God’s presence.
Well, yes, the Atonement is capable of restoring us to spiritual life, but precisely when does it do this? I think it's only at the resurrection when we're restored to God's presence.
I find a useful distinction made by the MormonWiki:
There are two ways we are cut off or separated from the presence of the Lord, and this distinction sometimes causes confusion
Our first parents were cut off both temporally and spiritually from the presence of the Lord. (Alma 42:7)

The resurrection . . . redeemeth all mankind from the first death—that spiritual death; for all mankind, by the fall of Adam being cut off from the presence of the Lord, are considered as dead, both as to things temporal and to things spiritual. (Helaman 14:16)

In other words, being cut off from Heavenly Father's presence is called a "temporal separation," and being cut off from the Holy Ghost's presence is called a "spiritual separation." The temporal separation (from Heavenly Father) is sometimes called the first spiritual death, or the first death (2 Nephi 9:15; Alma 11:45; 12:36; Helaman 14:16; Doctrine & Covenants 29:41). The spiritual separation (from the Holy Ghost) is sometimes called the second spiritual death, or the second death (Revelation 2:11; 20:6, 14; 21:8; Jacob 3:11; Alma 12:16, 32; 13:30; Helaman 14:18–19; Doctrine and Covenants 63:17; 76:37). This terminology may have been chosen because it refers to the sequence in which the two deaths occur in every individual's life—we are first separated from Heavenly Father when we come to earth for our mortal lives (the first death); then we are separated by degrees from the Holy Ghost when we sin (the second death).
This distinction is useful and seems to be supported by scripture though only subtly. It’s a difficult but necessary distinction.
