title: What Does it Mean to Make The Lord’s Paths Straight?

body.text: John 1:23
He said, I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias.

John the Baptist echos the words of Isaiah, making clear the connection of this prophecy to his time, that he is preparing the way of the Lord. But what is this about making the Lord’s paths straight? Does it mean that the Jews had to clean up their act in order for the Messiah to come? Because it sort of seems like the opposite had to be true—the Jews had to be wicked enough to crucify their own God.

Perhaps some had to be righteous to believe and have faith to see great miracles brought forth by Him while others would harden their hearts. Perhaps the preparation of His path entailed the change of heart and ways of the select few who listened to and heeded Christ.

Alma, when speaking to the people in the land of Gideon, references this scripture over a hundred years before the coming of Christ urging that people to heed the advice already and begin preparing the Lord’s paths. It’s odd because Christ’s mortal ministry wasn’t to any of the people in this audience so I ask why they were encouraged to be part of this preparatory movement of the Lord’s path. Although I’m not sure the answer to this question, digging into this section is very interesting.
19 For I perceive that ye are in the paths of righteousness; I perceive that ye are in the path which leads to the kingdom of God; yea, I perceive that ye are making his paths straight.
20 I perceive that it has been made known unto you, by the testimony of his word, that he cannot walk in crooked paths;
Luke 3:5
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;
neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning
James 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
from the right to the left, or from that which is right to that which is wrong; therefore, his course is one eternal round.

21 And he doth not dwell in unholy temples; neither can filthiness or anything which is unclean be received into the kingdom of God; therefore I say unto you the time shall come, yea, and it shall be at the last day, that he who is filthy shall remain in his filthiness.
Revelation 22:11
He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.
Alma references some ideas and wording which are somewhat exclusive to the New Testament. For instance, “shadow of turning” only appears once in the Book of Mormon and once in the New Testament.

The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.

I bring this scripture up to show that Paul suggests women pray and prophecy, and presumably do so in church. This seems to contrast with 1 Cor. 14 mentioned above where Paul says women should keep silent in church and not speak.

There’s Deborah from the Old Testament in Judges 4 who is described as a prophetess and judge of Israel (Judges 4:4) but this is somewhat irrelevant in the discussion as we’re talking about women’s role in the ecclesiastical church and priesthood. I just want to point this out so it’s not brought up as a red herring.

I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling; likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works. Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor. Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

This teaches that women are to submit to their husbands and not exercise authority over them. The bit about childbearing being their way to salvation is interesting. What is it referring to and what does it mean?
JD 1:66, Brigham Young, Education

I am not quite so strenuous as some of the ancients were, who taught that if the women wanted to learn anything, to learn it at home from their husbands. I am willing they should come to the meetings and learn, but some of the ancients proscribed them in this privilege, and would confine them at home to learn through their husbands. I am a little more liberal than they were...
Genesis 3:16 (ESV)
To the woman he said, “I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be contrary to your husband, but he shall rule over you.”
JD 9:305, Brigham Young, The Love of Truth and Righteousness, Etc.

When our first parents fell from their paradisiacal state, they were brought in contact with influences and powers of evil that are unnatural and stand in opposition to an endless life. So far as mankind yield to these influences, they are so far removed from a natural to an unnatural state—from life to death. Adam and Eve did not sin because it was in their nature to love sin, but, as Paul says in his Epistle to Timothy, “Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression. Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety.” The enemy of all righteousness deceived the woman, and Adam went with her that man might be, and that she might be saved in childbearing.

Brigham Young's view, based on this sentence and his influence in the temple ceremony depiction of the fall conveying the same sentiment of Adam following Eve for the sake of reproducing and obeying the Father's command to multiply and replenish is very interesting. But it suggests that Adam was not deceived and Eve was not his deceiver. This has some issues since almost every reference to the fall says that Eve, or both Adam and Eve, was deceived or beguiled. In what way was Adam deceived if not by Eve?

Anyway, it seems that Brigham Young interpreted 1 Tim. 2:15 as being a reference to Eve being redeemed from the fall because Adam chose to unite with her in her fallen state so as to be able to multiply and replenish with her. I hesitate with this interpretation. Where is the beguiling? How does it reconcile with the rest of scripture on the subject? Yet, this interpretation is forced upon latter-day saints via the Temple Endowment depiction of the creation and fall.

Perhaps this view isn't wrong after all. Paul does say that Adam wasn't deceived but only Eve (1 Tim. 2:14). Orson Pratt has a very interesting quote on this and gives a suggestion that 2 Nephi 2 may be saying that if Adam had not fallen he, and not Eve, would have remained in the garden and had no children. And he would have had no children because Eve would have been cast out and he remain, a lone man.
JD 1:290 Orson Pratt, A General Funeral Sermon, Etc.

But there is a very curious saying in the Book of Mormon, to which I now wish to refer your minds; it reads thus: “Adam fell that man might be; and men are, that they might have joy.” (2 Ne. 2:25) Says one, “If Adam had not fallen, then there could not have been any posterity.” That is just what we believe; but how do you get along with that saying which was given previous to the fall, where he was commanded to multiply and replenish the earth? (Gen. 1:28)

How could he have multiplied and fulfilled this commandment, if “Adam fell that man might be?” Let me appeal to another saying in the New Testament: “Adam was not deceived; but the woman, being deceived, was in the transgression,” (1 Tim. 2:14) says the Apostle Paul. Well, after the woman was deceived, she became subject to the penalty; yes, after she had partaken of the forbidden fruit, the penalty was upon her, and not upon Adam; he had not partaken of the fruit, but his wife had.

Now, what is to be done? Here are two beings in the garden of Eden, the woman and the man; she has transgressed, has broken the law, and incurred the penalty. And now, suppose the man had said, “I will not partake of this forbidden fruit;” the next word would have been, “Cast her out of the garden; but let Adam stay there, for he has not sinned; he has not broken the commandment, but his wife has; she was deceived, let her be banished from the garden, and from my presence, and from Adam's presence; let them be eternally separated.”

I ask, on these conditions could they fulfil the first great commandment? They could not. Adam saw this, that the woman was overcome by the devil speaking through the serpent; and when he saw it, he was satisfied that the woman would have to be banished from his presence: he saw, also, that unless he partook of the forbidden fruit, he could never raise up posterity; therefore the truth of that saying in the Book of Mormon is apparent, that “Adam fell that man might be.” (2 Ne. 2:25) He saw that it was necessary that he should with her partake of sorrow and death, and the varied effects of the fall, that he and she might be redeemed from these effects, and be restored back again to the presence of God.

I’ve never given much credence to the idea that Adam deliberately chose to fall, not being deceived, but made an informed decision to fall in order to uphold that first commandment to multiply and replenish the earth. I’ve thought that the so-called commandment of “multiply and replenish the earth” is an act of creation from God to man, not a moral instruction. God invoked the same words to all life, “Let them be fruitful and multiply.” Are we to think that God was giving moral instructions to each of His creations or rather that He was designing their genes and creating in them the processes and faculties that would enable them to reproduce?

Thinking of this instruction this way also dissolves the supposed dilemma of God’s paradoxical commandments of multiplying and not eating the fruit of the tree of knowledge—for it seems that Adam and Eve could only follow one or the other and not both of these commandments. Can God give incongruent commandments? What a dilemma.

The only other way to reconcile this dilemma as far as I can tell is that you have to concede that Adam and Eve actually good multiply and replenish in the garden while not also partaking of the forbidden fruit.

And so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled. Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good.

Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct. Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious. Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

title: Can the Church Apostatize in the Latter Day?

body.text: Daniel 2:44

And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
Excerpts from Three Addresses by President Wilford Woodruff Regarding the Manifesto

The Lord will never permit me or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray. It is not in the programme. It is not in the mind of God. If I were to attempt that, the Lord would remove me out of my place, and so He will any other man who attempts to lead the children of men astray from the oracles of God and from their duty.
Matthew 16:18 (KJV)
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

If there is a God, does he reveal itself to man or expect anything from us? If not, then our lives are negligibly affected by his existence; this is the functional equivalent to non-existence of God. The truth of a thing only matters if it’s existence is consequential. E.g., in a math equation, if this is the only equation and we are , then the only things that matter for us are  and . If it were asserted that the following were true: , it wouldn’t matter for us because it has no bearing on us or our world. The same is true for a God who makes no demands or manifests Himself in any way.

So, for our discussion, if we say there is a God then we mean a God who interacts in our reality. And if this God exists then we might well ask what religion is His. For if this God exists and interacts with our species but does not establish true doctrines regarding Himself and reality towards us, we must be left to conclude that He doesn’t care about us and perhaps has little or no expectations of us, and such a God’s existence would be negligible.

But concerning the God who does make demands and requirements and who does care for us at all, it’s reasonable that He would establish an order of His demands and requirements and lay forth such unto us. Why He doesn’t reveal Himself in all transparency and interact with us in a more apparent way is a question we must resolve, for it is our case. But if we’re to think that He doesn’t establish a religion among us then we’re conceiving of a God who is a spectator or a passerby. Perhaps such a God would be as the overseer of a simulation who watches His creation flourish and dwindle and evolve and dissipate but never interacts with the simulation or the constituents of such except in ways that do not reveal his identity or purposes.

title: Where Did Lehi Get His Priesthood?

body.text: Lehi makes thanks offerings, including burnt offerings, to the Lord from the time of his arrival in the wilderness after departing from Jerusalem (1 Nephi 2:7; 5:9; 7:22). Several years later, in the promised land, Nephi “[consecrates] Jacob and Joseph, that they should be priests and teachers” (2 Nephi 5:26)
This article addresses the topic but I don’t have time to read it fully and summarize it here. Finish this later.

Charity is love, but a certain kind of love. In English, love has many meanings so it can be unclear what exactly is meant by it. This isn’t the case in other languages such as Greek. “Charity”, when translated from the New Testament, comes from the Greek word , which means “love: esp. brotherly love, charity; the love of God for person and of person for God” (). This meaning is distinguished from éros (sexual love), philia (friendship), and xenia (hospitality).
Paul elaborates on charity in 1 Corinthians 13.
Corinthians 13:1-14:1
13:1 Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
13:2 And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
13:3 And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
13:4 Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
13:5 Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
13:6 Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth;
13:7 Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
13:8 Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
13:9 For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
13:10 But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
13:11 When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
13:12 For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
13:13 And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
14:1 Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.

Paul says what charity does and what we are without it (nothing), but still the meaning of the word can be evasive. When one considers the dramatic consequence of being deficient in charity it becomes perplexing how we could have missed this superlative ranking of the attribute or quality of charity. Then comes to mind the Master’s words on loving God and others:
Matthew 22:37-39

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
To which he adds in Mark 12:31 “There is none other commandment greater than these.”
Mormon, in a sermon where he describes how to “lay hold upon every good thing” (Moroni 7:20), gives a strikingly Paul-like teaching of charity:
Moroni 7:42-47
7:42 Wherefore, if a man have faith he must needs have hope; for without faith there cannot be any hope.
7:43 And again, behold I say unto you that he cannot have faith and hope, save he shall be meek, and lowly of heart.

7:44 If so, his faith and hope is vain, for none is acceptable before God, save the meek and lowly in heart; and if a man be meek and lowly in heart, and confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ, he must needs have charity; for if he have not charity he is nothing; wherefore he must needs have charity.

7:45 And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
7:46 Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
7:47 But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

Mormon’s final description of charity being the pure love of Christ calls to mind the beginning of his sermon where he gives the analogy of the bitter and good fountain bringing forth water of their own purity or lack thereof.
Moroni 7:8-10

For behold, if a man being evil giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God. And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing, for God receiveth none such. Wherefore, a man being evil cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.
This metaphor of the bitter fountain seems to reference Jesus’s analogy of the good tree and good fruit:
Matthew 7:17-19

Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

Mormon, in his analogy, likens the fountain to men bringing forth good or evil gifts and teaches that the intent of the heart must be pure if the gift is to be deemed good (Moroni 7:9). Perhaps his emphasis on charity is to be interpreted as the purity of heart required to bring forth good gifts and actions. If this is true, it would make sense how Paul and Mormon could claim “if ye have not charity, ye are nothing” (Moroni 7:46; 1 Cor. 13:2-3).
This interpretation is strengthened by Mormon’s similar style of writing though Mormon is speaking of his bitter-water/bitter-fountain idea and not explicitly charity at this point of the sermon:
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor , and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
(1 Corinthians 13:3)
For behold, God hath said a man being evil cannot do that which is good; for if he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent it profiteth him nothing. (Moroni 7:6)
And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing, for God receiveth none such.
(Moroni 7:9)

The extension of the metaphor Mormon appears to be intentional to charity. On a side-note here, Mormon appears to be fluent in his understanding of the New Testament by his ability to pull a teaching of Jesus about good trees bringing forth good fruit and tie it together with Paul’s sermon on charity.
Other helpful quotes on charity
Charity Never Faileth, Gordon B. Hinckley

If there be any within the sound of my voice who have harbored grudges, who have let hatred develop in their hearts one toward another, I ask you to make the effort to turn around. Hatred always fails and bitterness always destroys, but “charity never faileth.”
In Conference Report, Oct. 1986, Ezra Taft Benson

The final and crowning virtue of the divine character is charity, or the pure love of Christ (see Moroni 7:47). If we would truly seek to be more like our Savior and Master, then learning to love as He loves should be our highest goal. Mormon called charity “the greatest of all” (Moroni 7:46).

The world today speaks a great deal about love, and it is sought for by many. But the pure love of Christ differs greatly from what the world thinks of love. Charity never seeks selfish gratification. The pure love of Christ seeks only the eternal growth and joy of others.
CS Lewis  |  “Love Thy Neighbor,” in The Joyful Christian (New York: Touchstone, 1996), 197.

It is a serious thing to live in a society of possible gods and goddesses, to remember that the dullest and most uninteresting person you talk to may one day be a creature which . . . you would be strongly tempted to worship. . . . There are no ordinary people.
CS Lewis - Mere Christianity
But the Christian thinks any good he does comes from the Christ-life inside him. He does not think God will love us because we are good, but that God will make us good because he loves us.
Marvin J. Ashton  |  Ensign, May 1992, p. 19

Real charity is not something you give away; it is something that you acquire and make a part of yourself.  And when the virtue of charity becomes implanted in your heart, you are never the same again.  It makes the thought of being a basher repulsive.

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don’t judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet.  Charity is accepting someone’s differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn’t handle something the way we might have hoped.  Charity is refusing to take advantage of another’s weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us.  Charity is expecting the best of each other.

title: Women vs Men Presiding
metadata_raw: The Family: A Proclamation to the World | #Women #Men #Preside
refs_raw: The Family: A Proclamation to the World

body.text: Today the Relief Society presidency of our ward spoke in sacrament meeting and between the second and third speakers the conducting member of the bishopric stood up and gave some words. At one point he said something like,
“If women were in charge in this church we’d be lightyears ahead of where we are now because of how far behind we are as brethren.”

This particular man speaking has a quirk where he attempts to be humble by demeaning himself and others whenever he’s complimented or a compliment is implied. Today when he said this it bothered me a lot. He apparently intended to sound humble but instead his words became a twisted criticism of all men, including the presiding men in the Church, including God who designed the order of presidency.

If women would do a better job at directing the work of salvation and presiding in the Church that implies a deficiency in God’s design and work. I find the statement to be inaccurate and to have a negative effect on the men in this church. Men already struggle to be engaged and active in the Church, we don’t need degrading comments about us implying we’re not good at doing our jobs and the women would do better.

Comments like this have a negative impact on the minds of everyone in our Church suggesting to us all that the men stink and women are better. Especially for our young men who we hope to grow up to become strong leaders in the Church, how are they going to feel hearing their own male leaders say that women are much better than them at the callings they’ve been called to and insinuate that men lack spirituality and presiding characteristics? I understand that it’s an attempt to be humble but I think it has egregious ramifications and seriously backfires.

Some men appear to be very uncomfortable with the pattern of men presiding in the Church and they attempt to soothe their discomfort by making statements such as these or by watering down the definition of “preside” in an attempt to totally remove that calling from men.
The Family Proclamation

By divine design, fathers are to preside over their families in love and righteousness and are responsible to provide the necessities of life and protection for their families. Mothers are primarily responsible for the nurture of their children. In these sacred responsibilities, fathers and mothers are obligated to help one another as equal partners.

This excerpt from The Family Proclamation states that fathers preside. While fathers and mothers are obliged to help each other as equals, it is fathers who preside over their families and this pattern extends also to the church—the presiding priesthood authorities and men. That’s God’s design. Presiding means to lead, act as a president. God Himself presides over all His children as Adam does over the human family. This doesn’t mean women aren’t important or equals, but they have not been given this calling by God as men have. I think we’d do well to stop ignoring this doctrine or struggling against it by twisting scriptures or watering down doctrines.

title: Loving God more than the world

body.text: Moroni 7:47
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

I’ve heard some people say that this definition of charity can mean that charity is having the kind of pure love that Christ has for others or that it means having a pure love for Christ. I had always laughed off the latter interpretation finding it semantically incorrect. Whether it’s exegetically accurate, there may be utility to the concept of it. We are commanded, “love the Lord your God” ().

I’ve wondered how I am to love God. If I were commanded to love some random person named George who lived in Germany but whom I didn’t know and couldn’t know, how could I love him? I can’t conjure love out of thin air and place it where I’d like. Love must flow naturally, as if from a source outside of me. Perhaps I can allow it or stifle it, but I cannot create it. Also, it seems that love flows most easily when I know the individual. I may not need to know them in order to love them, I think that’s only a correlation that’s been common in my experience.
Can I love God without knowing Him?
1 John 2:3-6
3 And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments.
4 He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
5 But whoso keepeth his word, in him verily is the love of God perfected: hereby know we that we are in him.
6 He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked.
So one indicator that we know God is that we keep His commandments. This sounds consistent with John 14:15:
John 14:15
If ye love me, keep my commandments.
But I don’t think it means necessarily that anyone who keeps the commandments loves God (), only that those who love God keep His commandments.
1 John 2:15
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
Another teaching is this, that loving the world is mutually exclusive with having the Father’s love in us. This also is consistent with Jesus’s teachings—
Matthew 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Additional relevant verses:
6 Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not: whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him.
9 Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
10 In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother.
1 John 4:19
We love him, because he first loved us.

In 1 John there’s a lot of talk about loving others. It teaches that we ought to love others because God loved us and that if we love others we have God in us. God is love. But even heathens can have love toward one another so what do we mean? And how can we simply love God merely because He supposedly loves us?
I want to love God, but how do I? Perhaps this moves beyond the intellectual realm. I can’t love God by studying, perhaps. How do I get that experiential love of God?
1 John 5:3
For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.

Is loving God summed up in keeping His commandments? Not particularly. Even the Pharisees who were condemned by Jesus kept the commandments. But they kept them by their own willpower and volition and it was a burden on them. The commandments teach us to do that which is contrary to the carnal will and state of man. But if we truly have God’s love in us, this scripture teaches that keeping the commandments won’t be a burden but will flow naturally and with ease. This reminds me of Mormon’s teachings on giving good gifts and doing so not grudgingly.
Moroni 7:8
For behold, if a man being evil giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God.
Only someone who’s motivated by love for God can keep the commandments. Otherwise, they are a burden that lead us to resent and strain.
Moroni 7:10
Wherefore, a man being evil cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.
An evil man can’t please God because he is motivated by the fleshly desires.
Romans 8:7-8
7 Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
8 So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
This idea is expounded by King Benjamin:
Mosiah 3:19

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

So this all makes sense but the question still remains for me, how can I love God? How do I get that initial love in me? I realize that Christ died on the cross and that’s a great price to pay for me, but how can I turn my knowledge of that into love? I suppose I should be grateful at the very least, but how can I just start loving God?

title: How does Jesus Christ make Heavenly Father’s plan possible?

body.text: ●Adam and Eve exist in the Garden of Eden in an immortal and innocent state
○God’s commandment not to partake of the tree of knowledge of good and evil—“thou shalt surely die” (Genesis 2:17).
●The serpent tempts Eve and she and Adam partake of the forbidden fruit gaining knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 3:1-22)
Genesis 3:13-15

14 And the LORD God said unto the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life:

6 For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection, and the resurrection must needs come unto man by reason of the fall; and the fall came by reason of transgression; and because man became fallen they were cut off from the presence of the Lord.

7 Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.

8 O the wisdom of God, his mercy and grace! For behold, if the flesh should rise no more our spirits must become subject to that angel who fell from before the presence of the Eternal God, and became the devil, to rise no more.

9 And our spirits must have become like unto him, and we become devils, angels to a devil, to be shut out from the presence of our God, and to remain with the father of lies, in misery, like unto himself; yea, to that being who beguiled our first parents, who transformeth himself nigh unto an angel of light, and stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder and all manner of secret works of darkness.

10 O how great the goodness of our God, who prepareth a way for our escape from the grasp of this awful monster; yea, that monster, death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit.
11 And because of the way of deliverance of our God, the Holy One of Israel, this death, of which I have spoken, which is the temporal, shall deliver up its dead; which death is the grave.

12 And this death of which I have spoken, which is the spiritual death, shall deliver up its dead; which spiritual death is hell; wherefore, death and hell must deliver up their dead, and hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies, and the bodies and the spirits of men will be restored one to the other; and it is by the power of the resurrection of the Holy One of Israel.

13 O how great the plan of our God! For on the other hand, the paradise of God must deliver up the spirits of the righteous, and the grave deliver up the body of the righteous; and the spirit and the body is restored to itself again, and all men become incorruptible, and immortal, and they are living souls, having a perfect knowledge like unto us in the flesh, save it be that our knowledge shall be perfect.

title: The Gift of Righteousness—Given, not Earned

body.text: I’ve heard some speak of the atonement of Christ saying that it gives us an opportunity to try again—to wipe away our sins that we’ve committed and to give us a chance to give it another go, as if, given enough attempts, we’ll eventually be able to get rid of our sinful ways and be able to live without any sin. There are parts of this that have truth and parts that are misleading.
If the atonement were merely a second (third, fourth, …) chance, it would be insufficient.
Romans 3:20
…by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight…

Paul hits on this point pretty hard. We are incapable of keeping the deeds of the law, no matter how many runs we get at it. The way back to God isn’t by exerting an insane level of willpower and temperance to keep the law. Rather, it seems it is by pleasing God through faith and belief in Christ.
Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
If we can have the Spirit in us then we walk after a new law and have a new mind.
Romans 8:8-10

So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God. But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. And if Christ be in you, the body is dead because of sin; but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
Romans 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
This is somewhat odd leaving us to consider how we reconcile the demands of the law with this new walk with the Spirit. As James said:
James 2:26
For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.

Following the coming forth of The Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 13:39), chapter 14 begins the era where, “if the Gentiles shall hearken unto the Lamb of God” (1 Nephi 14:1), they will be privileged to “be numbered among the house of Israel” (14:2) and live as a “blessed people upon the promised land forever” (ibid). Verse 3 describes how the places where the mother of harlots, the great and abominable church (most likely parts and variations of the Catholic and Anglican churches), are established will be destroyed. As I read this I thought of the wars that preceded the Restoration of which this might be referring to.

Then, following this destruction, comes a time where God begins a new work, “a great and marvelous work” (14:7). This will be a great test for the Gentiles “either to the convincing of them unto peace and life eternal, or unto the deliverance of them to the hardness of their hearts and the blindness of their minds unto their being brought down into captivity, and also into destruction, both temporally and spiritually, according to the captivity of the devil, of which I have spoken.” (ibid)

It’s stated that even after that great destructive period of the great and abominable church that, still, the numbers of the church of the Lamb of God are few (14:2). Then it described what I thought might be an allusion to the two world wars which took place almost entirely in Europe where these churches were headquartered and most established. Perhaps that’s where the corruption was and perhaps the most corrupt facets and leaders of these abominable organizations which participated in works of darkness were destroyed in the world wars. I’m not thinking so narrowly as to categorize the whole Catholic church as abominable, but probably some leaders and divisions of it were what this chapter referred to.
I can’t tell what wars it’s referring to, the Revolutionary war, the war of 1812, the world wars…?

And it came to pass that I beheld that the great mother of abominations did gather together multitudes upon the face of all the earth, among all the nations of the Gentiles, to fight against the Lamb of God.

And it came to pass that I, Nephi, beheld the power of the Lamb of God, that it descended upon the saints of the church of the Lamb, and upon the covenant people of the Lord, who were scattered upon all the face of the earth; and they were armed with righteousness and with the power of God in great glory.

title: Automatic Writing: The Means of Translating the Book of Mormon

body.text: The referenced Wikipedia article describes automatic writing as: “a claimed psychic ability allowing a person to produce written words without consciously writing.” Here are some renown examples.
Patience Worth (Pearl Lenore Curran) Produced with Google’s Gemini

Patience Worth was a purported spirit channeled by Pearl Lenore Curran (1883-1937) between 1913 and 1937. Curran claimed Patience was a 17th-century English woman who communicated through automatic writing, a process where Curran would hold a Ouija board planchette (the moving piece) and allegedly receive messages spelled out by an unseen force.

Curran, a housewife with limited formal education, produced a vast amount of literary work attributed to Patience Worth. This included seven books, poetry, short stories, plays, and letters—totaling nearly four million words. The authenticity of Patience Worth as a spirit is highly debated. Psychologists and skeptics believe Curran created Patience as a subconscious invention, possibly influenced by her own knowledge and interests.

Despite the controversy surrounding her origins, Patience Worth's literary output was significant. Her work received positive reviews from critics and literary figures of the time. Notably, five of her poems were included in a prestigious poetry anthology, and her first novel was praised by the New York Times.

The Patience Worth case is a fascinating example of automatic writing. It highlights the potential for the subconscious mind to produce complex and creative work. However, it also raises questions about the validity of claims of spirit communication and the potential for self-deception.

Patience certainly is an interesting example. In the late 19th century and early 20th century, spiritualism was peaking in America with alleged psychics, fortune telling, ouija boards, seances, etc. But how could Pearl have produced her literature if not via spiritual contact? The feat would be impressive and quite surprising given her limited writing ability and education. Whether or not the spirit and identity of Patience Worth actually existed is an unanswered question. Perhaps a spirit really was communicating with Pearl but forged the identity of Patience Worth for fun or for some other reason.
Many Mansions and Dr. Carl Wickland's Spirit Communications Produced with Google’s Gemini

Many Mansions (1950) is a controversial book by Dr. Carl Wickland detailing alleged communication with a spirit being named "A" through a process called "hypnagogic regression." Dr. Wickland was a psychiatrist who used hypnosis in his practice. In "Many Mansions," he describes sessions where a patient, Robbie Peterson, would enter a sleep-like state and supposedly channel a spirit being "A." This technique aimed to regress Peterson to past lives or access spiritual realms.

While in this state, Dr. Wickland would pose questions about the afterlife, spirit beings, and other metaphysical topics that "A" would then answer. The sessions were not conducted in isolation. Dr. Wickland invited colleagues and friends to witness these communications, lending some credibility to his claims.

"Many Mansions" compiles the information gathered during these sessions. "A" discusses various spiritual topics like the nature of reality, the afterlife, and the purpose of life. Despite the book's popularity, it has been heavily criticized by skeptics. They argue that Peterson likely fabricated the information while under hypnosis or that Dr. Wickland orchestrated an elaborate hoax. There's a lack of objective evidence to support the claims of spirit communication.

"Many Mansions" remains an intriguing, if controversial, account of alleged spirit communication. It offered a glimpse into the growing interest in hypnosis and past-life regression in the mid-20th century. However, the lack of verifiable evidence and the possibility of hypnosis-induced suggestion make it difficult to conclusively determine the source of the information presented in the book.
Are these people accessing the spiritual realm and communicating with the dead?
The Urantia Book: Divine Revelation or Channeled Text? Produced with Google’s Gemini

The Urantia Book (1955) is a spiritual and philosophical text claiming to be a divine revelation presented by celestial beings. Published in Chicago, it offers a unique perspective on God, creation, and humanity's place in the universe.The origins of The Urantia Book are shrouded in mystery. There's no identified author, and the book claims to have been presented through a process it calls "papers." This has led to several theories about its inception:

●Divine Revelation: Proponents believe the book is a literal transmission of knowledge from higher beings. They point to the book's vast scope and complex cosmology as evidence of its non-human authorship.

●Channeling/Automatic Writing: Similar to Patience Worth, some suggest the book might be the product of automatic writing or channeling by a medium. An unidentified person might have received the information in a trance-like state.
●Human Authorship: Skeptics posit that the book is the work of one or more individuals, possibly drawing on various religious and philosophical sources.

Unfortunately, there's no verifiable evidence to support any of these origin theories. The "papers" remain unexplained, and attempts to identify a human author have been unsuccessful. The Urantia Book shares some thematic similarities with other channeled texts and spiritualist movements popular in the early 20th century. This connection fuels skepticism about its divine origin.

Despite the controversy surrounding its origins, The Urantia Book has garnered a dedicated following who appreciate its unique perspective on spirituality. However, the lack of clear authorship and the "channeled text" claim continue to be points of contention.

The Urantia Book's origin story aligns with the concept of automatic writing, where a person acts as a conduit for information from an unseen source. The similarities to Patience Worth's case highlight the potential for the subconscious mind to produce complex and creative work, even if the source is not truly spiritual.
The Fox Sisters and the Hydesville Rappings: A Catalyst for Spiritualism Produced with Google’s Gemini

The story of the Fox sisters and the Hydesville rappings is a pivotal moment in the history of Spiritualism. In 1848, Margaret ("Maggie") and Kate Fox, aged 14 and 11 respectively, living in Hydesville, New York, claimed to be communicating with a spirit through a series of raps, tappings, or knocks, on the walls and furniture of their home.

According to their account, the mysterious raps began shortly after the death of a peddler who supposedly stayed at their house. The sisters claimed they could communicate with the spirit by asking questions and receiving answers through a rapping code—a single rap for "no" and multiple raps corresponding to the alphabet or numbers.

News of the rappings spread quickly, attracting curiosity seekers and investigators. The sisters, along with their older sister Leah, began holding séances where they would communicate with the spirit on behalf of others. These séances became popular, drawing believers who interpreted the raps as messages from deceased loved ones.

The Fox sisters' story resonated with a growing interest in the afterlife and spirit communication during the mid-19th century. Their experiences helped spark the Spiritualist movement, a belief system that emphasized communication with the deceased. Despite the popularity of Spiritualism, the Fox sisters faced skepticism. Critics accused them of trickery, suggesting they produced the raps themselves by cracking their toe joints or using other methods.

In 1888, Maggie Fox publicly confessed that the raps were a hoax, damaging the credibility of Spiritualism. However, the movement continued to grow, and the Fox sisters remain symbolic figures in the history of spirit communication. Whether a genuine encounter with the spirit world or a clever prank, the Fox sisters and the Hydesville rappings had a significant impact. They contributed to the rise of Spiritualism, a movement that continues to influence ideas about death, the afterlife, and human potential.
Helena Blavatsky and Theosophy: Unveiling Ancient Wisdom Produced with Google’s Gemini

Helena Blavatsky (1831-1891) was a Russian mystic, writer, and co-founder of the Theosophical Society. She is considered a key figure in the development of Western esotericism and the concept of the "New Age" movement. Blavatsky's central belief revolved around the existence of an "Ancient Wisdom," a unified body of esoteric knowledge passed down from a hidden brotherhood of adepts throughout history.

In 1875, Blavatsky co-founded the Theosophical Society in New York City with the aim of reviving this "Ancient Wisdom" and promoting universal brotherhood. Theosophy blended elements of Eastern religions like Hinduism and Buddhism with Western philosophical and mystical traditions.

Blavatsky claimed to have been trained by these hidden adepts, whom she referred to as "Masters." She allegedly received theosophical teachings through various means, including astral travel, clairvoyance, and communication with these Masters on different planes of existence. Blavatsky's writings, particularly "Isis Unveiled" (1877) and "The Secret Doctrine" (1888), outlined her theosophical ideas. These books were controversial but widely read, sparking interest in Eastern religions and esoteric thought in the West.

Blavatsky's claims of hidden knowledge and communication with Masters were met with skepticism from scholars and academics. Accusations of plagiarism and the fantastical nature of her writings cast doubt on the veracity of her theories. Despite the controversy, Blavatsky's influence on 20th-century esotericism and alternative spirituality is undeniable. The Theosophical Society became a springboard for other spiritual movements, and her ideas resonated with those seeking alternative explanations for consciousness, reality, and the cosmos.
Aleister Crowley and Enochian Magic: Angelic Dictation or Elaborate Ploy? Produced with Google’s Gemini

Aleister Crowley (1875-1947) was a controversial British occultist, writer, and ceremonial magician. He claimed to have received a profound revelation through automatic writing in 1904, which formed the basis for his Enochian magical system. Enochian magic is a complex system of ceremonial magic based on a supposedly angelic language channeled by Crowley. He described communicating with a non-human intelligence named Aiwass over a three-day period. Aiwass dictated the content of "The Book of the Law," a central text of Crowley's magical philosophy.

Crowley allegedly used a technique known as astral scrying to facilitate communication with Aiwass. This involved ritualistically preparing himself and then gazing into a black mirror to receive visions and information. The received messages were recorded through automatic writing.

Crowley's account of his Enochian experiences has been met with widespread skepticism. Critics suggest the entire episode was a hallucination or an elaborate mystical hoax perpetrated by Crowley to bolster his credentials as a magician. Regardless of its origins, Enochian magic has become an influential system within Western occultism. Crowley's writings on the subject have been studied by magicians and mystics seeking to explore altered states of consciousness and unconventional spiritual experiences.

Crowley's use of automatic writing to channel Aiwass parallels other instances discussed previously. It raises questions about the potential of the subconscious mind to produce complex and symbolic material, even if the source isn't truly supernatural.
Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon
Now I’d like to give Gemini a chance to draw parallels between these examples and Joseph Smith. This is not my writing, but that of Google’s Gemini, a large language model.
The Book of Mormon and Automatic Writing: Echoes of Spirit Communication? Produced by Google’s Gemini

The concept of Joseph Smith producing the Book of Mormon through automatic writing is a theory debated by scholars and religious adherents alike. This theory finds parallels in several historical cases where individuals claimed to receive messages from spirits or unseen entities. Let's explore these connections:

●Spirit Communication as a Theme: All the cases discussed previously (Patience Worth, The Urantia Book, The Fox Sisters, Helena Blavatsky, and Aleister Crowley) share a common thread: the belief in communication with spirits or higher beings. Joseph Smith's experience with Moroni, the angel who allegedly guided him to the golden plates, aligns with this theme.

●Automatic Writing as a Method: While Smith didn't explicitly mention automatic writing, the act of dictating the Book of Mormon to scribes while looking into a seer stone presents some similarities. In automatic writing, the writer may enter an altered state and receive information unconsciously. Whether Smith experienced a similar altered state is open to interpretation.

●Rapid Composition: The speed with which the Book of Mormon was supposedly produced (around 90 days) mirrors the rapid output seen in some automatic writing cases. This raises questions about whether Smith was accessing unconscious knowledge or previously encountered information.
Important Considerations
●Lack of Evidence: There's no concrete proof that Smith used automatic writing. His accounts of revelations and communication with spirits rely on faith testimonies.

●Alternative Explanations: Believers in the Book of Mormon's divine origin offer alternative explanations for its creation. They emphasize Smith's role as a prophet chosen by God to translate an ancient record.

●Motives and Context: Understanding the religious environment of Smith's time is important. The early 19th century saw a rise in interest in spiritualism and divination. This context might have influenced Smith's experiences and beliefs.
Conclusion

The possibility of automatic writing being a factor in the creation of the Book of Mormon remains a theory. While parallels exist with other cases of spirit communication, the absence of concrete evidence makes it difficult to definitively conclude. Ultimately, belief in the Book of Mormon rests on faith and personal interpretation of historical accounts.
Final Thoughts

Pretty good, eh? Of course, I don’t agree with this theory as a refutation of the authenticity of the Book of Mormon. I believe the Book of Mormon is an authentic historical record of the ancient inhabitants of America. But I am open to the idea that perhaps Mormon or Moroni conveyed the translation of the words to Joseph Smith through a spiritual dictation process involving the Urim and Thummim or the seer stone.

title: Alma Eats Bread and is Filled

body.text: And it came to pass that the man received him into his house; and the man was called Amulek; and he brought forth bread and meat and set before Alma. And it came to pass that Alma ate bread and was filled; and he blessed Amulek and his house, and he gave thanks unto God. And after he had eaten and was filled he said unto Amulek: I am Alma, and am the high priest over the church of God throughout the land.
1.First comment on this is the similar wording to 3 Nephi 18, “”had eaten and [was] filled”. I don’t know if it’s a meaningful similarity but here’s the referenced section:
3 Nephi 18:3-5

And when the disciples had come with bread and wine, he took of the bread and brake and blessed it; and he gave unto the disciples and commanded that they should eat. And when they had eaten and were filled, he commanded that they should give unto the multitude. And when the multitude had eaten and were filled, he said unto the disciples: Behold there shall one be ordained among you, and to him will I give power that he shall break bread and bless it and give it unto the people of my church, unto all those who shall believe and be baptized in my name.
2.Secondly, it’s interesting that while Amulek apparently set out “bread and meat”, it’s only mentioned that “Alma ate bread”. Did Alma only eat bread or for some reason did they only mention bread ?

title: An Appeal for Mercy from Scriptural Accounts

body.text: In Easter Christianity the Efche, or , is a fundamental spiritual practice. I read about it in The Mountains of Silence, a book where a journalist interviews an Athonite monk. The prayer goes: “Lord Jesus Christ, son of the living God, have mercy on me a sinner”. This prayer is found to have been recited by monks as early as the 5th century B.C. It has scripture foundations in the following sections:
Matthew 15:22
And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.

And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimæus, the son of Timæus, sat by the highway side begging. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, and say, Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me. And many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou Son of David, have mercy on me. And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called. And they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee.
This plea for mercy, I’ve found, is quite prevalent in not only the New Testament, but all throughout scripture. It often precedes great moments where God’s mercy and power are manifest.

Zeezrom is delivered from his feverish suffering after Alma prays a variant of the Efche on his behalf.

This has a stark similarity with Lehi’s experience in his vision as well as the popular Easter Orthodox version of the prayer. Alma was delivered from his dark night into a joyous experience.

title: Great Spirit and Great God—A Lamanite notion of God

body.text: A popular Book of Mormon story is Ammon, a royal Nephite, who has a dramatic conversion and then proselytes among the Lamanites and converts many of them, including two kings. Alma 18 dictates Ammon teaching King Lamoni about God. King Lamoni is quite unfamiliar with the God of the Nephites; e.g., King Lamoni’s father, when asked by Aaron if he believes in God, responds: “I know that the Amalekites say that there is a God, and I have granted unto them that they should build sanctuaries, that they may assemble themselves together to worship him. And if now thou sayest there is a God, behold I will believe” (Alma 22:7).

King Lamoni, in Alma 18, refers to his notion of God as “the Great Spirit”. There are 18 occurrences of “Great Spirit” in the Book of Mormon and they all occur in Alma 18 and refer to King Lamoni’s notion of God. Needless to say, this exclusive phrase is one unique to King Lamoni and is how he expressed his idea of God.

After King Lamoni’s conversion, as well as the conversion of his brother (probably the king of Midian) and father, he convenes with all the Lamanite converts in the land of Midian to discuss their stance on the matter of impending threats from non-converted Lamanites. At this point, King Lamoni’s father had appointed his son to be king in his stead “and he called his name Anti-Nephi-Lehi” (Alma 24:2) and then King Lamoni’s father died in that same year. Anti-Nephi-Lehi, the brother of King Lamoni, gives a speech to the newly converted Lamanites in the land Midian and uses the phrase “Great God”, much like King Lamoni’s usage of “Great Spirit” but perhaps more properly referring to the Abrahamic God.

In this speech made by King Anti-Nephi-Lehi, he uses the phrase “Great God” 5 times and these are the only instances of such phrase in the Book of Mormon, showing it to be just as exclusive and unique as “Great Spirit”. This is a testament to the continuity of the Book of Mormon plot. It makes sense that King Lamoni and his brother might carry their cultural notion of God into their converted conception of God, relating it to their previous notion.

Also, in case a reader wonders why I said that King Anti-Nephi-Lehi is the one giving the speech in Alma 24 rather than King Lamoni, I’m not entirely confident that it was King Anti-Nephi-Lehi, but since the identity of the speaker is “the king” (Alma 24:17) and King Lamoni is always elsewhere referred to as King Lamoni, I’m assuming that “the king” refers to their current king, King Anti-Nephi-Lehi. This seems to be the most reasonable interpretation.
D&C 8: Two gifts for Oliver
The first gift is mentioned in verse verse 3 and is “the spirit of revelation” but the second gift is called “the gift of Aaron” (verse 6).

1 Oliver Cowdery, verily, verily, I say unto you, that assuredly as the Lord liveth, who is your God and your Redeemer, even so surely shall you receive a knowledge of whatsoever things you shall ask in faith, with an honest heart, believing that you shall receive a knowledge concerning the engravings of old records, which are ancient, which contain those parts of my scripture of which has been spoken by the manifestation of my Spirit.
2 Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart.
3 Now, behold, this is the spirit of revelation; behold, this is the spirit by which Moses brought the children of Israel through the Red Sea on dry ground.

4 Therefore this is thy gift; apply unto it, and blessed art thou, for it shall deliver you out of the hands of your enemies, when, if it were not so, they would slay you and bring your soul to destruction.
5 Oh, remember these words, and keep my commandments. Remember, this is your gift.
6 Now this is not all thy gift; for you have another gift, which is the gift of Aaron; behold, it has told you many things;
7 Behold, there is no other power, save the power of God, that can cause this gift of Aaron to be with you.

8 Therefore, doubt not, for it is the gift of God; and you shall hold it in your hands, and do marvelous works; and no power shall be able to take it away out of your hands, for it is the work of God.
9 And, therefore, whatsoever you shall ask me to tell you by that means, that will I grant unto you, and you shall have knowledge concerning it.
10 Remember that without faith you can do nothing; therefore ask in faith. Trifle not with these things; do not ask for that which you ought not.

11 Ask that you may know the mysteries of God, and that you may translate and receive knowledge from all those ancient records which have been hid up, that are sacred; and according to your faith shall it be done unto you.

Now I’ll point out that the first gift, the spirit of revelation, is not the gift used for translating. What seems to be the case is that the urim and thummim are referred to as the gift of Aaron and they are used for translating ancient records and for receiving knowledge of other things.

13 Now Ammon said unto him: I can assuredly tell thee, O king, of a man that can translate the records; for he has wherewith that he can look, and translate all records that are of ancient date; and it is a gift from God. And the things are called interpreters, and no man can look in them except he be commanded, lest he should look for that he ought not and he should perish. And whosoever is commanded to look in them, the same is called seer.
14 And behold, the king of the people who are in the land of Zarahemla is the man that is commanded to do these things, and who has this high gift from God.

17 But a seer can know of things which are past, and also of things which are to come, and by them shall all things be revealed, or, rather, shall secret things be made manifest, and hidden things shall come to light, and things which are not known shall be made known by them, and also things shall be made known by them which otherwise could not be known.
18 Thus God has provided a means that man, through faith, might work mighty miracles; therefore he becometh a great benefit to his fellow beings.

Mosiah also had this gift of Aaron, it seems. The gift is the physical possession of the means for translation—“the means of those two stones which were fastened into the two rims of a bow” (Mosiah 28:13)—and the commandment (or gift) of God to use it. Mosiah used this gift and medium to translate the ancient Jaredite records (Mosiah 28:11-13).

In response to D&C 8:11 where God urges Oliver to ask to know the mysteries of God, King Limhi, after learning of King Mosiah’s possession of the interpreters, identifies a consistent purpose of such instruments—“these interpreters were doubtless prepared for the purpose of unfolding all such mysteries to the children of men” (Mosiah 8:19).
Another reference that may be relevant is Alma 37:23, though it remains somewhat cryptic.
Alma 37:23

And the Lord said: I will prepare unto my servant Gazelem, a stone, which shall shine forth in darkness unto light, that I may discover unto my people who serve me, that I may discover unto them the works of their brethren, yea, their secret works, their works of darkness, and their wickedness and abominations.
This stone uncovers hidden things, from “darkness unto light”. Ammon taught King Limhi that the interpreters used by the seer, King Mosiah, had the same ability:
Mosiah 8:17

But a seer can know of things which are past, and also of things which are to come, and by them shall all things be revealed, or, rather, shall secret things be made manifest, and hidden things shall come to light, and things which are not known shall be made known by them, and also things shall be made known by them which otherwise could not be known.
A last reference is D&C 6, a revelation received right around D&C 8, also directed to Oliver Cowdery.
10 Behold thou hast a gift, and blessed art thou because of thy gift. Remember it is sacred and cometh from above—

11 And if thou wilt inquire, thou shalt know mysteries which are great and marvelous; therefore thou shalt exercise thy gift, that thou mayest find out mysteries, that thou mayest bring many to the knowledge of the truth, yea, convince them of the error of their ways.
12 Make not thy gift known unto any save it be those who are of thy faith. Trifle not with sacred things.

This gift must be the “gift of Aaron”, as it’s called in D&C 8. It apparently can allow Oliver to find out mysteries, just like the interpreters for King Mosiah. Oliver was, or could have been, a seer. The injunction to “trifle not” appears in both contexts (D&C 6:12; 8:10), further supporting my theory that both sections refer to the same gift, which is the gift of Aaron, not the gift of the Spirit of revelation. It seems to be referring to urim and thummim, or interpreters, or seer stones, etc.

In conclusion, D&C 8 supports the idea that seer stones, urim and thummim, were in use in 1829 April when this revelation was given and the language of their usage and purpose is consistent with teachings from the Book of Mormon.

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.

And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:
Ether 4:15

Behold, when ye shall rend that veil of unbelief which doth cause you to remain in your awful state of wickedness, and hardness of heart, and blindness of mind, then shall the great and marvelous things which have been hid up from the foundation of the world from you—yea, when ye shall call upon the Father in my name, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, then shall ye know that the Father hath remembered the covenant which he made unto your fathers, O house of Israel.
Thou shalt offer a sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in righteousness, even that of a broken heart and a contrite spirit.
ChatGPT 4 on the subject
Breaking Down the Words

Broken Heart: In scriptural language, a "broken heart" refers to a heart that is humble, submissive, and open to God's will. It suggests a state of deep sincerity, where one recognizes their own weaknesses and is fully dependent on God. It is not about being emotionally crushed, but rather being spiritually open and willing to be molded by God.

Contrite Spirit: A "contrite spirit" is a spirit that feels genuine remorse for sins and shortcomings, coupled with a strong desire to repent and change. The word "contrite" comes from the Latin contritus, meaning "crushed or worn down with grief." This doesn’t mean one is left in despair, but rather that they are humble and sincerely seek forgiveness and transformation through Christ.
